samples.result:
# The Last Crossing

On the last morning of the ferry, someone left a refrigerator on the east landing. It stood with its door open and a paper sign taped to the butter compartment: STILL GOOD.

Ruth went down with her coffee to investigate. The refrigerator smelled faintly of oranges. Inside it, on the middle shelf, was a single blue ice tray, empty except for a dead wasp.

The sign seemed an ambitious claim, but she supposed the person who had written it knew more about the refrigerator than she did.

At six, she unchained the gate and started the engine. The river was low enough that a shopping cart had emerged near the pilings. By afternoon, if the level kept dropping, she would be able to see what was in it. There was usually something in it. The river was not a person, whatever the poets at the library liked to say, but it did have a habit of putting things inside other things.

The first passenger was Mr. Teague, who had taken the 6:10 to the west bank every weekday for thirty-two years. He used to work at the bakery. Now he crossed to read the newspaper in a café where they got a different newspaper from the one he got at home.

“Fridge yours?” Ruth asked.

“No,” he said, in a tone that suggested she had made a personal remark.

He handed her a nickel. The ferry had been free since 1998, but that was the year his wife died, and he had aged into certain habits without bothering to distinguish which ones belonged to grief. Ruth put the nickel in the jar with the others.

“See you at four,” he said on the far bank.

“Three forty-five is the last return.”

“I know what the sign says.”

She waited.

“I’ll see you at three forty-five,” he said.

The bridge had opened on Monday. It was a clean, pale structure a mile downstream, with a lane for bicycles and a series of decorative openings through which, if you were unfortunate enough to drop your phone, you could watch it fall for quite a long time. Ruth had walked across with everybody else. From the middle, she could see the ferry’s entire route. Seen that way, it was a discouragingly small piece of water.

At the opening ceremony, a county commissioner had said that the bridge would bring both halves of the town together. Ruth wondered what he thought she had been doing all these years, but she was willing to concede that he meant at night, in winter, with an ambulance. She had once carried a woman in labor during a thunderstorm. It had taken eleven minutes, and for all eleven the woman had squeezed Ruth’s wrist so hard that Ruth felt it the following day. If anybody had suggested a bridge at the time, she would have voted for it on the spot.

Still, it was one thing to want the bridge and another to be told how happy she must be about it.

At seven fifteen, her brother came down the ramp carrying two cartons of eggs. He set them on the bench and stepped back onto the landing.

“Get on or get off,” Ruth said.

“I’m off.”

“You’ve left eggs.”

“They’re for you.”

“I don’t need twenty-four eggs.”

“Neither do I. That’s how you got them.”

Cal had been raising chickens for six months. He had a particular talent for beginning hobbies that became other people’s work. At Christmas he had given Ruth a sourdough starter with a name and a feeding schedule. She had put it in the refrigerator and forgotten about it until May, by which time it looked capable of feeding itself.

“You coming this afternoon?” she asked.

“For what?”

She looked at him.

“Oh,” he said. “I didn’t know you wanted me to.”

Ruth had wanted him to figure out that she wanted him to. Until he said it, she hadn’t realized how much work that required of him, or how little it required of her.

“Three forty-five,” she said.

“Okay.” He stood there another moment. “You need a ride home after?”

“I have my car.”

“I know. It was an offer, not a theory.”

He went up the ramp. Halfway to the road, he stopped at the refrigerator and tested the seal with his thumb.

At nine, a woman and a boy came aboard with a folding chair. The woman set up the chair although there were two perfectly good benches. The boy pressed his face between the railings. He wanted to know how deep the river was, and Ruth told him it depended where you asked.

“Here,” he said.

“About twelve feet.”

He considered it. “If you stood on my mom’s head, and I stood on yours?”

“I’d want to talk to your mom about it first.”

The woman laughed. She said they used to ride the ferry when he was a baby, because it was the only place he would sleep. She had spent whole afternoons going back and forth. Did Ruth remember?

Ruth had a faint recollection of a red blanket. What she remembered more clearly was a young woman who got on in the rain one day without a coat. Ruth had offered her the old sweater she kept in the wheelhouse. The woman said no, then yes, then cried while trying to get her hand through the sleeve. Ruth had steered one-handed so she could hold the cuff open. She didn’t know if it was this woman. There had been a lot of rain and a lot of people.

“Was there a red blanket?” she asked.

“Yellow,” the woman said. “I still have it. I put it under the washing machine when it shakes.”

At the west landing the boy announced that he wanted to cross again immediately. His mother folded her chair and said they would walk back over the bridge. It seemed to Ruth that the boy would protest, but he wanted to see how the decorative holes worked.

By eleven the sun had burned through the cloud cover. Ruth opened the wheelhouse windows and found, under the logbook, a letter she had been carrying for four months. It was from the county and informed her of the disposition of the ferry. She liked that word. It made the boat sound bad-tempered.

The parks department was going to take it upriver and use it to carry maintenance crews out to the islands. The benches would come off, and someone would paint over the blue stripes. Ruth had been invited to train the new operator, but she’d declined. The boat was easy to drive. The hard part was getting the hang of the approaches, and at the islands there would be different approaches for somebody else to get the hang of.

She folded the letter and put it in her pocket. Then she got it out again and read the second page, which she had never read. The county wanted the keys left in the lockbox and the fuel tank at least a quarter full. Further down was a blank headed OPERATOR REMARKS.

Ruth took out her pen. She had never found a way to stop the rattle in the port window except to wedge a folded coffee sleeve into the frame. The fuel gauge stuck at half for about an hour after you filled the tank. When you shut the wheelhouse door too hard in cold weather, the latch could drop on the inside and lock you out. She had spent that particular February crossing steering with a boat hook through the open window, in full view of a passenger who was polite enough to look at his sandwich the entire time.

She wrote down all three things. There was room for a fourth, but she couldn’t think of one until she started to put the pen away.

*The horn is louder on deck than you think.*

At noon an unfamiliar man came aboard, saluted, and asked if he could scatter his father’s ashes. He had a white paper bag with a bakery logo on it. Ruth said he could if he wanted, but the wind was blowing straight down the deck, and he might not get the result he was picturing.

The man looked at the bag.

“It’s rolls,” he said. “I was going to ask where a person could scatter ashes. My sister has the ashes.”

“Oh,” Ruth said. “Well. That’ll be easier on your rolls.”

He sat on the bench and opened the bag. His father had grown up on the east bank and moved away at seventeen. As far as the man could tell, he had spent the next sixty years threatening to move back. His children were trying to decide how literally to take him.

“Did he ever mention a particular spot?” Ruth asked.

“He always talked about the bakery.”

“You can’t scatter him in the bakery.”

“I figured.”

They ate the rolls, which were shiny on top and just underdone in the middle. Ruth suggested a place upstream where the town had put in a couple of benches. The man asked what you could see from there.

“Mostly the people on the other bench,” she said. “But it’s nice in the evening.”

His sister was driving in from Ohio. He decided he would take her to look at it before they did anything. When they reached the landing, he thanked Ruth for her help. He left the last roll in the bag for her, and later, when she had it with coffee, she found that it was the only one with raisins.

Around two the people with cameras began to arrive. A girl from the local paper asked Ruth how many trips she’d made, and Ruth said she didn’t know. The girl asked if she could make an estimate.

“How exact do you need it to sound?”

The girl lowered her phone. “My editor said not to come back with ‘countless.’”

Together, on the back of the county letter, they worked it out. They subtracted the winters the river froze and the year the gearbox went, then added the Saturdays Ruth had covered for Eddie before he retired. They arrived at forty-one thousand, which Ruth distrusted immediately. It was possible to imagine a thousand crossings. She could account for almost that many by thinking about the times she had carried a particular dog. But forty-one thousand was just a big number on the back of a letter. It gave her no more idea of where the time had gone than the mileage on her car.

“Say around forty thousand,” Ruth told the girl.

“Did you ever get bored?”

“Oh, absolutely.”

The girl looked up, pleased, and Ruth saw that this was going to be the quote.

At three thirty, there was a line down the west ramp. Ruth walked along it counting heads. Two bicycles counted as four people, a rule she had made up long ago and could no longer explain, except by asking anybody who disputed it to stand where the bicycles were.

She counted thirty-one. The limit was thirty.

“You can leave me,” said Mr. Teague from the back. “I know how to walk across a bridge.”

Before Ruth could answer, one of the cyclists rolled his bicycle out of line. He said he had been planning to try the new bike lane anyway. This left room for Mr. Teague and, a minute later, for Cal, who came down the ramp with his shirt sticking to his chest. He’d parked on the east bank and walked over the bridge.

“What for?” Ruth asked.

“So I could come back with you.”

He said it plainly, almost impatiently. She was glad he hadn’t said it in a nicer way, in front of all those people.

Mr. Teague offered her his nickel. She got the jar from the wheelhouse and let him drop it in himself. The jar was an old glass one, with a chip on the rim and a picture of a peach. He lifted it a little to see what it weighed.

“You know,” he said, “I started doing that because I had so damn many nickels.”

“Where’d they come from?”

“My wife used to find them in the laundry. Put them in a bowl for me to take upstairs.” He set the jar back down. “I never took them upstairs.”

Ruth blew the horn. Everybody on deck jumped except Cal, who had put his fingers in his ears. When she looked back a moment later, he was helping Mr. Teague settle onto the bench. She untied the line, looped it over the rail, and went inside to take the ferry out.

There was applause as they left the landing. It stopped fairly quickly. A man in a blue cap kept clapping after everyone else had quit, then looked around and quit too. People adjusted their bags and moved out of the sun. Mrs. Avery from the post office told her husband not to take any more pictures of her from below. One of the bicycles tipped over with a sound that made several people think of something they had forgotten to do at home.

Halfway across, Cal came into the wheelhouse.

“Anything I can do?”

“Get me those eggs before somebody sits on them.”

He brought them inside. There was a dark spot on the bottom of one carton where an egg had broken. He held it over the wastebasket and picked out the shell. Ruth watched him wipe each of the neighboring eggs with a paper towel. He turned them gently in his big hands. It was the sort of thing she would have told him not to bother doing if she’d had her hands free to take the carton away from him.

“Where do you want them?” he asked.

“Leave them there. Can you get the line when we come in?”

“I don’t know how.”

“I’ll show you.”

She slowed the engine a touch early so there would be time to tell him where to stand and what to do. When the landing came alongside, he dropped the loop short of the cleat. On his second try he got it over, and Ruth reached down from the wheelhouse to show him how much slack to leave. By then everybody was already waiting at the gate, looking past it toward the road.

On shore, somebody had closed the refrigerator door. Ruth watched the passengers pass it and start up the slope, some turning left toward the parking lot, others heading for the shops. Mr. Teague stayed at the foot of the ramp, studying the printed schedule. She was going to call out to him when he took a pen from his pocket, peeled the schedule out of its plastic sleeve, and turned it over. He wrote something on the back and slid it in again. Then he put on his hat and went home.

Ruth had three things left to do: record the engine hours, check the fuel, and put the keys in the lockbox. She did them in that order. The last one took the longest because she had to find a screwdriver to pry the ferry key off her ring. Her house key was almost the same shape, and for years she had told them apart by touch, by a little notch in the boat key that caught her thumbnail. She worked the screwdriver around until the key came loose. The ring went back in her pocket feeling no lighter at all.

Up on the landing, Cal had opened his truck. He was taking junk out of the bed so there would be room for the refrigerator. So far he’d removed a bent rake, a pail full of smaller pails, and a folding lawn chair Ruth recognized as hers.

“You know if it works?” she asked.

“No.”

“You know where you’re putting it?”

“No.”

She handed him her eggs and took hold of the refrigerator on the side with the hinge. They shifted it a few inches before discovering that neither had a grip. Cal fetched a blanket from the truck, and they tipped the refrigerator onto it and dragged it to the tailgate. The whole operation took ten minutes. Twice they had to stop laughing before they could lift.

When they were done, Ruth went back down to see what Mr. Teague had written. On the back of the schedule, in small square letters, was *THANK YOU RUTH*. Underneath, after what must have been some thought about available space, he’d added *AND EDDIE*.

She left it in the sleeve. Coming back up the ramp, she looked down between the pilings. The water had dropped another inch or two, and she could see a pale oval in the shopping cart. For weeks she’d been hoping it was a porcelain sink. It was a hubcap. She stood there long enough to make sure.

Cal called from the truck to ask about supper. He was going to fry some eggs, he said, if she knew anybody who wanted eggs.

Ruth looked toward her car. Tomorrow she could walk over and get it. She’d have to go the long way, which meant she could stop in the middle of the bridge, if there weren’t too many bicycles, and see what the new operator made of the landing.

“Let’s go,” she said, and got in on the passenger side.

# The Department of Misplaced Things

On the first Monday in March, a man came into the lost-property office and asked whether anyone had turned in his kitchen window.

“The whole window?” I said.

“Just the view.”

I had been working for the transit authority for eleven years. I knew not to laugh until I was sure a person meant to be funny.

“What could you see from it?”

“A brick wall, mostly. And the top of a pear tree.”

He set a photograph on the counter. It showed a narrow kitchen with a yellow kettle on the stove. Beyond the glass was a wall, and above it a little patch of white blossom. The photograph had been taken at an angle, as though the person holding the camera hadn’t wanted to get up from the table.

“They pulled the building down last week,” he said. “I thought there might be a form.”

I gave him the form for items lost on a bus. Under *Route*, he wrote the address of the building. Under *Distinguishing features*, he wrote for quite a long time, went over one word until he made a hole in the paper, and handed it back.

What he had written was: *Some mornings there were two pigeons, but generally one.*

I told him we would call if anything came in.

By noon we had received four gloves, a lunch bag containing an immaculate orange, a sealed envelope addressed to the tax office, and a trombone. The driver who brought the trombone had found it on the last bus of the night. He had heard a noise going around a corner and looked in his mirror to see the case rolling down the aisle.

“I thought it was a coffin,” he said.

“It’s four feet long.”

“I didn’t say I thought it was my coffin.”

I logged the trombone and brought the gloves to the sorting table. None matched. People ask whether we make pairs out of the unclaimed gloves, and the answer is that we used to. Then we noticed that almost all the gloves were left-handed. The drivers had theories. You take off your left glove to check your watch. You take off your right glove to check your phone, but because you need your right hand again, you put the glove in a pocket instead of balancing it on your knee. Our cleaner, Sal, said the right gloves were all falling down the far side of the seats, where the drivers didn’t look. She went out with a ruler one afternoon and came back with a fork, a ten-pound note, and no gloves.

She kept the tenner. I washed the fork.

The office occupied the back of the old bus station and had a public entrance through a painted blue door. Above the door was a sign, **LOST PROPERTY**, which Sal said was the only honest sign in the building. Above the dispatch window, for instance, there was a sign that said **INFORMATION**.

On the other side of my office was a storeroom. The first rack was for things lost that week, the second for things lost that month, and the rest for things whose owners had surprised me by managing without them. There was a full set of dentures in a margarine tub. There was an air fryer, which a driver had carried in with both arms and the expression of a man who had been asked to take a baby he did not know. There was a shoebox with a dozen undecorated gingerbread people inside. Before throwing them away, Sal turned them all over. On the back of one, someone had scratched an H.

“Guess he was in charge,” she said.

In April, the transit authority announced that it was closing the station. Buses would still stop outside, but tickets would be sold online and drivers would take their breaks in portable cabins by the ring road.

My manager, Peter, brought me the news in person. He didn’t sit down because he had brought a bicycle and was holding it by the handlebars.

“Is that for me?” I asked.

He looked at the bicycle. “God, no. Sorry.”

They planned to send lost property to a warehouse in Telford. People would be able to see their belongings in photographs on a website. If they recognized an item, they could pay to have it posted back.

“What about the orange?” I asked.

Peter did not know about the orange. It had been a long morning, and I told him about it in greater detail than it warranted. He listened, his right trouser leg still tucked into his sock. We had gone to school together. He used to draw tiny shoes on all the worms in the illustrations in his biology book. I could see him trying to work out whether I was making a serious objection.

“You won’t have to go to Telford,” he said. “We’ve got something for you in permits.”

After he left, I called the man who had lost his view. It was the first time I had opened his file since he’d filled out the form. His name was Mr. Venn.

“I’ve got nothing to report,” I said, “but I thought you should know we’ll be closing at the end of June.”

“That’s all right,” he replied. “I’ve been back.”

“To the house?”

“To the street. You can see right through to the next street now. There’s a lighting shop over there. I lived in that kitchen forty years and didn’t know there was a lighting shop.”

I asked him what had happened to the pear tree. He said he had forgotten to look.

That evening, I went home and opened the bottom drawer of my bedside table. I was looking for the key to my father’s old flat. I found it underneath a short charging cable and a packet of morning glory seeds my daughter had given me when she was seven. She was twenty-three now, working in a hotel in Rotterdam. Whenever we spoke, she was either getting ready to go to work or had just got home and was taking off her shoes. I knew exactly the sound of her hotel shoes hitting her floor.

I had kept the key because there had been nobody to give it back to. The housing officer had changed the lock while my father was in hospital. Apparently there had been a problem with the boiler, and the key they had on file didn’t work. My father said good, at least somebody had finally been round to look at the boiler. He told the story several times in the hospital, always crediting a different engineer. One of the people he credited had been dead since 1994.

On the day I went to clear the flat, the housing officer left the new key in a lockbox. I took out six bags of clothes, two wooden chairs, a television, and a cardboard box containing every rubber band my father had ever removed from anything. I found the old key only when I got home. I don’t remember putting it in my pocket that morning, but I must have stood in my own hallway, with my coat on, patting around for it as I had done whenever I went to see him.

I put the key back in the drawer and took out the seeds. The packet said to soak them overnight, so I put them in a cup. When I told my daughter, she said she had no memory of buying me seeds.

“Were they a birthday present?”

“Mother’s Day, I think.”

“I remember giving you a snail.”

“I remember the snail.”

“Did it die?”

“Not at our house.”

I could hear her shoes hit the floor. There was a pause, then she asked me what I’d done with the snail. I told her I’d put it in next door’s garden. She laughed so suddenly I took the phone away from my ear. She remembered which neighbours we’d had then.

At work the next morning, a woman was waiting for me at the blue door. She had lost a book on the number six. It was not a library book, she said, and she didn’t know the title. She was fairly sure it was green.

“Have you read any of it?”

“Most of it. I was about six pages from the end.”

I asked her what happened in it.

“A woman leaves her husband. Or he leaves her. You get both sides.”

We had six green books, of which three were about gardening and one was a driving test manual from 2008. She picked up one of the novels and frowned at the cover.

“That’s not it,” she said, “but I’ve read that one as well.”

I gave her the other novel. She opened it near the end, read a few lines, and closed it again.

“Have you found it?” I asked.

“No,” she said. “But they’ve got a dog, so I’d better not start there.”

She went home with the title written on the back of a bus ticket. I watched her through the door as she put the ticket in her coat pocket, took three steps, then took it out and put it in her purse instead.

As the closing date approached, I put up a notice asking people to collect anything they had been meaning to collect. A man phoned to ask whether we still had an umbrella he’d lost in 1986. I said no. He said it was a very good umbrella. I said I was sure it was. He said I sounded exactly like the woman who had been there in 1986. I hoped for both our sakes that he was wrong.

An elderly couple arrived for a walking stick and argued amiably about which of them had lost it. Someone came for the air fryer, bringing the receipt and a wheeled shopping bag. The trombone was claimed by a girl of about fifteen on a Wednesday just before closing. She came alone, in a school uniform, and asked whether I needed proof.

“What have you got?” I said.

She opened the case. Inside, between the bell and the lining, was a folded letter from the school music department informing her parents that she had been selected for the county band. It looked as though she had folded it and unfolded it a great many times.

“I didn’t tell them I lost it,” she said.

“Your parents?”

“The band.”

She put the letter in her blazer pocket and lifted the case. At the door, she turned and asked what day it had been found. When I told her, she said, “Oh. So you had it the whole time.” She looked down at the case with an expression that made me think she might give it a kick. Instead, she tightened one of the buckles, which was loose.

On the last Friday in June, Peter came to help us pack. He had a roll of labels and three colours of marker. We drank tea out of paper cups because Sal had already taken the mugs home. Around four, the man with the missing view came in with a white carrier bag. This time I recognized him before he spoke.

“I checked,” he said. “It’s still there.”

He had taken a picture of the pear tree from the street. In the picture the tree looked shorter than he’d expected. One side had grown flat against the wall, which had been cut down to about waist height. Someone had set a can of cola on the exposed bricks.

“That’s my window,” he said, pointing to a space above and to the left of the tree.

He took a second photograph from the bag. In this one he had stood where the kitchen would have been. There was the tree, at more or less the right angle, and behind it, in broad daylight, the lighting shop. The lights were on in the display window. Sale tags hung from a chandelier. Parked out in front was a dirty blue car.

“I thought if I waited, he’d move,” Mr. Venn said. “But he was waiting for somebody too.”

He handed me the bag, which contained two pears. They were not from the tree. He had bought them on his way over and wanted me to know that if they turned out not to be ripe, I could put them in a paper bag with a banana.

After he left, Peter asked whether the photographs needed to go in the shipment. I said they didn’t. We put them in an envelope with the original form, and I took them home.

I started in permits the following Tuesday. My desk was near the window, but I found that if I moved my monitor about six inches to the right, I could see the bus stop. I watched people step down into the road and reach back for children or shopping bags. One afternoon, I saw Sal getting off the number six in her ordinary clothes. She was carrying a cake tin. I knocked on the glass, and she looked up at the floor above mine. I waved with both arms. She looked down, spotted me, and tipped the tin forward a few inches so I could see what I was missing.

Only one of the morning glory seeds came up. I had planted them all in the same pot, so I didn’t know which one it was. For weeks it had two small leaves and otherwise gave me very little to report. Then in August it caught hold of the string I’d tied to the drainpipe and went up the side of the house. I went out every morning to see whether it had flowered. The morning it did, I had been on my way to put the bins out and was wearing one slipper and one shoe.

I took a picture for my daughter. It came out badly. The flower was a little blue smudge in the top left corner, and in the middle, sharp and bright, were the bins. She texted back, *Is that the green one we used to keep the snail in?*

It wasn’t. We’d had a red bucket then, which I remembered because the snail had crawled under the lip and we’d tipped the whole thing upside down trying to find it. My daughter had lain with her cheek on the paving stones and inspected it from underneath. She was the one who had found the snail; I had forgotten that until now. I called to tell her. She didn’t pick up, and a minute later she sent me a picture of her feet in clean black shoes. She was at work.

I left the flower alone and took the bins out. In the alley, one of my neighbours was moving a dresser with the help of a woman I didn’t know. They had got it as far as the corner, where one leg had snagged on a drain cover. The woman held her end up with her knee while my neighbour tried to see what was wrong. I put the bin down and helped them lift the dresser clear. It was light once there were three of us, and we went a long way without speaking, threading it past the bins and a parked car with its mirrors folded in. At the van we set it down. The top drawer slid open. Inside was a single brass handle, loose among the pale rings left by things I couldn’t identify. My neighbour picked it up, said, “Oh, there you are,” and put it in her pocket.

# The Things We Kept in the Depot

On the last Friday of every month, I baked whatever was in the freezer and called the bus drivers in to eat it. This was not an official duty. My official duty was lost property, but people left food on buses and the council had never issued a satisfactory instruction about it. I threw away anything with meat in it. Bread I could usually identify through the bag. The unmarked tubs I left alone until they became a problem for the next person.

For nineteen years there was no next person. Then the council sold the depot, and on a Thursday in April a man in a wool coat came to measure my shelves.

“Will these be coming with you?” he asked.

“Where am I going?”

He put his tape measure away. I think he’d been told that conversation had already happened.

The new depot would have a locker by the dispatch window. Anything too big for the locker would be photographed and disposed of after seven days. I was offered three mornings a week answering calls from home. The woman from Human Resources said I could do it in my pajamas. She meant this kindly, but I’d spent the first winter after my divorce going whole days in my pajamas and didn’t consider it much of a benefit.

I was given until the end of May to clear the room.

It was amazing what you could get rid of if you stopped believing its owner was on the way. The charity shop took thirty-one umbrellas, a mandolin, and a pair of roller skates with the original paper still stuffed inside. The man who bought scrap metal weighed the walking frames and offered me eleven pounds. I said I’d think about it. He said he’d be back on Tuesday, although neither of us believed he would.

The lemon tree came in on the number 8 on May 14. Ray carried it through dispatch with his jacket wrapped around the pot. There was soil all down his front.

“Someone’s going to want that back,” I said.

“You always say that.”

The tree was waist-high and had one lemon, green on the side that faced the window. Somebody had tied it to a bamboo stake with strips cut from an old shirt. There was a crack in the pot, neatly bridged with two loops of wire.

“An old bloke got on with it at the hospital,” Ray said. “I thought he’d get off at the garden flats, but he took it all the way to the exchange. I found it after I’d turned round.”

“Did you see him get off?”

“Saw him wait for me to lower the step. I assumed he had it.”

I wrote *tree, lemon, terracotta pot* in the book. The book was a duplicate pad left over from when a driver could hand a passenger a receipt for a parcel and carry it unaccompanied to the other end of the route. Sometimes a driver still did this, but only for somebody he knew.

By Wednesday the tree had dropped six leaves. I watered it. On Thursday it dropped nine, and I looked up what to do and discovered I shouldn’t have watered it. I moved it out of the draught. By Friday it had dropped so many that I stopped counting.

That afternoon my daughter, Alice, came to help me pack. She was thirty and had recently acquired a car big enough, she said, to make her popular with the wrong people. She brought two kinds of tape.

“Which boxes are going to yours?”

“None of them.”

She put down the tape. “I thought you wanted me to take your personal stuff.”

I showed her my personal stuff: a fork, a cardigan, one photograph of her on a donkey.

“God,” she said. “There was a woman behind that donkey charging by the minute. Do you remember?”

I remembered the woman chiefly because she had said there was no need to buy a photograph; we were welcome to take our own. I’d bought one anyway. Alice had been too old for the ride and wanted it so badly she’d tried to pretend she didn’t.

She slipped the picture out of its plastic stand and put it in her coat pocket. I almost asked for it back. Instead I asked how the new job was going.

“I didn’t take it,” she said.

I’d told three people she had.

“You sent me that message with the champagne glasses.”

“That was when they offered it.”

“Oh,” I said. “Well, you could have told me.”

“I just did.”

She opened a box and held the flaps together while I taped the bottom. We had always been good at the part that required two people and didn’t require talking.

The last person to claim anything in the ordinary way was a man who’d lost a shoe. He rang at nine in the morning and described it, including the square of cardboard he’d put under the insole. I found it in a bag marked *assorted trainers* and told him he could come before four.

“What about the other one?” he asked.

“You said you lost one.”

“I did. But I threw the other one out when I got home.”

He lived on the far side of town and understandably didn’t want to make the journey for a shoe he couldn’t use. We both stayed on the line a little longer than we needed to. Then he thanked me for finding it.

I put the shoe in the rubbish. At lunchtime I took it out again because the man had sounded as if he might change his mind. It sat on my desk for the rest of the week, taking up about as much room as my telephone.

The following Monday Ray brought in a note. Someone had handed it to him on the number 8. Written on the back of an appointment card were the words *Did the tree make it?*

There was a telephone number. I rang and got a man who said his name was Len.

“Yes, we’ve got it,” I said. “You can collect it any weekday before four.”

“I don’t want to collect it.”

“Well,” I said, “what do you want?”

There was a little scrape on the line, the sound of a telephone changing hands or a chair being dragged closer.

“I suppose I wanted to know where it ended up.”

I looked over at the tree. In the morning light the bare tips of the branches were almost white.

“Funny place to leave it,” I said.

“I tried the library first. They thought I was bringing it in for them to look after while I chose a book.”

“Were you?”

“No. But I did choose a book. Then I had to take that back as well.”

He’d moved out of his flat the previous week. His new room had a window that started six feet above the floor. He’d put a request on the noticeboard in the laundry asking whether anyone wanted the tree, but someone had taken it down to put up a warning about leaving things on the noticeboard.

I asked how old it was.

“Twenty-three. Older than any lemon tree you’d buy on purpose. Is the lemon still on it?”

“Yes.”

“Is it yellow?”

“Mostly.”

“You can have that,” he said.

After we hung up, I stood over the pot trying to get a finger under the wire without breaking it. There was a folded strip of rubber between the wire and the clay, protecting the rim. I’d never have thought to do that. I’d probably have used a new pot.

I rang Alice to see if she wanted a lemon tree. She said no, but asked why I was whispering.

“I don’t like talking on my mobile in the office.”

“Is there anybody else in the office?”

“No.”

She waited. I could hear something running in the background, perhaps a tap.

“Why didn’t you take the job?” I asked.

“Because it was in Bristol.”

“I thought you liked Bristol.”

“I do. I also like where I live now. I can like somewhere without moving there.”

She told me she’d worked out what the train would cost, and she’d actually gone as far as looking at rooms. One woman had wanted a deposit before Alice could see the place. Another had said she was welcome to use the kitchen as long as she didn’t cook anything that smelled like cooking.

“Why didn’t you ring me then?” I asked.

“Because you’d have found me a room.”

She wasn’t accusing me, which made it harder to say what came to mind. I got as far as “I could have,” and stopped.

“Yes,” she said. “I know.”

The tap, if it was a tap, went off. She asked what I was doing on Sunday. I said I wasn’t sure. She said she would come for lunch if I liked, but could we decide what to eat on the day? I said we could. When I hung up, it struck me that she might come and find there was nothing in the house. I made myself sit at the desk until the urge to write a shopping list passed.

On the last Friday, Ray brought sausage rolls from a bakery. He said he’d thought about putting them in an unmarked bag and leaving them on his bus for me to find, but he couldn’t trust the schoolchildren. We ate them with the door propped open. Without the shelves the room made a surprising amount of noise. We could hear a man in the yard reversing a bus and another man telling him, with steadily increasing disbelief, that he still had plenty of room.

At two o’clock, Len came in. I knew him because he looked straight at the tree. He wore a blue shirt with two mismatched buttons at the bottom, not that anyone would have noticed if he’d tucked it in.

“I said I wasn’t coming to collect it.”

“You did.”

He put a carrier bag on the desk. Inside were a handful of plant ties, a bottle with its label washed off, and a saucer big enough to take the pot.

“The chap downstairs always said he’d have that saucer when I was done with it,” he said. “Then when it came to it he only wanted it for his dog. The dog had a perfectly good bowl.”

I asked him to look at the leaves. He touched one of the remaining ones with the back of a finger.

“It doesn’t like moving,” he said. “It’ll do that again next time.”

“Will it live?”

“I don’t know. It always has.”

He bent to pick something out of the soil, a shred of foil that must have come from a cigarette packet. Then he straightened up and asked who was taking it.

I said I was.

Until I said it, I hadn’t known that I was. My flat had a shallow bay window, with enough room if I moved the small table on which I kept things I meant to take upstairs. Most of those things, on reflection, had been downstairs so long that upstairs could manage without them.

“Have you got help getting it there?” he asked.

I said I could call my daughter.

“Don’t lift it by the trunk,” he said.

We stood either side of the desk for a moment. He looked at the tree again, then picked up a sausage roll. He ate it neatly over the carrier bag, shook the crumbs into the rubbish, and left to catch his bus.

Alice came at four. She took one look at the pot and went out to get an old bath towel from the car. We wrapped it around the clay and carried the tree between us. Halfway across the yard she told me to stop. I said I was all right. She said she wasn’t asking whether I was all right; she had a bit of wire in her thumb.

We set the pot down. It was a tiny puncture, barely worth a plaster, but it bled quite freely. I handed her a clean tissue and waited while she pressed it to her thumb. Above us someone in dispatch had taped a piece of paper to the window saying *WE ARE STILL OPEN*. They’d have to go up there and peel it off in the morning.

“Did you get everything you wanted?” she asked.

I thought of the photograph in her coat pocket. I hadn’t seen it since she’d put it there and I didn’t know whether it was on her mantelpiece or still in the pocket, working its way through a hole in the lining.

“Yes,” I said.

We moved the tree the rest of the way with the wire on my side.

For the first two weeks at home, the lemon did nothing. Then one morning I found it on the carpet. It had landed on its stalk and made a little hole in itself. I rang Len to tell him. The number, it turned out, belonged to the desk at the place he’d moved to. A woman fetched him, and while I waited I heard her say, some distance from the telephone, “No, it’s the lady about your tree.”

I wondered how many calls he got that she could tell them apart.

“Was it yellow underneath?” he asked.

I turned it over. “Yes.”

“Well, there you are.”

I offered to bring him some. I meant a cake, or a jar of curd, something I could carry on the bus and present to him without either of us having to account for the journey. But he took me literally.

“How much lemon do you think there is?” he said.

After we’d hung up, I cut it across the middle. The skin was very thick and there wasn’t much inside. I squeezed half over some potatoes. The other half I left face down on a saucer until Alice came by.

She said she’d eat whatever I was having. It was too early for dinner and too late for lunch. We stood in the kitchen and ate the cold potatoes with our fingers. She squeezed the rest of the lemon over them, catching the pips in her palm, then rinsed her hands at the sink. I nearly told her that the lemon had taken almost a year to grow. Len hadn’t actually told me that. I’d read it somewhere and wanted it to be the sort of thing he’d know.

Outside, the number 8 went past. The route hadn’t changed with the depot, though the bus now made a left at the end of our street instead of a right. I still noticed every time. Alice didn’t look up. She was telling me about a woman at work who had gone on holiday and given her a key so she could water the plants. There were forty plants, she said. One of them had an instruction to be misted on alternate days, and the spray bottle was the size of a thimble.

“Have you done it?” I asked.

“Every other day since Tuesday.”

She went on to tell me which plant was her favorite. I thought it would be the one with the instructions, but it was an ordinary geranium on the landing. She hadn’t been asked to water that one. She didn’t even know if it belonged to the woman. It was just there each time she put the key in the door, and when she came out again she could tell by the smell that someone had beaten her to it.

samples.result:
# The Last Thing in Lost Property

The last thing anyone came to claim was a door.

“A door to what?” I asked.

The girl considered this. “That depends which way you’re going.”

She was fourteen, perhaps fifteen, and had arrived on the last afternoon of the municipal lost-property office with a canvas shopping bag and a claim ticket on which someone had written, in pencil, BIG FLAT THING. This was typical of our drivers. One of them had once handed in a cello as POSSIBLE GUITAR. For three weeks, its owner and I had been victims of the word *possible*.

“Was it lost on a bus?”

“On the forty-six.”

“Was it attached to the bus?”

“No.”

I asked the second question out of habit. We had rules about fixtures.

Behind me, the shelves were bare except for a pair of yellow swimming fins and a lunch box that smelled, even after six months, astonishingly of oranges. Everything else had been collected, donated, or put on the truck for the depot across town. At five, I was to leave my keys in an envelope on the desk. On Monday, a man named Craig would come to measure the room for a coffee franchise. I knew his name because he had already come once, two weeks early, and asked me whether the floor was level.

“It was when I started,” I told him.

The girl gave me the ticket. On the back was the number of the bus and, in the upper corner, a little drawing of a fish.

“That’s my fish,” she said. “In case you were wondering.”

“I was wondering about the door.”

“Oh. It’s green.”

There was a green door in the office. It was behind the filing cabinet, where we had put it after discovering that a door leaning against a wall invites people to open it. Two visitors had tried. The second had looked at the handle in his hand as if it had betrayed him personally.

I led the girl around the counter.

“Is that it?”

She put her palm on the green paint. “I need to see underneath.”

Together we pulled the door out. It was heavier than I remembered. A strip of brown felt had been glued along one edge, and there was a dent near the lock, exactly the right size to have been made by the back of a spoon. On the unpainted side, written in pencil, were the words:

*Fifty people: six onions unless Mrs. N. is coming.*

The girl crouched down.

“That’s it,” she said. “Mrs. N. is my grandmother.”

“Does she like onions?”

“She brings her own. She thinks no one else cooks them long enough.”

Below the onions were other pencilled notes, some in English, some in a language I didn’t recognize. A line of arithmetic ended in a small, angry cloud. Someone had drawn the outline of a hand and written *JUNE 2019* inside it. The girl put her hand over the drawing. The fingers of the drawing stuck out past hers.

“That’s my brother’s,” she said. “He was twelve. Disgusting, really, how fast he grew.”

I got a release form.

“Name of owner?”

“Everybody.”

“I’ll need a name I can put on the form.”

“Put my grandmother.”

“Did she own it?”

The girl thought awhile. “She paid for the hinges.”

I had a supervisor I could call. She had told me that if there were any unresolved claims on the final day, I should call. She had also told me that her son was going to read a poem at school at four, the first time he had agreed to speak in front of anybody since Christmas. It was four twelve. Whatever the proper disposition of the door, there was no need to involve a boy reading a poem.

“Where are you taking it?” I asked.

“Number eight, Larch Street.”

I knew the building. The ground floor had been a laundrette, then a shop that sold phones and repaired shoes, sometimes in the same transaction. The upper floors had balconies just deep enough to stand on if you didn’t mind your toes sticking through the railings.

“How did it get on the bus in the first place?”

“With difficulty,” she said.

She looked at me to see if I would let her get away with that. When I didn’t say anything, she sat on the edge of the counter and told me.

The door had come off the old boiler room in the basement of number eight. For eleven years it had lain across two trestles on Thursday evenings. Dinner had started with three women waiting for their washing to finish and ended up feeding anybody who turned up at seven. In warm weather they carried the door into the yard. Renters came and went, and some of them still returned on Thursdays, even after they had moved farther away than you would think anyone would travel for lentils.

Then the building changed hands. The new owners found water coming in behind the basement wall, and while the repairs were being done, the room had to be cleared. A man in an orange vest pointed to a skip and told the girl’s brother, who had come to help his grandmother, that anything nobody wanted should go in there.

“He thought the man was going to throw it out himself,” the girl said. “So he took it.”

“Where was he going?”

“To our uncle’s. He has a shed.”

“How do you accidentally leave a door on a bus?”

“You get off at the front to ask the driver to open the back. He doesn’t understand you because you’ve put your earphones in your pocket without turning the music off, and you think he’s saying yes when actually he’s saying stand clear.”

I laughed. The girl didn’t.

“He went all the way to the terminus after it. Then he told Gran he’d got it into the shed. He’s been going over to our uncle’s every Thursday for a month so she’ll think he’s checking on it.”

“Does your uncle know?”

“My uncle thinks he’s finally taking an interest in him.”

I laughed again, and this time she did too, though she tried to disguise it as a cough.

The door had arrived from the terminus on Tuesday. Until then it had been propped against a vending machine with a handwritten sign reading OUT OF ORDER. Quite a lot of lost property was not lost in the interesting sense. It was six feet away, being mistaken for a sign.

I put the form down between us.

“If I put your name, will you sign for it?”

“Yes.”

“Can you carry it?”

“Yes,” she said, without the same conviction.

She opened her shopping bag. It contained a skein of thin blue rope, a folded dish towel, and two apples. One apple had a bite out of it. She took it out, examined the bite as if it might have happened in transit, and took another.

Her name was Leila. She signed with a tiny, tidy signature that looked nothing like the fish.

We tried the rope first. The idea, as I understood it, was to make a kind of shoulder strap. With the door upright, Leila managed three steps before it swung outward and knocked the fins off the shelf. We tried putting the towel between the rope and her shoulder. This helped her shoulder but did nothing for the fins.

“We could get the forty-six,” she said.

I looked at her.

“Yes,” she said. “I know.”

I had a small cart in the cupboard, a folding thing with red wheels that I used for boxes of paper. It belonged to me, though it had been in the office long enough to acquire a municipal sticker and a dent made by someone who had never admitted borrowing it. If we laid the door on the cart and tied it down, one of us could hold each end. Larch Street was less than a mile away.

I looked at the clock. Four thirty-eight.

When I first took the job, my husband used to meet me at five and we would walk to the market. He liked to stand at the fish counter asking questions he already knew the answers to. “What would you do with these?” he would ask, pointing to the sardines, and the fishmonger, who knew perfectly well what he would do with them because he had told him every Friday for eight years, would explain again about the lemon and the salt.

After he died, I worked late on Fridays. There was no practical reason for it. At five the buses made one kind of noise outside the office, and at six they made another; by staying late I could leave to the wrong noise.

I’d intended to work late on this last Friday too. I had even left myself a drawer to clear. It contained a spare cardigan and some stamps. I could have emptied it in nine seconds.

“Get the other end,” I told Leila.

We laid the door green side down on the cart and passed the rope under it twice. I unplugged the kettle, put the stamps in my pocket, and carried the cardigan out under my arm. After a week of saying goodbye to people who had been coming in for years, I had thought there would be something left to do at the office itself. There wasn’t. The municipal envelope had a window too low for the address printed on the sheet inside. I adjusted the sheet, put the keys in, and left it on the desk.

Outside, Leila took the front end of the door and set off faster than I could comfortably walk.

“Have you told anybody we’re coming?”

“No.”

“Do we have somewhere to put it?”

She didn’t answer.

At the crossing, a man eating chips from a paper carton asked if we’d install it for him.

“Depends what you’re paying,” Leila said.

He offered a chip. She accepted, so he gave me one too. The light changed before he had time to put vinegar on either of them.

Halfway down Larch Street we lost one of the wheels. It came off on a slope and rolled back past us in a leisurely way, as if reconsidering its destination. Leila ran after it. I stood with the door tilted against my hip, trying not to scrape it along the pavement, while a woman watering the plants outside a hairdresser’s watched me from across the street.

“Is that the table?” the woman called.

“It’s a door,” I called back.

“Yes, I know it’s a door. Is it the table?”

The woman put down her watering can. Her name was Denise, and she had done hair on Larch Street for twenty-three years. She fetched a pair of pliers, a bent nail, and a man named Louis, who had been waiting for his daughter to finish getting her hair braided. Louis knelt on the pavement and repaired the axle while Leila stood with both arms around the end of the door.

“I thought you’d all finished with that,” Denise said.

“We were waiting for the room,” Leila said.

“It’s finished. They’ve got exercise bikes in it now.”

Leila looked at her.

“Only three,” Denise added, as though the number might help.

Louis spun the wheel. It wobbled but stayed on.

We didn’t go any farther for a minute. I could see the balconies of number eight from where we stood. Someone had hung a white shirt over one of the railings. Its sleeves kept lifting in the wind.

“Your gran hasn’t been down there, then,” Denise said.

“She has,” said Leila. “She’s been three times. She told me the workmen must be having trouble with the floor.”

Denise picked up her watering can and took it inside. When she came back, she had a plastic chair, which she set on the pavement. None of us sat in it.

“My brother’s in the shed now,” Leila said. She was looking at her phone. “He says our uncle’s showing him how to sharpen a pair of shears.”

“Tell him we’ve got the door,” I said.

“He’ll want to know where to take it.”

“Tell him where it is.”

She typed with both thumbs. Then she looked up at Denise.

“Does your water come out hot enough to wash dishes?”

“Hot enough to remove skin,” Denise said. “Why?”

Leila bent over the door to loosen the rope. “I’m calling my gran.”

That first Friday dinner nobody cooked. This has been disputed since, chiefly by Denise, who says that buying a hot chicken and cutting it into eight uneven pieces constitutes cooking. Louis brought the trestles from the cupboard under his stairs, where they had been all along. The woman from the corner shop brought paper plates and stood at the end of the table explaining that she couldn’t stay, right up until somebody took her coat.

Leila’s brother arrived with their uncle, who was carrying a pair of freshly sharpened shears. Their grandmother arrived last. She carried a jar of onions and a bottle of washing-up liquid in a bag that also contained, for reasons she never explained, a single clean sock.

Leila’s brother looked at his grandmother and began, “I can explain.”

“I should hope so,” she said. “I’ve been paying your uncle five pounds a week to keep you out of that shed.”

Their uncle put the shears down. The boy looked from one to the other, and it wasn’t until both of them laughed that I realized they were lying, and not particularly well.

We set the door green side up. There was a brisk discussion about whether it could stay in the hairdresser’s overnight. It couldn’t: Denise had a wedding party at nine and needed all her floor. Louis offered his hallway, provided it was gone before his daughter’s bicycle came out in the morning. Nobody knew where it would go after that. Leila put a paper plate over the hole where the handle had been.

I sat down when the chair became free. Somebody had brought sardines, the cheap kind in a tin, and I pulled back the lid and put a few on my plate. Leila passed me a lemon half without my asking. I squeezed it hard enough to get a seed in my eye. For a minute I could see nothing on that side but a bright, watery blur, and when it cleared everyone was still there, reaching over one another for bread.

A few weeks later I went past the old office. The floor, it turned out, was not level. Craig had solved this by raising one end of the counter, and now the little glass case full of pastries stood exactly where our shelf of ownerless umbrellas had been. I bought a coffee. It was good. I had been hoping it wouldn’t be.

The door acquires a new address every so often. It spends most weeks, at present, standing on edge in Louis’s hallway. His daughter has learned to wheel her bicycle past it without catching the pedals, though not without complaining. There is talk of asking the new owners for the basement on Friday evenings, since nobody has ever seen all three exercise bikes in use at once. There is also talk of staying on the pavement until the weather makes us stop. People get up from dinner and go to the bus stop, and people coming home on the bus see us and sit down.

Last Friday I arrived early. Leila was there, rubbing at a blot of candle wax with her thumbnail. She had a pencil tucked behind her ear. I asked if she needed it for school.

“No,” she said. “Turn this over with me a second.”

We tipped the door up off the trestles. The old notes were still there, darker in some places from the grease that had worked its way into the wood. Leila found a space alongside the angry cloud, took the pencil from behind her ear, and wrote *If raining, ask Denise*.

Then she squatted down and added, smaller, *Ask nicely*.

# The Things That Still Worked

On the first Monday after her father’s funeral, Agnes put a notice in the repair shop window: IF YOU LEFT SOMETHING HERE, PLEASE COME GET IT.

By noon, three people had come in to ask what she meant.

“Anything,” she told them. “A lamp. A toaster. Whatever you brought him.”

“No, but what do you mean by *get*?” asked Mrs. Bell, who had taught Agnes fractions and still spoke to her as if a better answer were available with effort. “Do you mean it’s ready?”

Agnes looked at the shelves behind the counter. There were two sewing machines, four fans, a bread maker, and an electric fireplace with a handwritten warning attached to it: NOT THE SWITCH. There were also several dozen objects whose purposes were less apparent. Her father had kept each repair’s screws in a separate baby-food jar. Some of the jars had more information on them than the repairs did.

“I mean I’d like you to take it home,” Agnes said.

Mrs. Bell considered this. “I’ll come back when you know.”

She left without saying what she had brought.

Agnes’s brother, Daniel, arrived with sandwiches and a roll of orange stickers. They were to mark everything that could go in the skip. He had ordered the skip for Friday, which Agnes thought was early, though she had been the one to tell him to stop asking her when he should order it.

They ate on stools behind the counter. Across the street, a man was washing the windows of the pharmacy, moving the same little crescent of water back and forth. The sandwich Daniel had bought for Agnes contained an ingredient she had disliked for thirty years. She took it out and set it on the wrapper.

“I know,” he said. “They don’t make them without it anymore.”

“It’s a tomato. They could start.”

“He used to give me his.”

“Dad?”

Daniel nodded. “On Thursdays.”

Agnes hadn’t known about Thursdays. She folded the tomato into the corner of the wrapper so it wouldn’t leak onto the bench.

Their father’s filing system consisted of a receipt spike, a school exercise book, and the conviction that he would remember. On the first page of the exercise book was a drawing of a bird. On the second was a list of the dimensions of the shop window. The repairs began on page three, proceeded in reasonable order through page eleven, and then resumed, upside down, at the back.

Agnes read the entries out while Daniel searched the shelves.

“‘Yusuf, amplifier, sound goes when warm.’”

“Got it.”

“‘Janice, iron, unreliable.’”

“Could be any of these.”

“‘Mr. Lee, radio. He knows.’”

“Knows what?”

“Maybe it was a difficult conversation.”

Daniel put the radio on the counter. In the battery compartment they found a key wrapped in a five-pound note.

“Do you think Mr. Lee knows about that?” he asked.

“I think we’ve reached the limit of what we can infer about Mr. Lee.”

They made a row for items with owners and a row for items without. By three o’clock the second row had taken over the first, and Daniel had stuck orange dots on a broken umbrella, two telephone directories, and a tin of buttons. Agnes peeled the dot off the buttons. Then she put it back. She had buttons at home. She didn’t use those either.

Just before closing, a woman came in carrying an empty shopping bag. She was perhaps seventy, with a neat white fringe and a green coat fastened wrong at the bottom. She introduced herself as Ruth and asked for her tape recorder.

“What sort?” Agnes said.

“Rectangular.”

“Any particular color?”

“It was the sort of gray they used to make things when they didn’t want you to think about color.”

Daniel found it under a work lamp. It was heavier than it looked and had a handle with grooves for four fingers. A jar of screws was taped to the top. Inside the cassette compartment was a tape with TUESDAY written on it.

“Did he fix it?” Ruth asked.

“We don’t know,” Agnes said.

“Well. Is there somewhere we could plug it in?”

Daniel found the lead. When Ruth pressed Play, there was a click, followed by a low rushing sound. Something struck a hard surface twice. A voice, too far from the microphone to be intelligible, rose and fell.

“That’s right,” Ruth said.

They listened. The sound continued. It might have been rain or a badly tuned radio. After a while there came a squeal, and Ruth pressed Stop.

“That’s not right,” she said.

Agnes waited for her to say what was on the tape. Instead Ruth took a ten-pound note from her purse, smoothed it on the counter, and asked if they would mind keeping the recorder another day.

“I’m not sure what another day would do,” Agnes said. “Neither of us knows how to fix it.”

“No, I know. I saw your notice.” Ruth looked down at the note. “Of course you don’t want to keep things.”

Agnes gave her back the money. Ruth put it away and opened her shopping bag. Daniel lowered the recorder into it by the handle, steadying the bottom with his other hand. All three watched the bag stretch into its new shape.

“What’s on the tape?” Agnes asked.

“The old swimming pool,” Ruth said. “I used to work there. I went in on the last day before they drained it.”

Agnes remembered the pool. You could pay twenty pence for a cup of hot orange drink afterward. It came from a machine, hot enough to buckle the cup.

“I thought you might say somebody’s voice,” she said.

“People do think that.” Ruth gathered up the handles. “I knew everybody there. I don’t particularly want to hear any of them.”

After she left, Daniel asked if Agnes remembered how their father used to count the tiles at the bottom of the deep end.

“He said he did,” Agnes said.

“I saw him doing it once. He got to the other side and held up eight fingers.”

“The pool was wider than eight tiles.”

“Yes,” said Daniel. “I never asked him about that.”

On Tuesday morning Agnes changed the notice. She added a deadline and her phone number, and beneath that, in smaller letters: WE DON’T KNOW IF IT’S READY.

People began coming in. Janice identified her iron by a scorch mark on the handle. Yusuf collected the amplifier and said he would put it somewhere cold. A man took home a fan that proved to belong to somebody else, then returned with it and brought the correct fan’s owner, who turned out to be his former wife. They hadn’t seen each other in six years. They discussed which one of them had originally bought the fan until Agnes offered it to the first person to pick it up. Neither did.

At lunch Daniel brought a bag of rolls and a block of cheese, and they made their own sandwiches. He cut his roll on the diagonal, which she had never seen anybody do to a roll.

“Did you come every Thursday?” she asked.

“Most of them.”

“How long?”

“Since he stopped driving, I suppose.”

That was four years. Agnes had lived less than an hour away for all four of them. She had called their father on Sundays from the supermarket car park, usually while deciding whether the ice cream would survive a second errand.

“You could have said,” she told him.

“What would I have said? We’re eating sandwiches?”

“I might have come.”

“You might have.” Daniel put down the knife. “Do you remember when he was in hospital and you asked me to bring him clean pyjamas? And I said I had?”

“Yes.”

“I hadn’t. I brought him mine. I couldn’t find his. He wore them for three days, and I kept thinking you’d get there and tell me where he kept his pyjamas. As if he’d even put them in the same place twice.”

“In the airing cupboard,” Agnes said. “Behind the towels.”

“See, that would have been good information.”

She couldn’t tell if he was angry. She was, but not in a way that gave her any useful thing to say. Outside, a delivery van pulled up, blocking their view of the pharmacy. They sat in the dimness and finished their lunch. When the van left, both of them blinked.

That afternoon Agnes found an invoice for six swimming lessons tucked into the frame of the shop mirror. The pupil’s name was Daniel’s, the date twenty-eight years earlier. Along the bottom, where the instructor was meant to initial each lesson, there were four blue ticks and two empty boxes.

She handed it to him.

“Oh,” he said. “I told Dad I’d learned. I could get across if I pushed off hard enough.”

“Did he believe you?”

“He came swimming with me the next week.”

Daniel turned the invoice over. The back was covered in sums. Their father had been working out how much it would cost to put a shelf over the front door. There was no shelf over the front door.

On Wednesday, Ruth called the number on the sign. She asked if Agnes could help her get the sound off the tape before it broke.

“My nephew says there’s a way to do it on a computer,” she said. “But he lives in Sweden. He’s very available from Sweden.”

Agnes said she could try. Ruth brought the tape around, without the recorder this time, in an envelope from the building society. Borrowing a cassette player from the library took two phone calls and a walk across town. Setting it up took the rest of the afternoon, largely because Daniel insisted he had the right cable and went home twice to get it. At last a green line began to wobble across Agnes’s laptop screen.

Without the squeal, there was more to hear. The rushing sound was water moving through the pool’s circulation system. Once they understood that, other noises separated out: a foot dragged across wet tile, a door scraped, a coin or a key landed on a bench.

“That’s me putting down the locker keys,” Ruth said.

“Were you the last one there?”

“Except for the manager. He kept following me around telling me which lights I could turn off. He’d been there six months. I’d been there thirty-one years.”

There was a pause on the tape when the water seemed to grow louder. Then came the soft clack of a light switch. Ruth closed her eyes. A second clack followed.

“Changing rooms,” she said. “Then the showers.”

Agnes realized she was waiting for an announcement, some remark that would make it clear this was the last day. Instead, after another minute, Ruth’s recorded voice said, “I’ve got your mug,” and the manager said, “Oh, cheers.”

The tape kept going for nine minutes after they left the building. At first they listened to Ruth walking. Then she got on a bus and sat down. Somebody a few seats away was giving directions to a café that Agnes knew had since become a dental surgery. Ruth leaned over to stop the tape.

“You can leave the bus on,” she said, changing her mind. “I’d forgotten the café.”

On Thursday morning it rained hard. Water came under the shop door, as it always had, and Agnes went to the back for newspaper. Behind a crate of old plugs she found a narrow board with a strip of rubber fixed along one edge. It fit exactly at the foot of the door. Once it was in place she could see two little pencil arrows, one on the board and one on the frame, pointing at one another.

There were things her father had finished. She kept finding evidence of them in places where there was no reason to look until something went wrong.

At noon Daniel appeared with a flask and two sandwiches from the usual place. They sat on the stools. Agnes gave him her tomato, and he ate it.

“I stopped calling on Sundays last summer,” she said. “Not completely. But I’d miss one and then I’d think I had to call properly, when I had time.”

“He went out on Sundays,” Daniel said.

“Where?”

“I don’t know. Sometimes he’d tell me where he’d been and I’d know he hadn’t. He said he went to a kite festival once. I looked it up. It had been canceled.”

“Maybe he went and found out it was canceled.”

“I hadn’t thought of that.”

A truck drove over the puddle by the curb. They watched water sweep over the pavement and stop a foot short of the door.

“I don’t actually think we need the skip,” Daniel said.

Agnes looked around. They had cleared almost everything customers had come back for. Of what remained, much could go to the charity shop or the electrical recycling depot.

“What about the fireplace?”

“Mrs. Bell says it’s hers.”

“Did she say what’s wrong with it?”

“She says it’s the switch.”

They laughed, but not very much, because what they both wanted, suddenly and with some force, was for the door to the back room to open and their father to come out and object.

It didn’t, of course. The radiator came on. Daniel got up to see if there was enough hot water for a second cup of tea.

On Friday, a man from the skip company phoned to say he was ten minutes away. Daniel had forgotten to cancel. Agnes was about to ask what the cancellation fee was when she looked up at the long workbench. It was anchored to the wall, and its top had split lengthwise where a vise had been bolted down. The new tenant had asked for an empty shop.

“Actually, bring it,” she said.

It took until midafternoon to get the bench out. The bolts had been painted over so many times that Daniel had to chip around each one before he could turn it. Agnes held up the loose end while he worked on the last bolt. She’d spent five days wondering what she might take home, rejecting a soldering iron, a chipped mug, and a radio that wasn’t theirs to keep. Now, with the weight of the bench against her ribs, she found she didn’t want so much as a piece of it. She wanted him to hurry. It was a great relief when he did.

In the space where the bench had been, the wall was painted a yellow neither of them remembered. Daniel leaned against it, breathing hard. Agnes went to the counter, found a pencil, and drew a little bird on the yellow paint.

“What’s that?” he asked.

“A bird.”

“Which way is it facing?”

She looked at it. She had given it a beak at both ends.

“Both,” she said, and left it like that.

They had agreed to give the keys to the landlord on Monday. There was no more work to do, but Agnes came back on Saturday for the narrow board that kept the water out. She had decided to leave a note explaining it to the new tenant. She set the board in place, opened the door to check it would still swing, and stood on the pavement with her keys in her hand.

Across the street, the pharmacy was busy. A woman came out with a paper bag, stopped to put on her glasses, and went back in. A boy on a bicycle waited at the crossing long after the cars had stopped. In the flat above the shop, someone drew a bath; water knocked in the pipes for a moment and then ran steadily.

Agnes took out her phone. She opened the voice recorder, thinking she might keep the sound of the street. But a bus went by, then another, and neither sound was the one she was waiting for. She put the phone away without recording anything. A minute later she took it out again and called Daniel.

“Are you doing anything?” she asked.

“Fitting a shelf.”

“How’s that going?”

There was a long pause. She heard something being set down.

“I’ve just put the kettle on,” he said.

“Good,” she said. “I’ll come over.”
