samples.result:
# The Practice Room

The room cost nine dollars an hour, and you could say anything in it except “I’m only practicing.”

That was my mother’s rule. She had painted it on a scrap of plywood and hung it at eye level beside the light switch. People liked to argue with it before they went in. What if they were practicing? What if the whole reason they’d come was to practice? My mother would listen, then ask whether they wanted the hour or not.

I inherited the room, the rule, and the little building that contained them in February. By April I had agreed to sell the building to a woman named Yvonne who wanted to open a bakery. She made excellent bread in a kitchen scarcely larger than her car. I had a job three towns away, a leaking roof at home, and no particular wish to spend my Saturdays listening through a wall.

“You can’t actually hear anything through the wall,” my brother, Daniel, said when I told him.

“I know.”

“Then why did you say it?”

“Because that’s what it feels like.”

He considered this. Daniel took a long time answering questions and very little time asking them. It had made him an exasperating child and a surprisingly good nurse.

“When do you close?” he asked.

“End of the month.”

“I’d like to book an hour.”

I opened the calendar. “What for?”

He looked at me.

“Right,” I said. “Sorry.”

The room had started as a typing office. Our mother did résumés, divorce petitions, church bulletins, whatever someone could bring her on paper and pay to have put onto another piece of paper. She was a fast typist and a poor speller. When she wasn’t sure of a word, she called the public library and asked whoever answered to use it in a sentence. She said it was a way of getting her money’s worth out of her taxes.

One afternoon a man came in with a letter he wanted typed to his daughter. He had written only her name. Our mother put a sheet in the typewriter and asked him what came next. He said he would know if she left him alone for a while.

She went to the diner. When she came back, he was gone. On the sheet he had typed, in the middle of the page, the word LISTEN. He had left two dollars under the ashtray.

I don’t know whether that story was true. She told it whenever someone from the newspaper came by, and twice, when it appeared in print, I noticed that the daughter’s name had changed. But the rent went up, typing went out, and the practice room persisted.

Its furnishings were simple: two chairs, a box of tissues, a clock you couldn’t hear, and a folding table with one short leg. One chair had arms and the other didn’t. People sometimes asked which one they were supposed to sit in. Mom said if they knew the answer to that, she could save them nine dollars.

I used to think the room was for speeches. Then, in high school, my friend Kelsey booked it to practice being told no. She wanted me to sit across from her and refuse to give her a job at the swimming pool.

“We don’t think you’re a good fit,” I said.

“Why not?”

“You’re not a strong swimmer.”

“I’m a very strong swimmer.”

“You’re not a strong swimmer and you’re argumentative.”

She burst into tears. I gave her a tissue, and she said, “Don’t be nice. We have forty minutes left.”

She got the job. The first week, she called me from the changing room to say they’d put her on the concession stand. She hadn’t considered that there might be a third thing that could happen.

During the last month I opened the building on Saturdays. There were fewer bookings than I expected, though people stopped in to tell me they’d always meant to make one. Some asked if my mother had ever used the room herself.

“She had a key,” I told them.

It was the sort of answer she would have given. At the time I was pleased by that. It took me several weeks to hear how annoying it was.

Yvonne came by on the second Saturday with a tape measure and her son, Milo. The boy wore yellow rain boots though it hadn’t rained in days. While his mother measured the front window, he drew six rectangles on a piece of paper and gave it to me.

“It’s the bread,” he said.

Each rectangle had a small door.

“So you can go inside?”

“So you can see if there’s raisins.”

He didn’t like raisins and regarded their concealment in bread as something adults did to him personally.

Yvonne measured the threshold to the practice room. She planned to make it her kitchen, but the oven she wanted wouldn’t fit through the door. I told her the partition wasn’t load-bearing. I had checked, hoping that perhaps it was. I don’t know what I thought that would accomplish. A bakery could have two rooms.

“Do you want the chairs?” she asked.

“I don’t think so.”

“Do you want to think about it?”

“Yes,” I said, surprised at how cheaply I could buy another week.

Daniel’s booking was at four on the last Saturday. At three fifty-five he arrived with a grocery bag. I thought he might have brought a prop, but the bag contained coffee, two oranges, and a sleeve of the plain biscuits our mother liked. He put everything on the counter and took out his wallet.

“You don’t have to pay.”

He handed me a ten. “Then give me two hours.”

I gave him a dollar in change.

While he was in there, I wiped the windowsills and emptied the bottom drawer of the filing cabinet. It contained a pack of playing cards with no queens, an expired coupon for an oil change, and thirty-three keys. I tried the keys in the front door, one after another. None fit. I imagined my mother receiving each one: a customer setting it down to look for exact change, a friend asking her to water a plant, a man with an old lock in his pocket who wanted to know what on earth she supposed it went to. She could throw away a perfectly good pair of shoes because she was tired of the sound they made on the stairs, but a key, apparently, always stood a chance.

At five Daniel came out and sat beside me on the bench under the window.

“Did you get it said?” I asked.

“No.”

“You can go back in.”

“I’d like you to come with me.”

I looked at the room. From the bench I could see one chair leg and a white scrape on the baseboard. I had made that scrape at thirteen, trying to get the filing cabinet out by myself after my mother said it couldn’t be done. It couldn’t be done by myself.

Daniel picked up the grocery bag. I followed him.

He sat in the chair without arms. I took the other one. Then he stood up and dragged his chair around so that we were side by side, facing the empty wall.

“This is how I had it,” he said.

“All right.”

“I’ve been trying to ask you this since January.”

I waited. He took an orange out of the bag and set it on the table, where it rolled into the tissue box.

“Did she ask for me?”

Our mother had died in her own bed on a Wednesday morning. Daniel had been there until midnight; I had been there after. In the months since, he had asked me a great many questions about that morning. Had she slept? Did she get cold? Did the hospice nurse arrive before or after six? I answered carefully, with the exasperation of someone being asked to show her work for an answer she hadn’t wanted to get right.

“No,” I said. “She didn’t ask for you.”

He nodded.

“She asked if it was going to snow. I said I didn’t think so.”

“Was that all?”

“She asked me to take her socks off.”

He bent down and flattened the grocery bag between his palms. I could hear the paper crackle.

“I went home because I wanted to,” he said.

“I know.”

“I had clean clothes in my car. I told you I was going home to change, but I had clean clothes in my car.”

“You’d been there since Sunday.”

“I wanted to sit in my own kitchen. I wanted to open a drawer and have everything in it be mine.”

He said this with the plainness he used to describe things that had happened at work, at an hour when I did not want to hear about work. Usually I interrupted. I pushed the tissue box toward him a little, then stopped. He hadn’t cried. I didn’t want to give him another thing to do.

“I was glad you went home,” I said.

He turned to look at me.

“I wanted to be there by myself.”

“Oh,” he said.

It wasn’t an especially charitable truth. For three days he had been the one who knew how to move her without hurting her, which of the pill bottles we still needed, and how to moisten the little sponge without dripping water down her neck. At one point our mother opened her eyes and asked me to get Daniel, though I was already holding the thing she wanted. I had gone to get him. I remembered, with some shame, the particular care I had taken not to close the door too loudly.

By the time we were alone she had very little need of either of us. Still, it mattered to me that the room was quiet and that I was the only person there to notice.

“I thought you might believe you left me with something I didn’t want,” I said. “You didn’t.”

Daniel placed the folded grocery bag on his knee. “That’s not what I thought.”

I waited.

“I thought maybe she wanted me back and you didn’t call.”

The clock above the door had a second hand. I’d always disliked its silence. Now I discovered that if you looked directly at it, its small advance was as irritating as any sound.

“Would you have called me?” I asked.

“Yes,” he said. Then he rubbed his thumb along a crease in the bag. “I don’t know. I hope so.”

I thought about our mother asking for her socks off. I had taken one off easily, turning it inside out at the heel as I pulled. The other caught on a toenail. She had opened her eyes and watched me struggle, and I remember thinking she was about to tell me how to do it. She didn’t. I had spent weeks making that silence into a kind of trust. It might have been exhaustion. I could keep both versions without having to choose, provided I didn’t tell the story too often.

“If she’d asked for you,” I said, “I would have wanted not to call. But I think I would have.”

Daniel leaned back. His chair bumped the wall.

“Okay,” he said.

We sat without speaking for a while. Through the window, high enough that all we could see was sky, the light changed. Daniel dug his thumb into the orange. He got one piece of peel off and handed me the fruit, then picked up the second orange and started on that one. He had done this since we were children: begun the hard part for me and left the rest. Whenever I tried to thank him he said he liked peeling oranges, which was clearly untrue. He peeled them badly and hated the white stuff under his nails.

“Who were you talking to before I came in?” I asked.

“Nobody. I was trying to get comfortable in the chair.”

“For an hour?”

“Not quite. I spent ten minutes getting it to stop rocking.”

He tipped it with his foot. Under the short leg was a folded dollar bill.

“Do you want that back?”

“Leave it,” he said. “It’s finally level.”

On Monday morning I met Yvonne to hand over the keys. I gave her the two that opened the building and showed her the drawer with the other thirty-three. She examined one at random. It had a round head with a tiny letter B stamped into it.

“My dad had a tin of these,” she said. “When he moved, we found the tin and no locks. In the new house there were six locks and no keys. For a while he acted like the two problems might cancel each other out.”

She put the key back. I offered to take the drawer home and she told me not to worry about it. She had a boy who liked keys.

I took the chair with arms for my bedroom, where it became, immediately and with no period of adjustment, a place for trousers. Daniel didn’t want the other one. Yvonne kept it by the bakery door for customers waiting out the rain or making a phone call. She left the dollar under the leg until the floor was replaced. After that, she said, she spent it.

The first week the bakery opened, there were long lines; the second week, there weren’t. Yvonne said this was a relief, though she checked the street whenever I went in. There was a narrow window into the kitchen where you could see her turning out dough, her wrists white with flour halfway up to her elbows. The old clock was mounted over the cash register. It was seven minutes fast. Everyone who worked there knew, and nobody fixed it.

One morning I was waiting for a loaf to be sliced when the woman in front of me asked whether this was the place that used to have the room. The young man at the register called back to Yvonne, who nodded through the window.

“Is there another one somewhere?” the woman asked.

Nobody knew of one. I could have told her that she didn’t need a special room. She could practice in a parked car, in the shower, on a long walk just far enough behind somebody that they wouldn’t think she was talking to them. I could have told her the chair by the door was the same chair, though I doubted that was what she wanted.

She bought a bun and carried it over to the chair. She set the paper bag in her lap, took out her phone, and held it for a long time without looking at it. The young man slid my bread across the counter. We both watched the woman by the door, and then, at almost exactly the same moment, we found reasons to look somewhere else.

“Would you like a bag?” he asked me.

The loaf was already in a bag. He saw that as soon as he asked. I said no, thank you. He nodded, and began brushing crumbs into his palm with the side of his hand.

By the time I got outside, the woman had put the phone to her ear. I walked the length of the window without turning my head. Then I went back in, because I had forgotten the bread. The young man had it ready for me. Neither of us looked at the chair this time. I took the loaf home and cut two thick slices for lunch, following the channels the machine had already made. The knife kept slipping into the next one. Finally I put it down and pulled the bread apart with my hands.

# A Map of Places to Sit

The first bench my father put on the map was not a bench. It was a low wall outside the dentist’s office, built to contain three hydrangeas and failing, by late July, to contain any of them. He backed into the flowers, sat, and started his stopwatch.

“What are we timing?” I asked.

“How long before somebody comes out and tells me I can’t sit here.”

Nobody came out. Across the road a man carried a sheet cake sideways out of the supermarket, discovered what he had done, and went back in. My father watched with the grave interest he generally reserved for people trying to reverse a trailer.

“Two minutes,” he said.

“Is that enough?”

“For what?”

I had no answer. He put a blue dot on the map.

The map was a free handout from the council offices. On one side were the streets of Bellwether, with little pictures of the clock tower and the war memorial. On the other side was an advertisement for a housing development that had been cancelled after somebody found a protected newt. My father had taken six copies. The council woman had asked whether he was expecting visitors. He had said he hoped not.

He was seventy-four and had recently begun having trouble walking. This was not how he described it. He said his legs were getting less interested in the second half of a journey. Home to the bakery was no problem. Bakery to home was sometimes a matter of stopping outside the betting shop and pretending to read the racing results until he could make it to the corner.

The council had removed the benches from the high street in March. The notice said they were being taken away for refurbishment. By June, someone had unscrewed the little brass plaques from their backs and put them in a drawer at the council offices. My father knew this because he had gone in to ask when the benches were coming back and had been offered, instead, a plaque. He could choose whichever one he liked.

“I didn’t know any of the dead people,” he told me. “It seemed forward.”

I was staying with him for two weeks while the bathroom in my flat was being redone. I had brought a laptop, three novels, and the belief that I would be useful. In the first four days I reorganized his kitchen cupboards, arranged for a grocery delivery he did not want, and suggested that he move his bedroom downstairs.

“Downstairs where?”

“The dining room.”

“Where would I have dinner?”

“You could have dinner in the kitchen.”

He thought about this for a moment. “Where would I have breakfast?”

I got angry, although he had scarcely moved. Later I put the mugs back on their original shelf. He had kept them beside the kettle, which was where I would have put them if I’d been trying to make the kitchen easier to use rather than trying to make it look as though I had done something.

The map was his idea. He wanted to find a way to the bakery that did not depend on a sudden interest in horses. I volunteered to go along. I had work to do, but my father liked to leave the house at eleven, and at eleven I generally began looking at property listings in places where I had no intention of living. I could spare the time.

We developed a key. A blue dot meant somewhere you could sit without buying anything. A green dot meant you probably ought to buy something. A circle around either meant there was a backrest. The bus shelter got a blue dot with a question mark because the seat consisted of a narrow metal ledge pitched at an angle. My father tried it and found that it required most of the muscles he was hoping to rest.

“Good place to get your trousers wet,” he said. “We should have a symbol for that.”

By our third outing he had begun to ask people. The florist told us you could sit on the concrete step beside her shop as long as it wasn’t Thursday, when the flowers came. A woman posting a letter directed us to the cemetery, where there were three benches and a fourth if you counted the lid of a water tank. A boy in school uniform told us that if we went into the carpet shop and acted like we were waiting for our mum, the man would let us sit on the stairs.

“How old do you have to be?” my father asked him.

The boy considered it. “Probably younger than you.”

We eventually found a route to the bakery by way of the dentist’s wall and the church porch. It added six minutes and avoided the betting shop. My father bought four buns to celebrate. He ate one standing outside the bakery, which I thought was an eccentric way to mark the occasion, but the icing was coming off on the paper and he didn’t want to waste it.

On the way back we found a woman sitting on the dentist’s wall. She had a red shopping trolley and a packet of frozen peas balanced on her knee. My father kept walking. At the corner he stopped and examined the map.

“You could have sat beside her,” I said.

“There wasn’t room.”

“There was loads of room.”

“For the two of us, yes. Not for the two of us and her wanting to be on her own.”

He said this without looking up. I went back to the supermarket and bought a bottle of water we didn’t need, to give him a reason to stay where he was. When I came out, he had been joined by the woman with the frozen peas. They were talking about the price of washing powder. Before she went on, she asked whether he was all right. He said he was waiting for me. That seemed to satisfy them both.

On Friday I took the map to the copy shop.

I meant to make two copies, one for him and one to leave at the bakery. The woman behind the counter asked what it was, and when I told her, she said her mother had stopped coming into town after the benches went. She had assumed it was because the bank had closed. Her mother had a habit of doing three errands at once and objected to anything that brought the number down to two.

The woman made twenty copies and charged me for two.

By Monday there were none left at the bakery. Someone had photographed one and put it on the Bellwether community page, where people immediately began arguing about whether we were encouraging loitering or failing to encourage it in enough parts of town. The florist rang to ask if we could make the bit about Thursdays bigger. The churchwarden rang to say there was no need to make anything bigger, but that a man had eaten a whole rotisserie chicken in the porch and left the bag.

“Was he sitting down?” my father asked.

There was a silence. I could hear the clock in the hall.

“Yes,” the churchwarden said.

“Well,” my father said, and then, apparently thinking better of whatever he had meant to say, promised to go down and get the bag.

On Tuesday the dentist came out.

We were not sitting on his wall at the time. We were across the road, waiting for a gap in the traffic. He waved the map at us. My father waved back. A van went by, and when it was quiet again the dentist said, “Could I have a word?”

He was younger than I’d expected, and he had the exhausted courtesy of someone who had already spent the morning asking people to open a little wider. A patient had tripped over somebody’s shopping trolley on Monday. It had been on the pavement in front of the wall. The patient hadn’t been hurt, he said, but she could have been.

I started to explain that the map was unofficial. In the middle of the explanation I heard myself making the argument that because nobody had asked us to do something, nobody could ask us to stop.

My father said, “We’ll take you off.”

The dentist folded the map twice, lining up the edges carefully. “My dad used to sit there,” he said. “When he came to pick me up. He’d get here half an hour early. Drove me mad.”

He looked back at the wall. In the heat the hydrangeas had gone limp over the pavement.

“I don’t mind people sitting,” he said. “I mind not knowing what I’m supposed to do when there’s a problem.”

My father asked if his dad was still driving. The dentist said yes, unfortunately, and for a little while the two of them talked about the roundabout by the bypass. Then we all went our separate ways.

At home I drew an X through the blue dot. My father watched me do it.

“You don’t have to press that hard,” he said.

I had made a hole in the paper. I taped it from the back, over the newt development.

That evening he brought out one of the other copies. Almost all the places we had marked clustered around the high street. In the streets to the east, where there were rows of council houses and a long incline to the health centre, we hadn’t put anything at all.

“I never go up there,” he said.

“You don’t have to.”

“No. But other people do.”

We set out the next morning. Halfway up the hill there was a bus stop with no shelter and a sign advertising a service that ran on Tuesdays and Fridays. It was Wednesday. A woman in slippers stood at the gate of the nearest house, shaking crumbs off a tea towel. My father asked her if there was anywhere to sit.

“Here, if you want,” she said.

She went inside and came back with two folding chairs. One had a picture of a tropical fish on the seat. She set them up inside her gate and told us to mind the step. My father sat on the fish.

The woman’s name was Jean. She had worked at the health centre until it moved to the top of the hill. Her husband, who was inside watching the snooker, used to bring a chair out for a particular man who walked to his appointments. The man always wore a tie. He had diabetes and a small dog and had been dead six years. Jean knew his appointments used to be on Wednesdays because Wednesday was when her husband went out to bring in the bins, and one day he had left the chair open on the pavement and the bin lorry had backed over it. They’d bought the fish chair after that.

“Can we put you on our map?” I asked.

“No,” she said. “I don’t want people knocking.”

“Fair enough,” my father said.

“But you can finish sitting.”

We did. Somewhere inside the house the snooker audience applauded. Jean folded her tea towel into thirds over the gate and told us about a woman who had tried to get a bench installed at the bus stop. The council had sent a form asking the woman to estimate how many people would use it. She had written back that the people in a position to find out were the ones who could stand there all afternoon.

“Did they write back?” I asked.

“Probably. She liked a letter. I think half the pleasure was getting one back.”

On the way down the hill I walked ahead and then had to wait. My father came slowly after me, touching the tops of walls where he could. It occurred to me that he had known on the way up exactly what the way down would cost him. I had been thinking of the hill as somewhere we were going to look.

At the bottom, he asked me to hold his elbow. I did, and immediately began steering him toward a front step.

“Just hold it,” he said.

We stood there until he was ready.

In the second week the council put one of the old benches back. It was outside the bakery, which had complained about people leaning on the window. There was a fresh coat of varnish and a pale oblong on the back where the plaque had been. My father took a cloth in his pocket, in case the varnish was still tacky. It wasn’t. He sat and moved his hands along the grain of the seat. Then he got up again because a woman with two carrier bags was coming and he thought she might be put off if he looked settled. She walked straight past him into the bakery. He sat back down.

We made a new edition of the map. The bench got its blue dot and its circle. The dentist’s wall disappeared. We added a note about the florist’s deliveries and a dotted line up the hill, where there was still nowhere to sit unless Jean happened to be shaking out her tea towel. We did not put that on the map.

My father said he’d take twenty copies to the council offices. I asked what he wanted them to do with the maps.

“Look at them.”

“And then?”

He slid the copies into a supermarket bag so the edges wouldn’t curl. “Well, I’ll be there. They can ask.”

I didn’t go with him. The plumber had called to say he’d finished my bathroom and left the key with the upstairs neighbour, who was going away the next morning. I packed my laptop and the three novels, two of them unread. Before I left I wrote my father a list of the food in the fridge, then threw it away. He had bought most of it himself.

At the station my train was delayed. There were two benches on the platform, both occupied, and I watched a woman walk past them to the far end, turn, and walk back. She was carrying a bunch of flowers wrapped in brown paper. The paper crackled each time she changed hands. I had spent two weeks watching people do things that might or might not mean they needed to sit down. I still couldn’t always tell.

A man on the bench next to me stood when the train was announced. I put my bag between my feet and moved over, though there was enough room already. The woman came and sat. She kept the flowers upright on her lap, holding them by the paper with both hands. We waited. The announcement had been for a train on the other platform.

After a while she turned to me. “Gladioli,” she said.

I had been trying to think what they were called. My mother used to buy them when they were cheap, which they often were, because they were inconvenient to get home. She used a tall glass vase that leaned to one side unless you put something under it. My father used to fold a corner of the newspaper and slide it under the base. Then at breakfast he’d ask who had taken the sports section.

I could have told the woman some of this. There was time. Instead I said they were a good colour. They were pale green, a colour I hadn’t known gladioli came in. She tipped the bundle a little so I could see the buds all the way up.

“Those ones at the top won’t open,” she said. “Not unless I cut the bottom ones off when they go. I always forget.”

When my train arrived, she stayed where she was. I’d assumed she was getting on it too. Through the window I saw her set the flowers down on the bit of bench I’d left, then reach over to tuck the loose paper underneath them. Before the train pulled away, a man came out of the station carrying two cups. She took the flowers straight back onto her lap. He sat down beside her, close enough that she could take the lid off his cup while he held it.

samples.result:
# The Things We Came Back For

On the morning the city decided to close its lost-property office, Nina found a front door in the umbrella bin. It was a narrow blue door with a brass letter slot and four small panes of glass. Someone had wrapped a dish towel around the knob. The tag, in the handwriting of the night porter, said: *Number 14 bus. Rear seat.*

Nina had worked in the office for seventeen years. She knew how someone could leave a cello on a bus, and how an accordion could travel all the way to the airport before its owner noticed. A door was different. She went upstairs to ask the porter how it had come in.

“Sideways,” he said.

He was eating an orange. He offered her half, and she took it. By the time she got back downstairs, there was already a man waiting at the counter.

“I’m looking for my umbrella,” he said. “Black.”

Nina looked at the door. It had displaced perhaps sixty umbrellas, which lay in a heap on the floor.

“Anything distinctive about it?”

“It opens.”

“You’d be surprised,” she said.

Together they tried eleven umbrellas. The man recognized his by a faint smell of fried onions. He had once held it over a grill at his daughter’s wedding while the cook finished a tray of sausages. He told Nina this apologetically, as though he had been caught making up a reason to miss the umbrella. She handed him a form and watched him write his address in the careful block capitals of a person who had spent his working life being asked to write more legibly.

The city’s letter lay beside her keyboard. It was dated three weeks earlier. Lost property would henceforth be handled by the transit website, which would match descriptions to photographs and inform claimants when their belongings were available for collection at a warehouse beyond the airport. Nina had been offered a position there. The warehouse was two buses and a twenty-minute walk from her flat. The letter described it as easily accessible.

She carried the blue door to the back room and stood it against a cabinet. At the bottom, where the paint had chipped, she could see a previous life in yellow. She photographed it, entered the dimensions, and selected *Other* from the inventory menu. Much of the world, once it had been separated from its owner, turned out to be Other.

Her colleague Dev arrived at ten with two coffees and a roll of red stickers.

“Anything over ninety days,” he said. “We’re meant to mark it for disposal.”

“We’ve always been meant to.”

“Yes, but now they’ve bought stickers.”

They started with the shelves nearest the boiler. Dev called out accession numbers while Nina checked the dates. A wool hat with a cigarette burn. Three mobile phones, all older than Dev’s daughter. A pair of shoes in a bakery bag. Inside one shoe was a receipt for the other shoe, purchased on a different day. Nina remembered logging them. For months she had wondered whether there was someone who bought shoes one at a time, and under what circumstances that arrangement worked.

At eleven a woman called looking for a tin of buttons.

“What kind of tin?” Nina asked.

“Shortbread. The royal wedding.”

“Which royal wedding?”

There was a pause.

“Oh,” the woman said. “I was thinking there’d only been the one.”

She meant Charles and Diana. Nina found the tin under a gym bag. There were buttons inside, but also a key, a French coin, and a paper envelope containing a milk tooth.

“Could you check for a green button like a leaf?” the woman asked.

Nina tipped the contents onto her desk. There was a leaf, though she might have called it a feather.

“That’ll be it,” the woman said. “I’m in my slippers. Tell me your opening hours.”

“Until six today. Until four tomorrow. Then we’re closing.”

“Well,” the woman said. “I’d better put my shoes on.”

Nina’s father had brought her to the office for the first time when she was nine. They had lost a paper bag containing six peaches and a pair of trousers he had just paid to have shortened. Nina remembered being more worried about the peaches. It was July, and her father had chosen them by lifting each one to his nose. The woman behind the counter returned the trousers and told them the peaches had gone soft. On their way home, her father stopped at the same stall and bought two more, one each. Nina ate hers down to the stone. Her father took a bite of his and frowned.

“You can’t buy the same peach twice,” he said, which was the kind of statement he made when something had disappointed him and he preferred to leave the exact nature of the disappointment unspecified.

For years after he died, Nina’s mother kept his trousers in the wardrobe with the dry cleaner’s paper folded over the hanger. Eventually she gave them away. The wardrobe was no easier to close afterward. There were plenty of other things in it.

Around noon Nina posted a photograph of the door on the neighborhood message board. She left out the towel and the yellow paint, so a claimant would have something to describe. By one, the photograph had been shared forty-three times. Someone suggested it belonged to a house that had been demolished the previous spring. Someone else identified it as a stage prop from a play about a woman who marries a ghost. Two people offered to buy it, and a third wrote, *If this is the one from our kitchen, please do not give it back to my husband.*

None of them could describe the towel.

At half past one, a boy arrived with his grandmother. He had lost a paper crown on the number 8. He was six, he said, and the crown was from when he was five, which had been yesterday. His grandmother carried a shopping trolley full of potatoes. She looked tired enough to sit down on the floor if Nina didn’t get her a chair.

“What color was it?” Nina asked.

“Gold.”

“Was there writing on it?”

“Six.”

“I thought you said you wore it when you were five.”

“Only till three twenty-two,” said the boy.

Nina checked the number 8 crate. There were two scarves, a paperback about birds, and a pharmacy bag with someone’s blood pressure tablets. No crown. She told him things sometimes took a day or two to come in. He considered this, then asked whether he could look under the desk. The crown was not there either, but he found a pencil Nina had dropped that morning and returned it to her.

“Can I have that in a form?” he asked.

She gave him a receipt for one pencil, signed and dated. He folded it into his coat pocket. His grandmother got up and let him pull the trolley to the lift. It bumped hard over the metal threshold, and he stopped to look back, as though the office might have lost a potato.

By three the woman with the button tin had come and gone. She had brought an empty tote bag and a friend who waited outside. When Nina handed over the tin, the woman opened it, picked out the envelope with the tooth, and put the envelope in her coat pocket. She closed the lid without looking at the buttons. Through the glass Nina saw her show the envelope to her friend, who put both hands over her mouth. Then the two of them moved out of sight. Nina went to put away the chair she had brought out for the boy’s grandmother. Instead, she sat in it for a while.

Dev had been thinning a collection of water bottles. From the back room came the intermittent pop of their lids.

“Do you want the warehouse job?” she asked him.

“They haven’t offered it to me.”

She looked up.

“They said mine was a customer-facing position,” he added. “Whereas you apparently face the stock.”

He brought out another crate. Nina had trained him four years earlier, when he was twenty-three and so nervous about getting claims wrong that he made a man describe the contents of his lunch before surrendering a lunchbox. The man had said *sandwich*, inaccurately. Inside was a note from his wife telling him that if he forgot to buy cat food again, he could explain himself to the cat. Underneath the note was a slice of quiche. Dev had accepted the man’s claim after hearing him read the note aloud.

“What are you going to do?” Nina said.

“Go home at six,” he said. “I’ve actually got plans.”

He had never told her about his plans before unless they required a shift change. She almost asked him what they were, then realized he might simply mean to go home at six and have the evening to himself.

They had a late lunch. Dev went out for chips, and Nina ate hers at the counter. Across the hall, a workman took down the sign that directed people from the station entrance to the office. Nina watched him fill the holes with putty. He had a small brush with which he dabbed at the wall until the patches blended with the old paint. When he left, she could still see where the sign had been. She imagined that by tomorrow she wouldn’t be able to.

At five the man with the umbrella came back. He had left it at the bakery while buying bread.

“I thought, if they’re going to send it anywhere, it’ll be here,” he said.

Nina phoned the bakery. The umbrella was still there, propping open the kitchen window. The baker wanted to know how soon the man could come, as the windowsill was already getting wet.

“You can take the bus,” Nina said after hanging up.

He looked out at the rain. “It’s only two streets.”

She watched him start off, carrying the loaf under his jacket. There had been a tear in his umbrella between two of the ribs, she remembered. In serious rain he’d have got wet either way.

At twenty to six, a woman in paint-stained jeans came in and asked if Nina had a door. She was dripping. Her hair appeared to have been cut recently and with some impatience.

“What’s around the knob?” Nina asked.

“A tea towel. Lemons on it. It was so the knob wouldn’t scratch anybody.”

“Was it always blue?”

“No, it was yellow. I painted it blue last Tuesday. Is the glass all right?”

Nina fetched the door. The woman crouched to examine the panes and stood up with one hand resting against the wood.

“I left it on purpose,” she said.

Nina had already uncapped her pen. “We do get that.”

“At first I was just getting off to make a phone call. Then I watched the bus pull away and thought, there, now that’s done.”

The door had come from the house where the woman grew up. Her mother was selling the house and had offered her anything she wanted, and for some reason she had chosen the door from her old bedroom. The buyer didn’t mind taking it off the hinges, though he had asked her not to remove anything else while he was at work. Including, he’d added, the radiators. She’d been so offended by this that she carried the door all the way to the bus stop without pausing, even when she passed the café where she ought to have stopped to get something to eat.

“Do you have somewhere for it?” Nina asked.

“No. My flat’s got enough doors. It might have one too many, actually. I can’t open the oven if the kitchen door’s open.”

She ran a finger over a dent beside the letter slot.

“Why is there a letter slot on a bedroom door?”

“I asked for one for my twelfth birthday. I thought my brothers would write me letters. They mostly put socks through it.”

The woman laughed. Nina moved the form to the dry end of the counter. She knew the part of this encounter that came next: a name, the date, a signature where indicated. But the woman was still examining the door. She opened the letter slot from one side and held it open while she peered through from the other, which required her to put her cheek on the edge of the wood. Nina could see her eye through one of the panes.

“My mum’s not dead,” she said, straightening. “You’d think, with all this.”

“Did she like the blue?”

“She said it looked all right. Then she asked if I wanted the rest of the tin.”

The woman signed the form. Nina offered to help her carry the door to the bus stop, but she shook her head. She had called her brother. He was bringing his van, and she expected him to spend the entire journey suggesting places where they could get rid of it. When Nina asked what she would tell him, the woman said she didn’t know yet. First she was going to make him help carry it up the stairs.

At six, Dev clocked out. Nina heard him jog up the station stairs, then stop and come back for his scarf. He snatched it from the peg on his way past without saying anything, and she managed not to say anything either.

She had intended to stay late sorting the last shelves. Instead, she pulled the red stickers off a crate they had done that morning and carried it out where she would see it first thing. The shoes in the bakery bag were there. She checked the receipt again. It was for one shoe, with a handwritten note she hadn’t noticed before: *left to follow*. Perhaps the shop had sold the display shoe and was waiting for the other one to come from another branch. She had imagined a whole customer around a temporary problem with stock.

She put the receipt back. Tomorrow someone might come for the shoes. If not, both were in good condition, and she would put them in the donation sack rather than the bin. She made a note to bring an extra sack from home. Then she took the warehouse letter from beside the keyboard, folded it into quarters, and put it in her pocket. She hadn’t decided about the job. She could ride out there on Monday and see what the twenty-minute walk was like. There might be a pavement all the way. There might even be somewhere good to get lunch.

Upstairs, the rain had stopped. The buses were pulling in with their lights on, though it was still light enough to see everybody through the windows. At the stop, the woman and her brother were making room in the van. He was lifting a toolbox out of the back while she steadied the door against her hip. Nina waited a little way off, ready to help if they needed another pair of hands. The brother found somewhere for the toolbox, came around to take the heavy end, and together they slid the door in flat. Before he shut the van, the woman reached through and undid the towel. She folded it once and wiped the rain off the glass.

samples.result:
# The Borrowed Table

The summer I worked at the library, we lent out a folding table so often that its reservation list ran longer than the one for the new Stephen King. It was six feet long, with a white plastic top and gray steel legs. It had been used at two weddings, a councilman’s fish fry, and the sale of everything in a house whose owner had gone to prison. I knew these things because people told me, usually while I was trying to fit the table back into the closet.

People apologized for bringing it back dirty. They didn’t apologize for telling me what had happened around it.

Once a woman said, “We put the cake right here,” and rested her hand on a faint pink stain. I waited for the rest. There wasn’t any. She looked at the stain a little longer and then went out through the automatic doors.

That summer I was twenty-six and living in my childhood bedroom. My father had died in February. My mother had taken a job that started at six in the morning, and sometimes when I came home at nine at night I found her sleeping on the couch with one shoe off. I would put the kettle on, then turn it off before it boiled. I had never lived with another adult so carefully.

My brother, Paul, lived forty minutes away. He called on Sundays and asked how Mom was doing. I told him she was fine, and he thanked me as if I had gone to check on a pipe under his sink.

In August he called on a Wednesday.

“Do you get a discount on tables?” he asked.

“Everything’s free, Paul.”

“I mean, can you jump the line?”

It turned out he and his girlfriend, Nina, were getting married at the courthouse. Afterward they were going to have lunch in our mother’s yard. Nobody had asked our mother yet. Paul had counted fourteen people, though he thought the woman Nina worked with might bring her husband, who had recently bought a motorcycle and wanted to go everywhere on it.

“When?”

“Next Friday.”

“Why next Friday?”

“That’s when Nina’s mother can get here.”

I opened the reservation book. The woman ahead of him was having a yard sale on Saturday and planned to pick up the table as soon as we opened Friday. She had made her reservation six weeks earlier.

“You could have given us a little warning,” I said.

“If we gave everybody warning, everybody would have things to say.”

I did have things to say. The first was going to be that Dad would have wanted to be there. I heard it in my head and hated it immediately. Of course Dad would have wanted to be there. That was one of the things death had cost him, not a point I could score off Paul.

“I’ll ask about the table,” I said.

Our father had made a dining table himself. He’d made it in the basement, which was where he made everything, because from the basement he could shout questions to whoever was in the kitchen. He finished the top before realizing it wouldn’t go up the stairs. For three nights we ate dinner to the sound of him taking it apart.

The table seated four most of the year. There were two leaves in the hall closet, wrapped together in a crib blanket. On Thanksgiving, Dad would grab one end, Paul the other, and they would pull while I watched the gap. If the runners stuck, Paul let go first. He couldn’t stand to do a thing that wasn’t working. Dad could keep trying long after everyone wished he’d stop.

Two years before Dad died, he and Paul had stopped speaking. The actual quarrel was about a lawn mower. Paul had borrowed it. Dad had driven over to get it without calling and found it outside in the rain. What got said after that depended on who was telling it. Dad told his side in the kitchen, and Paul told his in the car on the way to a grocery store. Neither of them asked me to carry a message. They just told me things that would be pointless for me to know unless I carried them.

Paul came to the hospital in February. Dad was heavily sedated by then. When I went down for coffee, Paul was in the chair beside the bed, scrolling through his phone. When I came back, he was standing by the window. I have no idea what he did while I was gone. It took me a while to understand that he might not know what I did, either, on all the afternoons I had been there without him.

At dinner that night I told my mother I thought Paul might call.

“He did,” she said. “I said they could have it here.”

“Are you sure?”

She picked a cucumber slice out of the salad bowl with her fingers. “I’ve been watering that grass all summer. I may as well show it to somebody.”

I asked what she thought about taking the dining table outside.

“Oh,” she said. Then, after a minute: “It’s heavy.”

She didn’t say we couldn’t. But I knew how heavy it was. The week after the funeral I had tried to slide it away from the wall to retrieve a case for Dad’s glasses. I had shifted it just far enough to uncover a pale stripe in the floorboards. The case turned out to be empty.

At work the next day I called the woman with the yard sale. Her name was Helen. Before I could finish explaining, she said no, she really needed the table all day Friday.

“People see you putting things out,” she told me. “They stop. You can do half your business before the sale starts.”

I said I understood. She hung up. Ten minutes later she called back and asked who was getting married.

“My brother.”

“Is he young?”

“Twenty-nine.”

“Oh,” said Helen. “I thought maybe he had to.”

I laughed so hard that my supervisor looked up from the printer. Helen waited.

“He doesn’t have to,” I said.

“Good for him, then. But I still need it Friday.”

My supervisor suggested a party rental place over by the highway. They had tables, but the delivery fee was ninety dollars and they closed before I got off work. I called Paul to pass along that information. In the background I could hear Nina asking whether he had told me the other thing.

“What other thing?”

“We said no presents,” Paul said.

“That’s fine.”

“And Nina wanted to ask if we could borrow Dad’s blue cooler.”

I said yes to the cooler, hung up, and spent the rest of the afternoon getting angry at Paul for the ease with which he had asked. I knew exactly where the cooler was. I knew there was a bag of badminton birdies in it and a receipt from a gas station in Ohio, where Dad had bought ice on the way to a reunion. I wanted Paul to have to come over and open it himself. I also hoped he wouldn’t throw away the receipt. I wouldn’t have been able to explain what I thought he ought to do with it.

On Thursday, a man returned the folding table twenty minutes before closing. He was wearing a blue shirt with his name stitched over the pocket. I had seen him around town for years and always thought his name was Glen. The shirt said BOB.

“Anything wrong with it?” I asked.

“Not that I noticed.”

I folded down the legs to check. A piece of tape on the underside had collected enough lint that you could see where the edge of a tablecloth had been.

“What’d you use it for?” I asked. I had never asked anyone before.

“My daughter’s moving into a place with no counters. We made pierogies.” He reached into his pocket, came up with his keys, and looked at them in surprise. “I was supposed to bring you some.”

“That’s okay.”

“No, it’s not. She packed a little bag.”

He went out to his truck and came back with a grocery sack knotted at the top. Inside was a takeout container with six pierogies and a plastic fork. I said thank you. He said they were better hot, although he liked them cold, too, which was good because they had probably been cold for a while.

I ate one as soon as he left. Then I called Paul from the circulation desk and told him I would help him get the dining table out of the house, but he would have to come over that night so we could figure out how.

It was almost ten when he arrived. Nina came with him. She was wearing her grocery store uniform and had brought a bag of peaches with bruises shaped like thumbprints. My mother made tea, and we all stood around the table eating peaches over the bag. Nobody wanted to get a plate dirty.

Paul crouched to look underneath. He had brought two socket wrenches in different sizes, both wrong. I went down to the basement and found Dad’s set on the workbench. There was a socket missing, but it wasn’t the one we needed.

The bolts came out easily. That was a surprise after years of hearing Dad swear at things that wouldn’t come apart. Each pair of legs was attached to a crosspiece. Paul held the legs steady while I backed out the last bolt, then carried them to the porch one pair at a time. When he came back, there was nothing between the tabletop and the rug but his knees and mine. We tipped it up sideways.

I had never seen the underside. Dad had drawn pencil lines where he planned to put the runners. He had got one measurement wrong and crossed it out so thickly it looked as if he had tried to make a hole in the wood. Off to one side were three circles in red crayon, one inside the next.

“Did you do that?” I asked Paul.

“Probably you,” he said.

Nina turned on the porch light and held the screen door open with her hip. My mother followed us outside with the bolts in the pocket of her robe.

“Will it sit flat out here?” she asked.

“No,” said Paul. “But we can make it.”

*

The courthouse ceremony took eleven minutes. I know because we parked at a meter, and when we came out there were nineteen minutes left. Nina’s mother cried before anything happened and then was all business. She got photographs on the steps, including one of Paul holding Nina’s purse. When Nina tried to take it back before the picture, her mother said, “Leave it. He’s fine.”

At home, the yard looked the way it does when you come back for something you forgot: familiar and completely unprepared for you. There were no flowers on the table yet, and we hadn’t brought the chairs outside. My mother had bought paper napkins, and the wind lifted three of them straight out of the package. Nina caught one against the back steps with her foot.

Paul and I fetched the leaves from the hall closet. He carried the bundle out and unwrapped it on the grass. The crib blanket had yellow ducks around the border. Nina’s mother came down the steps with the flowers in a jug and asked whether she could use it. She spread it on the ground for the woman with the motorcycle husband, who had brought their little boy. The boy touched a duck with one finger, then lay on his back and kicked at nothing.

The first leaf went in fine. With the second there was a problem: one of the little metal pins wouldn’t meet its hole. Paul gave his end a shake. I told him not to. He gave it another shake anyway. Then we stood there looking down at the same crooked inch of table.

“You have to lift it on your side,” he said.

“I am lifting it.”

“You’re pulling.”

He was right. I lifted. There was a dry knock as the pin slid in. From across the yard my mother called, “Good, because the chicken’s here,” and somebody went out front to help her.

We used an old seed catalog under one leg to level the table. Then we put down the chicken and a bowl of sliced tomatoes, and Nina’s mother asked where she should sit. The motorcycle husband said he didn’t care where he sat as long as somebody passed him a tomato. It turned out he had come in a station wagon. He and Paul discussed the motorcycle briefly, but neither one seemed to know how to get the conversation past the fact of its purchase.

Halfway through lunch, Paul got up and went into the house. He came back with a big spoon for the potato salad. As he reached across me to put it down, he said, quietly, “I thought I was going to see him when I came out here.”

I thought he meant that morning. “You mean before the wedding?”

“Just now,” he said. “Coming out the back door.”

I looked at the back door. From where I was sitting I could see through it to the kitchen and all the way down the hall. Dad had usually sat at the far end of the table, facing the stove, in a chair with a dish towel folded over the back because one of the spindles had a rough spot. We’d left that chair inside. Nina’s mother was at the far end now, sitting on a metal chair from the garage, buttering a second roll for the boy.

“I do that in the grocery store,” I said. “I think I see him by the bread.”

“He never bought bread.”

“I know. It’s always some other guy.”

Paul sat down. He ate a little more, and after a while he held up his glass for Nina to fill. She filled his and mine, too.

That evening, when everyone had gone, the three of us took the leaves out. My mother shook the crumbs off the crib blanket and wrapped the leaves again. Paul offered to bring the table inside, but she said she wanted to sit there for a while. I brought her a sweater. Then I brought out the rest of the peaches. We could hear the neighbor running water into a metal bucket. There was a house two streets over where someone practiced the trumpet, and one of us would say something and then stop so we could hear how far the trumpet got that time.

When Paul got up to leave, my mother remembered the cooler. He went down to the basement for it. He was gone long enough that I almost went after him. Then I heard him call up through the floor, in the same impatient key my father used to use.

“Who put birdies in the cooler?”

“Your father,” my mother called back.

“Well, does anybody want them?”

It was a fair question. The badminton net had rotted years earlier, and nobody could say where the rackets were. My mother looked at me. I shook my head.

“Bring them up anyway,” she said.

On Saturday I went by Helen’s yard sale. I told myself it was on my way to the store, which it was if you took the road by the cemetery. The library table was out on the lawn with its steel feet sinking into the dirt. Helen had put the books at one end and the dishes at the other; in the middle was a cardboard box of electrical cords with a sign that said PLEASE TAKE.

“Did he get married?” she asked.

“He did.”

“Did he look happy?”

I thought of him coming through the screen door with the potato spoon. I thought of the courthouse steps, where Nina had finally got her purse back and Paul, with nothing left to hold, had reached for her hand.

“Yes,” I said.

I bought a green bowl for a dollar. Helen wrapped it in newspaper, though I told her I was only going a few blocks. As I straightened up, the table shifted and a stack of saucers began to slip. Helen caught them with both hands. I held the table steady while she went looking for something to put under the leg. She came back with a paperback she hadn’t been able to sell, slipped it under the foot, and told me to let go. I did. The saucers stayed where they were.

# The Door on Platform Four

On the last Friday before the station closed, a man came to lost property looking for a glove.

“Left or right?” Elsie asked.

“I’d have to see it.”

She tipped the glove basket onto the counter. It contained seventeen gloves, not one of them apparently made for the same kind of weather. The man picked through them with tenderness. He tried on a red mitten and held his hand up between them.

“Mine was black,” he said.

She waited.

“I suppose I could become the sort of person who wears red.”

“You’d have to become the sort of person who wears one.”

He took it anyway. Elsie recorded the transaction in her ledger as *red mitten, released by mutual agreement*. Strictly speaking, it was the seventeen remaining umbrellas she was supposed to be finding homes for. Gloves did not retain much water and could go into the donation sacks without special arrangements. The umbrellas, having spent several years leaking privately into a copper tub, had developed the character of a small wetland.

At six, a replacement bus would make its first run from the curb outside. The station would stop handling passengers, although freight trains would still pass through, which Elsie considered unnecessarily theatrical. It would be like closing a theater but leaving the actors inside to perform for one another.

She had worked there for twenty-three years. People kept asking what she planned to do on Monday. She planned to buy washing powder, a fact that disappointed them so reliably she had begun to say she was considering Portugal.

At eleven, Dean from signaling came in with a sandwich and nodded toward the door.

“Still got that, then.”

The door he meant was not the one he had come through. It was a green interior door propped against the shelves, displacing two boxes of scarves and a single ski. Someone had removed the handle but left the hinges attached. Its lower panel contained a small square of plywood, fixed in place with screws that did not match.

“Two people coming to look at it,” Elsie said.

“Two people have lost a door?”

“One of them says he has. The other says it’s hers.”

Dean put his sandwich down to consider this distinction. “Well,” he said. “They can have a side each.”

It was the kind of thing Dean said when a problem belonged to somebody else.

The door had arrived on Tuesday aboard the 14:12 from Harford. According to the conductor, a passenger had loaded it into the bicycle compartment and gotten off at Marsh End to help his wife down the steps. The train had departed before he could get back on. The conductor had brought the door to Elsie with no particular urgency. It was already a door without a room; a few additional miles, he seemed to feel, could hardly make it more lost.

Elsie had photographed it for the station’s notice page. Usually those posts traveled no farther than the people who wanted to know why the lift was broken. The door did better. Within an hour, a stranger had written, *Have you tried knocking?* By Wednesday, the joke had been made thirty-eight times, and two people had sent her private messages.

The first was from a young man named Tariq. His grandfather had been on the train. Could he pick up the door Friday, after his shift?

The second was from a woman named Vivien, who wrote: *I scratched my name into the top edge of that door in 1983. Please check before you give it to anyone.*

Elsie had gotten the step stool. The name was there, in deep, ragged capitals, partly filled with green paint. Beside it was a much smaller word she couldn’t make out. She sent Vivien a message and asked when she could come.

*Friday,* Vivien replied. *I’ve waited this long.*

At two fifteen, Tariq arrived in a bakery apron with a floury handprint on the hip. He was younger than Elsie had expected. People who wrote *after my shift* in messages always sounded middle-aged to her.

“My granddad says it has a patch where the cat flap was,” he said.

“What happened to the cat?”

“Nothing. That was the problem with the flap. Every cat in the neighborhood could work it except ours.”

Elsie led him behind the counter. He put his palm flat against the plywood patch, almost as if checking it for a temperature.

“That’s his work,” he said. “He’s the only man I know who’d go out and buy screws because he didn’t have enough and then use the wrong ones anyway.”

“Why was he taking it on a train?”

“He was bringing it to me. I’m moving, and he thought I’d need a desk.”

Elsie looked at the door. “Did you tell him you needed a desk?”

“I told him I needed a kettle. He’s got a very complicated way of listening.”

He smiled, then took out his phone and photographed the plywood. He sent the picture to his grandfather. Almost immediately the phone rang.

“Yes,” Tariq said. “I’m here. Well, I wouldn’t have sent you a picture of it from somewhere else.”

He listened for a while.

“No, I haven’t got it yet.”

He glanced at Elsie. She shook her head, and he turned away a little, as though that might make his half of the conversation private.

“Apparently there’s another lady.”

Vivien arrived at half past two in a light rain, carrying a folded supermarket bag. She was tall and very upright, with wet silver hair and a coat the same green as the door. At the counter she took a photograph out of the bag and turned it around for Elsie to see.

Two girls in nightdresses were standing together in front of a yellow door. One was laughing; the other had drawn her chin back into her neck in anticipation of whatever the laughing girl was about to do. They had the same narrow feet.

“I’m the one who looks like she’s being held hostage,” Vivien said. “That’s my sister, Carol.”

“Was it your bedroom door?”

“Bathroom. There were six of us and one bathroom. We spent half our childhood outside that door.”

She pointed to a black crescent below the handle. It was still there on the green door. Elsie had mistaken it for a knot in the wood.

“Our mother hung a hook there for the bath mat. The hook came off with the mat one day, and Carol put it back with the biggest nail she could find. It went right through. Dad sawed the end off from the other side. Took the whole afternoon. We were meant to be going to the beach.”

“Did you go?”

“Yes. It was a terrible beach. We had a wonderful time.”

Tariq had come out from behind the counter. He and Vivien looked at each other. Then he pointed to the door in the photograph.

“Was that number fourteen?”

“Number six.”

“Oh,” he said.

“Before they knocked through and did the flats again,” Vivien said. “They changed the numbers. I went back once and rang my old bell and a man told me I was standing in his kitchen.”

“That might have been my granddad.”

“No, I was standing in his kitchen. He’d left the back door open and I’d walked in.”

They thought about this.

“Still might have been him,” Tariq said.

Elsie fetched the step stool. Vivien climbed to the second tread without taking off her coat and passed two fingers over the top edge of the door. Her expression did not change. After a while she asked whether they had a torch. Tariq took out his phone and switched on the light.

“Can you read the little word?” Elsie asked.

“‘Out,’” Vivien said.

She climbed down.

“It was supposed to say ‘Vivien, keep out.’ Carol got as far as my name before she realized nobody would see it up there, so she left me to finish it. I didn’t know how to spell ‘keep.’ Not with a penknife, anyway.”

“You said you scratched your own name.”

“I did say that.” Vivien brushed green dust from the tips of her fingers. “It sounded more convincing.”

For a moment they all looked at the photograph, still lying on the counter. Then Tariq said, “Did you want to take it home?”

Vivien folded the supermarket bag into a smaller square. “I thought I would. On the way here I started wondering what I’d do if you let me.”

“I was going to make it into a desk.”

“Would you sand it down?”

“I was probably going to put my laptop on it and call it a desk.”

Vivien gave this the consideration it deserved. Outside, a train rolled in and the floor began to tremble. The umbrellas knocked lightly together in their tub.

“How much room have you got?” she asked.

“For a desk?”

“For a door.”

Tariq showed her a photo of his new room. Elsie went back to packing scarves, although nobody had asked her to leave them alone. She had spent much of her working life learning not to watch people too closely when they had just found something. Once, a man reunited with a canvas shopping bag had sat down on the floor and cried. He’d told Elsie, after several minutes, that there was nothing in it but leeks. It had been a very bad week, he said, and he hadn’t wanted to go back to the shop.

By three thirty, the photograph and the door had been formally released to Vivien and Tariq, respectively. Vivien had asked him to send her a picture of the desk when it was done. He had asked if he could photograph the photograph. She held it up against the green door so the nail mark in the picture almost met the real one, and he took three shots, apologizing each time for the glare.

Then he tried to lift the door by himself.

It was heavier than it looked, especially at the end he wasn’t holding. He took two steps toward the exit and came back, walking backward with great dignity.

“I can get my cousin,” he said. “He finishes at seven.”

“We close at six.”

“Oh,” he said, and looked at the wall clock. “Tomorrow?”

Elsie had been answering this question all week in one form or another. She was surprised to find that she could no longer bring herself to say no.

“Where are you going?”

He gave her an address six streets away.

“I’ll take the other end.”

Vivien offered to help, too, but the geometry of the door defeated them. She settled for carrying Tariq’s apron, which he’d taken off at last, and holding traffic at the crossings with a look of concentrated displeasure. Elsie had always liked walking in the rain if there was something to do with her hands. The three of them went slowly, catching their breath at the corner where the butcher’s had become a shop that sold tiles. They declined assistance from a man who offered it, then had to ask him to move his bicycle.

At the entrance to Tariq’s building they discovered that the door wouldn’t go around the first bend in the stairs. They stood with it angled between them, staring up at the landing. From somewhere above came the sound of a child practicing the same four notes on a recorder.

“Was there always a chance of this?” Vivien asked.

“There was always a chance of a lot of things,” said Tariq. He took out his phone. “Now I’ve got to tell Granddad.”

He put the call on speaker so he could use both hands. He explained the stairs.

“How much are you short?” his grandfather asked.

Tariq looked at Elsie, who held her thumb and forefinger a few inches apart.

“About three inches.”

There was a pause.

“Have you tried turning it over?”

Tariq closed his eyes. “It’s the same size on the other side.”

“Yes,” his grandfather said. “But you’ve got the hinges sticking out toward the banister, haven’t you?”

They looked. The top hinge had caught against an upright. Elsie lowered her end and Tariq lifted his. Vivien reached between them and folded the hinge flat against the wood. Together they eased the door around the bend until its weight shifted and Tariq stumbled up a step with it.

“Got it,” he said.

“Good. There’s a kettle in the post, by the way.”

“You bought me a kettle?”

“I posted you a kettle. It was ours. Your gran hates it.”

The recorder stopped. Somewhere a grown person said, with great feeling, “Much better.”

Tariq’s flat smelled of fresh paint and toast. He had two low filing cabinets ready in the corner. They set the door across them, green side up, then stood back. It sat a little high. The old handle hole looked absurdly large without a handle in it, and the plywood patch made an uneven place where a person might reasonably want to put a cup. Tariq set his laptop down and opened it. The door held.

“I can bring you a cork coaster,” Vivien said. “For that bit.”

“I’ll get one.”

“I’ve already got the coaster,” she said, with such impatience that Elsie had to turn toward the window.

From the window she could see the tracks on their raised bed behind the houses. A train went past, and although the rain had softened the glass, she could make out the figures inside: a person in a white shirt, a person standing up too early, someone reaching overhead into the luggage rack. She started to calculate when they would arrive. It was a calculation she made three or four times an hour without ever calling it math. Then she remembered that Dean was holding down lost property while she was gone, and that it was more than likely he had eaten the second half of his sandwich over her ledger.

She said goodbye. Vivien stayed behind to help decide where the kettle ought to go.

Back at the station, the man with the red mitten was waiting at the counter. He had brought a black glove with him.

“Right hand,” he said, laying it down.

“You found it?”

“I found the one I wasn’t missing. I thought you might want it. In case somebody else is trying to become a different sort of person.”

Elsie accepted it. After he left, she put it in the basket. Then she took it out again and put it in her coat pocket. Her kitchen window, which was painted shut through most of the year, had recently developed a draft, and a glove would plug the gap until she did something about it. She owned better gloves, but she wanted those for her hands.

At six she locked the office and handed over the keys. There was no ceremony at the station. A few people had stayed to see the last train, but by the time it pulled out most of them were looking at their phones, checking where to catch the bus. Elsie went outside with them and found that she knew the driver. He’d left a thermos on the train the previous winter. She had put it aside because he’d covered it with pictures his daughter had drawn on sticky labels.

He opened the doors. “You coming?” he asked her.

She had walked home the same way for twenty-three years. The bus would take her the other way around, past a row of houses whose back gardens she knew from the platform. She had often wondered about the fronts.

“Where do you stop?” she asked.

“Where do you want to get off?”

Elsie thought. “Is there a shop that sells washing powder?”

“Several,” he said.

She got on.
