# The Things Nobody Came Back For

On the last day of the lost property office, a man came in for a ladder.

“What sort of ladder?” Ada asked.

“Aluminum. Six rungs. One foot’s got a sock on it.”

“What color sock?”

“Green, unless somebody’s washed it.”

Ada looked at him. He looked back. In thirty-one years behind the counter, she had developed a reliable sense of when a person was joking about a ladder.

“How did you lose it?”

“I lent it to a man called Brian.”

“Did Brian leave it on a bus?”

“I wouldn’t put it past him.”

The office accepted articles recovered from city buses, the municipal swimming pool, and the public portions of City Hall. It did not, as a rule, intervene in disputes with Brian. But this was the last day, and Ada had already packed her lunch in a bag she meant to take home, rather than in a container she would wash on Monday. She went to look.

There was no ladder. There was a single green sock, but it was too small even for a modest ladder, and she decided not to mention it.

The man took the news well. He said he’d always had his doubts about Brian. Then he asked what would happen to everything nobody collected.

“Clothes to charity. Electronics to recycling. Anything valuable goes to auction.”

“What about the rest?”

“Depends what it is.”

He nodded as though she had confirmed something he’d long suspected.

“Good luck with Brian,” she said.

“Oh, Brian’s dead,” the man said. “That’s why I’m having to do all this myself.”

After he left, Ada took the green sock off the shelf and put it in her cardigan pocket.

The office occupied a former ticket booth at the west end of the bus station. Its window had a shallow dish cut into the counter so coins could pass from one side to the other, although Ada used it mostly for pushing tissues toward people. People cried more often than you might expect. They cried after telling her they didn’t care about the purse, only about what was inside it. They cried when she found the purse. Once a woman had come for a thermos and cried because it was the wrong red thermos, then apologized so strenuously that Ada had made tea in it.

Starting Monday, the city would run lost property out of a depot beyond the ring road. There would be an online form. Ada had been offered a place at the depot, three mornings a week, but the only bus that went there stopped on the opposite side of six lanes of traffic. When she pointed this out, the man from the city suggested she drive.

“I never learned,” she said.

“Well,” he said, with the gentle encouragement of a person imagining an entirely different problem.

At eleven, her daughter phoned.

“Remember,” Ruth said, “I’m coming at four to help.”

“There’s nothing heavy.”

“That’s not the only kind of help.”

Ada had been hearing variations on this sentence since Ruth was fourteen, and still hadn’t found an answer that didn’t prove her daughter’s point.

“Bring a coat,” she said instead. “It’s cold in here.”

By noon Ada had dealt with two claims for black umbrellas and one for a bicycle helmet memorable chiefly because its owner described it as humiliating. She found that one straightaway. The owner put it on to leave, and she understood what he meant.

Then she unlocked the cupboard under the sink and took out the wooden box.

It was the size of a loaf of bread, with a sliding lid and a half-moon worn into one end where a thumb had opened it, perhaps thousands of times. There was no lock. Inside were forty or so slips of paper, each with a date on the front and a sentence on the back.

*March 3. I returned the drill before he asked.*

*April 18. We ate outside in our coats.*

*June 9. I told her the real price.*

The box had been found eleven months ago on the Number 6, tucked behind the heater. Ada had registered it as WOODEN BOX WITH PAPERS. She had not registered what she thought it was, because the register had no field for that, and because her opinion changed every time she opened it. At first she’d thought the slips recorded achievements. Then she read *August 4. I let the call go through to the machine.* It could have been an achievement, of course. She had no way to know.

The last slip was dated November 21.

*I can get there by myself now.*

She had put up a notice inside the Number 6. Nobody called. After ninety days, she moved the box to the cupboard under the sink so it wouldn’t go out with the unclaimed goods. This was not something she did with objects simply because she liked them. She liked the small brass telescope that went to auction in May. She liked a yellow scarf with two intricate and deeply ugly horses on it. The box was different in a way she wouldn’t have cared to explain to the city, whose eventual decision on a wooden box containing used paper would likely have been both sensible and quick.

At one, a young man appeared at the window, breathing hard.

“Did anybody turn in a set of keys?”

Ada set the box on the floor.

“What sort?”

“House keys.”

“How many?”

“Three. Maybe four.” He held his hands apart, as if the keys were a fish whose size he was trying not to exaggerate. “There’s a white plastic thing.”

“A tag?”

“A tooth.”

From the second drawer Ada took a set of keys attached to a white plastic molar. The young man shut his eyes.

“I haven’t even got to the worst part of my day yet,” he said.

“Do you know when that’s scheduled for?”

“Half past two.”

She pushed the keys through the dish. He explained that he was clearing out his father’s flat. The keys were to his own place; he’d had to leave the flat that morning to collect the hired van, and while he was out his sister had started on the kitchen. At half past two she was going to ask him to decide what to do with the plates.

There were twelve plates, he said. Their father had lived alone.

“The odd thing is,” he said, “I can remember every time we needed more than four.”

Ada waited. But he didn’t tell her about any of those times. He put the keys carefully into an inside pocket, zipped it shut, and thanked her.

She ate her sandwich. Then she opened the wooden box and turned the slips over one at a time, looking for identifying details she might have missed. On one, the writer had pressed hard enough to emboss the paper, but it was just another date. Another had been torn from the corner of a bill. On the reverse were three letters of an address, too close to the cut to tell whether they belonged to a street or a name.

She had once shown Ruth a few of the sentences. Ruth thought they sounded like homework from a therapist.

“What kind of homework is ‘We ate outside in our coats’?” Ada had asked.

“The kind you get when all your other sentences begin with ‘I.’”

Ada had wanted to object and couldn’t quite. She’d raised a person who could make a remark like that over a plate of chips and then ask if you were going to finish them.

Around two the drivers began coming in to say goodbye. Mel brought her a packet of biscuits from the vending machine, still warm because he’d got it jammed and had to reach through the flap and work it free. Frances gave her a card. There was a drawing of a bus on the front with *SORRY YOU’RE LEAVING* on its destination display.

“To be clear,” Ada told her, “I’m not the one who decided to leave.”

“I know,” said Frances. “But there wasn’t a card for what they did.”

They stood for a little while, looking out at the station. A bus reversed into its bay with the steady, apologetic beeping Ada had long ago stopped hearing unless nothing else was being said.

“Do you remember that notice I put up on the Six?” Ada asked.

“The box?”

“You remember it?”

“You made me take the first one down because I put it over an advert for a missing cat.”

“It was an old cat. I didn’t think it could afford to lose a week.”

Frances leaned an elbow on the counter. “Was it wooden? About this big?”

Ada reached down for it. Frances took it in both hands and slid the lid back an inch. Then she closed it.

“I think it’s mine,” she said.

“Think?”

“No. It is.”

For eleven months Ada had imagined asking the person who claimed it to identify a sentence. She had settled on the drill, the earliest one in the box, because surely everybody could remember a drill they’d returned without being asked. Now she found she didn’t want to administer the test. She did, however, want to know why Frances had let her make a second notice.

“I saw it,” Frances said, when Ada asked. “I was driving the Six that week. I drove around with the notice behind my head for five days.”

“Why didn’t you say?”

“I thought you might have read them.”

Ada could have said she had to look through the contents in order to log the item, which was true. She could have added that she had kept the contents together and secure, which was a little less true if you took into account the occasion with Ruth and the chips.

“I read them,” she said.

Frances turned the box so the worn end faced her. She fit her thumb into the half-moon.

“My sister made it,” she said. “In school. The lid used to stick.”

Ada waited for the rest. Frances ran her thumb over the end of the box a few times. Out in the station a driver called to someone that the next one would be along in twenty minutes. The person he was talking to said they’d already waited twenty minutes, which both of them knew was beside the point.

“Were you putting them in as they happened?” Ada asked at last.

“Some of them. Some I wrote a long time after.” Frances looked up. “I put the date I remembered it. Sometimes I couldn’t have told you when it actually happened.”

This upset Ada’s theory of the box, although she couldn’t now have said what her theory was. She had thought about those dates so often that there was weather attached to some of them.

“The coats,” Ada said. “I always pictured that one in March.”

“We were on the ferry,” Frances said. “Middle of summer. Everyone else had gone inside. We’d paid extra for the crossing in daylight and my sister said she wasn’t eating a sandwich under a strip light after what it cost us.”

Frances laughed before she got to the end of the sentence, and Ada could hear, in the speed of it, that she had told this story before. Maybe to someone who’d laughed in the right place. Maybe to someone who’d been there and said that wasn’t what she’d said at all.

“Are you taking it?” Ada asked.

“Yes,” Frances said. She put it under her arm. Then she put it down again, opened her work bag, and moved her lunch tin and a paperback until she could fit the box flat at the bottom.

At four, Ruth arrived in a coat too thin for the weather and carrying a roll of packing tape on her wrist like a bracelet. Ada had one drawer left. They went through it together. There were rubber bands knitted into a single perished mass, a sheet of stamps with one stamp missing, and the manual for a kettle that had caught fire in 2009. At the back was a photograph of Ruth at seven, sitting on the counter with her feet in the dish.

“I didn’t know you had that,” Ruth said.

“Neither did I.”

In the photograph Ruth was eating a pear. Ada remembered the cardigan she was wearing better than she remembered the afternoon itself. It had been a nursery cardigan, and by then the sleeves were so short Ruth had insisted on wearing gloves with it even indoors. There was one glove on the counter. The other hand, bare, held the pear. As Ada looked, she remembered that the pear had been hard, and that Ruth had spent a long time working away at one spot with her loose front tooth.

“Did Frances come?” Ruth asked.

“Yes. How did you know?”

“She texted me last night. I told her if she wanted it back, she had until four.”

“Did you know it was hers?”

“Not till last night. I called some of the drivers about signing your card. She asked if you still had a wooden box. I said I didn’t know, but I knew where you kept it.”

“You could have told me.”

“I almost did.” Ruth took the tape off her wrist. “She asked me not to.”

Ada got up to check the hooks behind the door. For a moment she had resented both of them, Frances for making her wait, Ruth for knowing where to look. It had been pleasant, in a private way, to have something that was waiting with her. She’d spent a certain number of quiet afternoons hearing footsteps slow outside the booth and thinking: *This will be the person.* She was glad Frances had come. It took her a little while, standing at the empty hooks, to be glad without reservation.

At five they turned off the light. The station was still running, and the new sign on the window referred all inquiries to a web address that looked, to Ada, needlessly difficult to copy down. A woman approached the booth while they were waiting for their bus. Ada watched her peer in, read the sign, and lift her phone to photograph it. Then the woman walked away. It hadn’t occurred to Ada that you might photograph the sign.

“Mum,” Ruth said, “where do you want to go?”

“Home, I suppose.”

“We can do that.”

Two buses came and went before theirs. Ada put her hand in her cardigan pocket and found the green sock. In daylight she could see a little ridge of darker green running all the way across the toe. Somebody had darned a child’s sock. It was such a small job that Ada could imagine putting it off for a month, or doing it immediately to avoid doing something else.

She took out the sock to show Ruth, who turned it inside out to see how the mending had been done.

“Have we missed it?” Ruth asked, looking up.

“Not yet.”

A bus rounded the corner with the interior lights on. Ada had stood in this bay in every season, after long days and after days she couldn’t account for at all. There were people who boarded here whose claims she remembered by the objects they’d lost, and people she recognized only because for years they had sat in the same seat. Tonight she and Ruth went upstairs. They got the front seats, which had always been Ruth’s favorites.

At the first red light Ada pulled out her phone. Her contacts still included a plumber who’d moved to Spain and a neighbor she’d never liked, but not Frances. She asked Ruth for the number.

She typed: *What did you have in the sandwiches?*

It was a nosy question, and possibly Frances had already told her as much as she wanted to tell. Ada held the phone for most of the ride home without sending it. Then, just as Ruth reached across her to ring the bell, she pressed send.

The answer came while they were walking up the hill.

*Egg. We used to get them every time. I don’t even like egg.*

A second message followed.

*Actually I think that time mine was cheese.*

Ada stopped under a streetlight to read both messages again. Ruth, a few steps ahead, stopped too and put her hands in the pockets of her inadequate coat. The hill was steep there. Ada put the phone away and took her daughter’s arm, and the two of them finished walking home.

# The Department of Unclaimed Things

On the morning the city abolished its lost-property office, a man came in to claim a ladder.

“How long ago did you lose it?” Mara asked.

“Forty-three years.”

She looked up. He had the mild, expectant face of someone who had just asked for a glass of water.

“Do you remember where?”

“Outside my house. Or it was my house then. I put the ladder up to paint the bedroom window, and my wife said the baby had finally gone to sleep, so I came inside to see. I meant to go back out.”

“And when you did?”

“We had supper. Then it rained for three days. By Sunday the ladder was gone.”

Mara explained that the city generally kept things for ninety days, with exceptions for items of unusual value. She left out the fact that, by noon, the city would no longer keep things at all.

“I thought I might have lent it to someone,” the man said. “I’ve spent forty-three years being a little annoyed with everyone I knew then.”

“Why look for it now?”

“I was annoyed with somebody else this morning and realized I could actually ask him.”

Mara opened the city’s inventory. There were two ladders: an aluminum stepladder recovered from a tram shelter and a wooden ladder retrieved from the canal last November. The man considered both descriptions.

“Mine was wooden.”

“Was it painted?”

“I never got as far as opening the paint.”

She took him down to the basement. The canal ladder had seven rungs, one of them split, and smelled faintly of the canal despite having spent a winter beside a radiator. The man put his hand on it.

“Well,” he said. “That’s not it.”

Mara waited for him to take his hand away. He didn’t.

“You can have it if you want,” she said. “Though I wouldn’t climb it.”

“I wouldn’t climb mine either, at this point.”

They carried it up together. At the door he handed her a claim ticket. She had assumed he didn’t have one. It was a yellow rectangle with a number in the upper corner and a blue ink drawing of a ladder on the back.

“My daughter made that,” he said. “She was six. Not the baby in the story. The next one. She went through a period of giving me receipts for things.”

After he left, Mara turned the ticket over. Under the ladder her predecessor, or her predecessor’s predecessor, had written, *No ladder matching description found. Please try again in thirty days.*

Apparently he had.

At nine, the truck arrived. Two men in orange vests began moving the contents of the basement into the street. A woman from Procurement stood by with a clipboard to determine which objects were suitable for resale. She put a green sticker on a saxophone, a red one on a damp box of wigs, and no sticker at all on a portrait of a boy holding a fish. After some thought she turned the portrait to face the wall.

“Are we taking the shelves?” one of the men asked.

“Those belong to the building.”

“Are we taking the building?”

The woman checked a separate sheet. “Not today.”

Mara went upstairs. Her desk drawers were empty except for a packet of instant soup and the index card she had been carrying from job to job since she was twenty-two. In her brother’s handwriting, the card said: *If they ask about the goat, you were never in Belgium.*

Her brother had written it on the train home from their aunt’s funeral. There had been no goat, and Belgium had been their aunt’s home for twenty years. He’d slipped the card into Mara’s coat pocket while she slept. She found it at customs and began to laugh so hard that the officer moved her out of the queue.

For years she had thought the card would be the thing she would save from a fire. Now that she was actually clearing out a desk, she put it in the bag with the soup and felt mildly cheated. There ought to have been more occasion to it.

The telephone rang.

“Lost property,” Mara said.

“I left a blue jar on the number four bus,” said a woman. “It’s about the size of a large orange.”

“When?”

“Yesterday afternoon. This is extremely important.”

Mara looked through the morning deliveries. Gloves, keys, a transparent bag containing one black shoe and a flyer for a second shoe at half price. At the bottom sat a blue jar with a screw top.

“Can you describe what’s inside?”

“Rice.”

Mara lifted the jar. Something shuffled against the glass.

“Only rice?”

“Yes. How soon can I get there?”

“I don’t know where you’re coming from.”

“Neither do I, exactly. I got off the bus.”

Mara talked the woman to a street sign, then told her how to get to the office. She set the jar aside. A moment later she moved it farther from the edge of the desk.

By ten the street outside looked like the yard of a house whose occupants had separated on unusually generous terms. There were badminton rackets, school uniforms, an electric kettle, a red bicycle with no saddle, and a saddle with no bicycle. A pair of matching suitcases had been lost six months apart, on different bus routes. They had finally met in the basement, where Mara stored one inside the other.

People began to stop. The woman from Procurement explained that nothing could be sold until it had been assessed and listed. A young man asked whether he could have the fish portrait.

“You know him?” she asked.

“No.”

“What do you want it for?”

“My flat is very quiet.”

She looked at him, then at the boy, who had the startled expression of someone beginning to suspect the fish was not going to help. She gave the young man the portrait.

This started something. A delivery cyclist took a pair of ski goggles. A woman in a cream suit tried on a purple wig from the damp box, examined herself in the side mirror of the truck, and asked whether it came in any other colors. One of the men in orange found a tape measure he said was better than his, then pulled his own from his pocket and showed Mara precisely why. The woman from Procurement made a new column on her sheet and labeled it *Other*.

Mara’s brother called at ten thirty.

“Are you a private citizen yet?” he asked.

“I’ve got an hour and a half.”

“Come for lunch. I’ll make you a sandwich that reflects your former rank.”

He lived across the city, in the house he had moved into after his divorce. For the first six months he had owned one plate and seventeen lamps. Mara used to go over on Thursdays to watch television with him. He switched on every lamp as the daylight went, without ever mentioning it. Recently he had acquired a dining table, and at Christmas he’d asked her to bring chairs.

“What rank was that?” she said.

“You tell me how thick to cut the cheese.”

She said she would call him later. Then she took the index card out of her bag and called him back.

“Why Belgium?” she asked.

“What?”

“On the note about the goat.”

There was a pause. She could hear a cupboard opening.

“Because I bought you a goat,” he said. “At the station. A little wooden one. You said you didn’t want anything to remember the trip by, so I was going to hide it in your coat and give you the card as well. Then I dropped the goat between the train and the platform.”

“You never told me that.”

“I thought you’d be upset.”

“I’d have been delighted about the goat.”

“No, I mean I thought you’d be upset that I’d dropped it. You were upset when I ate the last pear.”

She remembered the pear. They had been in their aunt’s kitchen, in the middle of deciding what to do with thirty years of jam jars. He had asked her whether she wanted half and she’d said no. When she heard him bite into it, she had to go out into the garden. There, for want of anything else to do, she righted a fallen flowerpot. It was full of ants, which had presumably preferred it the other way.

“Cut the cheese thick,” she said.

At eleven the woman arrived for the blue jar. She was younger than Mara had imagined and wore a coat with one sleeve turned inside out. She spotted the jar on the desk, put both hands flat on the counter, and exhaled.

“I’m sorry,” she said.

“What for?”

“I was going to tell you there were ashes in it, in case you didn’t take the rice seriously. Then I thought if you found it you might open it and be disappointed.”

“Is the rice special?”

“No. I mean it’s not a special kind of rice.” She picked up the jar. “My son’s teacher gave everybody a bean to germinate. We’ve been waiting for it for a week. I moved it from the windowsill on Tuesday, and for two days he’s been asking me if I threw it out. He’s at his dad’s now. I was taking it over to show him.”

“The bean’s in there?”

“In a little envelope. The rice is to keep it dry. I looked it up.”

Mara wondered why the woman had decided the bean needed drying when the whole point had been to get it wet. There was probably an afternoon’s worth of explanation in that coat alone.

“Would you like to use the phone?” she asked.

The woman dialed from memory. A man picked up, and they exchanged a few words in the clipped, overly courteous way Mara recognized from listening to her brother call about a missing school jumper. Then there was a long wait. The woman shook the jar once, quietly, as if whatever was in it might answer first.

“Hi,” she said at last. “Remember how I said I put it somewhere safe?”

She listened.

“No,” she said. “You were right about the bus.”

Mara went outside to give her some privacy. The sack of lost keys was still by the steps. Nobody wanted those. People would pick up keys only on the off chance they recognized their own, and just then there was nobody there to try. Mara crouched and sifted through them. There were keys so new you could still see the price of having them cut written in pencil on the paper tag, and keys rubbed smooth at the shoulders by people who had used them every day. One was attached to a flat stone with a hole in the middle. She couldn’t imagine carrying the stone around in her pocket. She could imagine, very well, finding it on a beach and looking for a use for it.

She had worked in lost property for fourteen years. She was good at persuading people to tell her what was actually missing. They might start with the make of a briefcase, but after a little while they would tell her about the broken clasp, the stain on the lining, the smell of a banana they’d forgotten the previous summer. Their certainty came back as they talked. Sometimes it was a pleasure to break the news that the office had no such thing, because by then they knew exactly where else to look.

Other times a person came in with as little information as possible. A woman had once asked about a teddy bear and then, with evident reluctance, revealed that it was actually a rabbit, that its name was Frank, and that it was hers. Mara had found the rabbit in the drawer labeled *Small Animals*. For reasons nobody at the office could remember, this was also where they put false teeth.

She’d liked the job best on days when everybody got what they came for. There hadn’t been many of those. The closest she could remember was a rainy Tuesday when three nearly identical umbrellas had been returned to their owners. An hour later, one of the owners had come back to say she had the wrong one. The other two were never heard from again. As far as Mara knew, they were satisfied.

At half past eleven, one of the men in orange asked what he should do with an upright piano. There had been some confusion about its status. A previous manager had brought it in for an office Christmas party and never taken it home. For eighteen years the staff had been filing reports on top of it. Nobody knew whether it still belonged to the manager, who lived in Spain, or whether it had become municipal furniture through uninterrupted use.

“Can anybody play?” Mara asked.

The woman from Procurement said that she could, a little. She sat on a box of unclaimed scarves while the two men held the piano steady on the truck’s lift. One note didn’t work and another didn’t stop working when she took her finger off it. She played the tune again, shifting it up, and it went much better. Mara knew it without knowing its name. She waited for the bit she could hum. It turned out to be the end.

“My mother liked that one,” the woman said. She examined her hands, then pulled down the fallboard. “She thought I should do it professionally. She’d never heard a professional.”

At six minutes to twelve the truck left, taking the piano and the keys. The woman from Procurement shook Mara’s hand and asked if she wanted the clipboard.

“Is it yours to give away?”

“It is now,” she said.

Mara went through the ground-floor rooms one last time. The office already smelled different. The objects had brought in their own weather: bus heaters, wet wool, hand cream, the dry heat of handbags left in the sun. Underneath it all was the cool mineral smell of a room whose windows didn’t open.

A girl was waiting at the counter when Mara came back. She was perhaps twelve, with a schoolbag open at the top. Mara nearly told her about the zip, but the girl reached into the bag and took out an envelope instead.

“I found this at the cash machine,” she said.

Inside were two twenty-pound notes and a receipt with the balance still showing. The balance was less than the amount withdrawn. Mara counted the money, though there was very little counting to do.

“Will they come here?” the girl asked.

“Not here. We’re closing.” The girl put a hand out for the envelope, and Mara gave it back. “But the bank’s just down the road. They might be able to work out whose it is.”

“I already tried the bank. The guard said it wasn’t their cash machine.”

“Which machine?”

“The one at the bank.”

Mara looked at the clock. It was twelve. She turned the sign on the door, locked up, and put the keys through the letterbox as instructed. They landed with a sound exactly like keys being put through a letterbox: intimate, ordinary, nothing a person in the street would turn to look at.

“Come on,” she said to the girl. “Show me which guard.”

They walked past the empty patch where the truck had stood. In the window of the café next door, the girl noticed her open schoolbag and stopped to close it. Mara held the envelope while she did. Across the road somebody was carrying a bouquet upside down, shedding water onto the pavement. A bus swung around the corner and Mara took half a step toward it out of habit. She had been catching that bus at the same time, from the same stop, for years. Once, when she’d missed it three mornings in a row, the driver asked on the fourth if she’d been on holiday. She had told him yes. It seemed kinder than telling him about her alarm clock.

The bus pulled away. There would be another one in ten minutes, and one ten minutes after that. The girl tugged on her zip, which had caught in the lining.

“Here,” Mara said. “Hold this a second.”

She handed back the envelope and worked the cloth loose. The trick was to pull the zip a little farther open before trying to close it. When she was done, the girl slid the envelope inside herself. Then she took it out again and carried it in her hand, ready to show the guard.

# The Door on the Number Nine

On the last Thursday of the municipal lost-property office, a woman came in and asked if we had a door.

“What sort of door?” I said.

“The sort you’d notice.”

There was a white line on the floor that people were meant to stand behind while I searched. The woman stood exactly on it, her boots neatly covering the words PLEASE WAIT HERE. She looked about thirty. She had come without a bag, which I took as evidence that she really did expect to leave with a door.

“What bus?”

“The nine. Last Tuesday. Around two.”

“Did you leave it on the bus yourself?”

“Yes.”

“By accident?”

She considered this. “Eventually.”

Behind me were three hundred umbrellas, a dentist’s model of the lower jaw, and a slow cooker containing a serving spoon and no other evidence of a meal. By five the following afternoon, whatever remained would be divided between a charity van and a skip. On Monday the city would outsource lost property to a company whose collection point was in an industrial estate across the river. The company’s website was already up. Its illustration showed a woman being reunited with a purple suitcase, both of them apparently delighted.

I had worked in the office for nineteen years. In that time I had learned that a person who has genuinely lost something is rarely good at describing it. Ask what color their wallet is and they will tell you where they bought it. Ask how many keys were on the ring and they will tell you what the keys open, starting with a house they no longer live in. People attempting to claim someone else’s phone, on the other hand, tend to know the make, model, and retail price.

The woman’s name was Lina. She described the door as blue on one side and white on the other, with a brass handle that pinched if you turned it too far. Then she said, “There’s a little hole near the bottom where my brother tried to put a bolt on his side. He was seven. It didn’t occur to him he’d have to drill all the way through.”

“Was it his bedroom door?”

“It was everybody’s bedroom door at some point.”

I checked the register, though I knew there was no door in it. On Tuesday we’d had a tennis racket, a bag of onions, and half a set of curtains. I remembered the curtains because the driver had submitted two reports, one for each panel, and our software wouldn’t let me persuade him they were traveling together.

“I can ask the depot,” I said. “Leave me a number.”

Lina wrote it on the back of a business card. The front said she was a piano tuner.

“Do most people tell you it’s just been tuned?” I asked.

“No. Most people tell me nobody plays it, as if that ought to have helped.”

She left. I put the card beside the phone, then moved it under the stapler so it wouldn’t get swept into the recycling. I had spent the morning deciding which office supplies were mine. I could account for the mug and the cardigan. The stapler defeated me. I remembered buying it, but I also remembered filling in a form to be reimbursed, and I couldn’t remember whether I’d ever handed in the form. There was no one left in our department to ask.

At the depot a dispatcher called Ben answered. I knew Ben by voice alone. For years he’d told me to hang on a second and then left me to listen to whatever he was eating.

“A door,” he said. “Like off a bus?”

“Off a house.”

“Why would it be on a bus?”

“I was hoping you’d tell me.”

He put me on hold. Through the little speaker came a recording that urged me to consider a career in municipal transport. It listed a pension, discounted travel, and the opportunity to make a difference to someone’s day. The recording had been suggesting this to municipal transport employees for as long as I could remember. Then Ben came back and said yes, there had been a door.

“It’s in the drivers’ room. You want it?”

“Someone does.”

“Ah,” he said. He sounded disappointed.

“Is that a problem?”

“No. We’ve just had our lunch on it.”

By the time I arrived at the depot the next morning, the door had been cleared except for a bottle of hot sauce and a deck of cards. It lay across two filing cabinets in a room with a sink, a kettle, and a notice about the correct procedure for reporting a broken chair. Under the notice was a broken chair.

The driver who’d found the door was called Jo. She was sitting at its far end doing a crossword. I recognized her handwriting before she introduced herself. On lost-property slips, Jo had a way of describing things in terms that made you hope they would be claimed. A WOOL HAT, MUCH MENDED. A CAKE TIN WITH A CAKE STILL IN IT. Once, memorably, A PHOTO OF TWO MEN WITH A FISH THEY ARE CLEARLY VERY PROUD OF.

“She got off to help a man with a pushchair,” Jo said. “Back wheel caught between the bus and the curb. The man got his wheel free and she walked off with him, talking. I waited a bit. In the end someone rang the bell.”

“You could have called after her.”

“I did. I called, ‘Your door!’ She looked right at me and waved.”

Jo set down her pencil. We both looked at the door. On the side facing up, someone had painted over the handle, and years of hands had worn the paint away in a ragged oval. Near the bottom there was a little hole.

“I thought she was giving it to us,” Jo said. “Which was a peculiar thing to do. But it had been a peculiar thing to bring in the first place, so I gave her the benefit of the doubt.”

I called Lina. She said she could come at half past three, between an upright and a baby grand. I asked if she would need help getting the door home. There was a pause long enough for me to hear her turn a page.

“I’m not taking it home,” she said. “My brother’s coming.”

I went back to the office for the final afternoon. Word of the closure had traveled in unpredictable ways. A man came in looking for a pair of binoculars he’d lost in 2006. A woman who’d received three reminders that we had her gym bag turned up to tell me, in person, that we could keep it. Two boys inventoried our stock of footballs with the concentration of surveyors. They found theirs when one of them remembered there was a dog bite in it. His brother said no, that was a hole from the fence. They took the ball, still arguing, both with a hand on it.

Just before three, a woman telephoned about a stuffed rabbit. I asked what it looked like.

“It looks as if it’s been in the washing machine too many times,” she said.

We had four rabbits that met this description. I carried the phone to the shelf and read off their distinguishing features: one ear, green dress, red ribbon, no face.

“Oh God,” the woman said. “No face.”

She was at work until six. I told her I would leave the rabbit at the newsagent’s next door. The newsagent, who had spent nineteen years sending people over to me when they tried to hand lost things to him, said he would make an exception. Then he asked whether we had an umbrella he could borrow.

I gave him a good one.

At half past three I put up the sign that said BACK IN TEN MINUTES. There was no sign for what I meant. I had filed everything that needed filing and emptied the drawer where I kept teabags. I took my cardigan and left the stapler beside the phone.

Lina was already at the depot. She and Jo had turned the door over, blue side up. There were pencil lines near the hinge, each with a date and an initial. Some had been crossed out and redrawn. At the top of the highest line, someone had written IN SOCKS.

“My dad,” Lina said when she saw me looking. “He objected on the grounds that my brother had better socks.”

She put one finger against the lowest mark. It stood a little higher than her knee.

“The builders let me take it,” she said. “They’d put it out with the wood. I went past on my way to a job and there it was. I had to go knocking on the next house to borrow a screwdriver to get the hinges off. Then I missed two buses because the drivers wouldn’t let me on with it.”

“Technically,” Jo said, “neither did I.”

“No, you opened the middle doors and looked the other way.”

“I needed to look that way for unrelated reasons.”

Lina smiled, then checked the time. Her brother was late.

I had assumed the markings were why she wanted the door. So when she asked Jo for a cloth to wipe them off, I said, rather sharply, “Why would you do that?”

Jo found a cloth but didn’t wet it. She set it down by Lina’s hand.

“I thought I’d take a picture first,” Lina said. “Then he could paint it.”

“Your brother?”

“He’s got two bits of kitchen counter balanced on a clothes horse. He says he likes to eat standing up, but he’s been saying that since February.”

I tried to imagine the door in her brother’s kitchen. What I pictured instead was my own father at our kitchen table, working his thumbnail under a drop of dried candle wax. He had done this whenever the wax was there and sometimes when it wasn’t. I couldn’t remember the color of the table. I could remember the noise his thumbnail made against it.

Lina’s brother arrived at four, carrying a tape measure. His name was Sami. He had the same habit Lina did of looking down when he needed to consider a question. When he saw the door he said, “Oh, that one,” with the vague irritation you might reserve for an appliance someone had called you over to fix.

“You don’t have to take it,” Lina said.

Sami pulled out the tape. “I didn’t say I wasn’t taking it.”

He measured the door in both directions, wrote the figures on his hand, and then measured it again. Lina took out her phone and photographed the pencil marks. She did it in sections, shading each patch with her free hand because the light from the window caught the paint. Sami waited until she was done. Then he put his heel against the bottom of the door and stretched the tape up to the line marked IN SOCKS.

“He was right,” he said. “I had hiking socks. Remember those green ones?”

“You wore them to bed.”

“They were comfortable.”

“You wore them in the bath once.”

“That was a different pair of socks.”

For a little while the disagreement required all their attention. I sat in Jo’s chair. Her crossword had one entry left. The clue was *Keep for later*, seven letters. I counted out *reserve* and *set aside*, the latter one letter too long. Jo looked over my shoulder and said, “It’s ‘put by.’ I’ve got two letters wrong somewhere.”

They had come in Sami’s car, a small hatchback with a rear seat that would fold only if you reached through the boot and tugged a loop of webbing. We carried the door out together. It was heavier than it looked and the handle swung open against my wrist. I turned it too far and it pinched.

“Told you,” Lina said. She was at the other end. She couldn’t possibly have seen.

The door went into the car corner first. The boot wouldn’t close over it. Sami inspected the gap. He took the door out again and shifted the passenger seat forward until the headrest nearly touched the windscreen. This time the boot came down. Lina went to open the passenger door and saw what he’d done.

“I’ll take the bus,” she said.

Sami stood with his keys in his hand. “You could come and show me where you think it should go.”

“Have you got anything to put it on?”

“The clothes horse.”

Lina looked through the rear window at the door. “It’ll flatten the clothes horse.”

“Probably,” Sami said. “You could come and watch it happen.”

She got in. There wasn’t room for her knees, so she sat sideways, and Sami reached around her to work the seat belt. As they pulled away, I saw her stretch a hand behind her head to stop the brass handle rattling against the window.

It was twenty to five. I could have gone straight home, but I walked back to the office. The newsagent tapped on his glass as I passed and held up the rabbit by one ear, then set it upright next to the till. He had put it in a paper bag and folded down the sides so that its featureless head stuck out.

Inside the office, I took down the sign. A young man was waiting behind it. He’d lost a black glove on his way to work that morning. We had a whole drawer of black gloves, but none could have come from that morning: the last depot delivery had been the day before. I told him so. Then, because in ten minutes there would be no practical reason not to, I opened the drawer.

He tried on three before he found a right-hand glove that fit. The cuff was a different length from the one he’d brought with him. He pulled down his sleeve and the difference disappeared.

“How much?” he asked.

I shook my head.

He put his hands in his pockets, took them out again, and thanked me. From the window I watched him stop at the corner and take off both gloves to answer his phone.

At five the building manager came for the keys. She offered to wait while I looked around, but I’d already looked around. I handed them over and went outside. A number nine was pulling up across the street. I had never taken it home; it went a longer way, past the swimming baths and over the railway, before joining my usual route. I caught it anyway.

The bus was nearly empty. In the middle, opposite the doors, there was a broad space with two folding seats. I sat in one and tried to work out how Lina had stood with the door. Flat against the window, perhaps, one boot braced behind it for the turns. Or on its long edge across both seats, with the handle jutting into the aisle. Neither seemed right. I thought I might ask Jo, and then remembered Jo hadn’t been looking.

At the swimming baths, an old man got on with a bunch of flowers wrapped in newspaper. He sat across from me and set the flowers on his lap. At the next stop he moved them to the seat beside him to get at his phone. He made a call. Nobody answered. When we reached the railway he stood up, put his phone in his pocket, and stepped toward the doors.

“Your flowers,” I said.

He came back for them. He looked a little annoyed with himself and a little annoyed with me for having witnessed it. Then, as the doors opened, he tucked the newspaper more securely around the stems and said, “She’d never have believed me.”

I didn’t ask who. There wasn’t time, and I liked the way he said it, with such certainty about a conversation he was now not going to have. He stepped down to the pavement. I moved to the window seat and rode the rest of the way home.

# The Things People Came Back For

The heaviest thing anyone ever left on a Bellweather bus was a tombstone. It rode the Number 6 all the way to the depot, propped against the wheel well and wrapped in a beach towel. Our driver, Manny, thought it was a microwave until he tried to pick it up. Then he thought it was somebody’s ashes, which made him set it down so gently that he hurt his back.

It turned out to be a sample. The name on it was JOHN DOE, and the dates were 1900–1900. A man from a monument shop came for it on Tuesday. He said the lettering was what customers needed to see; he hadn’t thought about the dates until I pointed them out.

“Poor little guy,” he said, looking down at the stone.

Then he put it on a hand truck and wheeled it out.

I worked in lost property for eleven years. People assume the job is mainly about sorting things, but sorting takes up about twenty minutes of an ordinary morning. The rest of the time you are asking someone to tell you something about a black umbrella that would distinguish it from another black umbrella, and the person, who has never really looked at the umbrella, is discovering how much of their everyday life they have agreed not to notice.

One woman said her umbrella was black on top and dark underneath. We went through the rack together. She opened six umbrellas before she found hers. It had a loose spoke, which she recognized by the way it caught in her hair.

“That’s a terrible umbrella,” I said.

“Oh, absolutely,” she said, and took it home.

We kept things for ninety days. At the end of each month a charity took the usable coats, the bus company shredded the identification cards, and I carried the rest to a dumpster and discovered, once again, that I could throw away a child’s drawing if it was raining hard enough. On dry days I sometimes stood there reading them. One showed a woman inside a house and a much larger woman standing beside it. The caption said MY MOM AT WORK. There was no indication which woman was the mother, or what she did.

In my ninth year, the company announced that lost property would be moving to a warehouse at the airport. You would fill out a form online, receive a claim number, and pay for postage. The notice described this as bringing the service closer to passengers. If you lived near the airport, I suppose it did.

The union got me two more years at the depot. I spent the first year answering questions about the move and the second year answering the same questions more honestly. No, you probably could not get a bus to the warehouse. Yes, there would be a telephone number. No, I did not know if a person would answer it.

Three weeks before we closed, Manny brought me a wooden stool.

It was painted yellow, with four legs and an oval hole in the top for carrying it. One leg was shorter than the others. Somebody had cut it off cleanly and painted the exposed wood. It wasn’t broken, which was what made it so disagreeable to look at. Someone had gone to some trouble to make a stool that wouldn’t stand up straight.

“Found on the Six,” Manny said.

“Everything good is on the Six.”

“That’s because we brake so hard.”

He left it on my desk. I put it on the floor, where it rocked when I touched it with my toe. Later, when I needed to reach a box of school uniforms on the top shelf, I stood on my swivel chair rather than use it.

My father used to make stools. He also made bookcases, gates, rabbit hutches, and one kitchen table so wide that my mother made him take it apart and rebuild it in the room where it would spend the next thirty-seven years. He had a joinery shop behind the old post office. As a child I liked the shop best in winter, when the glue had to be warmed and you could put your hands around the pot. Outside, the street smelled of wet wool and bus exhaust. Inside, even the rubbish smelled good.

By the time the yellow stool came in, he hadn’t set foot in the shop for eight months. A dance teacher had bought the building, and he was living in a second-floor flat with a view of the chemist’s extractor fan. He claimed to like the fan. It went on at eight and off at six, so there was no need to look at the clock.

I went round on Thursdays with groceries. He always asked what he owed me, and I always told him, and he always gave me cash, including the pennies. Once I rounded down by eleven pence and he made me take it. On my way home I bought a packet of crisps I didn’t want. I sat at the bus stop eating them furiously, though I couldn’t have said what I wanted him to do instead. Refuse to pay, perhaps. Ask me to stay for supper. Buy his own bloody carrots.

That Thursday I took the stool with me. I filled out a movement slip first: REMOVED FROM INVENTORY FOR IDENTIFICATION. It was the same slip I’d used when the police took away a fishing tackle box that smelled of petrol. I wrote my own name in the box marked RECEIVING AUTHORITY.

My father turned the stool over on his kitchen counter. He ran a thumb over the short leg. I had expected him to enjoy identifying the wood, which was the sort of question he could answer while pretending not to enjoy it.

“Whoever painted this used a lot of newspaper,” he said.

Caught in the yellow paint under the seat was a scrap of print no bigger than a thumbnail. I could make out the bottom of an advertisement: SATURDAY ONLY.

“Why would somebody do that to the leg?” I asked.

He looked at me. For a moment he seemed to be waiting for the rest of a joke.

“Because the ground was high on that side,” he said.

We both looked down at his level kitchen floor. All at once I could picture the stool standing solidly somewhere. I felt foolish for having carried it across town.

“Would you like tea?” he asked.

I said yes. While the kettle boiled, he told me the dance teacher had phoned about the shop. She wanted to know if he could take away two benches he had left in the yard. He’d asked if he could come to see them before she threw them out, and she’d said of course, but he hadn’t been.

“Are they good benches?”

“They’re all right.”

“Do you want them?”

“Where would I put two benches?”

He poured the tea. There was a grey crescent in his cup where a teaspoon had worn the glaze away. I recognized the cup from the shop. I wondered how many things he’d taken because he wanted them and how many he’d taken because he happened to be holding them when somebody came in with a broom.

“What day can she let us in?” I said.

He didn’t answer right away. Then he went out to the hall, where he kept telephone numbers on a calendar from three years before.

On Saturday the dance teacher let us through a side gate. She was called Ingrid and wore thick socks with individual toes. She apologized for painting over the shop sign. My father said he’d painted over the previous man’s sign himself. I had never known there was a previous man.

“Did he do joinery too?” I asked.

“Sold aquarium supplies. Terrible damp in there when I got it.”

Through the new glass in the back door I could see a full wall of mirrors. I had a brief, stupid hope that if I looked at the right angle I might see the old room reflected instead of the new one.

The benches were under a plastic sheet in the yard. Dad had built them for people waiting to collect orders, though ordinarily if someone sat down while he was working, he found them a job. One bench had gone soft at the ends. The other was sound except for a slat that had come loose. He pressed on it, listened to it creak, and asked Ingrid whether she needed somewhere for people to put their shoes.

“They leave them right in front of the door,” she said. “I trip over them every night.”

He asked if she had a screwdriver.

She brought him a kitchen knife. He sent me out to buy screws and a screwdriver, and when I came back the two of them had taken their shoes off and were standing in the middle of the new floor. Ingrid wanted to know if a blemish in the wood would come out. Dad was showing her how to tell a nail stain from a scorch. Neither looked up until I set the packet of screws down. Then he asked me to hold the slat steady while he worked.

The rotten bench went into Ingrid’s skip. We carried the other inside. It was a good fit along the wall, and Ingrid sat on it to put her shoes back on. Dad asked if she would mind pushing it a little to the left, away from the door. She did. He asked her to put it back where it was. She did that too. On the way home he said there’d been another bench, years ago, with a back on it, and he wondered who had that one now.

The stool remained unclaimed. In our last week, a man collected a briefcase that had been with us for eighty-seven days. There was nothing in it except a receipt for the briefcase. A girl came in on behalf of her grandmother and left wearing three cardigans, none of them her grandmother’s. Her grandmother came in the next day to return two. The third, she said, she had washed and would like to keep. I said that seemed fair. It was the kind of transaction the airport system would struggle to accommodate.

On our last afternoon, a woman called to say she’d lost a stool on the Number 6. I asked her to describe it. She said it was green. I looked at the yellow stool, which I had put on the counter in full view of the door.

“Any chance it was yellow?” I asked.

“No,” she said. “I’ve had it twenty years. I know what colour it is.”

I took her number anyway. Ten minutes later she came in. She was wearing house slippers inside two supermarket bags, because it was raining and she hadn’t wanted to change her shoes.

“Yes,” she said, when she saw the stool. “That’s it.”

I asked her whether it had always been yellow.

“No idea,” she said. “It was my sister’s before I had it.”

I gave her the claim form. She picked up the pen and asked what the date was. I told her, then watched her write the date in the space for her name. She looked down at what she had done and crossed it out with such deliberate force that I heard the paper tear.

“My sister had another one,” she said. “A green one.”

She tucked the stool under her arm. I held the door for her. She made it halfway across the depot before turning and coming back.

“I can’t remember which stop I get off at,” she said.

She knew her address. It was on the other side of town, up a road I recognized because the buses could only go one way on it. We looked at the timetable together. I told her where to get off and wrote the name of the stop on the back of her claim receipt.

“Would you mind saying it again?” she asked.

I did. Then I walked her over to the bus. Manny had already gone home, but the driver knew me and said he’d give her a shout when they got there. She climbed aboard, took the seat nearest the front, and set the stool next to her with its legs pointing up. As I walked away I saw her put her hand around the short leg. She held it the way you hold the stem of a wineglass when someone’s trying to get past you at a crowded table.

At five I locked the office. Nobody asked for my key, so I kept it. The company offered me a job taking calls about late buses, and I took it. For the first few months people still asked to speak to the woman in lost property. It was hard to know what to say when they did. Sometimes I said, “You’re speaking to her,” and then we were both disappointed by what I could do.

Dad stopped asking what he owed me for the groceries. This happened because one Thursday I turned up with a loaf of bread and two pork chops and no carrots at all. He looked in the bag and asked whether I planned to stay. I said that depended on who was cooking. He took out a frying pan. The bread was stale by the time we got to the end of it, but he knew how to make it soft again, which involved running the loaf briefly under the tap and putting it in a hot oven. I’d have thrown it away.

Much later I had reason to go up the road where the woman with the stool lived. I won’t pretend I wasn’t looking for it. She’d given me a house number, but there were newer houses tucked in between the old ones, with letters after their numbers, and I couldn’t remember if hers had a letter. I slowed down at every gate. A man rinsing out a bucket asked whether I was looking for somebody. I said I used to work for the bus company. He waited a moment, then went back to rinsing his bucket.

At the corner, outside a narrow house with a blue door, there was a low wall that rose in three courses of brick beside the front steps. The top course ended about a foot short of the path. I stopped and looked at the space. You could set a stool there, with three legs on the path and the fourth on the brick. You could sit to tie your shoes or put down a bag while you looked for your keys. If the afternoon was warm, you could sit with your feet out and talk to anybody who happened to pass.

There was no stool. I had to catch myself from going up and knocking. I had no good question to ask anyone who might open the door.

The bus came back down the hill just as I reached the stop. It was early, for once, and I had to run. Inside it was too warm. Somebody had left a shopping list on the seat: eggs, washing powder, plums if good. I moved it over so I could sit by the window. Then I picked it up again to see if there was anything on the back. There wasn’t. I left it on the seat, flat this time, with the writing up.

samples.result:
# The Department of Minor Returns

The first thing anyone brought back was a door.

This was awkward because the sign above the counter said SMALL OBJECTS ONLY, and because the woman carrying the door had come on the bus. She had persuaded the driver to let her stand with it in the space reserved for folded strollers, on the grounds that it folded in a sense. She demonstrated by opening and closing it on one remaining hinge. The driver, who was late and had spent fifteen years learning which arguments would make him later, let her on.

“Where did you find it?” I asked.

“It’s mine,” she said.

“Then you don’t need us.”

“I know whose it was before it was mine. That’s the trouble.”

The door was painted yellow on one side and unpainted on the other. A little brass hook, too high for a child to reach, protruded from the frame. At the bottom was a black crescent where, the woman explained, a dog named Albert had once scratched to be let in.

“Is Albert the party you wish to return it to?”

She looked at me for a long time. I was twenty-three and still thought a joke could make most kinds of paperwork less humiliating.

“No,” she said. “Albert would have wanted to keep it.”

Our office occupied the old municipal baths, behind the library and below a clock that had been wrong for so long people gave directions by the wrongness. If you were meeting someone at noon, you could say, “When the baths say twenty past four,” and nobody would ask what you meant. The city had intended to put a youth orchestra in the building, then a court for parking appeals, then a museum devoted to the canal. What finally moved in was a woman named Ada, six metal shelves, and a budget line that could not, without amending an ordinance, be spent on anything other than returning property.

Ada was my supervisor. When I asked her what counted as property, she said, “If somebody comes looking for it, don’t start by telling them it doesn’t count.”

She came out from the back room and looked at the door.

“Do you have the house?” she asked the woman.

“Not anymore. They knocked it down on Thursday.”

“Do you have a name?”

“My sister’s. But we haven’t spoken in eleven years.”

Ada handed her our standard form. The woman filled in her sister’s name, her own phone number, and, in the box marked CONDITION, the words *better than you’d expect*. Then she went home on the same bus, in the same space, with her hands free. I watched from the window as she moved aside to let a man maneuver a stroller past her. She made a little flourish with both arms, as though she had herself invented the room he needed.

We leaned the door against the wall and put a numbered tag on the brass hook.

For a while we took in ordinary things. A set of dentures in a raspberry jam jar. A trumpet whose case contained, instead of a mouthpiece, eleven hard-boiled eggs. A photograph of a woman cutting the ribbon at the opening of a laundromat that still existed, though the woman did not. When I phoned the laundromat, the owner said she was his aunt and he would come on Saturday. He came on Tuesday. He stood at the counter touching the picture with one finger, just below his aunt’s shoes.

“I was there,” he said. “They made me hold the other end of the ribbon. I was furious they wouldn’t let me have the scissors.”

He kept looking. I began to wonder if he expected to see himself at the edge.

“Do you want an envelope?” I asked.

“No. I live over the shop. I’ll walk her home.”

That was our first completed return. Ada rang the little bell on the counter. Then she told me not to do it again unless we were both in the room; she didn’t want me to have all the fun.

The door stayed through winter. Sometimes I used its unpainted side as a clipboard, until Ada pointed out that I had pressed an impression of a set of dentures into the wood. We sent a postcard to the sister at the last address the woman knew. It came back marked NO SUCH NUMBER. I looked up the street and found that the numbers skipped from 16 to 20. Number 18 had disappeared into a driveway, and the house at 20 had a basketball hoop over its garage. You could see it on the city’s map. For months afterward, whenever I mailed something important, I caught myself picturing that hoop.

In February, a man brought in a red mitten. He had found it on the river path and attached it to a fence, where it remained for nine days. On the tenth day it rained. He took the mitten home and dried it over a radiator.

“Is there anything distinctive about it?” I asked, opening the ledger.

“It’s very small.”

“Anything else?”

“I used to buy them like this.”

He made a shape with his hands, indicating a child of intermediate size who might have been five or six. Then he put his hands in his pockets.

We did not find the owner of the mitten. In April he brought in a blue cap. In June, a tiny green shoe. He always stayed until I had written a description, and I began to understand that part of what mattered to him was watching the details go down. For the shoe, I wrote *one green canvas shoe, left, size seven, white rubber toe, considerably worn*. He asked me to change *considerably* to *a little*. I did. It made no difference to the prospects of a return, and by then I had learned to distinguish the rules Ada cared about from the ones I had invented because I liked the sound of my pen stopping.

My mother called every Sunday, usually while the kettle was on. She and my father had moved to a town where the grocery store sold frozen bait in the same freezer as the ice cream, which was her preferred example of how well they had adjusted. At some point in every call, she gave me a chance to report that I was leaving the baths for a better job.

“Anything on the horizon?” she would say.

There were a number of jobs I meant to apply for. I kept their descriptions in a folder on my desktop, sometimes after the closing dates, out of a reluctance I would have been hard put to explain. I liked coming in early and listening to Ada fill the kettle in the old dressing room. I liked how the pipes knocked when the heating came on. I also wanted a salary that would let me buy a winter coat without standing in the shop calculating my remaining days in the month. Mostly I wanted my mother to stop asking so I could tell her, without being asked, what I did all day.

One morning a boy of about twelve came in with nothing in his hands.

“I lost my brother’s laugh,” he said.

Ada had gone to the dentist. I was eating toast over the ledger, which she would not have allowed.

“When did you last have it?” I asked.

The boy pulled up a chair. His brother wasn’t dead, it turned out. He had moved two streets away with their father. They still saw one another, but the brother had developed a new laugh, an economical breath through his nose with which he acknowledged things on his phone. The old laugh was the one that came out when he tried not to laugh during dinner. It began, the boy said, with a sound like a duck being stepped on.

I didn’t open the ledger. It was clear to me that we couldn’t return a laugh, and pretty clear that the boy knew it, too.

“Can you do it?” I asked.

“No.”

He thought for a moment. Then he lowered his head and tried. The result was a rude little quack. From what he’d told me about the laugh, I imagined it wasn’t very close. But it was an excellent sound to hear in a tiled building at nine in the morning. I laughed, and so did he, though not in the way he had come in hoping to hear.

After he left, I tipped the toast crumbs out of the ledger into my palm. I did not make an entry. I’ve sometimes wished I had, because I can remember the brother’s laugh as described but can no longer remember the boy’s.

The letter telling us we were to close arrived in August, tucked into a shipment of stationery meant to last until the next financial year. Ada read it twice, worked the staple free with her thumbnail, and posted the second page on the front door. It explained that unclaimed objects would be transferred to central storage, pending appropriate disposal. The document had been written by someone who knew that *pending* was a good word to put before something nobody wanted to picture.

“How much time do we have?” I asked.

“Six weeks.”

“What are we going to do?”

“What we did yesterday. More urgently, I suppose.”

We moved the shelves into what had been the shallow end. With the objects laid out in daylight, they looked less like exhibits than the contents of an apartment whose tenant had stepped out in a great hurry. We found the owner of the trumpet; he said the eggs weren’t his. We found an engineer who could identify her own umbrella by the replacement screw in its handle, and an elderly woman who brought in the matching earring to one we’d held for a year. The two earrings lay together on the counter like shy cousins. Watching her put them on, I understood why she’d bothered. They made two very small flashes every time she turned her head.

I called the woman who had brought us the door. I must have sounded apologetic, because she interrupted to say it was all right, she knew her sister’s address.

“Since when?” I asked.

“Since before I brought it in.”

She told me where it was, in a town forty minutes away by train. She had written the old address on our form because it was the last one her sister had given her. The new one she knew from a nephew’s wedding invitation somebody had left face-up on a kitchen table.

“I was hoping you’d find her some other way,” she said.

I looked down the room at the door. In summer the yellow was almost too bright to look at, but a little rectangle below the handle, where an old sticker had been peeled away, was brighter still.

“Would you like the door back?” I asked.

“I want to know if she wants it.”

I said I could write and ask. The woman didn’t speak for a while. Then she asked whether I could send her whatever I wrote, so she could see it before it went out.

It took three drafts. In the first, I called the door an *item of possible sentimental significance*, which Ada crossed out so hard she tore the paper. In the second, I got halfway through explaining the circumstances under which we had obtained the door before noticing that I’d made it sound as though we had confiscated it. The one we sent said there was a yellow door at the municipal baths, that it had come from her old house, and that her sister had brought it to us. We would be open until the end of September. Here was our number.

The sister phoned the next day. Had it still got the brass hook? I said yes.

“Our mother put that up,” she said. “To stop the dog getting in. It didn’t stop him. He could get through if it was open even an inch. He’d lie down and push his nose into it.”

“Albert,” I said.

“No, before Albert. This was a much worse dog.”

She wanted to come on Friday. I asked if she wanted her sister to be there. She said she’d call her herself.

That Friday I wore a shirt without a missing button. This turned out to be the full extent of my involvement. The sisters met outside, where I couldn’t hear them. One held up a packet of biscuits for the other to see. After a while they came in together and stood at an angle to the door, as though waiting for someone on the other side to answer.

The sister who’d brought the door asked if we remembered what she’d written about its condition. I found the form. She read it aloud and they both laughed, although the other sister said, “Well, you would say that. You never could see a thing wrong with this color.”

“I picked that color,” the first sister said.

“I know.”

They stood looking at it a little longer. Neither of them had anywhere to put it. One lived in a narrow upstairs flat, the other in a house with doors that fit. We took it out to the pavement anyway, to see whether the fresh air would give anyone an idea. There it looked enormous.

In the end they took the brass hook. I fetched a screwdriver and held the frame while one sister worked the screws loose. She gave the hook to the other to hold, then went after the screws, which had rolled apart on the pavement. They left with the biscuits and the hardware in the same coat pocket. I propped the door against the counter one last time and rang the bell. Ada had to come out of the back room to ask what I thought I was doing.

“The hook,” I said.

“Oh,” she said. “Of course.”

On our final afternoon the man who had brought us the red mitten came in. I thought he might be looking for something new to hand over, but he wanted to know what would happen to the shoe. I explained about central storage. Then I asked if he wanted it. He looked startled, as if I had offered him one of my own.

“I wouldn’t know what to do with it,” he said.

We stood there awhile. In the end he went home without it. I was glad he’d come, though I still don’t know what he wanted me to tell him. Perhaps he’d hoped the shoe was already gone. I could have told him that, but the empty shelves behind me made it hard to say anything that wasn’t true.

The baths stood empty for seven years. When they reopened, as a branch library and community kitchen, I came down for the opening. The clock had been repaired. I arrived twenty minutes late, having gotten so used to subtracting them that I’d done it one last time.

Outside the kitchen was a long yellow bench. I went around behind it and put my hand under the seat. There, where you wouldn’t notice it unless you ran your fingers along the grain, was the little black crescent. I asked a volunteer where they’d gotten the wood. She said it had been lying in the building when they started work. There’d been just enough sound timber for a seat. They’d had to buy the legs.

I sat down. Through the open kitchen window I could hear someone hunting for scissors. A woman beside me was easing an orange out of a string bag. When she had peeled it, she offered me half, and I took it. It was colder than I’d expected, as though she had carried it all the way from her refrigerator just in time to share it with a stranger. I held the peel for her while she ate. Then we went inside to see if anyone had found the scissors.
