samples.result:
# The Sound of a Room With Someone in It

The first thing I learned at the Bureau of Unclaimed Sounds was how to open a bottle without hearing what was inside it. You held it under a thick felt cloth, turned the stopper a quarter inch, and waited for a little tug against your thumb. Then you let the stopper settle back. The tug meant there was still something in the bottle. If you didn’t feel it, you wrote EMPTY on the label and put the bottle in a crate for washing.

This was not as simple as it sounded. A bottle containing the last good laugh at a wedding might pull hard enough to bruise you. A bottle containing a man saying *I know* to his own reflection might barely pull at all. For my first three weeks, I wore a thumb splint and sent a great deal of despair to be washed.

My supervisor, Viv, said this was normal.

“In July,” she said, “we get a student.”

It was April. I understood that I was not to think of myself as temporary.

The Bureau occupied the basement of the central library, underneath the travel section. A surprising number of people came down looking for Italy. In a way, we had more of Italy than the travel section did: the bell above a bakery door in Bari, the elastic slap of wet bathing suits against a balcony in Genoa, seventeen versions of a particular whistle made by a particular grandfather in a village outside Lucca. But we couldn’t give anyone a route to Florence. We directed people back up the stairs.

What we kept were sounds that had gone astray. Most sounds finish exactly where they should. A spoon strikes a saucer; someone hears it; the matter is concluded. But a spoon can strike a saucer just as the person across the table finishes reading a letter. The sound lands a little too late. Nobody takes it in. Years later, when the café is being rewired, an electrician finds it wedged behind a baseboard.

The city distributed collection jars to its tradespeople. Plumbers brought in the best things and wanted the least credit.

One Monday a plumber named Fay brought us an onion jar with a square of masking tape on the lid. On it she had written: SECOND FLOOR, BACK BEDROOM, 18 MERCER.

“I nearly left it,” she said. “It came out when I took the radiator off. I thought it was the radiator.”

“What is it?”

“If I knew that, I’d have written it on the lid.”

She took a ginger biscuit from the tin Viv kept beside the intake forms. Fay was entitled to three biscuits per delivery, an arrangement she had negotiated herself and which we were forbidden to call a payment.

Eighteen Mercer was my father’s house. Or it had been. Six weeks earlier, after ninety minutes of signatures in a room with an artificial orchid, it had become the property of a dentist named Helen. Helen had two children and had asked whether the upstairs carpet was wool. I told her I didn’t know. Then I went home and looked up how to determine whether a carpet was wool, which involves setting a little of it on fire. I was glad I hadn’t known.

Fay ate a second biscuit and put the third in her coat pocket.

“Does he still live there?” she asked.

“No,” I said.

She nodded. She knew he had died. She was offering me a question I could answer without saying it.

By regulation, when a member of staff recognized an address, the jar had to be passed to another member of staff. I put it on Viv’s blotter. She finished peeling an orange, wiped her hands, and took down the red ledger.

“Anything you want me to know before I open it?”

“He was alone in the house for a while.”

“How long?”

“Twenty years, more or less.”

“I meant toward the end.”

“So did I.”

This was unfair to my father, who had friends and a standing Thursday lunch with a woman called Penny. It was also unfair to Penny, who had telephoned me on the morning he died and then, because I was on a train, telephoned again to tell me to get off at the right station. I had never thanked her for the second call. I had been considering staying on the train to the coast.

Viv took the jar into the listening room. I heard her chair scrape. The room was soundproof except for that particular scrape, which had got into the wall years ago and made itself heard whenever it liked.

When she came out she had written a description on a yellow card.

INTERIOR. ONE PERSON PRESENT. NO SPEECH.

“You have first claim,” she said. “If you want it.”

“I don’t remember what the rules are about family.”

“You remember all the rules about family. You typed them up last Tuesday.”

I took the yellow card. In the space marked DURATION she had written eleven seconds.

My father and I spoke on Sundays. This had not always been the arrangement. It began when I moved across town and discovered that forty minutes on a bus could, if properly managed, become a distance as insurmountable as the Atlantic. At first we called each other whenever we had something to say. Later we called on Sundays. I don’t remember who proposed this, but I remember the relief of having arrived at terms.

A typical Sunday call went like this: he told me what he had bought at the market, and I told him what I ought to buy at the market. He asked how much I had paid for something. I told him less than I had paid. Then sometimes, when we had exhausted what could be pretended about vegetables, one of us said something we had meant to keep to ourselves.

Once he told me that after my mother left, he had walked around for a year with a library book in his bag because he liked to imagine she might call and ask him to meet her somewhere, and he didn’t want to have to sit there doing nothing while he waited.

“Did you read it?” I asked.

“Twice. It wasn’t much good.”

I waited for him to tell me the title. He wanted me to ask. I knew that and still didn’t ask, for reasons I could not have explained even then. On Sundays I sometimes rationed my interest, as if I were afraid he would notice how much I had.

I put the yellow card in my pocket and left the jar on Viv’s desk.

“You can take it home,” she said.

I told her I didn’t have a place for it.

Two days later Helen came in. She found the basement without asking for Italy. She wore a long raincoat with a bright blue lining and carried a glass measuring cup in a paper bag.

“Fay says this belongs to you,” she said.

It was my father’s measuring cup, the one with the numbers rubbed off above the half-pint mark. I had left it in the bathroom on purpose. On the last morning, I’d gone from room to room with a bin bag, disposing of lightbulbs too dim to be worth keeping and socks nobody would wear again. In the bathroom I found the measuring cup by the sink. He used it to rinse his hair. I washed it, dried it inside and out, and put it back precisely where I had found it. I’d had the idea that the new family might use it for the same thing.

“Thank you,” I said.

“We would have kept it, only there are no numbers on it.”

“There are some numbers.”

“Yes,” she said. “I suppose there are.”

I could see her deciding whether to tell me something. I assumed it would be a defect in the house. I prepared to defend the drains.

“My daughter likes the back bedroom,” she said. “She says it’s the only room where she can hear the rain without seeing it.”

“Has she got the bed under the window?”

“She’s got it along the other wall.”

For twenty years I had considered that the wrong wall. I tried, briefly and with real effort, to imagine putting my childhood bed against it. Then I realized I’d already done so. My father had moved it there when I had pneumonia at nine because the window was drafty. I remembered the wardrobe on my left, where it had no business being. On the day I went back to school he moved the bed to its old position, and I had been cross with him for deciding I was well.

Helen said she ought to go. It was raining. As she reached the stairs, I asked if I could see the room sometime.

“Of course,” she said. Then she came back to the desk and took out her phone. “Would Saturday actually work? If we don’t pick a day, I’ll forget, and you’ll think I was just saying it.”

On Saturday I carried the onion jar to Mercer Street in a padded lunch bag. I hadn’t listened to it. On the bus I kept fitting my hand between the jar and the bag’s foil lining whenever we turned a corner.

Helen’s daughter was called Bea. She was twelve and not particularly pleased to meet me. Her mother had asked her to tidy the bedroom out of respect for my feelings, which from Bea’s perspective was a novel and unwelcome extension of my rights as the former occupant.

“You don’t have to show me anything,” I told her.

“I already put it all away.”

This seemed to settle the matter in favor of a tour. She showed me the desk where my father had kept his shirts and the small square on the wall where a sticker had taken off the paint. I said the sticker had been a frog. She said she liked the square better, and after a moment I found I did too.

“Do you want a minute?” Helen called from the landing.

“No,” I said, too quickly.

Bea sat down on her bed. A red charging cable trailed from beneath the pillow. There was a library book on the floor, open facedown. I could have read the title from where I stood. Instead I told them about the jar.

“Can you tell what they’re thinking?” Bea asked.

“No. Sometimes you can’t even tell what they’re doing.”

“Then how do you know it’s him?”

I said that I didn’t. This was the first time I had considered the possibility that the person in the jar was me.

I took it out of the bag. There was still a trace of onion smell around the lid. Helen asked if we should close the door, and Bea said yes, before her brother came upstairs and started making noises on purpose. Then Bea put her phone facedown on the bed, and I opened the jar.

For the first few seconds I thought Viv had made a mistake, that there was nobody present at all. There was the sound a room makes when the windows are shut and the door is open a little, a difference in the air that has no pitch but is there to be heard. A pipe ticked twice. Then somebody turned a page.

A faint roughness followed: a fingertip traveling down the edge of the paper. My father stroked the pages of books while he read. At family meals, when somebody else was telling a long story, he did it to the paper napkins. It used to drive my mother mad. I’d forgotten that. I was glad to remember it, and then, to my surprise, I was glad it had driven her mad. She had sat through a lot of long stories, with that faint noise coming from the end of the table, and sometimes a person wants to eat dinner without being asked to endure another tiny thing.

The sound ended with a bit of fabric shifting. I waited for more. I had spent eleven seconds in anticipation of the part I could tell somebody about afterward.

“Was that it?” Bea asked.

“Yes,” I said.

She picked up her phone, then set it down again.

“He must’ve been quite still.”

“He was good at that.”

What came to me then was not a scene from childhood. It was a Tuesday two summers earlier. I had been in the middle of something at work and had phoned my father because I needed to know the name of a man who had lived next door to us. He told me the name, and I said I had to go. Before I hung up I heard him say, “Oh, all right.” I had thought about that *oh* many times since his death. I’d pictured him sitting by the phone in the middle of a long day, getting up after I hung up with nowhere in particular to go. But now it seemed possible he had put down the phone and gone back to a book. Perhaps I’d interrupted him in a good part.

I put the lid on the jar. Downstairs Helen made tea. Bea came into the kitchen and asked where the measuring cup with no numbers had gone, because it poured better than the new one. I said I’d bring it back. On the bus home I kept my lunch bag on the seat beside me until a man got on with a folding shopping trolley. I put the bag on my lap and the man sat down. He smelled faintly of a swimming pool. For a while we both watched the same dog running along a fence, and when the bus got too far ahead of it he leaned forward to see if there was a gap at the other end. There was. The dog emerged at a trot, as if it had known all along where it was going.

In July we got a student. Her name was Sal and she had previously worked at an ice rink. She was better at opening bottles than I was. She could distinguish by touch between a shoe being tied and a shoelace breaking. After a fortnight, Viv entrusted her with the cupboard of disputed birds.

One afternoon a man arrived with a sample jar wrapped in a tea towel. He had found it on a high shelf while clearing out his mother’s kitchen. Her handwriting was on the label: THE SOUND OF A ROOM WITH SOMEONE IN IT.

“Can you check if there’s anything there?” he asked. “I opened it at home and couldn’t hear a thing.”

I brought out the felt cloth and loosened the lid beneath it. The tug was so slight I could easily have taken it for the pulse in my thumb. I tried a second time, holding the jar in my other hand.

“There’s something,” I said. “Would you like to use the listening room?”

He looked at the jar.

“Could somebody come in with me?”

I went with him. We sat side by side at the little table. He unwrapped the tea towel and spread it beneath the jar. It was a souvenir towel from a seaside town, printed with a map. A stain obscured part of the harbor.

When he opened the jar, we heard a woman set down a cup. There was a pause, then the small, dry click of a second cup touching the first. The man kept his hand on the lid. Neither of us moved to put it back on. Overhead, a library cart passed across the travel section and caught, as it always did, on the strip of metal between the carpet and the tile. I knew the sound well enough to tell you where it happened: just past the end of the shelf, where for years a chair had stood by a window. Sometimes somebody moved the chair to get a better look outside. Sometimes they turned it around so there would be a place for another person to sit.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
The first thing I ever fixed for money was a toaster that didn’t need fixing. Mrs. Vale brought it in wrapped in a beach towel. I plugged it into the wall behind my counter, put in two slices of bread, and waited. Out came toast.

“That’s what it does here,” she said.

I was twenty-three and had just painted REPAIRS on the window. I explained that appliances did not behave differently according to where they were. Mrs. Vale listened politely, then asked whether I had ever met a dog.

At her house, the toaster behaved exactly as she had described: it stayed down until the bread burned. The kitchen floor sloped toward the garden, and Mrs. Vale had put a folded beer mat under one foot of the toaster to make it sit level. It was the beer mat that jammed the lever. I trimmed it with scissors, and she gave me five pounds and the toast, which she scraped over the sink before buttering.

For years afterward, whenever I was about to tell somebody that what they said could not possibly be happening, I thought of Mrs. Vale. Sometimes I told them anyway. I was not a naturally wise person. I had just accumulated a useful number of occasions on which I had been wrong.

By the time I turned sixty, people mostly brought me lamps. You could still open a lamp. And on Wednesday evenings, after I closed the shop, I took the number six bus to my sister Ruth’s house for supper. If I sat on the left, I could see her kitchen from the bend in the road. She always left the oven light on, even when we were having salad. I once asked her why and she said she liked to check whether it had come on.

“Whether what had come on?”

“The oven light.”

This was the sort of conversation we had got very good at since her husband died. We could make an evening out of almost anything, provided neither of us said what we were doing.

In October a notice appeared inside the bus, just above the rack where people left newspapers for each other. From the first of November, the six would terminate at Bell Street. The last four stops would no longer be served. Ruth lived at the third of those stops, and the fourth was the little turning circle at the cemetery.

That Wednesday, everybody read the notice as they boarded. Mr. Akhtar, who rode as far as the swimming baths, moved his lips all the way through it. A boy in a school blazer took a photograph. One woman pressed the bell almost immediately afterward, though her stop was still a mile away. The driver, whose name was Pat, pulled over.

“Sorry,” the woman said. “I don’t know why I did that.”

“Take your time,” Pat said, and we all sat there for a few seconds while the woman decided whether to get off. She stayed.

At supper I told Ruth I could walk from Bell Street.

“You could,” she said. “In June.”

“It’s only twenty minutes.”

“Then I’ll walk the other twenty minutes to your shop.”

We ate in silence for a while. The meal was chicken thighs with rice and the soft carrots Ruth liked. I preferred them with some resistance, but that was a preference I exercised in my own home.

“What about the people who go to the cemetery?” she asked.

“They could write a letter.”

“You’re a person who goes to the cemetery.”

I put my knife down. Her husband, Alan, was buried there. So were our parents. Ruth went every Sunday, and I went when I had something particular to tell one of them, which was not often enough to claim any inconvenience.

“I’ll write one,” I said.

“Good. You can do it while I wash up.”

I wrote three paragraphs on a sheet torn from her shopping pad. Ruth dried her hands to read them, then crossed out *vital lifeline*. She said if I wanted someone to believe me, I should tell them where I went.

So I wrote that I went to supper at my sister’s on Wednesdays. I added the times of the buses I took there and back. Then I left the letter on the table while I went to find my coat. When I came back, Ruth had written, underneath my name, *I am the sister*, and signed hers.

The reply arrived nine days later. The decision, it said, had been made after a review of passenger numbers. An average of 1.8 passengers remained on board after Bell Street. I read this figure to Ruth over the phone.

“Which bit of you doesn’t come to supper?” she asked.

I appealed to Pat the following Wednesday. She was standing beside the bus at the depot end of the route, eating a pear before she opened the doors. I had come early because I thought she might tell me the review had taken place during the school holidays, or that the counting machine didn’t work. Instead she said the numbers sounded right. Some runs she took nobody past Bell Street at all. She turned the bus at the cemetery and drove back empty.

“Does it bother you?” I asked.

“The turning circle doesn’t,” she said. “It’s a lovely turning circle.”

She ate the rest of the pear, right down to the seeds.

“There’s a woman gets on at the cemetery on Sundays,” she said. “Always asks if it’s the last bus. Never wants to be told the time of the next one. Just wants to know that one isn’t the last.”

I asked if she meant Ruth. Pat said she didn’t know anyone’s name unless they’d left something behind.

A few days later a young woman came into the shop carrying a lamp shaped like a heron. The bulb went between its feet, so that when you switched it on the bird looked startled by something it had just caught. She said there was no hurry; she was moving, and the man who had given her the lamp might or might not move with her. Depending on what happened, she might come back for it or ask me to throw it away. I told her the switch would cost four pounds.

“It’s not really about the switch,” she said.

“No,” I said. “But I can do the switch.”

After she left, I tore a piece of cardboard off a box and wrote WHERE DO YOU GO ON THE SIX? I propped it in the window with a pad of paper and a jar of pens just inside the door. If nobody came in, I thought, at least I would have made a sign. Making a sign was one of the few stages of a public campaign for which I already had the equipment.

The first person to answer was the postman. He didn’t go anywhere on the six. He wanted to know if I knew someone who would buy a clarinet. The next person was a woman I recognised from the bus, though we had never spoken. She wrote for almost ten minutes, shielding the pad with her hand. When she left, I looked down and saw that she had drawn a map. It showed Bell Street, her house, and the hill between them. Halfway up the hill she had drawn a rectangle and labelled it *wall I can sit on if dry*.

Other people wrote down journeys that had nothing to do with the four stops. The boy in the blazer said he went to his dad’s. A man wrote *anywhere as long as the top front seat is free*, though the six was a single-decker. Three people wanted the old route back, by which they meant three different routes. Some had understood my sign to be a question, others a petition, and one a request for directions. I kept the page on which someone had written, in large capitals, TURN LEFT AT THE CHEMIST. It had the advantage of being immediately useful.

I sent copies to the council and received a friendly email from a woman named Leanne. She said she would pass them on. I believed she would. I had expected to find it harder to be angry with an impersonal organisation once I knew the name of a person inside it, but it turned out I could be quite angry with the council and still hope Leanne was having a nice lunch.

On the last Wednesday in October, Ruth asked me to stay until the late bus instead of taking my usual one. She had bought a pudding that needed forty minutes in the oven. While it cooked, she told me she was thinking of selling the house.

“You said you’d never move,” I said.

“I said I’d never move the piano. The piano can stay.”

Neither Ruth nor Alan had played it. They had bought it at an auction twenty years before because nobody else bid. When we were children, Ruth used to bring home sweaters she found in the school lost property box, on the grounds that if she left them there they would never get washed. Our mother made her take them back, but only after washing them.

“Where would you go?” I asked.

“I don’t know yet. I’ve only just told you.”

The pudding was still cold in the middle when we cut it. The oven light had come on but the oven, as it happened, had not. We ate the warm part at the edges and put the rest back in. Then Ruth got her coat. She wanted to ride the late bus with me.

“You’ll have to get back somehow,” I said.

“I’m aware of the situation.”

At the stop we waited under a streetlamp with a low, irregular flicker. Ruth said she hadn’t been on a bus at night since Alan was alive. I asked where they had gone.

“To get his car,” she said. “He’d left it at the garage. We got there and the garage was shut. There wasn’t a bus back for an hour, so we went to the pub, where he spent the entire time insisting he knew perfectly well it would be shut.”

“Did he?”

“Of course not. He’d brought the spare keys.”

She laughed, and then she kept her face turned toward the road for long enough that I began to study the streetlamp. It flickered twice, held steady, and flickered again. When the bus came, Ruth held out her hand to signal it, though we were plainly the only reason it was stopping.

Pat was driving. There were four other people on board, including the woman who had drawn the map. She had a bag of groceries on the seat beside her and moved it to let Ruth sit down. I sat across the aisle. At Bell Street nobody got off. The woman with the groceries asked Pat whether she planned to go straight on from there next week.

“I go round the roundabout and back,” Pat said.

“So you don’t get a break?”

“I get seven minutes at the roundabout.”

“Where do you go to the loo?”

“Nowhere in seven minutes.”

The woman considered this. “I’d write a letter about that.”

When we reached my stop, Ruth got off with me. It was cold, and I told her she could wait in the shop while I rang for a taxi. But she said she’d walk home from Bell Street. She had brought a torch. We stood on the pavement while Pat waited, both of us assuming the other would say whatever needed saying before Ruth got back on.

“Do you want me to look at the oven?” I asked at last.

“Yes,” she said. “But not tonight.”

The next Wednesday I shut the shop early and walked from Bell Street. I had dressed too warmly. By the time I reached the wall marked on the map, I was carrying my coat. The wall was dry, so I sat on it. From there I could see into a house where a little girl in pyjamas was practising the recorder. I couldn’t hear her through the glass, but I could tell she was making mistakes by the way she kept lowering the recorder to look at it.

A car slowed. It was the woman who had drawn the map, in the passenger seat of a small white hatchback. Her daughter was driving. They offered me a lift, and I took it, though Ruth’s house was only another five minutes away. The daughter said that from now on she would take her mother shopping on Wednesdays. Her mother said that was very kind, but she liked to go on Fridays. For the rest of the ride they discussed Fridays in the tentative, exacting way people discuss a date for surgery.

Ruth had made sandwiches. I took the back off the oven while she ate hers at the counter. There was a fault I could see and another I suspected. I told her not to use it until I could get the part. Then I asked if she wanted me to come with her on Sunday.

“To the cemetery?”

“Yes.”

“You can. But you don’t have to stand there the whole time.”

On Sunday it rained. We went in a taxi and took longer than expected because Ruth stopped to pull wet leaves off the stones of people she didn’t know. At Alan’s grave she bent down and set a supermarket bunch of carnations in the holder. There was already water in it. She poured some out so it wouldn’t overflow.

I walked over to the turning circle. Pat was right. It was a good one, wide and clear, with a view over a field where two horses were eating close together on opposite sides of a fence. There was a shelter, too, with room for three people on the bench if they didn’t mind touching. The timetable had been removed, but I could still see the clean oblong where it had been. I stood there a little longer than I needed to. In the rain it was pleasant to have a roof, even a roof that had lost its reason for being there.

By Christmas Ruth had looked at two flats and decided against both. The young woman came back for the heron. She had moved without the man, and I was prepared to hear that she no longer wanted the lamp. Instead she asked if I had a box. The heron would go by the front door, she said. In the new place there was no switch within reach when you came in, and she kept catching her foot on the mat.

I gave her a box and showed her where I had put the new switch, a broad one she could step on in the dark. She tried it out twice. Then she paid me, tucked the lamp under her arm, and went to catch the six.

It was nearly closing time. On the pavement I found one of the pens from the jar, washed down against the step after a day of rain. I brought it in and tested it on the back of the sign. It wrote at once.

I had been meaning to take the sign down. The papers were still there, curling at the edges, and the council had sent a second reply, much like the first. I turned the cardboard over. After a moment I wrote my sister’s new telephone number on it. She hadn’t moved house. She had got a mobile phone, and so far she had called me from the garden, the upstairs landing, and once from just outside her own front door, to ask whether I could hear her through the letterbox.

I could, I’d told her. But she ought to come in.

samples.result:
# The Spare Key

The first thing I found in my father’s coat was a receipt for six lemons. The second was a key with a paper tag that said NOT THE SHED.

He had been dead for twelve days, and I was beginning to resent how funny he could still be.

The coat hung in the back hall, where it had hung every November through March for as long as I could remember. It was brown, with a corduroy collar and a burn on one sleeve from the year he tried to teach himself to weld. My mother had died three winters earlier. Since then he had started buying his own clothes, mostly at the farm supply store. Whenever I complimented a shirt, he would tell me how much it cost. Whenever I didn’t, he would tell me anyway.

I put the key in my pocket and took the coat out to the car. Then I brought it back inside. I had been doing a lot of that.

My brother, Nick, was coming on Saturday with his van. We had agreed that he would take the furniture and I would deal with the papers. What he meant by *the furniture* was the good table and perhaps the bed. What he meant by *the papers* was everything else in the house, declining in size until we reached, at last, the pin that held two spare buttons to a card.

At eleven someone knocked on the back door.

It was a woman in a blue raincoat, holding half a cake on a plate.

“Is this a bad time?” she asked.

I told her that it was not a particularly good one, but that I had no reason to expect improvement.

She looked at me closely. “You must be Helen.”

The woman’s name was Ruth. She lived on Daley Street and worked at the pharmacy. I knew neither of these things until she told me. She knew that I lived in Leeds, that I taught geography, that I had once backed my father’s car into a water butt, and that I had a son who had been born with six fingers on his left hand.

“Five now,” I said.

“Yes,” she said. “Your dad gave me updates.”

She put the cake on the counter. One side had been cut cleanly down the middle, and icing sagged over the exposed edge.

“I’d have brought the whole thing, but I didn’t know I was going to bring any of it until I’d started eating.”

I got out two plates.

My father, it turned out, had kept a key for Ruth. On Monday a man was coming to service her boiler, and she couldn’t find her own spare. She had let her ex-husband have it when he moved out, so he could come back for his bicycle. The bicycle was still in the kitchen, but the spare key had moved with him to Hull.

“Which is the sort of thing he’s very good at,” she said. “Moving something that isn’t the thing you asked him to move.”

I took the key out of my pocket.

“Not mine,” she said. “Mine’s got one of those rubber hats on it. Green.”

We tried the biscuit tin in the hall. My father had kept keys there since my childhood, though none of us had ever called it the key tin. Inside were two golf tees, a small plastic cow, and twenty-three keys.

Three wore green hats.

“Well,” Ruth said, “I’ve been thinking I should get to know the neighbours.”

We spread the contents of the tin over the kitchen table. Some of the keys had labels. BOAT, said one. We lived forty miles from the sea, and my father had distrusted rivers on the grounds that you could never see what they were up to. Another said MARGARET—ASK FIRST. Margaret was my mother. A third said simply OH DEAR.

Ruth held up a narrow brass key.

“That might be the church.”

“Did he go to church?”

“Not in a religious capacity.”

“What other capacity is there?”

“He lowered a carpet cleaner down the cellar stairs on a rope once.”

I waited for the rest of the story. Ruth ate another bite of cake. Apparently that was the whole thing.

She took a green key at random and went home to try it. It worked. She rang to tell me, then rang again a minute later to ask if I’d found a wooden clothes peg among the keys. There was a woman called Jean, she said, who might want one of them back.

“Why a clothes peg?”

“Your dad said she never remembered the colour of her front door. I think he was making fun of her.”

The peg was at the bottom of the tin, firmly attached to a key.

“Red door,” Ruth added. “I don’t know why she’s got such trouble with it.”

By two o’clock I had eaten another piece of cake and made a list.

1. Ruth, green.
2. Jean, peg.
3. Boat?
4. Margaret.

I had planned to spend the afternoon separating my father’s bank statements from the offers to lend him money. Instead I walked over to Jean’s. I had lived in the town until I was eighteen. I could remember where the drains flooded, which gardens had once contained dogs, and the exact location of a public telephone that had been removed in 2003. I had no idea where any of the people lived.

Jean answered her red door wearing slippers with hard soles. She took the key, examined the peg, and said, “I wondered where that went.”

She meant the peg. It was one of a set made by her grandson in a woodworking class. He had carved a J into each half. One J was backwards.

“What happened to the others?”

“Most of them broke. He was only little.”

She turned the peg over a few times and asked if I’d like a cup of tea. I said I had better keep moving. At that point I still imagined I was running an errand.

BOAT belonged to a man named Arthur, who had built a canoe in a lockup behind the carpet shop. The canoe was too wide to get out. He knew this because my father had measured it for him. He had known it, in fact, for nine years.

“You could take the doorframe off,” I said.

“Oh, we considered it.”

“Or tip the canoe on its side?”

“Yes, we considered that too. Would you like to see it?”

He meant the canoe. I went with him to the lockup. It was pale and glossy and much prettier than I had expected. Arthur couldn’t tell me what kind of wood he’d used without telling me first about the man who sold it to him, and the man who sold it to him turned out to have a daughter I’d shared a desk with in primary school. By the time we got back to Arthur’s house I had learned that the canoe would fit through the door if Arthur took off the two handles he’d fitted to carry it by. It had taken him three weekends to make the handles. He wasn’t ready.

“Your dad used to come and sit in it,” he said at the gate.

“On the ground?”

“Yes, Helen. On the ground. Where did you think he sat in it?”

I hadn’t thought my father sat in a canoe at all. The one time I’d asked him to come boating with me, on a small ornamental lake with a café in the middle, he said if I wanted him to pay nine pounds for coffee I could at least give it to him on land.

“Did he get in properly?” I asked. “Legs all the way inside?”

“Of course. We both got in. I was at the back.”

There was no way to ask what I wanted to ask without sounding like an idiot. *What did he look like in there? Was he happy? Where did he put his hands?* Arthur had already given me everything he thought there was to give.

At home I turned on the kitchen light. It was only four, but the lawn had gone the greenish grey it went before rain. I took the key marked MARGARET—ASK FIRST to the small bureau in the sitting room. My mother had answered correspondence there. She owned three fountain pens, one of which worked. When I was a child she used to give me her airmail envelopes to hold up to the light, so I could see how little paper there was between our street and Melbourne.

The key didn’t fit.

I tried the little tin box where she’d kept foreign coins, then the old writing case upstairs. I tried the cabinet in the bathroom although it had no lock. I was standing on the landing holding the key against a screw head, which is how far I’d got with things, when Nick let himself in.

“You said Saturday,” I called.

“It is Saturday.”

He came upstairs in his work boots and sat on the top step. There was a white strip of skin on his wrist where he usually wore his watch.

“I left the van running,” he said.

“Why?”

“I don’t know. I suppose I thought I’d come in and you’d be standing next to a table.”

I sat down beside him and showed him the key.

“That’s for the little padlock on the back gate,” he said.

“There isn’t a padlock on the back gate.”

“There was when he wanted to cut down her lilac.”

I remembered the lilac. I didn’t remember anyone wanting to cut it down. By the time I started coming home with a child of my own, the lilac was gone, and there was a place beside the gate where my father could stand with his arms full and push it open with his shoulder.

“She locked it so he couldn’t get the wheelbarrow through,” Nick said. “I was here that weekend. I’d come for the drill.”

“Did you get it?”

“No. I got a cup of tea from each of them in a different room.”

For a while we listened to the van running. Eventually Nick went out and turned it off. When he came back we moved the table six inches, discovered the rug underneath was a different colour where nobody had walked on it, and put the table back. Then he fetched two mugs from the cupboard, chose one without a chip for himself, reconsidered, and gave it to me.

I could tell from the size of his van that he’d hoped to bring the table home. I could also tell that he had not cleared a place for it. His wife would have asked him where it was going, and he would have said, with the unreasonable confidence he generally reserved for household acquisitions, *I’ll find somewhere.*

“Did you want the table?” I asked.

“Yes. Not today.”

I told him about Arthur’s canoe. He didn’t laugh at first.

“Dad was in it?”

“Apparently they both got in.”

“Which end was he?”

“The front.”

“Right,” Nick said. “So he had to get past Arthur to get out.”

This was the first thing anyone had said about the canoe that took proper account of our father, who couldn’t sit in the middle of a row at the cinema. Even if the room was empty he wanted the aisle. I pictured him in the lockup with his feet stretched out, not asking Arthur to move.

Nick took the cake plate over to the sink. There was a thin curl of icing left at the edge, and he scraped it up with his thumb.

“Have you tried that key in the shed?” he asked.

I showed him the tag.

“Yes,” he said, “but have you?”

We went out in the rain. The key slid into the shed lock as easily as if we’d done this every day. I turned it; the door swung in and caught on a bag of compost. Nick pushed hard enough to get his head through and found the light.

The shed had a concrete floor and smelt of cold soil. There were four screwdrivers stuck upright in a flowerpot, though I had spent nearly an hour looking for one in the house. A bicycle pump hung off a nail. Along one wall my father had put up shelves and written directly on the wood in pencil: string, washers, good jars. Beneath *good jars* there was a single jar, with a crack running from the rim nearly to the base.

Nick pulled a garden chair out from under the bench and opened it. One of the straps had been replaced with a length of old belt. He sat down and looked at his feet.

“He always made me fetch the chairs,” he said.

“He made everyone fetch the chairs.”

“No, I mean when he came round to ours. He never sat down until I’d brought another one out for him. Even if there were already chairs.”

“Were the others any good?”

“Of course they were. I’d just bought them.” Nick picked at the old belt. “They were those low ones, though.”

I sat on the bag of compost. Rain on the shed roof made the room feel smaller. At first there was the sort of quiet in which I expected Nick to start talking, and then he didn’t, and I stopped expecting it. From where I sat I could see the lower half of the garden through the open door. The big slab we’d used for hopscotch was grey except for a hand’s width under the eaves, where it was white. The rain was getting in at one corner of the roof. A single drop landed on the back of my wrist. I moved my hand.

“Who do you think he was trying to fool?” I said, holding up the tag.

“Us, probably.”

“He didn’t have anything worth stealing.”

“Maybe he just wanted us to knock.”

We went through the rest of the keys after supper. Nick recognised the old garage key by a nick he had filed in it himself, at fourteen, so that he could find it in his pocket without turning on a light. We established that there were five keys to the back door, one to a bicycle lock in the canal, and at least two that had belonged to cars with windows you wound down by hand.

OH DEAR turned out to be a bottle opener. Once you knew, there was nothing else it could possibly be.

On Monday morning I washed Ruth’s cake plate and took it over. The boiler man had his head inside a cupboard. The bicycle was still in the kitchen, with a tea towel draped over the saddle. Ruth had made lemon curd and gave me a jar.

“Your dad brought me the lemons,” she said. “I told him to get four and he brought six. He said two of them looked a bit small.”

I wanted to know whether he’d carried them over in the paper bag or tucked them into his coat. I wanted to know if the lemons had rolled about on the counter and he’d had to stop one with his hand. I could have asked Ruth and she might have remembered. But the boiler man called out to ask her a question, and while she bent to look inside the cupboard I put the jar in my bag and let myself out.

Before I left town, I went to see Arthur again. I’d been thinking about the handles.

“They don’t have to come off forever,” I said. “You can put them back on outside.”

He gave me a long look. “Yes, I understand how screws work.”

I told him I could come back the following weekend. Nick could bring the van. We might be able to take the canoe somewhere.

“Where?”

I hadn’t got that far. There was a reservoir north of town, but I didn’t know whether you could put a boat on it. There was the ornamental lake with the café, if we could stand the looks we’d get from the man who rented out the pedal boats.

“Or just outside,” I said. “We could start with outside.”

Arthur put on his shoes. We walked down to the lockup and stood there looking at the canoe. He ran his fingers over one of the handles, and I saw why it had taken him three weekends. It was wide enough to get your whole hand through, with room left over, and rounded where your palm would go. The ends fitted so closely to the side of the boat that I couldn’t tell how they’d been joined.

“Show me how you did that,” I said.

He looked about for somewhere we could sit. There was a folding stool by the door, but only one. So he held the canoe steady while I stepped in, then passed me the stool to set on the floor beside us, where he could put his tea. I sat at the front. From down there I couldn’t see the handles at all. Arthur reached over my shoulder and showed me where to put my hand.

# The Number at the End of the Pier

The telephone at the end of Bellwether Pier had been disconnected for eleven years when it rang.

Nina was kneeling beside the fish-cleaning station, trying to persuade a rusted bolt to turn. She heard the first ring and thought it was a gull doing a good impression of something. At the second, she put down her wrench. By the third, she was inside the booth with the receiver to her ear.

“Jo?” a man said. “I’ve got the cake, but there’s a dog in the car.”

“What kind of dog?”

It was the question she would later regret asking first. There were so many better ones.

“Brown,” the man said. “I don’t think it’s a particular kind.”

Behind his voice she could hear the papery tick of a turn signal.

“You’ve got the wrong number,” Nina said.

“Is this not the pier?”

“It’s the pier.”

“Well, can you look around for Jo? She’ll be wearing a yellow coat. Tell her I’m at the roundabout and I can’t get the dog out without letting it into traffic.”

Nina stepped out of the booth. The pier was empty except for a gull examining the place where she’d put down her wrench.

“There’s no one here,” she said.

The man was silent for a moment. “Would you tell her I tried, anyway?”

Then the line went dead.

Nina hadn’t written down the time, but the call must have lasted less than a minute. When she thought about it that evening, though, it seemed to contain an unreasonable amount of weather. In the booth she’d smelled the wet wool of somebody else’s coat. The man had sounded warm, as if his car heater was on too high. Outside, it had been June, and she’d been working in her shirtsleeves.

---

Nina ran a hardware shop in Bellwether. Fixing things on the pier wasn’t her job; it was how she spent Wednesday mornings since her mother died. For most of her adult life she had spent them taking her mother to appointments. Now, when Wednesday came, she still found herself opening the shop an hour late, with the solemn sense that something had been booked.

She told Cal, who came in for a toilet gasket, about the call. He bought the gasket and borrowed a ladder. By noon he had removed the back of the telephone and could confirm that it had no connection to anything.

“The line’s been cut,” he said.

“I knew that.”

“Yes, but now you know it in a way that cost me forty minutes.”

He handed her a short length of wire with blue insulation. One end came away in flecks when she rubbed it.

“Put it back,” she said.

“It doesn’t do anything.”

“Then it won’t hurt.”

They put it back.

The following Wednesday, the telephone didn’t ring. Nina got the bolt out, drilled a new hole, and replaced a section of the fish-cleaning station that had gone soft. At eleven she went to the shop and found a man waiting to buy a single washer. He stayed for twenty minutes explaining why he needed it, which was one of the satisfactions and one of the hazards of selling things for seven cents.

The call came the next morning. A woman answered it on her way back from walking her terrier.

“My dad says to put the chairs in the shed,” said a child.

The woman asked which shed.

“The one with the swallows.”

Bellwether had more sheds than houses and more swallows than telephone subscribers. But the woman’s husband remembered an old boat shed on the north beach where a family called the Keenes used to hold dances. There had been swallows in the rafters. There had also been a child, now sixty-three and living in a suburb where the closest thing to a swallow was a silhouette on a car dealership’s sign.

The woman looked up the number of the sixty-three-year-old child. She felt foolish calling, and more foolish when he said that yes, from the age of eight, it had been his job to ring the pier and remind whoever was there about the chairs. His father worried about the varnish.

“Did they put them away?” he asked.

“Who?”

“The people you told.”

“I didn’t tell anyone.”

“Oh,” he said. He couldn’t seem to think of anything else to say, so after a while he thanked her.

---

By July, people were leaving folding chairs beside the booth, as if waiting for a bus. Someone compiled a list of calls in a school exercise book and tied it to the door with string. The first few entries were tidy and factual. Later, with no agreement as to the purpose of the book, people started adding remarks.

*Man requesting weather forecast, wouldn’t accept that I didn’t know.*

*Woman selling a green bicycle. Sounded in a hurry. I would actually buy it.*

*Heavy breathing, then somebody said, “No, the other end.”*

There were long stretches when nothing happened. Two teenage boys spent a night there and reported that when the sun came up, they suddenly had things to say to each other. They mentioned this as a complaint.

Nobody worked out a rule for the calls. Some were recognizably old, because of a shop name or a person who’d been dead for years. Others couldn’t be placed at all. A woman asked whether the mackerel were running, and when Nina told her they were, she yelled the news to someone on her end. It was the first time Nina knew for certain that an answer had got where it was going.

People began to ask Nina whether there was any way to request a specific caller. She told them no. They asked anyway. One man gave her a slip of paper with his brother’s name on it, folded twice and worn soft enough at the corners that she suspected he’d been carrying it long before he had a reason to give it to her.

She said she’d keep it at the shop. He nodded.

She put it in the till, under the pennies nobody wanted in their change.

Nina’s own mother had used the pier telephone. She’d worked summers at the ticket kiosk during the years when there was still a boat to the island, and sometimes, after closing, she’d called Nina to say that she was on her way home. There was nothing particularly tender about these calls. Often she was calling to ask Nina to turn the oven on. Once she called from the pier to ask whether Nina had seen her glasses, and Nina had said, “Mum, you’re wearing them,” which was a guess, but such a good one that she still thought of it as a thing she had seen.

She wanted to hear her mother say that she was on her way home. She didn’t want the conversation that would follow, in which she would have to decide whether to tell the truth or let her mother drive home expecting the kitchen to be lit.

If the telephone rang while Nina was passing it, she answered. She took some care not to pass it too often.

---

In August a woman named Harriet came into the shop and asked to see the book.

Nina told her it was still tied to the booth.

“No,” Harriet said. “I mean the one where you’re keeping the real information.”

Harriet wore dark glasses and was holding a small, much-folded map of Bellwether. Nina recognized it as one that had been given away inside boxes of a certain breakfast cereal. It showed an aquarium that had never existed. Nina knew because, as a child, she’d spent an afternoon trying to find it.

“What would the real information be?” she asked.

“Dates. Names. How somebody gets through.”

There was no edge in the woman’s voice. She spoke matter-of-factly, as if Nina had told her how much a door cost and she was asking whether that included the hinges.

Nina found a stool and brought it around the counter. Harriet sat without taking off her glasses. She’d come from two hundred miles inland, she said. Her husband had grown up in Bellwether. She knew he’d used the phone as a boy because he’d once told her a story about calling it from his house. He and his friends would use it to find out whether the tide was high enough to jump off the pier.

“He’s not dead,” Harriet said. “I just want to talk to him when he’s fourteen.”

Through the front window, Nina watched a man pass carrying a lampshade. It was tilted over his head to keep the sun out of his eyes.

“I wouldn’t tell him anything,” Harriet went on. “I’d ask him what he had for lunch. And he’d think, why is this woman asking me what I had for lunch? But he’d tell me.”

“Would he?”

“Oh, yes. He always liked to talk about his lunch.”

After a little while Harriet took off her glasses. She looked tired and a bit embarrassed, but not as though she’d been crying.

“Yesterday,” she said, “he had soup. He wanted some bread to go with it. He went all the way around it. The thing you put in the metal thing. Then he looked down at his soup. He said, ‘I don’t think I want it that much.’”

Nina didn’t know what to offer her. She thought of telling Harriet about her mother, which would have been true but would also have required Harriet to sit there and hear about her mother. Instead she closed the shop for lunch and walked with her to the pier.

The booth stood on four square feet of concrete. Someone had wedged the door open with half a brick. The book twisted slowly on its string.

“Does it matter who picks up?” Harriet asked.

“I don’t think so.”

“Then wait with me for a bit.”

They sat in the folding chairs. A boy caught a fish too small to keep and had to be persuaded to put it back. From where Nina sat, she couldn’t see the fish, only the boy’s hands held carefully apart after he released it, as if it were still there.

The phone didn’t ring.

At two, Harriet said she ought to start driving. She put her glasses on, folded the cereal map, and asked if there was somewhere in town to get a good loaf of bread. Nina sent her to the bakery that would still be open. She watched Harriet walk back down the pier. Halfway along, Harriet stopped and stepped aside so a man with a bucket could pass, though the pier was wide enough for both of them.

As soon as she was out of sight, Nina went into the booth and picked up the receiver. She didn’t dial a number. There was no dial tone, and the metal plate with the instructions had been pried off years before. Still, she waited a few seconds to see what would happen if she was the one who wanted to make a call.

Nothing happened, not even the faint crackle you sometimes get from a phone you know is dead. She set the receiver back in its cradle. A black crescent of somebody’s hair was caught in the cord.

---

In September the town council voted to remove the booth. The concrete underneath it was failing, but worse, from the council’s point of view, was that an engineer had now written a letter saying the concrete underneath it was failing. Nina attended the meeting. So did Cal and the woman with the terrier. They’d expected to have to argue that the calls were real. Instead the chair of the council said he’d taken one himself and still wasn’t keen on being the person who let a telephone booth fall on a child.

They agreed it could be moved. Someone suggested the museum, which had limited hours and already contained two phones that didn’t work. Cal offered the front of his garage. Then Nina said there was room outside the hardware shop.

On the morning the booth was due to come out, she went down with a broom. It seemed wrong to have people lift the thing and discover it was full of cigarette ends and shrimp tails.

She swept around half a brick and two buttons and a small coin so corroded she couldn’t tell what country it came from. She held the coin up to the light. The telephone rang.

“Hello?” she said.

There was a little pause. She heard a breath taken not to speak but to put off speaking.

“Hi, love,” said her mother. “Is your mum about?”

Her mother could only have been twenty or so. The voice went up at the end of the question in a way it hadn’t for years. Nina remembered it from when she was small, when her mother would sometimes speak differently to a stranger and Nina would tug at her sleeve, wanting her usual voice back.

“No,” Nina said. “She’s out.”

“Oh. I meant to catch her before she left.”

A young man asked a question in the background. Nina’s mother covered the mouthpiece, but not firmly enough.

“I’m doing it,” she told him. “Go and see about the cake.”

Nina set her broom against the door.

“Are you Jo?” she asked.

A laugh came through the receiver. “Who did you think it was?”

Nina could picture the yellow coat now. It had hung in the cupboard under the stairs all through her childhood. There was a tear inside one pocket where she used to put her fingers and feel a second, secret pocket between the lining and the coat.

“Is the dog all right?” Nina asked.

“What dog?”

“Never mind. What should I tell her when she gets in?”

Nina’s mother hesitated. When she spoke again, she’d dropped the voice for strangers.

“Tell her I didn’t mean what I said about the dress. I’ve had a look in the glass here and she’s right. It wants taking up.”

Nina’s grandmother had been a dressmaker. Nina remembered a tin of chalk and a carpet that snagged under the kitchen door. She tried to picture her mother standing on the carpet with her arms held out. There had been a whole house in the years before Nina lived in it, and she couldn’t furnish a single room without borrowing from what came after.

“And ask her to come down,” her mother said. “There’s plenty for everyone.”

“I will,” Nina said.

The line went quiet. Nina held the receiver for a little longer. Then she put it down, picked up her broom, and swept the dirt she’d collected into a dustpan. She put the coin in her pocket.

---

It took three men and a van to move the booth. When they set it down outside the hardware shop, one of its feet didn’t touch the pavement. Nina went inside for a shim.

The telephone never rang again. The next spring someone took the receiver off its hook and left it dangling, and a customer brought it in, thinking it had broken off. Nina went out and showed him where it went. There was a little trick to setting it in the cradle so it wouldn’t slip.

She saw Harriet once more. Harriet came into the shop with a man in a blue cap. There was no reason for Nina to be sure who he was until Harriet asked him whether he wanted to see the pier, and he said yes, but wasn’t there somewhere they could get lunch first?

Nina took them to the café herself, in part because it was awkward to give directions while the pavement was being dug up. They ordered at the counter. The man chose a cheese sandwich. The café had started offering several kinds of bread, and the girl at the till listed them so quickly that even Nina had trouble following.

Harriet looked at the basket behind the counter. She didn’t speak for him. She put a finger on the glass, first in front of one loaf and then another, giving him time to look.

“That one,” he said at last. Then, with considerably more certainty, “Will you cut it in triangles?”

The girl said she would. Nina stayed while they found a table. Before going back to the shop, she bought a slice of cake. She ate it outside, standing in the sun, and kept the paper plate cupped in her palm until she’d picked up the last of the crumbs.

# The Things We Put Under Tables

On the first Tuesday in March, a woman brought a table leg to the library and asked if she could leave it there until Thursday.

“It isn’t a donation,” she told Martin, who was at the desk. “I want it back.”

Martin had been a librarian for twenty-three years, long enough to know that most requests contained a second request that would reveal itself if he waited. He waited.

“I’m having lunch with my sister,” the woman said. “If I bring this, she’ll ask about the table.”

He tied a paper tag around the leg and put it in the cupboard where they kept the folding chairs. On Thursday she returned with a bakery bag containing two buns, one for him and one for herself. She ate hers standing at the desk and told him that her sister had asked about the table anyway.

“What did you tell her?”

“That it wobbles.”

“Does it?”

“Of course it wobbles. I took a leg off.”

Her name was Ada. She had recently moved into one of the flats over the pharmacy, and the table had belonged to her mother. Her sister wanted it. Ada didn’t particularly want it, but every time she imagined her sister sitting at it, she wanted it very much. The leg had come loose during the move, and Ada had been carrying it to the hardware shop on Tuesday when she realized she was about to be late for lunch.

“What did the hardware shop say?” Martin asked.

“I didn’t go. I liked having somewhere to come on Thursday.”

She brushed the sugar from her fingers, took the leg, and went home.

By June the library was due to close. This had been announced in January in language that allowed people to think it might not happen. The library would be *transitioning out of its current premises*. Residents would continue to enjoy *a robust range of services*. There would be *a mobile presence*. The mobile presence, when it arrived for a trial run, turned out to be a white van with room for a driver and six crates of books. A seventh crate could be accommodated if the driver brought sandwiches instead of a lunch box.

Martin had been offered a job at the central library. The commute was an hour and ten minutes on a good day. He had calculated this by making the journey on three consecutive mornings, although nobody had asked him to. On the third morning he bought a coffee near the new building and watched a man feed bits of croissant to a pigeon with one foot. He tried to picture this becoming the sort of thing he knew about his workplace: which pigeon came, and where the man bought his croissant, and whether anyone in the café would let Martin pay tomorrow if he forgot his wallet. It would happen, he supposed. He resented that it would happen.

The week after Ada collected her table leg, someone left a bicycle pump behind the radiator. Then a boy asked if he could keep his papier-mâché volcano on top of the returns trolley while he went swimming. Martin said yes to the volcano, no to the top of the trolley. A woman from the florist’s brought in a key to her back door for the girl who watered her plants. By the end of March, the folding chairs had been moved into the staff room. Martin put a notebook in the cupboard to record what came in and what went out.

His colleague Nisha found the notebook while looking for a chair.

“You’ve started a cloakroom,” she said.

“No coats so far.”

“Good. It’ll be a surprise when you get one.”

She turned the pages. Among the items waiting to be collected were three paving samples, an empty violin case, a blue saucepan, and a sealed envelope addressed to a man called Frank, who came in daily to check the weather in cities where he no longer knew anybody.

“What’s in the envelope?” she asked.

“I don’t know.”

“I wasn’t asking you to open it. I was asking if you already had.”

Nisha took a chair and went back to the children’s room, where she was making a cardboard tunnel for the toddlers to crawl through. The toddlers crawled through it twice and then sat on it. She made another one the following week. Nisha had accepted a job at the central library in January. She lived twenty minutes from it, and her new hours meant she could collect her daughter from school on Wednesdays. She had apologized when she told Martin, then become annoyed with him for making her feel she had to apologize. All he’d said was “Right,” but he knew he had got a fair amount into that one word.

In April an estate agent came to measure the building. He wore clean white trainers, which made the stepladder he carried look particularly dirty. While he measured the children’s room, a boy named Louis followed him around and wrote down all the numbers. Later Louis made a plan of the building in which every room was the same width, but the staff bathroom ran for nearly forty metres. He had written down a date as one of the measurements.

“You could fix that,” Martin said, when Louis showed him.

“I know,” Louis said. “But look how many sinks we can have.”

The estate agent asked what the library would be taking with it. Martin said he didn’t know. He knew about the computers and the books, but not about the round mirror above the stairs in which you could see the tops of people’s heads before they saw you, or the framed photograph of the library opening in 1968. In the photograph a girl on the far left was eating an apple. The photographer had caught her looking at the mayor with her mouth open, about to take a bite. Martin had spent years hoping she’d come in and identify herself. People had identified the mayor, the mayor’s wife, and a dog in the background that Martin had initially taken for a bundle of rags. Nobody knew the girl.

Ada came in again on a wet Saturday. She had a drill in a moulded plastic case and wanted to know if Martin knew how to use it.

“Somewhat,” he said.

“How much is somewhat?”

“I own a drill.”

“So do I. Look at us.”

They laid the case open on the desk. The drill had belonged to her husband. There were four bits, a dead spider, and an instruction booklet in languages none of them could read. Nisha came over and showed them how to fit a bit. She’d put up shelves in her daughter’s bedroom the previous weekend. The shelves leaned down at one end, she said, but her daughter had arranged the books in ascending order of height and appeared to be satisfied.

Ada was quiet while Nisha demonstrated the drill. Then she asked if she could have a go. Martin found a piece of scrap wood in the staff room and took it out to the back steps. Ada drilled two holes. Her first was tentative and shallow, but on the second she pushed so hard that when the bit came through she put a little hole in the step as well.

“Well,” she said, peering into it. “It won’t be my deposit.”

She had already given the table to her sister. Her sister had put it in the kitchen with the loose leg against the wall, where it held perfectly well as long as nobody dragged the table forward. Ada had been over for lunch twice. The drill was for a hook in the hall of her new flat. She was tired of keeping her bag on the floor.

By May the cupboard had acquired a name. It was called the Cupboard, with a small pause before it. People came in and asked, “Could I put this in the Cupboard?” sometimes without giving any indication of what *this* was. A delivery driver left a bunch of daffodils for his mother, who was supposed to collect them at four and forgot. Martin put them in the blue saucepan with an inch of water. When the saucepan’s owner arrived, she carried it out with the daffodils still in it. The following morning she brought back the flowers in an olive jar and left a note apologizing for taking them home. She had understood at the time that the flowers weren’t hers, she wrote. She simply hadn’t been able to think of a second thing to do with her hands.

The work of closing the library picked up. Martin and Nisha took turns calling people whose books had been overdue for so long that the computer no longer showed the fines in days. A man returned an atlas he’d borrowed in 1989. He said the atlas belonged to him by now, which seemed a reasonable position, although it left Martin wondering why he’d walked a mile in the rain to give it back. Between sections, bare metal shelves began to appear. People who’d used the library for years suddenly had trouble finding the toilets. Without their usual landmarks they would get as far as the reference section and turn the wrong way.

On the penultimate Friday, the council sent over a sheet headed LOCAL DISPOSAL, with columns for condition and estimated value. Martin started with the staff room kettle. Nisha took the sheet from him and wrote her name next to it.

“Is that allowed?” he asked.

“We can put it in the Cupboard if you like.”

They laughed harder than the joke warranted. Then Martin asked what she thought they ought to do with the cupboard itself.

“Leave it,” she said. “It’s part of the building.”

“I meant the things in it.”

“Call people.”

“I have. Most of them are coming.”

“Who isn’t?”

There was the violin case, whose owner had gone to live with his father and whose mother said she couldn’t be expected to know what he wanted. There were the paving samples. There was a wool scarf that had appeared in the cupboard overnight, the only item anyone had deposited without speaking to him. There was a biscuit tin containing three photographs of a greenhouse. The woman who had left the tin assured Martin she would be in on the last day. What she wanted him to do if she didn’t come was a question she seemed to find insulting.

“Take the violin case,” Nisha said. “You keep talking about it.”

“I don’t want a violin case.”

“Okay,” she said. She set the disposal sheet down between them. “What do you want?”

Martin looked at her. From upstairs came a familiar short squeal: the sound of somebody trying to open the window that only lifted two inches. He wanted to say he didn’t know. What came out was that he wanted her to complain to him about the new library, even though it would be closer to her house and very likely the chairs would be better.

“Oh, the chairs look dreadful,” she said. “Have you not seen the chairs?”

He had. He’d sat in three of them on his third visit, carrying his coffee from one to the next like a man trying to get out of the sun. He told her so. She wanted to know which three. They spent the remainder of their break comparing the new chairs.

On the final day, it rained until noon. The first person in was Frank, who had come for his envelope. He opened it at the desk. Inside was another envelope, addressed to him in his own handwriting, with an old stamp glued to the corner.

“I used to send my grandson things when he was at university,” Frank said. “I always put an envelope in so he could send something back. He never sent one back until now.”

“Did he write anything?”

Frank shook the inner envelope. A key fell out.

“New flat,” he said. “He told me he was making a spare. I thought he’d forget.”

He put the key on his ring, removing a stiff little tag from the dry cleaner’s to make room. He didn’t check the weather.

The woman with the greenhouse photographs came at three and opened the tin to check that everything was there. Martin had seen only the top photograph. She showed him the other two. They were nearly identical, except that in the second one someone had opened the greenhouse door, and in the third there was a hand in the upper left corner, reaching for a vent.

“That’s me,” the woman said.

“Who took them?”

“I did. The camera had a timer. It took me all afternoon to get my hand in.”

She put the photographs back in the tin. The greenhouse had been dismantled years ago and she intended to build another one, smaller this time. She couldn’t remember which way the vent had opened. She held the tin out towards Martin, as though he might want to check again, and then tucked it under her arm.

Ada came in just before five. Martin thought she might want help with another hook, but she said she had a favour to ask. Her sister was bringing the table over to the flat on Sunday. They’d agreed to eat at it on alternate weekends and move it back and forth between them. Her sister drove a hatchback. The table fitted in the hatchback if nobody wanted to ride in the passenger seat.

“This seems like something you’ll do twice,” Martin said.

“Once,” Ada said. “I’m counting on her getting fed up and buying her own.”

She wanted to borrow an old paperback she’d seen on the sale trolley, a long novel about two women who spent their whole lives living next door to each other. The cover showed them in different seasons, with one up to her ankles in snow while the other stood in a garden of huge pink flowers. Martin told Ada she could have it.

“I know. But can you put a date in the front?”

He found the old stamp in a desk drawer. They’d stopped using it when the self-checkout machine arrived. The rubber wheels were small and difficult to turn. He set it for a Thursday three weeks away and stamped the book.

“Where do I bring it?” Ada asked.

It was the kind of joke she made with a straight face, and he was about to take it that way. But she had her bag open and was waiting. He told her about the café near the central library, how it had a narrow table out front where you could sit even if you hadn’t bought anything yet. He could be there around a quarter past twelve on Thursdays, if that happened to be a good time.

“It might be,” she said. “I’ll see how I get on with the book.”

At six, Nisha unplugged the kettle and put it in her bag, where it stuck out at an angle. Martin looked in the cupboard once more. The paving samples had gone. The scarf was still there. He took it out and found, behind it, a short strip of wood with a hole in each end. He recognized it as the piece he had fetched for Ada to practise on. At some point he had brought it back inside and put it away.

“Ready?” Nisha called from the door.

“One minute,” he said.

He went to the staff room, where the folding chairs had left parallel marks on the floor. The little staff table had been cleared. Without the kettle or the pile of mugs, you could see the pale ring a plant pot had made before the plant died and somebody threw it away. Martin put his hand on the table and leaned. It tipped towards him, just enough to make him remember how he always set a full cup down near the middle.

He crouched and slid the scrap of wood under the shortest leg. It was too thick. When he leaned on the table again, the wobble had moved to the other side. He took the wood out, carried it to the door, and put it in his coat pocket. Then he went back for the scarf. It was mild outside, but Nisha was wearing a jacket without a collar. She said no when he offered it to her, then changed her mind halfway across the car park. He waited while she shifted the kettle from one arm to the other and wound the scarf around her neck.
