# The Door on the Number 6

On the first Monday in November, someone left a door on the Number 6 bus.

It was a full-sized interior door, painted green on one side and white on the other, with a brass knob and three empty hinge slots. Along the green edge were pencil marks recording the heights of two children, Annie and Lou, at intervals between 1998 and 2009. Lou, who had started out considerably shorter than Annie, overtook her in the summer of 2006. Whoever held the pencil that day had drawn a little crown above his name. Someone else had crossed it out.

The driver, Mo Sadiq, brought the door to Lost Property at the end of his shift.

“How do you leave a door on a bus?” I asked.

“You get off without it.”

“But surely you’d notice.”

“I noticed,” Mo said. “I thought she was coming back.”

He propped it against the wall beside the umbrella bin. It fell over while he was signing the intake form. We propped it up again, this time with a crate of unclaimed water bottles at its foot.

“Which stop?”

“End of the line. She asked me to wait while she found a trolley. I waited six minutes. Then another bus came up behind me.”

“Did you get a name?”

“No. I did get a look from the other driver.”

On our inventory system the closest available category was *Building Materials*, which had been added after a man lost twelve bathroom tiles. He came back for them nine months later and was offended to learn that we had not kept them. He had spent those nine months, he told me, looking for a match.

I entered *Door, green/white, one knob*. There was nowhere in the form to put Annie and Lou, so I added them under *Distinguishing Features*.

My colleague Bev arrived at eleven, carrying a paper bag that had gone translucent with butter. She put two pastries on a napkin, considered the door, and asked if we’d been burgled.

“Other way round,” I said.

She went over to read the marks. “They’ve measured them in shoes.”

“How can you tell?”

“This one’s got ‘no trainers’ next to it. You only write that after somebody’s cheated.”

Bev had three children and six grandchildren and was generally able to reconstruct an entire domestic dispute from less evidence than that. She took a bite of pastry and went to turn on her computer.

By Wednesday the door’s owner had not called. We did get a call about a cello, which turned out to be a viola, and another about a pair of prescription sunglasses with navy frames, which narrowed our stock to nineteen. A man came in looking for a shopping bag containing a raw chicken. We told him we would not have kept the chicken overnight. He said that was fine; it had been Saturday.

The terminal stop on the Number 6 was at the top of Mercer Hill, outside a row of shops built around a concrete square. There was a pharmacy, a barber, a vacant travel agency, and a hardware shop that still displayed its prices on fluorescent cardboard stars. I went up on my lunch break and asked in the hardware shop if anyone had borrowed a trolley.

“Hundreds of people borrow our trolley,” said the man behind the counter.

“On Monday?”

“Oh. No, we’re shut Mondays.”

He came outside with me and pointed to the travel agency. The shops shared a narrow loading yard, he explained, and the travel agent used to leave a flatbed trolley there. It was probably still around, unless his landlord had taken it.

The travel agency window was papered over from the inside. In one corner, someone had missed a triangle of glass, and through it I could see the lower half of a poster advertising Mauritius. Six identical bare feet advanced across the sand.

I thanked him and went back down the hill on the bus. I hadn’t expected the trip to take my whole lunch break, but I ate a packet of crisps and watched the backs of houses slide past. When I got back, Bev had taken a call from a woman who had lost a gate.

“Three feet high, wrought iron,” she said. “I nearly asked if she’d consider something in wood.”

The reason I wanted someone to collect the door had nothing to do with the rules. We were supposed to keep it for twenty-eight days. After that the depot could dispose of it, and I’d have been happy not to fill out the forms. The trouble was that my father had recently moved into a flat and become convinced I wanted his workbench.

It was seven feet long. I lived on the second floor. I’d been saying no, kindly at first and then with increasing mathematical detail, for most of the autumn. His response was to send me photographs of it from different angles, as though the obstructing fact of its size might disappear if we looked at it from the end.

The door had started turning up in this argument even though my father knew nothing about it. He’d text *Bench?* and I’d look up at the line marked *Annie, 12, after swimming*. He had made me a bookcase when I was nine. It leaned alarmingly to the left and I’d taken it to the tip when I moved out of my first flat. I hadn’t told him. I was forty-one and sometimes still had the feeling that if I took a wrong turn I might find him in the queue at the tip, holding the bookcase.

I called him on Thursday.

“Did you ever mark my height on anything?”

“No,” he said. “We rented.”

There was a pause in which I could hear the sound of him doing something to a piece of paper.

“Your mother did,” he added. “On the back of the airing-cupboard door. There was wallpaper in there and she figured nobody would notice. I noticed.”

“What happened to it?”

“How would I know? We moved out in 1989.”

He had hung up before I realised that for the first time in weeks we’d spoken without mentioning the bench.

On our second Monday with the door, a man in a cycling helmet came in and said, “I believe you have part of my kitchen.”

Bev called me from the back. The man had taken his helmet off by the time I came out and was standing with it tucked under his arm, looking younger than I’d expected, though of course I knew exactly how old he was. He put his forefinger on the crossed-out crown.

“Annie thinks that was her,” he said. “It wasn’t. It was me. Mum said if I was going to behave like that, she’d measure us again in the morning, when everyone’s taller. I didn’t understand the science but I understood the threat.”

“Was it your mum who left it?”

“My sister. She’s currently in a field in Wales with no reception. I’ve got nine messages from her, all sent within a minute of each other, starting with ‘Don’t be cross.’”

The kitchen, he said, had belonged to their mother. She was alive and well and was at that moment in a tile showroom with somebody named Graham. She’d sold the house and given Annie and Lou a weekend to take whatever they wanted, provided that it wasn’t listed in the particulars. Annie had found the door in the shed, where it had been since a renovation.

“Where’s it going?” I asked.

He looked back at me. “I haven’t the faintest idea.”

It was the first thing he’d said that sounded rehearsed. I handed him the release form. He began filling out his address, stopped at the postcode, and looked over his shoulder at the door.

“Could I leave it here till Friday?”

I said yes. It was well within the twenty-eight days, although I would probably have said yes anyway. He put the helmet back on and fastened the strap.

“The worst of it,” he said, “is that she said there was some stuff in the shed I might want, and I told her to chuck it all. Now I keep thinking about what else was in there.”

“What was in there?”

“A lawnmower, mainly.”

On Friday a woman in muddy boots was waiting outside when I opened up. She was standing in the cold with two cardboard cups, and when I unlocked the door she asked if I was the person she’d been giving trouble to.

“You haven’t given us trouble,” I said. “Apart from the thing falling over once.”

She held a cup out to me, then held it back. “Do you take sugar? Because I panicked and put it in both.”

It was very sweet tea. I drank it next to her while we waited for Lou, who had borrowed a van and was trying to find a place to park it. Annie was reading the height marks. She got to *after swimming* and put her cup on the counter.

“Our pool used to have a hair dryer that came down over your whole head. I wish someone had saved that.”

“You could have brought it in,” I said. “We’d have kept it for a month.”

She laughed, then stood away from the door and looked at it with her head tipped back.

“I promised Lou I wouldn’t make him take it,” she said. “I have a room in a shared house and there’s barely space for a second towel. But if I’d gone into the shed the following week and it hadn’t been there, I’d have thought about it for the rest of my life. This way I’ve thought about it for eleven days and I am absolutely sick of it.”

Lou pulled up outside and put the hazard lights on. Bev came in from the depot yard. The four of us carried the door out, though there was only really work for two. At the van Annie noticed a little gluey rectangle low on the white side. She asked Lou if he remembered the cat flap. He said no. They stood holding the door between them while she tried to tell him about the cat that preceded the cat he knew, until the driver of a laundry truck put his head out the window and asked if we meant to be much longer.

When they’d gone, I found a dry leaf on the floor where the door had been. I swept it into a dustpan and, since I already had the broom out, swept under the umbrella bin. There was a pound coin under there. I put it in the tea fund.

That evening I went to see my father. He’d stored the bench in the garage behind his old house, which hadn’t sold yet. When we let ourselves in, I found he’d taken the vice off. Four clean circles showed where the bolts had been. 

“Where’s the vice?”

“Chap across the road wanted it,” he said.

“Did he want the bench?”

“Didn’t ask him.”

We stood on either end of it. I had come expressly to ask what he wanted me to do with the bench, but suddenly this seemed a ridiculous question to put to someone who had been telling me what he wanted for two months. Instead I asked him how he’d made it.

He pulled a stool up and showed me where he’d drawn a square around a knot in the wood so he wouldn’t put a bolt through it. He’d run out of pencil and drawn the last side with a ballpoint pen. He showed me a burn where he’d set down a hot saucepan while trying to flatten a warped bit of plywood. He’d made the legs longer at first, and shortened them after one week of work that had given him a pain between his shoulders.

“I thought you bought the legs,” I said.

“From where?”

He seemed so genuinely puzzled at the prospect of a shop that sold legs that I remembered another question I’d meant to ask him years earlier. When I was little, one of the legs of our kitchen table had come loose and he’d fixed it overnight. In the morning, the table stood an inch shorter. I’d always wanted to know whether he’d made a mistake and cut the other three to match.

“Of course,” he said. “Did you think I did it for fun?”

He laughed so hard he had to sit down on the stool. I dragged another one over and sat across from him. He was wearing two different socks, which had become more common since he’d started doing his own laundry. I asked where he wanted to have supper.

A week later, the chap across the road decided he wanted the bench after all. He and his son carried it over, and my father stood in the road saying, “Mind the drain,” until they cleared the curb. Then my father went home to his flat. The chap sent him a picture once he’d put the vice back on. He’d put it on the opposite end. My father showed me the picture on his phone and said it was a sensible arrangement for a left-handed person, though he was fairly sure the chap was right-handed.

We never heard from Annie and Lou again. There was no reason we should have. Once, at a flea market, I saw a green door laid across a pair of trestles, covered in little porcelain animals. I went around to the other side to check the edge. The knob was in the wrong place. I bought a fox with one ear missing, which I keep on my bookcase. It was thirty pence because of the ear. The woman wrapped it in a page from a newspaper and told me to carry it upright, a precaution whose logic I could not see but followed all the way home.

In December someone left a roasting tin on the Number 6. It was wrapped in a towel and still warm when Mo brought it in. For once he knew the owner’s name: a woman called Ruth who made dinner on Sundays for her brother, then took the leftovers home on the bus. Mo knew where she got off. He said he could drop it back on his next run, but he didn’t want to spend the whole route smelling roast potatoes, so I wrote her a note and took it up myself after work.

Ruth wasn’t in. Her neighbour, a boy of about eleven, came out in slippers to see what I was doing. I told him about the tin. He said he would take it, and when I offered him a receipt he said, with great courtesy, that he didn’t think he was allowed to sign things. Then he thought better of taking the tin at all. We stood under the little porch between the two houses. A light came on in Ruth’s front room, but it turned out to be on a timer.

In the end he went inside and brought out a dining chair. He set it by Ruth’s front door so she wouldn’t have to bend down to pick the tin up, and I set the tin on it and tucked the note under the towel. Then he asked me to wait while he fetched something else. He came back with a second chair.

“She might put the tin on the ground,” he said, “and use the first one to sit on. She does that when she gets back from the shops. This one’s for the tin.”

We left them side by side. As I went down the path, he called after me to ask if there were any potatoes left. I said I hadn’t looked. He waited until I reached the pavement and then lifted the corner of the towel. I could see him quite clearly from where I was, but he must have thought I’d gone. He put the towel back, straightened the note, and went in.

# The Things We Carried for Free

On the last day of the bus depot, a woman came to claim a door.

“Front or interior?” I asked.

She considered this. “Interior, but it used to have a letter slot.”

“What color?”

“Which side?”

Already she was doing better than most people. People think they know their possessions until you ask them to describe one. A man will tell you he has worn the same hat for twenty years, then look you straight in the eye and say it might be brown.

“Cream on one side,” she said. “Green on the other. There’s a brass knob. The bottom is cut crooked because the floor was crooked.”

I put my pencil down. “We’ve got your door.”

“Oh,” she said, and sat in the chair by the counter. “Good.”

She didn’t get up again right away.

Behind me, everything still unclaimed was sorted into boxes. The charity shop would collect what it wanted at four. A salvage man named Len was coming at five. The city had given us orange stickers for things that could be sold and blue ones for things to be thrown away. Len had been buying goods from us for thirty years and knew from experience that he could wait for a sticker to change color.

I had put an orange one on the door. It had good hinges.

“How did you lose it?” I asked.

“I left it on the bus.”

“I know that part.”

“Is there a form?”

“No,” I said. “I’m curious.”

She told me that the previous Tuesday she’d taken the Number Six from Chalmers Street. The driver had helped her put the door in the wheelchair space. Then a man in a wheelchair had got on, so they moved it behind the driver. At the hospital, a passenger fainted. The woman had got off to help and ended up holding a stranger’s handbag while a nurse attended to him. By the time she gave the bag to the nurse, the bus was gone.

“I had the idea that if I walked fast enough I could catch it,” she said. “I walked two stops before I thought about what I was doing.”

I asked why she’d waited a week to come in.

“I did call. The person on the phone asked if I meant a doormat.”

That would have been me. For the last month I’d been answering all the calls, including ones about timetables, complaints, and whether the new depot would sell the same potato cakes. It wouldn’t. The potato-cake woman had been offered a place there, but she’d measured the counter and found she couldn’t turn around with a hot tray in her hands.

“Let me get it,” I said.

The door had spent the week upright between a golf bag and a box of library books. In that light the green looked nearly black. When I brought it out, the woman stood and ran one finger along the edge, feeling for something. Her finger stopped at a dent near the top hinge.

“Yes,” she said. “That’s it.”

I offered her the pencil and the ledger. She wrote Ruth Bell in the column marked CLAIMANT. In the column marked RELATION TO OWNER, she wrote daughter.

“Is there anyone coming to help you with it?” I asked.

She examined the door as though it had gained weight during its time with us.

“I thought I’d get the bus.”

“Where to?”

“Plover Street.”

I told her there had been a diversion since Wednesday. It would let her off at the foot of the hill.

“That doesn’t sound very far,” she said.

“It isn’t, without a door.”

We stood looking at it. People had carried large things on our buses. Window frames, prams with the babies taken out and held like parcels, a bathtub on a quiet Sunday. Once a man boarded with a rolled carpet, and when the driver asked what he was doing with it, he said, “Taking it to my sister’s,” with such injured dignity that she apologized and drove on. But you needed a driver who would say yes, and these days they were watched by little cameras, including one whose sole apparent purpose was to prove there had been room for further passengers.

“I finish at five,” I said. “I can help you carry it.”

Ruth looked at me. “You don’t have plans?”

I did have plans. I’d bought a bottle of beer and left it in the fridge at home. Somewhere around five thirty I meant to open it. Beyond that the day was poorly organized.

“My plans can move,” I said.

She went across the road for something to eat. At four she came back with two custard tarts and helped me box up the things the charity-shop people would take. She was better at it than I was. I had spent thirty-four years matching objects to their owners, which made me reluctant to separate anything that had come in together. Ruth persuaded me that a clothes hanger found inside a suitcase did not have to go wherever the suitcase went.

“Someone packed that hanger,” I said.

“And I hope they have another one.”

We emptied the suitcase. Under the lining was a receipt for one night at a hotel in a town neither of us knew. It was dated nine years ago. The suitcase had been with us for eleven weeks.

“Have you ever looked people up?” she asked.

“Sometimes.”

“Does it work?”

“Sometimes,” I said. I told her about a school clarinet with a name on the case. The mother had come in furious because they’d already bought another clarinet. She asked why we hadn’t called sooner. I said we’d called the school the day it came in, which only made her angrier, because now she had to decide whether to go to the school on her way home.

“And sometimes,” I said, “you get a surprise.”

“What kind?”

“A man left a cake on the Number Four. He came in two days later and was genuinely relieved we’d eaten it.”

At half past four, a driver named Sanjay put his head through the open window and asked if he could have the clock. It was a big square clock, now four minutes slow. It had spent twelve years being four minutes fast, which suited everyone better.

“Where would you put it?” I asked.

“Kitchen. My daughter’s learning to tell time. At school they have a clock with no numbers on it. How’s she supposed to learn anything from that?”

I fetched the stepladder. There was a clean square on the wall behind the clock, bordered on one side by a smear where I used to press a finger to steady it while changing the battery. Sanjay tucked the clock under his arm. His own bus wasn’t due out for another ten minutes, but once he’d got what he came for, neither of us seemed to know how to prolong the visit.

“See you,” he said.

“See you,” I said, which was possible. He would still be driving the Four. I had just never had much reason to go anywhere on it.

At five, Len arrived and took the golf bag, the shelving, and a portable radio that picked up a station from across the water whenever it rained. I’d been told to leave the keys in an envelope and push it through the office letter slot on my way out. I did this carefully, only to remember I’d left my cardigan inside. I stood with my hand against the glass for a moment. Then I knocked, just to see how it felt. It sounded exactly as it had when I was in there ignoring people before opening time.

Ruth picked up her end of the door.

“Ready?” she said.

We caught the Six. The driver made us wait until everyone else had got on, then came down the steps and showed us a way to turn the door that neither of us had thought of. He held it steady while we got ourselves arranged. He’d driven a removal van for his uncle, he told us. The uncle used to charge by the hour and could make a long afternoon out of a wardrobe.

At the foot of Plover Street, we got the door off by ourselves, though for part of the operation I was standing in the road with my end up in the air while Ruth, invisible on the other side, said, “Wait, wait, wait.” The driver waited too. When we were clear he gave the horn a little tap and pulled away.

We carried it to the first lamppost and set it down.

“Do you want to know why I’ve got it?” Ruth asked.

“I’d like to.”

“My brother asked for it. I said no.”

She leaned her shoulder against the green side. The light was going and little chips in the paint were showing white.

“Our mother moved to a flat in February. She left us to clear the house. My brother wanted the door; I wanted him to take the freezer. It was a perfectly good freezer, and I got so annoyed with him for making me deal with it that I told him the clearance people had already taken the door. Then, of course, I couldn’t let them take it.”

I waited. It wasn’t clear yet why the door mattered to her brother, but it seemed clear enough why she was carrying it.

“He used to deliver his own mail through it,” she said. “When we were little, it was on the front of the house. Later my mother got a new front door and moved this one to the kitchen. He used to write letters to himself and push them through from the hall. He’d go round through the dining room to pick them up.”

“What did he write?”

“Oh, mostly he told himself he’d won things. A horse, once. That one upset him. He was about six, and there was a point later in the day when he forgot there wasn’t a horse.”

We picked up the door again. As we climbed, the knob pressed into the soft part of my wrist. I tried a different grip and found that I could wedge my fingers into the letter slot. Ruth heard the little brass flap lift.

“Mind it doesn’t bite,” she said.

At the second lamppost we traded ends. I asked whether her brother lived with her, on Plover Street.

“No. He lives in Leeds.”

I let that settle between us.

“I know,” she said. “I’ll have to make a phone call eventually. I wanted to get it up the hill first.”

A boy in slippers came out to put a bag of rubbish in a bin. He watched us go by and asked why we were carrying a door. Ruth said we were taking it home. He looked back at his own front door, as if testing how much he would mind if we came back for it.

Her house was five doors farther up. There were three steps to the entrance and a narrow turn into the hall. She wasn’t sure where she wanted to put it. We got it inside, turned it, and backed it against the dining-room wall. Then she changed her mind and we turned it around again so the green side faced out. I made sure it couldn’t slip. Ruth went to put the kettle on.

From where I sat, the old door looked like a new way into the room. I knew perfectly well I’d just carried it there, but every time I glanced up I felt aware of a space beyond it. Not a kitchen, exactly. More the size of a hallway where a child might kneel to write a letter, taking care to put his own address at the top.

Ruth brought two mugs. She’d made my tea very strong and hers so weak you could see the bottom. We talked for a while about the price of things. Then she asked if I had anything from the depot.

“I had a cardigan,” I said.

She was kind enough to laugh. I hadn’t meant it as a joke, but after a moment I laughed too.

On my way down Plover Street, I stopped where we’d first put the door down. My fingers had stiffened in the shape of the letter slot. I opened and closed them a few times. Across the road a man was washing a single dinner plate at his kitchen window. He set it in the rack and wiped his hands, and the light went off.

The next morning, I called the city about my cardigan. A young man told me I could fill in a lost-property form online. I said the cardigan wasn’t lost. I could tell him exactly where it was.

“That’s useful,” he said. “There’s a box for that.”

I filled in the form. It asked for the route number, the date of travel, and a description of the item. I thought the cardigan was gray, but the longer I sat in front of the screen the more I remembered it blue. My wife had bought it for me at a market on a trip we took years ago. I could remember what we’d eaten for lunch that day and the animal on the pub sign. I could even remember my wife pulling a loose thread from the cuff and winding it around her finger while she waited for change. None of that settled the color.

I wrote *two pockets, one with a hole in it*. In the box for the location I wrote *back of the chair by the window*. Then I pressed send. A little wheel turned, and the city thanked me for my report.

Three days later Sanjay rang my bell. He’d been sent back to the old depot for a first-aid kit, and he brought the cardigan in a plastic bag. It was green. Not a doubtful green, either. He stayed for a cup of tea and showed me a photo of his daughter standing on a kitchen chair, reaching up to move the hands of the clock. She’d learned to tell the hour but was still suspicious of the minutes. Whenever she got an answer wrong she turned the hands until it was right.

I didn’t hear from Ruth again until well into summer. She sent a postcard of a park in Leeds. On the back she’d written, *He says I could have just told him about the freezer.* Underneath that she’d given me the route number, the stop, and directions from the bus shelter to her brother’s house. He was having some people over for lunch. If I came, she said, I was not to bring anything.

I went. Her brother met me in the back garden, where he was putting out chairs. He and Ruth had laid the door across two trestles. The knob was gone, and he’d fitted a wooden plug in the hole, but he hadn’t touched the letter slot. When somebody spilled a little wine, a red drop made its way down through the brass flap and landed on his shoe.

“Oh, good,” he said, looking down. “I wondered if that still worked.”

There were seven of us. The door was narrower at one end, and the plates there had to be staggered to make room. Ruth sat opposite me and passed a bowl of potatoes. When everyone had been served, there was one left, and she cut it in two and put half on my plate and half on hers. Neither of us had asked for it, but I ate my half, and she ate hers.

# The Drawer Marked Thursday

On the last Thursday of its existence, the lost-property office opened at eight, as usual, and at eight-oh-three a man came in for a cow.

“Not recently,” he said, anticipating the question. “Nineteen seventy-four.”

Nora put down her coffee. She had been told to expect a certain amount of nonsense on the last day. The newspaper had run an article under the headline *City to Close Its Attic*, with a photograph of Nora holding a trombone she had specifically asked not to be photographed with. Now people were coming in to say goodbye to objects they had never owned.

“Was the cow lost on municipal transport?”

“On the number six.”

“The six went across the river in those days.”

“Yes,” said the man. “She liked bridges.”

He took off his cap. He was perhaps eighty, with the smooth, pink scalp of a newborn mouse. From his coat he produced a photograph of two boys next to a cow. One boy wore a tie, the other a paper crown. Behind them stood a bus with its doors open.

“That’s me with the crown,” he said. “The cow’s name was Margaret. My brother swore he handed the driver sixpence for her fare. I wondered if there was a record.”

“You don’t want the cow, then.”

“My wife was very clear on that point.”

At the back of the office were forty years of ledgers. There had been sixty years once, but a pipe burst in 1998. Nora found 1974 on the second shelf, between a sandwich press and a cardboard box marked *TOES*, which contained the detachable feet of a dressmaker’s dummy.

They turned the pages together. The man smelled faintly of oranges. There was no cow, but on the fourteenth of June they found an entry for a paper crown, recovered from the upper deck of the number six.

“Oh,” the man said.

Nora waited.

“I’d have said I wore that home.”

She offered to photocopy the page. He said no, then yes. While the machine warmed up he told her that Margaret had belonged to a dairy that lent her out for school fêtes. His brother had been allowed to walk her home, but it had begun to rain. The driver had made everyone get off before he let them bring the cow aboard. This part the man remembered very well: nine or ten passengers waiting at a bus stop in the rain while a cow looked at each of them in turn from inside the bus.

“Was your brother wearing a tie for the fête?”

“He wore one every day that summer. He thought it made him look employable.”

“Did he get a job?”

“No,” the man said. “He was eleven.”

Nora handed him the copy. He folded it carefully around the photograph and put both in his inside pocket. At the door he stopped to put his cap on.

“My brother’s still alive,” he said, as if he had forgotten to give her the most important piece of information. “I’m going to ring him up.”

By nine, a florist had retrieved a single boot, a student had tried on four identical navy jackets and rejected all of them, and a woman had returned an umbrella she’d collected in 2016.

“It wasn’t mine,” the woman said. “I thought I’d get used to the handle.”

Nora accepted it. There was no procedure for this, but at five o’clock there would be no procedures for anything.

The office was closing because the city had contracted its bus routes to three companies, none of which wanted to pay for a shared room full of wet gloves. Each would have an online form. Passengers would be asked to identify the operator of the bus on which they had left their belongings. Nora had taken the bus to work for twenty-seven years and could not have done this herself. The buses were all blue. Whenever the city changed contractors, it took longer to repaint a bus than to change the name of the company that owned it.

She did not object to closing as fiercely as people seemed to want her to. The office was damp, the wages bad, and there was a patch in the ceiling shaped like Australia that had recently acquired Tasmania. When she told people she worked in lost property, they leaned forward and asked her the strangest thing anyone had ever left on a bus. Nobody asked how many hours she spent on hold with the supplier of the padded envelopes.

Still, on Monday she would wake up and have nowhere she was expected at eight.

At ten, her daughter called.

“Have you found it?” Alice asked.

“Good morning to you too.”

“Good morning. Have you found it?”

Nora looked toward the filing cabinet. The bottom drawer had a label that said *THURSDAY*. The others said *KEYS*, *WALLETS*, and *GLASSES*. The label dated back to a weekly arrangement with a driver who had retired before Alice was born. Nobody remembered what they had arranged.

“I haven’t looked yet.”

“You said you would last night.”

“I said I would today.”

“You also said you would in April.”

Nora held the phone away and examined it. When Alice was ten she used to answer any correction with *approximately*. She had come up with this on her own. Three times seven was twenty, approximately. She had fed the rabbit, approximately. Her teacher had written *A pleasure to have in class* on her report and then, in a different pen, added *when present*.

Now Alice was thirty and professionally exact. She installed exhibitions in museums. Last winter she had flown to another country to supervise the movement of a blue bowl from one room to another. The bowl was not particularly old, she told Nora. It was, however, deeply insured.

“I’ll look,” Nora said.

“Will you call me if you find it?”

“Yes.”

“Even if it’s broken.”

“Yes.”

Alice hung up. Nora took an elastic band from the desk and slipped it around her wrist. She did that when there was something she needed to remember. By the end of most days she had three or four, and no idea what any of them meant.

At lunchtime, Hal came down from the depot with a cake. He drove the fourteen and had spent most of his working life bringing Nora whatever people left behind. He had brought her a wedding dress in a bin bag, a shoebox containing two live hamsters, and, on their third anniversary, a grocery-store orchid with its price written on the pot in permanent marker. The orchid was the only one of these things she still had. It bloomed every February on a windowsill in her flat, which Hal had not seen in seven years.

The cake said *THANK YOU NORMA*.

“They charged by the letter?” she asked.

“I told them Nora twice. They were quite sure I meant Norma.”

He put it on the counter and went out again to get paper plates. When he came back she had scraped away the M with a teaspoon. There was a gap between the R and the A, but unless you knew what had happened, it just looked as though the person icing it had got tired.

“Did Alice ring you?” Nora asked.

“Last week.”

“And?”

“I said you’d know where it was.”

“Fat lot of help.”

“I thought you did know.”

“I know where it ought to be.”

Hal took off his jacket. Underneath he was wearing a shirt she had given him for Christmas when they were still married. It had once been dark green. It was now the color of the inside of a cucumber.

“I can look,” he said.

Nora wanted to tell him it was her office and she could look for things in her own office. Instead she handed him the key to the bottom drawer.

It stuck. It always did. Hal pulled harder. Nora put one hand on top of the cabinet to steady it. It annoyed her how easily they still did certain things together.

Inside were a packet of seeds, two pairs of children’s mittens on strings, a disposable camera, and a clear plastic bag containing a little red shoe. There was also a smoked-glass ashtray Nora had been meaning to take home since the smoking ban, although she did not smoke and could not remember ever having liked it.

Hal lifted out the shoe.

“No,” Nora said.

“I know. I was just looking at it.”

She had forgotten how small it was. A baby shoe, hardly bigger than her thumb. The sole was clean. Someone had called about it three days running, asking if the other one had turned up. Finally Nora had said, gently, that she thought the other shoe must be somewhere else.

“Well, of course it is,” the caller said. “I have it.”

That had been years ago. Looking down at the shoe now, Nora realized the woman hadn't been asking her to find the other one at all. She must have been asking if this one had turned up, always saying *the other one* because there was already a shoe on her kitchen table. Nora wondered how many times they had each put down the phone thinking the other was an idiot.

“The camera?” Hal said.

“No.”

He laid it back in the drawer.

When Alice was nine she had made a radio program with Nora’s father. They called it *The Six O’Clock News* and recorded it at eleven in the morning. Her father reported that the postman had been seen on the avenue in shorts despite the temperature being eleven degrees. Alice interviewed the rabbit. At the very end, after a long pause in which they apparently thought the tape had stopped, her father asked Alice if she wanted an egg.

Nora knew all this because her father had played the tape for her once, in his kitchen. He had died several weeks later, in a grocery store. There had been a carton of eggs in his basket, a fact that Nora had never found a useful place to put.

The tape had come to the office in a shopping bag full of his things. Nora had brought it in to listen to on the little cassette player she kept by the kettle. She got as far as taking it out of the shopping bag. There was a knock at the hatch, and a woman was there for a wallet, and after that Nora could not remember a single thing that had happened for the rest of the day. She was almost sure she had put the tape in the bottom drawer.

She was also almost sure she had put it in the pocket of her raincoat.

She had given the raincoat to charity twelve years ago.

Hal cut the cake. They ate standing up at the counter. A man approached the hatch, saw them eating, and started to back away.

“Come on,” Nora said. “We’ve got plates.”

He didn’t want cake. He wanted his lunch. A grey insulated bag, left on the fourteen the previous afternoon. Hal had found it and put it in the depot fridge. He called up to get someone to bring it down.

“Don’t trouble anybody,” the man said. “I’ll walk up.”

“Do you work near there?”

“No. I’ve got all day.”

He had retired on Tuesday, from a shop that sold glass for greenhouses. On Wednesday he’d got on the fourteen with a packed lunch because he had been getting on the fourteen with a packed lunch since the birth of his second child. He’d gone two stops past the shop, got out, and walked along the canal until he felt ready to go home.

“Any plans?” Hal asked him.

“People keep asking me that,” the man said. He thought for a moment. “I might start buying tomatoes that need to be sliced.”

He did have a piece of cake, after all. He took it away in a paper napkin, holding it flat on his palm. Through the front window Nora watched him give a small, instinctive wave of thanks to a driver who’d stopped to let him cross. The cake tilted. He saved it against his coat.

At a quarter to five Alice arrived. She had taken the afternoon train without telling anybody and came through the door trailing the strap of a large blue bag.

“You can’t leave that there,” Nora said, pointing to the strap. “Someone will trip.”

Alice picked it up.

“I haven’t found it,” Nora said.

“All right.”

“I might have left it in a raincoat.”

“All right.”

“I should never have brought it here.”

Alice looked into the office, at the bare shelves and the faint outlines left by years of notices. Hal had taken the remaining boxes upstairs. There was a clean square on the wall where the clock had been.

“Can I see the drawer?” Alice asked.

Nora showed her. There was nothing in it now except the red shoe, which she hadn’t been able to decide about. Alice took it out and turned it over.

“Was I good on the radio?”

“You kept asking the rabbit the same question.”

“What was the question?”

“‘How’s the grass these days?’”

Alice smiled. Nora hadn’t remembered that until her daughter asked. Now she could hear the exact rise at the end of *days*. She could hear, too, the sound her father had made in the background. She’d always thought he was clearing his throat. Suddenly she could see him at the kitchen table with a hand over his mouth, trying not to laugh into the microphone.

“What else?” Alice said.

Nora told her about the postman. Alice remembered the shorts but thought they might have belonged to the milkman. They disagreed over which rabbit it was. Alice said that she had pronounced her own name wrong at the beginning because she’d been trying to give herself an accent. Nora didn’t remember that, but she remembered how her father had said *Do you want an egg?* The way he’d asked it, the egg was obviously already on.

“Boiled,” Alice said. “He had those cups with the chickens on.”

“One had a duck.”

“No, you always said it was a duck. It was a chicken with a funny beak.”

Nora opened her mouth to argue, then realized she would have to go over to Alice’s flat and look. She had given her the cups when she moved out.

At five Hal came down to collect the keys. Nora gave him the one for the cabinet and the two for the hatch. Then she locked the front door from the outside. There was nobody waiting to get in. Across the street the florist was sweeping soil off the pavement in two different boots.

Alice asked if she wanted to get something to eat. Nora said she did. She had eaten little more than icing all day. They started toward the bus stop, and halfway there Nora felt an elastic band cutting into her wrist. She took it off and put it in her pocket, where her fingers found the shoe.

“Oh,” she said. “I’ve gone and taken this.”

Alice held out her hand, and Nora gave it to her.

The bus pulled up, blue like all the others. Alice let two people go ahead while she slipped the shoe into her bag. Then she moved the bag to her front, where she could see it, and followed her mother aboard.

# The Things We Put Aside

On the last Thursday of every month, the city sold the things nobody had come back for. Bicycles went first, then tools, then jewelry, then the boxes whose contents the auctioneer called miscellaneous. The umbrellas never sold. At the end of the afternoon, he would ask if anybody wanted an umbrella, and even on days when rain rattled against the high windows, people looked down as if he had asked for a volunteer to sing.

My mother ran the lost property office for thirty-one years. She kept a pair of dry socks in her desk and gave them to anyone who came in with wet feet. This was not city policy. City policy, as she explained it to me, was that adults were responsible for their own socks.

I worked there for six weeks the summer I turned seventeen. I remember this as the summer I was saving up to leave town, though when I recently found the envelope in which I’d kept my wages, I saw that I had written STEREO across the front. Evidently I intended to leave town by making my room louder.

The work was to take whatever the bus drivers, parks employees, and street cleaners brought us, give it a number, and describe it so that another person could find it. A green scarf was simple until you had eleven green scarves. Then you had to know about fringe and weave, and become willing to call something moss when you would ordinarily have called it green.

“Don’t write ‘old,’” my mother said one morning.

I was holding a leather briefcase with a broken clasp. Its handle had been repaired with fishing line, and there were dark half-moons on either side where somebody’s fingers had rested.

“How old do you think it is?” I asked.

“I don’t know. Neither do you. Write down the fishing line.”

She made a point of opening the briefcase herself. We were allowed to look for a name, but she didn’t want me reading people’s letters just because I had a city badge. Inside were a clean shirt, a toothbrush, and a wax-paper parcel containing six slices of boiled potato. She threw the potato away and took the shirt out to look for a laundry mark. Then she folded it along the existing creases and put it back.

At noon I ate my sandwich on the loading step. My friend Cal would sometimes come by on his bike and tell me what everyone else was doing. Ordinarily this was nothing, but he was good at making nothing sound like an event I’d missed. On the day of the briefcase, he told me six people had gone swimming in the quarry at midnight and nobody had thought to call me. Then he asked why I hadn’t come.

“I was asleep,” I said.

“See, that’s exactly what I told them.”

He took the pickle from my sandwich and rode away.

That afternoon a man came in for the briefcase. His shirt was buttoned wrong at the bottom, and he held a slip of paper my mother had given him on an earlier visit, before the driver had turned it in. He described the broken clasp. When she asked about the handle, he held his thumb and forefinger a little apart.

“Fishing line,” he said. “It’s the kind you can land a decent pike with.”

I thought he’d be relieved to get the briefcase back. Mostly he was anxious about the potato. He kept asking if it had gone bad, and my mother finally said yes, although she couldn’t have known. After he left, I asked why he’d brought a briefcase to carry a shirt and a potato.

“You could ask him,” she said.

This was one of her stock answers, and I hated it. Obviously I could ask him. The whole point of asking her was not to have to.

Three days later he came back with a plastic grocery bag full of something that knocked against the counter. He put it down and took out a jar of pickled beans for my mother and another for me. He had grown the beans behind his building, by the garbage cans, where the bricks held the heat. The jars were still a little warm. He said to leave them alone for a week before opening them.

Then he asked if we’d found a blue cap.

“Did you lose one?” I said.

“No, but I could use one.”

My mother laughed and told him to come to the auction.

The best thing I ever found was a notebook in the pocket of a child’s raincoat. On its first page, in slow block letters, somebody had written THINGS MY FATHER CAN DO. There were five entries:

1. Whistle with two fingers.
2. Put his hand flat on a hot car.
3. Know which dog it is by the bark.
4. Get the lid off.
5. Wake up when he says he will.

The next page was blank. I turned to it expecting a separate list headed THINGS MY FATHER CANNOT DO. At seventeen I would have found that funnier, and I assumed the child would, too. I copied the list onto the back of a bus schedule and kept it in my wallet. For a long time, whenever I got a new wallet, I moved the list into it. Somewhere along the way I stopped.

My own father lived four streets from us then. He cut hair in the front room of his house and used the back door so his customers wouldn’t hear him coming home with groceries. He was good at a number of things that wouldn’t have made the child’s list. He could persuade a person with very little hair to sit still for twenty minutes and feel that the attention was necessary. He could peel an orange without breaking the peel. He could also call our house, ask my mother if I was there, and somehow get off the phone without speaking to me.

On Wednesday evenings I took him dinner in a covered plate. This was my mother’s arrangement, though she always called it his. If he was cutting hair, I sat and waited. In the mirror I could see both of us without having to look directly at either of us. Once he asked how work was going and I said we’d had to throw away a man’s potato.

“Was it wrapped?” he said.

“In wax paper.”

“He must’ve been disappointed.”

It had taken my father three questions fewer than it had taken me to get there. I resented both of them for the rest of the evening.

In August there was a bicycle nobody could agree on. It was a small red road bike with drop handlebars and one white pedal. Two people claimed it within an hour, a woman and a boy of about twelve. The woman said hers had disappeared outside the post office. The boy said he’d left his at the swimming pool. Neither was where the bike had been found, but it had turned up in a drainage ditch, and my mother didn’t see why anyone would leave a bicycle in a ditch on purpose. She asked them independently to describe their bikes. They both knew about the pedal.

“Mine has a scratch right here,” said the woman, pointing to her own shin to show where the scratch would be on a bicycle.

“Mine has my name in it,” said the boy.

He told her he had rolled up a piece of paper and pushed it into the handlebars. His brother had shown him how. My mother got a screwdriver and pried off one of the end caps. Nothing came out. She tried the other one. We could hear something in there, but we couldn’t see it. I went to get a length of wire.

As I came back, I heard the woman ask the boy whether he’d written his name on a piece of green paper. He said yes. She picked up her purse.

“I remember now,” she said. “Mine had black pedals.”

My mother waited until the woman left before bending the wire into a hook. I thought this was tactful. Then the boy, who’d been standing out of the way with his hands in his pockets, said he’d ridden the bike to the post office once, when he went with his brother to mail a letter. He said it loudly, as if the woman had made it only as far as the door and might still hear him.

The paper inside the handlebar was green. It said MARTIN ORTIZ in neat capitals. Underneath, in smaller writing, it said BRING TO MY HOUSE IF FOUND. There was no address. My mother asked if he wanted to add one before she put the paper back, but he said he’d do it at home. He tucked the slip into his shoe. I held the door while he wheeled his bike out, and through the window we watched him ride down the sidewalk with one foot bare. His shoe, impossibly, was on the white pedal. He had slipped his foot out to check the paper and then, for reasons of his own, left it out. At the corner he stopped and put the shoe back on.

In September I went back to school. By then I’d bought the stereo, secondhand from Cal’s brother, and discovered that one speaker cut out unless I put a book on the wire. I used my chemistry textbook, which gave me an excuse not to bring it to class. The office went on without me. Occasionally my mother brought home a story, though more often she brought home an onion or some eggs she’d bought on her lunch break and asked me what I wanted for supper.

Much later, when she retired, the city gave her a clock. It was made of clear plastic, with the city seal suspended inside. With the clock came a letter thanking her for her dedication to the recovery of municipal assets. She kept the letter because the city manager had signed his own name, and this surprised her. The clock she put on the shelf over the washing machine, where it gained seven minutes a month until the battery ran out.

I helped her empty her desk. The office had moved by then, and most of the work was done on computers. There was a designated shelf for phones. When the phones lit up, you could see the names of the people trying to reach them. My mother said she was glad to be giving that up. She had spent years wishing lost things could tell you who they belonged to. Now the woman at the next desk sometimes had to listen to a phone ring with the word HOME on its face until the battery died.

In the last drawer I found one of the lost property tags we used to tie to things. It was stiff yellow cardboard with a string through the eyelet. I asked my mother if she remembered the man with the potatoes.

“No,” she said.

“The pickled beans. He brought us each a jar.”

“Oh, were those his?” she said. “They were good.”

I had forgotten what the beans tasted like. I could remember the warmth of the jar and that I had opened mine early, after only four days. I had eaten three beans over the sink and put the lid back on and said nothing. It seemed unfair that one of us should have the man and the other the beans, and that neither of us had kept his name.

There was a pair of socks in the drawer. I held them up and asked what she wanted to do with them.

“Take them,” she said. “You never wear sensible shoes.”

I was forty-three and wearing the same shoes she was. I pointed this out. She looked down at our feet.

“Then you know how they are in the rain.”

Last winter, on the bus home from work, I found a gray wool glove on the seat beside me. Or I thought it was wool. I rubbed it between my fingers, trying to decide what I would have written on the tag. The thumb had been mended in purple thread. The stitches went in every direction, holding a surprising amount of glove together.

At the next stop a woman got up from the seat in front of mine. She had been carrying two bags of groceries between her feet and had to drag one into the aisle before she could lift it. I asked if the glove was hers.

She set the bags down and searched one pocket and then the other. Out came a receipt, a square packet of tissues, a gray glove. She laid her glove on the back of the seat and I held mine beside it. Hers was smaller. The cuff was different.

“No,” she said. She put hers away and picked up the bags, then put one of them down again. “Would you mind pulling my sleeve down? It’s all bunched up in there.”

I tugged the cuff of her coat. She worked her hand farther out, enough to get a good grip on the bag. By then the bus had started moving again. The driver saw her standing there and stopped a second time, a few yards past the shelter.

I rode to the end of the line and brought the glove up to the driver. He put it in a paper bag and asked me where I’d found it.

“On a seat.”

“Which seat?”

I showed him. He wrote something on the bag. He was young, in a blue city jacket with the sleeves pushed up. On a shelf beside him he had a paperback lying open facedown. I wanted to know what he was reading, but I’d already made him get up and find a paper bag. I told him the thumb was mended with purple thread.

He looked inside the bag.

“So it is,” he said, and wrote that down, too.

The bus turned out of the loop and I started home on foot. At the corner there was a small grocery store that still put fruit outside in winter. I went in for an orange. The cashier rang it up, then looked at the conveyor belt to see if there was anything else. I had no reason to buy more than one. Still, I went back to the bin and picked out a second, and on the way home I called my father.

He doesn’t cut hair anymore. He answers the phone by saying his full name, as if he were still taking appointments.

“Do you want an orange?” I said.

“Is it a good one?”

I considered telling him it was firm for its size, or that the price had been reasonable. In fact I’d picked it for the long stem still attached to it, which had made it easy to lift out of the bin.

“I haven’t opened it yet,” I said.

He thought for a moment. “Come around the back. I haven’t shoveled the front.”

He met me in the kitchen, where he’d set two plates on the table. I gave him the orange with the stem. He dug his thumbnail in and started to turn it, bracing the fruit with his other hand. The peel came away in three pieces. He examined the largest one, set it on his plate, and held out his hand for my orange.

“I can do it,” I said, and then gave it to him anyway.

# The Bench at the End of the Line

On the first Monday in October, the number 6 bus stopped going to the sea. It still went to the supermarket, the hospital, and the roundabout where the furniture store had been. But instead of continuing down Lantern Road to the seawall, it turned behind the supermarket and waited beside the recycling bins. The new timetable called this the Seafront Interchange. You could see the sea from there if you stood on the concrete base of a lamppost and looked through a gap between two apartment buildings.

Someone had remembered to put a yellow bag over the sign at the old terminus. No one had remembered the bench.

I knew the bench because my father had eaten his lunch on it every weekday for twenty-seven years. He maintained the public toilets on the promenade, a job he described as having the great advantage that nobody wanted to stand over him while he did it. At twelve thirty he would lock his mop in the cupboard, carry a cheese sandwich across the road, and sit looking out over the water. When I was little and school was out, I sometimes joined him. He always gave me the half of the sandwich with the mustard. For years I thought he did this because he loved me, which he did, but it turned out he also hated mustard and couldn’t bring himself to tell my mother.

Two weeks after the route changed, I got a postcard from him. He’d been dead six years. It was a postcard I’d written to him in 1998, showing a glacier in Norway. My mother had found it behind a drawer and decided to send it back to me. Under my account of the price of a beer she had written: *Do you remember sitting on that bench with Dad? They’re taking it away Thursday.*

I rang her. She confirmed that she had mailed the postcard in an envelope, then taken it out of the envelope and mailed it on its own, because otherwise I might have put it down without turning it over. This was exactly the sort of thing she did whenever she had correctly guessed that I would find something upsetting.

“Who’s taking it away?” I asked.

“The people who take things away.”

“Did they put up a notice?”

“No, I asked them. They were taking away the bin.”

I had left town for university and returned at thirty-nine when a landlord in another city raised my rent by an amount I could not make into a joke. By then I worked from home, correcting the closed captions on training videos. I knew a great deal about ladder safety and the many ways a person could decline a gift from a vendor. My knowledge of who owned a bench was less extensive, but on Tuesday morning I found the council’s online form. Its categories included benches and bus shelters, separately. Under benches, you could report graffiti, damage, or a missing plaque. Removal, apparently, could happen only to a bus shelter.

I selected *Other*.

A woman called Elaine rang me before lunch. She worked in parking enforcement. I asked how my form had ended up with her.

“I selected *Other*,” she said.

Elaine had access to an inventory of street furniture. She read aloud the relevant line: “Lantern Road turning circle, seat, timber, one. Condition fair. Ownership unconfirmed.”

“Could I have it?”

“If it’s ours, there’s a process for disposing of it.”

“And if it isn’t?”

“Then there’s a process for finding out whose it is.”

“Which process are we in now?”

“Neither,” she said. “At the moment we’re talking on the phone.”

After work I went down to the promenade. The public toilets had been converted into a shop that sold ceramics three afternoons a week. Through the window I could see a stack of bowls with a blue glaze running over their rims. My father’s cupboard, assuming it was still there, would have been behind a pink curtain.

The bench was longer than I remembered. I sat in the middle and put both hands flat on the boards. There was a gouge near my right leg where somebody had once tried to carve a word, got as far as an M, and either thought better of it or had to catch the bus.

A woman in a supermarket uniform came up Lantern Road carrying two bags of groceries. She sat at the other end of the bench, took a carton of milk out of one bag, and put it in the other.

“They’ve moved the bus stop,” I told her.

“I know.”

I waited for her to go on, but she was watching a dog carry a stick across the beach.

“Do you know they’re taking away the bench?” I asked.

“Why would they do that?”

“Because they moved the stop.”

“What’s that got to do with the bench?”

Her name was Mari. She lived up the hill, in the red-brick flats behind the old lifeboat station. After a shift she liked to sit down before the last climb. There was a bench nearer her building, but it faced a window where a man ate dinner at five twenty-five every evening. He didn’t like to be watched and she didn’t like to watch him. They’d never discussed it. He just closed his curtains whenever she sat down.

I told her about my father. She said she remembered him, then described a man who couldn’t possibly have been him. I let her finish. The man in her story had once come out of the toilets wearing a woman’s hat someone had left on a hook, and had chased its owner half the length of the promenade to give it back.

“Maybe it was him,” I said, revising an opinion about my father’s willingness to wear a hat.

At home I wrote a letter to the council. The first draft began, *For nearly three decades, my late father served this community.* I deleted that and wrote, *People are still sitting here.* I attached a picture and sent it to Elaine, who replied that she had forwarded it to the relevant team. Then she sent a second message asking whether my photo showed bolts at both ends of the bench. I said I would check.

On Wednesday morning a white van was parked in the turning circle. Its driver, a man with a thermos balanced on his dashboard, said he had come to take measurements. I asked what for. He said he’d measure the distance between the bolts and send it to somebody who would decide what for. He let me hold one end of his tape measure.

“Did it need a new bench when it was a bus stop?” he asked.

“Not that I know of.”

“Sometimes the trouble starts when they stop calling it something.”

He took a picture of the tape stretched across the base. Before he left, he poured the last of his tea onto the ground with great care, as though watering a plant I couldn’t see.

I decided to spend Thursday on the bench. I had in mind the sort of protest where a worker arrives with a wrench and is obliged to have a conversation. I brought a sandwich, a raincoat, and a paperback I’d been carrying from house to house since my twenties. By nine I’d read the first four pages twice. Across the road, a delivery driver tried the door of the ceramics shop, put a box down, picked it up again, and drove away.

At ten my mother appeared. She had brought a cushion.

“I’m not making a stand,” I said.

“I can see that.”

She set the cushion down and sat on it herself. We watched the tide come in. Presently she asked if I remembered the big rows she and Dad used to have in the car. I said I remembered one, on the way home from a hardware store. Dad had bought a stepladder too long to fit in the boot. My mother had to fold herself into the back seat alongside it. The stepladder had knocked against the dashboard every time we braked.

“He bought the wrong one on purpose,” she said.

“How do you know?”

“He told me. The short one was out of stock and he couldn’t bear the thought of coming back on Saturday.”

We watched a gull drop a mussel on the concrete. Another gull came down and ate it.

“He could have said something about the mustard,” she said.

It hadn’t occurred to me that she knew. Apparently she hadn’t known until the morning he retired. He’d come into the kitchen while she was making his last sandwich and asked if, just this once, he could have it plain. She’d packed him a little pot of mustard on the side, in case he changed his mind.

At twelve thirty I opened my sandwich. My mother went home to have soup. At two Mari arrived with her shopping and asked whether I’d saved her a place. We sat at opposite ends, as we had on Tuesday, leaving room in the middle. A boy on a bicycle rode up to the yellow bag on the bus sign, squeezed it so the air came out at the top, then rode away.

Nobody came with a wrench.

Late in the afternoon Elaine called. The bench did belong to the council, but it wasn’t listed for removal on Thursday. She knew this because she’d spoken to the man in the van. He’d been sent to see whether they could move it to the Seafront Interchange, which didn’t have a seat.

“So they are taking it,” I said.

“They were looking at it.”

“What’s the difference?”

“Well,” she said, “you’re still sitting on it.”

I hadn’t told her I was sitting on it. I looked back at the flats, briefly imagining a parking enforcement officer at every window.

Elaine told me we could make a case for keeping the bench if we could show it was being used independently of the bus service. I said I had been using it all day. She asked if that was typical. I looked down at my paperback, which had begun to curl in the damp.

“No,” I said. “It isn’t.”

The next morning I took the bus to the recycling bins. I’d been so busy considering the people who no longer caught it at Lantern Road that I hadn’t thought about the people who caught it here. Two women waited close to the supermarket wall to stay out of the wind. A man with a walking stick leaned against the bin for clear glass. Every time somebody put a bottle in, he edged away, then edged back. When the bus pulled up, he stayed where he was until the others had boarded. I got on behind him. It was eleven minutes before the driver pulled out.

That afternoon I sent Elaine another email. I said the interchange needed a bench. I said the old stop needed one too. I’d nearly written that the council could surely find enough money for a second bench, but the figure they paid for one turned out to be high enough that I’d have wanted to ask a few questions myself. So I asked whether the council already owned one it wasn’t using. Elaine sent me a list of six. Two were marked *awaiting installation*, three were damaged, and one was at a school that had been demolished in 2017. We agreed the last one probably should have been taken off the list.

For three weeks, nothing much happened. The yellow bag tore and blew away. Now and then somebody waited at the old stop, and if I was passing I would show them where to go. One woman refused to believe me until she’d finished her cigarette, at which point she asked if I might help with her suitcase. We went by the long way up Lantern Road because it was the only route without steps. She stopped twice to rest, sitting on the suitcase while I held the handle so it wouldn’t roll away.

In November, the council put up a notice asking for comments on the bus route change. It was posted at the new interchange, where the people who could no longer get to the bus were unlikely to see it. Mari asked for a second copy and taped it inside the window of the ceramics shop. People put comments through the letterbox, which was not what the notice instructed them to do. The potter collected them in an unsold blue bowl and delivered them herself.

By Christmas there was a bench at the interchange. One of the damaged ones had turned out to have a sound frame, and someone in the council workshop replaced the boards. Its feet didn’t line up with the holes left by a previously removed bin, so they put it a little farther to the left. This gave the people sitting on it a view of the supermarket’s staff entrance. Mari, who sometimes caught the bus after work if she was tired enough, said that from there she could see who was sneaking out early. This considerably improved her opinion of the new stop.

The bench on Lantern Road stayed in place. I don’t know whether that was because of the emails and the comments in the bowl, or because once the interchange had a bench, nobody had a reason to finish the paperwork for moving ours. I meant to ask Elaine, but by then she was on leave and I had learned enough about the process to leave well enough alone.

In January a storm threw stones over the seawall and cracked one of the bench’s boards. I reported it under *Damage*. A week later I got a reply saying a crew had inspected the bench and found it in fair condition. I went down and sat on the cracked board. It pinched the back of my trousers when I stood up. I took a picture of the blue thread the crack had pulled loose and sent it in. A man came out with a new board. It was too long, so he went back to his van and cut it. He gave me the offcut, having mistaken my interest in the proceedings for an interest in wood.

I brought it to my mother. She was repotting a geranium on the kitchen table, with newspaper spread under it. The table rocked when she put her weight on it. I tried the offcut under the short leg and found it was thick enough to raise the foot on the opposite side.

“Your father would have kept that for twenty years,” she said. “Then he’d have gone out and bought a piece exactly the same.”

She found a bit of cardboard for the table. I took the wood home and put it beside my front door so I could remember to throw it out. It was there in March, when I wedged the door open with it to bring in a secondhand desk. Afterward I put it back beside the door.

By spring the new board had darkened to nearly the color of the others. One afternoon I walked down to the water with a sandwich, planning to eat it in my father’s old place. There was a man already there. His shoes and socks were off, and he’d arranged them in a neat line at his feet. It was too cold to be barefoot. I sat at the other end and unwrapped my lunch.

“I got them wet,” he said.

I nodded. I’d once come down here in my work shoes and misjudged how quickly the tide would cover the lowest step. It took all weekend for those shoes to dry.

“Is this a bus stop?” he asked.

“Not anymore.”

“Oh,” he said. Then he looked back out at the water and wiggled his toes in the thin sunlight. Neither of us got up.

### The Lost Property Office

The first sound anyone turned in was a laugh.

It came in a blue lunch box with a broken clasp. A bus driver named Dolores had found it on the last seat of the number 6, after the bus emptied at the depot. She set it on the lost property counter and lifted the lid. A child laughed once, with such force that he seemed surprised by it himself. Then the box was quiet.

“Is there a name on it?” asked Mr. Vale, who ran the office.

“On the box or on the laugh?”

They looked at each other. It was the first interesting question either of them had been asked that week.

Mr. Vale wrote *blue lunch box, containing one laugh* on a claim ticket. By Friday, he had acquired a whistle in a matchbox, the sound of rain on a particular kitchen roof, and a woman saying, “No, wait, let me start again.” The woman’s voice had been brought in by a window cleaner, who found it in a flowerpot four floors above the street. He couldn’t remember which building.

There were rules for umbrellas and wallets. Mr. Vale adapted them. To claim a sound, you had to describe it before he let you hear it. After ninety days, unclaimed sounds became municipal property. Nobody knew what the municipality might do with them. A clerk from the finance department suggested an auction, then asked if there was any way to estimate the reserve price of a sneeze.

Some sounds were easy to return. A baker claimed the squeak of his shop door, which had gone missing the same morning he oiled its hinges. A girl came for the first note of a song she was learning on the clarinet. She described it as “a duck finding out something bad.” Mr. Vale turned over the little envelope without checking.

Other claims took longer. Two brothers arrived separately for the sound of a shovel striking a stone. Both knew the small scrape just before the strike. Both could name the street where it happened. Mr. Vale asked what they’d been digging for.

“A pond,” said the older brother.

“A hole big enough to get us in trouble,” said the younger.

Mr. Vale put the shovel sound back on the shelf and told them to return together. They did, three weeks later, with a photograph of the hole. They were both in it, standing up to their knees, holding the shovel between them. Neither remembered who had taken the picture.

The office occupied a narrow room between the public toilets and the escalators at the bus station. Until the sounds began arriving, Mr. Vale had enjoyed the escalators. Their steady motor made it possible to work without noticing that he hadn’t spoken all morning. Now there were people at the counter who didn’t know how to describe what they had lost. He learned to move his tea out of the way when they began using their hands.

One afternoon a woman asked if he had the sound of somebody coming home.

“What sort of door?” he asked.

“Any door,” she said, and then, after a moment, “No. That was foolish.”

He showed her what he had anyway: a key dropped on a tile floor, a screen door that slapped twice, a shopping bag set down too hard. She listened to each. When he played the shopping bag again, she asked if she could hear what came next.

“Nothing comes next,” he said.

“I thought I heard an orange roll away.”

He listened again. She was right. He had filed the bag under *impact, miscellaneous*. He fetched a pencil and added the orange.

In December the city replaced the old escalators. For nine days the station was so quiet that Mr. Vale could hear people on the upper level deciding whether to take the stairs. On the tenth day, a contractor brought him a cardboard tube. Inside was the hum of the old motor.

Mr. Vale knew he could claim it. He could describe the thin rattle that started at half past six, when the station warmed up, and the little dip in pitch when a crowd got on. Instead he wrote out a ticket, slid the tube onto a shelf, and went to lunch.

He took the stairs. On the landing, a boy in a blue coat was laughing so hard that the woman with him had to set down her bags and wait. Mr. Vale recognized the laugh. He had expected to feel the satisfaction he felt when a lost wallet went home with the right person. Instead, he stood there wondering whether the boy might be embarrassed if a stranger said he had been keeping his laugh in a cupboard since June.

By the time he decided to say something, the woman had picked up her bags.

“Excuse me,” he called. “Did you ever lose a lunch box?”

The boy shook his head. The woman said, “You did. The blue one. You told me you threw it away because I put a pear in it.”

“I did throw it away.”

“Then how does this man have it?”

The boy considered this. “I threw it away on the bus.”

They came downstairs. Mr. Vale found the box and opened it. The laugh burst out. The boy went red.

“That’s not me,” he said.

“No,” said the woman. She took the box and opened it again. “That’s your brother.”

The boy leaned closer. “He couldn’t laugh like that.”

“He could before his front teeth came in.”

The boy tried it with his lips pulled back. It sounded nothing like the laugh in the box, but it made the woman laugh, and then it made Mr. Vale laugh. A man on his way to the toilets slowed down to see what was happening. Finding nothing he could explain later, he carried on.

The woman asked if they could keep the lunch box. Mr. Vale said that of course they could. He had her sign for it, though the ninety days were long past.

After they left, he took the cardboard tube down from the shelf. At closing time he carried it up to the landing and tipped it over the rail. The old hum filled the station. A few people glanced at the escalators. One man stepped aboard, rode all the way up, and never looked up from his newspaper.

When the hum was gone, Mr. Vale heard Dolores at the curb calling to a woman who was running for the number 6.

“Take your time,” she shouted. “I see you.”
