samples.result:
On the first Monday of every month, the city sold what it had found on the buses. The sale took place in a low brick building behind the depot, where the windows were too high to see through and the coffee came out of a machine that gave you a wooden stirrer whether you wanted one or not. I went because my father had left his umbrella on the number six. It was a black umbrella with a duck’s head for a handle. He’d been dead nine months, which meant it had been missing for at least nine months and a day.

The woman at the desk asked whether I had reported it missing. I said I hadn’t known it was missing until I cleared out his hallway. She turned her monitor so I could see the form. There was a field for the date of loss, and another for the approximate time. Neither accepted a dash. We tried leaving them blank. The computer outlined both fields in red. Finally she entered noon on the day I’d cleared the hallway. “That’s the day you lost it,” she said. I had been ready to dislike her, but this struck me as fair.

There were thirty-seven umbrellas in the sale, bundled in threes with masking tape. None had a duck’s head. I bought a bundle anyway. Outside, I opened the first umbrella and discovered it was meant for a child: yellow, with two fabric ears that stood up when the canopy opened. The second had a broken rib. The third was a promotional umbrella from a dentist’s office and said *OPEN WIDE* across two panels. This one worked. I stood beneath it in the depot yard, holding the other two, while a bus reversed into a bay with the slow, emphatic beeping of an appliance asking to be unplugged.

My father had driven a bus before I was born. I knew this from a photograph, not from him. In the photograph he was leaning out of the driver’s window in shirtsleeves, laughing at something beyond the frame. The bus was cream and green. When I asked him, once, what had been so funny, he told me the bus wasn’t supposed to be green. The city had ordered blue paint and someone had sent green, and by the time anyone noticed, they had done eleven buses. I asked what that had to do with the photograph. He looked at it again. “Nothing,” he said.

At the next sale I bought a lunchbox containing a fork and a small saltshaker. In June I bought a red scarf. The woman at the desk, whose name was Val, began putting the umbrellas aside so I could look at them before she taped them together. She didn’t ask about my father. She did ask if I wanted to know what happened to the things they couldn’t sell. I said I assumed they went to charity. “Most do,” she said, and opened a bottom drawer. Inside were seven single shoes. She shut it again. I had the sense she had meant to explain them and then thought better of it.

In July a man came in looking for a hearing aid. He said it was in a blue case and he’d lost it on the number six. Val brought out two blue cases. He opened the first and said it wasn’t his. He opened the second and said it wasn’t his either. Then he picked up the first one again, took out the hearing aid, and put it in his ear. Val asked him something. “Excuse me?” he said. She asked him again, louder this time. He took it out and looked at it with an expression of genuine annoyance. “Yes,” he said. “That’s definitely mine.”

That afternoon I took the six all the way to the end of the line. It terminated beside a supermarket. The driver switched off the engine, came down the aisle, and said she’d be going back in twelve minutes if that was what I was waiting for. I asked if she found many umbrellas. “Not as many as you’d think,” she said. People forgot them on mornings when it rained and cleared up. If it was still raining when they got off, they remembered. I thought of all the sunny afternoons on which my father might have walked home empty-handed, pleased to find the weather had improved.

In August there was a black umbrella with a carved wooden handle. It was a horse. Val set it on the desk between us, and I ran my thumb over its ears. On the underside of the handle someone had stuck a strip of white tape with a phone number written on it. We dialed from the desk. A young man answered. When I explained, he said, “Oh, he’ll be so embarrassed.” Then he asked if we could hold it until Friday. I said yes, although I didn’t work there and had no idea whether we could. Val took a tag from a drawer and wrote *FRIDAY* on it.

I had brought a picture of the duck umbrella to show her. It was a photograph of my father at a cousin’s wedding, taken just outside the reception hall. Someone inside must have called his name. He was half turned away, reaching for the door with his left hand, holding the closed umbrella in his right. Val looked at the picture for a long time. “Those doors were a nuisance,” she said. “You had to lift them by the handle or they’d catch.” It turned out she’d been married in the same hall. I’d been there twice and hadn’t noticed anything about the doors.

I stopped going to the sales after that summer. I still have the dentist’s umbrella. Last week, on the six, I saw a woman get up and leave a yellow umbrella on the seat beside her. I called out, and she turned, but she didn’t come back for it. She pointed through the window. We’d been underground by the station, and neither of us had noticed that it had stopped raining. I carried it down to her anyway. At the curb she pressed the button to make sure it was hers. Two small ears sprang up, and we both laughed.

On the first Tuesday of every month, the town of Bellwether auctioned off the things people had left on its buses. Umbrellas went in bundles of five. Telephones went in a cardboard box marked AS IS, which was also how the auctioneer described a wedding dress, a trombone, and a jar containing twenty-seven human teeth.

The teeth went for eleven dollars. The wedding dress took three months.

Mara worked the auction table. Her job was to write down what things sold for, which meant she knew that a good winter coat was worth less in February than in October, and that people would bid against their own spouses for a decent flashlight. She also knew enough not to try on the coats. There was always something in a pocket: a hair clip, a grocery list, a paper napkin with a telephone number. The coat was easy to sell. The napkin was not.

One Tuesday, just before the doors opened, the depot manager set a kitchen chair on her table.

“Number forty-six,” he said.

“How do you leave a chair on a bus?”

“Same way you leave anything. Get off without it.”

It was an ordinary chair, painted yellow except where the paint had worn away under somebody’s elbows. One leg was shorter than the others. Whoever had last sat in it had folded a square of newspaper and tucked it under the leg with a strip of tape.

Mara turned the chair over. The newspaper was dated May 17, thirty-one years earlier. On the exposed square, a supermarket advertised peaches for thirty-nine cents a pound. She tried to remember whether that was cheap even then. Her father would have known. He had kept a running account of what things ought to cost, and long after he stopped going to the shops he would send her out for a loaf of bread with an amount of money that expressed his disapproval.

She put the chair down and opened the doors.

By noon, everything had sold except the chair. Nobody wanted to carry it home. Mara understood. She had taken the bus that morning herself.

“You can put it out back,” the manager said.

Instead, she carried it to the bus stop. It was only two blocks, but there was no good way to hold it. She tried one hand under the seat, then both hands around the back, then an arrangement that left her looking through the slats. At the stop she set it down and sat in it. On the uneven pavement, the short leg turned out to be exactly the right length.

A man with a paper sack stood beside her. After a while he said, “Is that yours?”

“I suppose so.”

“Do you mind?”

She stood. He sat, setting the sack between his shoes. Its bottom was slowly darkening.

“What have you got in there?” she asked.

“A chicken. I was told it was frozen.”

When the bus came, he lifted the sack with both hands. Mara reached for the chair. Then she saw a woman coming down the sidewalk, walking in the careful, irritable way her father used to walk when there was farther to go than he’d counted on. Mara got on the bus without it. From the window she watched the woman put one hand on the back of the chair, test it, and sit.

The chair was still there the following Tuesday. Someone had moved it under the little overhang of the closed tailor’s shop, where it would stay dry if the rain came straight down. Two weeks later there was a cushion on it, the kind people tie to patio furniture. There was no way to tie it to the chair, so someone had tied its strings to each other.

Mara began to notice who used it. Schoolchildren sat in it sideways, with their legs dangling over an arm. A woman who caught the bus at six carried a folded hand towel to put on the seat. Once, after missing her own bus, Mara watched a man in a good suit eat three plums in the chair. He ate them with such concentration that he didn’t notice his bus pull up. Mara hesitated to interrupt, and by then it was too late. He looked up, saw what had happened, and took a fourth plum out of his bag.

In November the chair disappeared. Mara checked behind the tailor’s shop and asked at the depot, where the manager opened the lost-property cupboard without comment. Inside was a single roller skate, a tin of biscuits that rattled too much to contain biscuits, and a wedding dress.

“Another one?” Mara asked.

“Same one.”

She shut the cupboard.

Three days later the chair was back. It had been painted a yellow so bright it looked green next to the brick wall. The cushion was gone. So was the folded newspaper. Whoever had worked on the chair had glued a neat little block of wood to the short leg, so that it rocked on the pavement.

The next time Mara missed her bus, she sat down anyway. She tried keeping both feet on the ground, then crossing her legs. The chair tipped slightly every time she shifted her weight. She took a receipt out of her coat pocket, folded it twice, and slid it under the opposite leg. It worked. Only after she had done it did she look at the receipt. She had bought butter and a birthday card. The card was for her sister, whose birthday had been the previous Thursday. It was still in her bag.

At home, Mara took the card out and wrote, *I bought this on your birthday*. Then she looked at the date on her phone, crossed out *on*, and wrote *near*. The envelope was too wide for the little box outside her building, so she took it with her the next morning to post near the depot.

At the bus stop a boy was sitting in the chair, tying his shoe. His other foot was planted on the folded receipt. Mara waited until he finished before she asked him to lift it. The paper was wet through. She had the birthday card in one hand and the scrap in the other. When the bus came, she gave the boy the card to hold and crouched to fold the receipt one more time.

On the first Tuesday of every month, the library put its broken things on a table by the front door. Anyone could take one, provided they wrote down what they intended to do with it. Most people were honest. Beside a lamp with no cord, someone had written *Learn about lamps*. Beside a wooden duck with no head: *Make this worse*.

Nina took a clock that gained eleven minutes every hour. Under *Intended Use*, she wrote *Kitchen*. The librarian, who had been watching her over the rims of her glasses, said, “That’s a place.”

“It’s where I intend to use it.”

“Fair enough.”

The clock was yellow and had a second hand that moved with the earnest, slightly panicked energy of a person carrying soup through a crowded room. Nina hung it above the stove. It was three in the afternoon, and by dinner it would be nearly bedtime.

She had recently inherited the house from her father, who had kept a clock in every room, all set to different times. He claimed this was because he didn’t believe an hour should be allowed to arrive everywhere at once. In fact, he had never bothered to learn how to set any of them. For six years the microwave had read 0:00. When Nina was a teenager and came home late, he would consult the microwave and say, “Midnight exactly,” which meant she was in just enough trouble for him to put the kettle on.

The house had come with everything in it, including a dining table that rocked and a jar of screws whose original purposes could no longer be determined. Her father had saved the screws on the theory that whenever you threw one away, its purpose immediately revealed itself. Nina opened the jar, chose a short brass screw, and used it to hang the yellow clock. This was the first convincing evidence she had ever encountered in support of his theory.

At five thirty the following morning, someone knocked on the back door. It was her neighbor, Mrs. Vale, holding a casserole dish with a blue lid.

“I saw your kitchen light,” Mrs. Vale said.

Nina had left it on all night. She used to do the same thing when her father was alive and she went out somewhere he disapproved of. This allowed him to pretend he had fallen asleep in the chair by accident.

“What’s in the dish?” Nina asked.

“Nothing. I thought I’d start returning things before I forgot who they belonged to.”

It wasn’t Nina’s dish. She recognized it as the one Mrs. Vale had carried into the house a week after the funeral, full of baked apples. Her father had hated baked apples. He said they were what happened when you gave up halfway through a pie. Nina had eaten them cold, standing at the counter, and had washed the dish twice because washing it was the only task she could think of that had a definite end.

She said, “Do you want coffee?”

While the kettle heated, Mrs. Vale looked up at the clock. The hour hand was halfway to nine.

“Goodness,” she said, and sat down.

They drank two cups. Mrs. Vale told Nina that the man who had been delivering her newspaper for years had quit and that she had never learned his name. She knew he had a daughter in Ohio and that he couldn’t eat peaches. He had once shown her a photograph of a retaining wall he’d built. “I kept thinking it would be embarrassing to ask,” she said. “And then every year it got more embarrassing.”

“Call the newspaper.”

“And say what?”

“That you liked the wall.”

Mrs. Vale considered this. “I did like the wall. It wasn’t fancy, but you could see he’d thought about the water.”

When she left, she took the dish with her. Nina watched her cross the yard, balancing it flat in both hands as if it were full.

On the next first Tuesday, Nina carried the clock back to the library. The librarian lifted it to her ear, then looked at the face.

“Didn’t work out in the kitchen?”

“It worked out fine,” Nina said. “I think I’d like someone else to have it.”

There was no space for that on the form, so the librarian handed her a blank card. Nina thought about writing a warning. Instead she wrote *Gains eleven minutes an hour. Easy to hang.* She set the clock down between a sewing machine and a pair of binoculars through which everything appeared slightly green.

A boy in a red coat picked it up before she had reached the door. His grandmother, who seemed to have come in for the sewing machine, read the card aloud.

“Is that a lot?” he asked.

His grandmother counted silently, tapping one finger against her coat. “It’ll get about four and a half hours ahead every day.”

“Can it get a whole day ahead?”

“I suppose it can.”

The boy stood very still. “But how will you know when it does?”

His grandmother looked at the clock again. Then she looked up at the librarian, who shrugged. The boy tucked it under his arm and went over to the form.

Nina didn’t stay to see what he wrote. She went home and pulled the dining table away from the wall. The short leg had been shimmed with a piece of folded cardboard that had flattened over the years. She sat on the floor and unfolded it. It was the back of a packet of sunflower seeds. On the front, beneath a picture of three improbably tall flowers, someone had written a telephone number in pencil.

She called it. A woman answered, and Nina explained where she had found the number.

“Oh,” the woman said. “Did they ever come up?”

Nina remembered them then. Her father had planted them beneath the eaves, where there was hardly any sun. Only one had grown tall enough to reach the corner of the kitchen window. Whenever Nina did the dishes, she’d had to lean a little to the left to see its face.

“One did,” she said.

“Well,” the woman said, with the satisfaction of someone whose arithmetic had worked out, “that’s all he asked for.”

### The Bench at the End of the Line

On the last night of the Number 6, someone brought a cake. This was against the rules, but Len had been driving the route for twenty-three years and could no longer remember whether the rule was *no food* or *no hot food*. The cake was cold. He let it on.

“Where do you want it?” asked the woman holding it.

“Is it going to pay?”

“I’ve got exact change.”

She put two coins in the slot. Len printed the cake a ticket, and she carried it to the seat behind him, where it rode all the way downtown with LAST STOP written in blue icing.

At eleven fifteen, the bus was ordinarily empty except for a dishwasher named Ivo, who took his shoes off as soon as he sat down. Tonight, people kept getting on. There was a man Len recognized only when he folded his newspaper into quarters. There were twins who had once been small enough to turn around under the seat without bumping their heads. They were in their thirties now and seemed surprised to see each other.

“Did Mum tell you?” one asked.

“No,” said the other. “Did she tell you?”

They spent three stops trying to establish how they had both found out.

The city had not, strictly speaking, canceled the bus. It had made improvements. Starting Monday, riders could take the 14 to the hospital, cross six lanes of traffic, and catch the 22, which would deliver them almost anywhere the 6 had gone. There was a diagram. Len had studied it long enough to discover that a person could get from his first stop to his last in forty-seven minutes, provided they could walk briskly and the second bus waited while they crossed.

The second bus would not wait. Len knew the driver.

Near the old swimming pool, a girl pulled the cord. Len opened the doors. Nobody moved.

“Sorry,” she said. “I’ve always wanted to do that.”

“You’ve never pulled the cord?”

“My grandmother always did it.”

He shut the doors. In the mirror he watched her wind the sleeve of her sweater around her fingers. He thought he knew which grandmother she meant. For years there had been a woman who pulled the cord immediately after boarding, then looked straight ahead while the bus stopped at every corner between the pool and her house. Eventually she and Len had reached an understanding. She could pull it whenever she liked, and he would let her out at Maple.

At Maple, the girl stayed on.

The last stop was a triangle of cracked pavement between a shuttered florist and the river. The city had bolted a bench there in 1987 and painted it green. In summer, the slats gave off a hot, piney smell. In winter, the bench was a way to get colder than you would have thought possible while wearing pants.

Len pulled in at eleven fifty-eight. Nobody stood.

“What happens to the bench?” the woman with the cake asked.

Len turned off the engine. In the sudden quiet he could hear the river pushing something hollow against the bank.

“I don’t know,” he said.

It was the first question anyone had asked him about the changes that he couldn’t answer. He knew which fares would be honored, where to get a new schedule, and what wording to use if you wanted a real person to read your complaint. He had a card in his pocket with twenty copies of a telephone number, cut into strips because the depot wouldn’t pay to print leaflets. He had not thought to ask about the bench.

The woman peeled the lid off the cake. The icing had stuck to the plastic, leaving only STOP. She passed it around on brown napkins. Someone had brought a knife, but nobody had brought forks.

While they ate, Ivo stepped outside and crouched beside the bench. He came back to ask whether anybody had a socket wrench. The man with the newspaper did, though it took him a while to get it out of the packaging. He had bought it that afternoon to fix a loose toilet seat.

Len watched the two men through the windshield. One held up a phone for light; the other leaned so hard on the wrench that his heels came off the pavement. The first bolt gave with a noise loud enough for everyone on the bus to hear.

“Where are you taking it?” Len asked when they had finished.

This hadn’t occurred to them. They looked down at the bench, which was longer from underneath than it had been from above.

“My grandmother’s building has a laundromat,” the girl said. “People sit on the dryers.”

“That’s back up the route,” said Len.

Nobody pointed out that he knew the way.

The bench wouldn’t fit through the front doors. They got it through the back by turning it on its end, knocking one of the overhead lights loose. Len tucked the light cover into the pocket beside his seat. The twins stood in the aisle and held the bench steady, each bracing a foot against the same iron leg.

On the way back, they passed a man walking a little white dog. He saw the bus and began to run, waving his free hand. Len pulled over.

“Does this go downtown?” the man asked.

“Not anymore,” Len said. “Where are you going?”

The man named a street two blocks from Maple. He started to explain about his car, then about the person who had promised him a ride. Len lowered the bus so the dog could get on.

At the laundromat, there was just enough space for the bench under the window if they moved the trash can. The girl called her grandmother, who came down in slippers and a good wool coat. She put one hand on a slat and rubbed at a pale mark someone had left there long ago with a cigarette.

“You’ll want to put something under that leg,” she said.

The man with the newspaper folded a section into a thick square. Len held the bench up while he pushed it underneath. Then the grandmother sat down, bounced once to see if it would hold, and moved over to make room.

# The Museum of Ordinary Things

On my father’s last day at the lost-property office, he brought home a wooden leg. He stood it beside the umbrella stand, where my mother found it when she came in with the groceries.

“You said you were bringing home a plant,” she said.

“I did bring home a plant.”

The plant was on the kitchen table. My mother took off her coat, came back into the hall, and looked at the leg again. It wore a brown lace-up shoe. She bent to check the sole, although neither of us knew what she expected to find there.

“Someone must have come for this,” she said.

“Two people,” my father said. “It wasn’t theirs.”

For thirty-one years he had worked beneath the bus station, in a room with a high window that showed the feet of people waiting for the number seven. As a child I thought he knew them all by their shoes. Sometimes, when a pair of boots stopped right outside the glass, he would say, “There’s your Uncle Frank,” and I would run upstairs to find a woman eating an orange.

The office had a counter and two chairs. Behind the counter were shelves arranged by month. Wet things went on a rack by the radiator. Money went in a safe. Sandwiches were thrown away immediately, except for one which my father ate in 1988 and which my mother continued to bring up whenever he offered an opinion on food hygiene.

At twelve I spent a week there during the school holidays. I had imagined people would come in furious or weeping, but most were embarrassed. They began with an account of their day, as if the route to a missing glove necessarily passed through a dental appointment. My father listened. He was good at noticing the point where a story stopped being useful without making the person telling it feel they ought to stop.

On Thursday a woman came in for a blue bag. She described the handles, a broken zip, a white mark where she had leaned against a newly painted fence. My father fetched it. She looked inside and sat down.

The bag contained a pair of slippers and a tin of peaches. Her husband had gone into hospital on Monday. She had bought the peaches because he didn’t like the fruit they gave him there, which came already cut up in little bowls. He had died that morning. She’d remembered the bag on the way home.

My father asked whether she wanted a cup of tea. She said no. He made one for himself and one for me, and after a while she asked if there was any left.

I don’t remember what we talked about while she drank it. I remember she had a bus to catch, because my father went up to see if it was in yet. When he came back down, he carried the bag. She’d asked him to keep the peaches.

We had them on Sunday with evaporated milk. I told my mother where they came from, expecting her to put down her spoon. Instead she asked if I wanted the last half. I did. I ate it and turned my bowl sideways to get the milk that had collected under the rim.

After my father retired, the wooden leg stayed in the hall for three weeks. It was awkward to vacuum around, and sometimes, coming downstairs in the dark, my mother mistook it for him. This last objection puzzled me: the leg was much shorter than he was. She said she didn’t mistake it for *all* of him.

Eventually he took it to a cobbler, who stood it in the window to advertise repairs. My father worried the sign might imply the cobbler could repair the leg as well as the shoe. He went back to discuss it and came home with two pairs of insoles.

I moved away. The station was demolished and another built out beyond the ring road. The old site became flats with balconies too shallow for chairs. When I visited, my father liked to walk past and show me where his window had been. It took him a while to get his bearings. There was nothing left to measure from except the bend in the road, and they had softened the bend.

Years later, when we cleared my parents’ house, my sister found his lost-property ledger in a drawer with some takeaway menus. We sat on the stairs to read it. She went straight to her birthday, expecting, I think, to see an entry in his handwriting with something about her. There was a folding umbrella and a pair of prescription sunglasses. She ran a finger down to the next day. He’d taken the rest of the week off.

Inside the back cover he had written three phone numbers without names. My sister wanted to call them. I said they would belong to different people by now. She said even if they did, we could ask how long they’d had the number. We didn’t call. There was a man coming for the washing machine, and we had to find out how to turn off the water.

I took the ledger home. Most of the entries are crossed out. At first I thought this meant my father had reunited a great many people with their belongings. Then I remembered that things got crossed out when they went to the charity shop, too, or into the bin. There’s no way to tell from the line which happened.

One entry, near the bottom of a page in February, reads: *Child’s mitten, red, still warm.*

I think about those last two words. They couldn’t help anybody identify the mitten. By the time a parent came down the stairs, even if they came running, it would be cold. My father must have picked it up, felt the warmth through the wool, and put it down beside the ledger while he found his pen. I wonder how long it took him to decide to write that part. I wonder, too, if he had already written it before he knew he meant to.

### The Things We Keep Until Friday

On Fridays, the city sent a truck for everything nobody had come back for. The driver was named Len. He wore a clean shirt to do dirty work and never asked why a thing had been saved. At four, he backed up to the municipal lost-property office and waited for Ruth to open the loading door.

The office occupied the old weights-and-measures building, which meant that people sometimes came in wanting to know if their grocer was cheating them. Ruth always wished she could help. It would have been satisfying to put an onion on a scale and settle something.

Instead, she had umbrellas.

She had a clarinet with a note in the case that said, in a child’s handwriting, *Please do not make me play this at Grandma’s*. She had a single roller skate, size eleven, with four immaculate wheels. She had six copies of a book called *Getting Your Life in Order*, five of them left on buses and one found in the courthouse, where it had apparently been used to prop open a window.

And, beginning on a Tuesday in October, she had a kitchen drawer.

A street sweeper had found it on a traffic island. The drawer was pine, painted yellow, with a brass handle that had gone green around the screws. It contained two birthday candles, a screwdriver, red thread, a packet of soy sauce, and a key with a cardboard tag marked *NOT THIS ONE*.

Ruth put it on the shelf behind her desk. Several people asked about it, but nobody claimed it. A man collecting a briefcase reached in for the screwdriver without asking. Ruth held out her hand until he gave it back.

At lunch she ate an apple over the drawer, careful not to drop any seeds inside. She tried to remember what had been in the kitchen drawer of the apartment where she grew up. Batteries, probably. Her father’s reading glasses. A little wrench that came with something they no longer owned. For years after he died, she had been able to recall the sound of him searching that drawer. Now when she tried, what she heard was herself asking him what he was looking for.

About three weeks after the drawer came in, a woman in a blue raincoat stopped at the counter.

“Is that from a kitchen?” she asked.

“I assume so,” Ruth said.

“We had those handles.”

“Do you want to look at it?”

The woman said no, then took off her gloves. Ruth set the drawer on the counter.

The woman picked up the key. “My son used to write things like this. We had a switch in the hall that didn’t do anything, and he put a piece of tape over it that said ‘Don’t.’ I asked him why, and he said, ‘Because it doesn’t.’”

“How old is he?”

“Thirty-one. He works at an aquarium. I don’t know what he does there, exactly. He tells me and I come away with the impression he fixes the fish.”

She put the key back and collected the gloves she’d come for. They were black wool, joined at the wrists by a long cord.

“People laugh,” she said, threading the cord through her sleeves, “but I still have them.”

On the drawer’s last Friday, Len came in early. Rain was coming under the loading door, and he helped Ruth move a box of books out of its path. Then he went to get a broom.

“Do you want a drawer?” she asked when he came back.

“What for?”

She hadn’t prepared for this question. “It’s a good drawer,” she said.

Len turned it over. On the underside someone had written *14⅜* in pencil.

“It’ll be that wide at the back,” he said. “Maybe a little wider at the front.”

He took a tape measure from his pocket. It was a little wider at the front.

“Made it to fit,” he said, and set it down.

At ten to four a man came in carrying a new umbrella with the price tag still on it. He had lost an old umbrella. Ruth showed him the stand by the radiator, and he sorted through it, opening two of them despite the sign.

“It had a wooden handle,” he said. “My wife bought it for me on our honeymoon. We’d had a fight, and I walked out in the rain. She came and found me in a sandwich shop. She’d bought herself one, too. Hers was better.”

He tried the last umbrella. It stuck halfway open.

“She’s at home,” he said, though Ruth hadn’t asked. “She told me to buy a new one.”

He folded the old umbrella and put it back. Then he asked Ruth for scissors so he could cut the tag off the new one before he went out.

By four the rain had eased. Len took the books and the umbrellas, the roller skate and the clarinet. Ruth carried the drawer as far as the loading door. She stood there holding it while Len tightened a strap across the back of the truck.

“I could take it home,” she said.

Len tested the strap with his thumb. “Sure.”

She thought of her kitchen. The shallow cupboard beside the stove had a shelf at just the right height, though she’d have to move the colander. She could put the scissors in there, and the loose batteries from the windowsill. She could throw out the soy sauce.

Instead she put the drawer on the truck.

On Monday morning there was a message from a man whose kitchen cabinets had fallen off a trailer in October. Ruth called him back. He said he wasn’t after cabinets, which were easy enough to replace. He wanted a brass handle. They’d found eleven in the road and needed twelve.

She told him about the truck. He was quiet a moment, then asked whether she remembered what the handle looked like.

She drew it while he waited: two square feet, a low arch, a screw at either end. He said there was a man at the flea market who sold handles out of coffee cans. He hadn’t been sure what to ask for.

Ruth offered to mail him the drawing. After they hung up, she went over the pencil lines in ink so they wouldn’t rub off in the envelope.

### The Department of Unclaimed Things

On her third day at the Department of Unclaimed Things, Nora learned that a single glove was worth keeping for ninety days, but a pair of gloves only sixty.

“People come back for the single ones,” said Len, who had worked there since before the city put numbers on its bus stops. “They’ve got the other one at home reminding them.”

He showed her how to tag an umbrella without opening it and how to tell, by weight, whether a lunchbox needed immediate attention. At four he made tea in a kettle that had been left on the number nine bus in 2006. Its owner had never come, although Len had once received a call from a man who could describe the kettle perfectly but insisted he had lost it at sea.

“Could have been his,” Len said. “People are unreliable about where they’ve been.”

The department occupied two rooms beneath the central bus station. All day, buses shuddered overhead, stirring dust from the pipes. Nora had taken the job because her father had died in February, and by April she had discovered that she needed work with a very clear distinction between what had been done and what hadn’t. A thing was tagged or it wasn’t. Nobody asked her how she was doing unless she had lifted something heavy.

Her father’s apartment was still full. The landlord had given her until the end of the month to empty it. She had managed the refrigerator and one kitchen drawer. The drawer contained eight birthday candles, a screwdriver with a broken handle, and a takeout menu on which her father had written, in his square draftsman’s capitals, NO GOOD. She had thrown away the candles and the screwdriver, then taken the menu out of the trash.

One Tuesday, a woman came to the counter looking for a green bag.

“What was inside?” Nora asked.

“Another bag.”

“And inside that?”

“Nothing. I was on my way to buy potatoes.”

Nora fetched three green bags, none of them right. The woman looked relieved at the sight of the third, then disappointed when she touched it.

“Mine had a better handle,” she said. “I made it from the waistband of my husband’s trousers.”

Nora asked for a phone number.

“Don’t trouble yourself,” the woman said, and left.

That afternoon Nora found the bag tucked inside a folding shopping cart. Its handle had a buttonhole at one end. She set it under the counter. There was a shelf for things awaiting collection, but to put it there she would have needed a name.

On Thursday, Len brought in a loaf of bread.

“My daughter’s got into sourdough,” he said. “She talks about it like she’s having trouble with a horse.”

They ate slices at the counter with butter shaved off a cold block. Nora told him about the apartment. She hadn’t meant to, but he asked whether she wanted to take the rest of the loaf home, and she said there wasn’t room in the freezer. All the food people had brought her in February was still in there.

“How much time have you got?” he asked.

“Nine days.”

“I can bring my van on Sunday.”

She started to explain that most of the things weren’t ready to go. Len said Sunday was when he had the van. They could see what was ready then.

He arrived at nine with a stack of empty banana boxes. Nora had spent the previous evening making signs that said KEEP, DONATE, and RUBBISH. When she opened the door, he was holding two coffees and looking down at a small brass plate screwed into the doorframe. Her father had installed it to cover a hole where a chain lock had been.

“Nice work,” Len said.

Nora had passed that plate hundreds of times. She ran a thumb over it. One corner stood slightly proud of the wood.

They packed the books first. Her father had owned several books about canals and a paperback about how to win at blackjack. Nora opened that one and found an old bus ticket marking page seventeen.

“He took a bus to the casino once,” she said. “He came home with more money than he left with. A woman at the stop lent him five pounds for the fare and he walked home instead.”

“Did he pay her back?”

“He spent two Saturdays waiting for her at the stop.”

Len held the box open. Nora put the book in.

By noon, the apartment sounded different. From the kitchen she could hear Len drawing the tape across a box in the bedroom. She opened the refrigerator, forgetting she had already emptied it, and stood in the light from the little bulb. Then she unplugged it and propped the door open with a shoe.

On Monday, the woman came back.

“I thought you might,” Nora said, reaching beneath the counter.

The woman put both hands flat on the green bag. She pressed the buttonhole with her thumb.

“I’ve bought the potatoes already,” she said.

“You can still take it.”

“Oh, I know.” She looked up at Nora. “I’m trying to remember what else I need.”

They stood there while she thought. Above them a bus pulled out, and something in the ceiling gave its usual small knock.

“Onions,” the woman said at last. She folded the bag into a neat square and put it in her coat pocket.

That evening Nora took a screwdriver to the apartment. She undid the two screws in the brass plate and caught it in her palm. Behind it was a ragged hole, with a bright scrape where the chain had once pulled loose. She remembered that happening. She’d been twelve and angry, and had yanked the door open while her father was still telling her she couldn’t go out. He’d looked at the chain lying on the floor and said, with genuine interest, “Well, I wouldn’t have thought you could do that.”

She stood in the doorway for a minute. Then she fetched the shoe from the kitchen and used it to prop the front door while she carried the last box down. Afterward she came back up, screwed the plate into place, and locked the door. The new tenant would never need to know about the hole. Nora hoped that, sooner or later, they’d notice the brass.

### A Place to Put the River

The first thing we did after buying the house was paint over the line where the river had been.

It ran through the kitchen at the height of my hip, a faint brown seam interrupted by the stove. The previous owner, Mrs. Vale, had pointed it out during the inspection. She stood in the middle of the kitchen with her handbag hanging from both hands.

“That was a Tuesday,” she said.

The inspector asked what year.

“Oh, 1986. But Tuesday was the important part. I’d just washed the floors.”

On our first morning in the house, my brother and I opened a can of pale yellow paint. We were thirty and thirty-four, old enough to know that buying a house together was a questionable solution to several unrelated problems. His marriage had ended. My landlord had decided to sell. There was only one bathroom, and the stairs began directly behind the front door, so that if you came in too enthusiastically you could find yourself in the middle of going upstairs.

We painted the kitchen yellow because the hardware store had mixed five gallons for somebody who never came back.

By lunchtime the river was gone.

In September, my brother found a canoe in the garage. We had been parking beside it for three months without noticing. It hung from the rafters, upside down, its green hull almost black with dust. We got it down with considerable planning and no grace. Inside were two paddles, a wasp nest, and an envelope containing a photograph of Mrs. Vale standing knee-deep in water in our kitchen.

She was wearing a blue robe and holding a colander.

On the back someone had written: *Jean retrieving the potatoes.*

I put the photograph on the refrigerator. My brother took it down because the magnet was scratching the door. I put it back with a different magnet. This was more or less how we had been making decisions since childhood.

Neither of us wanted to go out in the canoe. We wanted to be the kind of people who went out in a canoe, which was different enough to keep it in the garage all winter.

In February a letter came for Mrs. Vale. It was from the hearing clinic and had *PERSONAL* stamped on the front in red. I called the number she had left us. She’d moved into an apartment across from the library, and I offered to bring the letter over.

“Would you?” she said. “I’ve been ignoring their calls for a week.”

Her apartment was hot and smelled of toast. On the windowsill was a row of stones, each with a date written on it in pencil. While she went to find the kettle, I leaned over to read them. Most were from the previous summer. One was dated April 9, 1991.

“I pick one up when I go for a walk,” Mrs. Vale said behind me. “Then I come home and put it down. There’s not a lot to it.”

I asked about the photograph.

“Oh,” she said, “he thought that was terribly funny.”

“Mr. Vale?”

“No, the man from the gas company.”

She told me the river had come in through the back door, which she’d opened to see how high it was. She could still shut the door, but by then there wasn’t much point. The potatoes floated out of a basket under the sink. She had been determined to catch them, because it was something she could see to do.

“What did you do with them?” I asked.

“Threw them away, of course.”

In March it rained for six days. My brother went down to the river each evening and returned with a report that meant nothing to me.

“It’s up to the bench.”

“Which bench?”

“The one you can’t see anymore.”

On the seventh morning, we woke to a woman knocking on the door. She lived two streets over and had been knocking on doors since five. The river had come into her yard. She recommended moving the cars uphill while we could. My brother started looking for his keys, and the woman, who could see them on the hall table from where she stood, reached in and handed them to him.

The water didn’t reach our house. It reached the end of the driveway and stayed there for half a day. All that time our cars sat at the top of the hill with the other cars, and people walked down in twos and threes to look at their houses. A man carried a toaster uphill under his arm. Nobody asked him why he had chosen the toaster.

Late that afternoon my brother and I took the canoe off its hooks. We set it on the driveway and sat in it, facing the river. Our feet were dry. The paddles lay across our knees.

“Do you know how to steer this?” he asked.

“No.”

“Good,” he said, and took his feet out of his wet shoes.

We sat there until the woman who’d knocked on our door came back down the street. She looked at us for a moment, then asked if there was room for one more. My brother moved forward. She climbed in, carefully, with a hand on each of our shoulders. She had been on her feet since before dawn.

The next time I visited Mrs. Vale, she wanted to know how close the water had gotten. I said I’d show her, and the following Saturday she came over. We stood at the mouth of the driveway. In the gravel there was a ragged line of leaves and little sticks, with a blue plastic clothespin caught among them.

From there I could see straight through the kitchen window to the yellow wall. I asked if she remembered exactly where the old line had been.

She came inside and considered the wall for a while. Then she put one finger against it, just below a light switch.

“Here,” she said. After a second she moved her finger down. “No. Here.”

I offered to get a pencil.

Mrs. Vale thought about it. “Have you still got that photograph?”

I showed her where it was on the refrigerator. She straightened it, although I hadn’t noticed it was crooked. Then she asked if we had any coffee, and I put the kettle on.

### The Lost Property Office

On the morning the city decided to close its lost property office, a man came in looking for a plum.

“Not a particular plum,” he explained. “Any plum would do.”

Nora, who had worked behind the counter for twenty-three years, told him they didn’t keep fruit. It was the sort of thing she usually said without looking up, but that morning she wanted to see who would come all the way down to the basement of the municipal building for a plum.

He was wearing a suit with one sleeve damp to the elbow.

“Did you lose one?” she asked.

“No. My sister used to bring me one when she picked me up from swimming. I’ve just been swimming, and I thought I’d see if I could get the rest of the afternoon right.”

“There’s a grocer on Bell Street,” Nora said.

“I know. I own it.”

He thanked her and left. For the next hour she thought about the damp sleeve.

At eleven, a woman from the city brought down several rolls of colored stickers. Green for auction, red for disposal, yellow for anything that might contain personal data. She stuck a green dot on a violin case without opening it.

“Wouldn’t you want to see if there’s a violin inside?” Nora asked.

“Is there?”

“No.”

The woman peeled off the dot. “Then you’ve saved somebody a disappointment.”

Nora waited until she was gone before opening the case. Inside were three sheets of music and a pencil worn down to the length of a thumbnail. Years ago, a boy had come in with his father to claim it. The father had described a blue case with brass clasps, which was accurate. But when Nora brought it out, the boy took one look and said, “Mine never had a handle.”

The father swore softly. The boy’s face did something Nora had not understood until much later: he was trying not to smile. For a few more hours, at least, he wasn’t going to have to practice.

She put the pencil in her pocket.

Her own daughter had lost a shoe at the seaside when she was six. Nora had made them walk the length of the beach twice looking for it. The girl had found a crab shell, a plastic dinosaur, and a piece of glass worn soft as soap. She had offered each in turn as a reason to stop.

At last Nora had carried her back to the car. She no longer remembered the shoe. She remembered the sandy foot bumping against her thigh.

At lunch she called her daughter and asked if she remembered the shoe.

“What shoe?”

“Never mind. What are you doing?”

“Eating an egg over the sink.”

“Is there something wrong with your table?”

“No, Mum. I just didn’t want to get a plate.”

Nora could hear a tap running. Her daughter asked how the packing was going, and Nora said she was making progress, which was true in the sense that the morning was gone.

By three, she had filled five boxes. By four, she was down to the umbrella stand. The office had once had a policy of keeping umbrellas for ninety days. Then the city reduced it to thirty, and then to seven. There were always about forty umbrellas. People lost them on the first clear afternoon after rain.

Nora took the stand upstairs and set it outside the front doors with a sign that said PLEASE TAKE ONE. On her way back down, she passed the grocer.

He was sitting on the basement steps. He had changed his jacket.

“I thought I’d try again,” he said.

“We still don’t have any plums.”

“I brought some.”

He showed her the paper bag. There were at least a dozen inside, greenish yellow, with small brown freckles. She had expected purple ones.

“Are these the right kind?” Nora asked.

“I haven’t tried one yet.”

She sat beside him, and he chose two. Hers was cold and so ripe that the skin broke under her thumb. She bent over her knees to keep the juice off her blouse. Beside her the grocer laughed, though he hadn’t taken a bite.

“She had a towel,” he said. “That’s what I forgot. She always brought a towel from home because I never dried myself properly. She’d make me stand behind the car and do my ears.”

“How old were you?”

“Thirty-seven.”

Nora looked at him.

“I was learning,” he said. “I’d been afraid of the water.”

He finished his plum, folded the pit into a corner of the bag, and went upstairs. He left the rest of the fruit with Nora. Through the stairwell window she watched him take an umbrella, open it to check the spokes, and put it back. It was a clear afternoon.

At five, the woman from the city returned with a caretaker. He rattled the handle after locking the office, then stooped to peer through the little window in the door.

“You’ve left the light on,” he said.

“I know.”

He waited. Nora had no explanation for him. After a moment he unlocked the door and turned it off himself.

Outside, somebody had taken the entire umbrella stand. Nora caught the bus to her daughter’s apartment with the plums on her lap. At each stop they rolled to one side of the bag, then settled back.

Her daughter answered barefoot, with a dish towel over her shoulder.

“You could have called,” she said.

“I did call.”

“You asked me about a shoe.”

Nora held out the bag. Her daughter looked inside, picked a plum, and went to eat it over the sink. Nora followed. From the kitchen window they could see a man in the building opposite trying to coax a cat in from a ledge. He was shaking a box of something the cat plainly did not want.

Without turning away from the window, Nora’s daughter took the towel off her shoulder and handed it to her. Nora wiped her chin. They stayed there long enough to see the man give up and the cat come in on its own.

The first sound my mother asked me to save was the kitchen drawer. Not her voice, not the song she used to sing while cutting my hair, but the drawer to the left of the stove. You had to lift it by the handle before you pulled. Otherwise it stuck, then came loose all at once and sent the teaspoons skittering to the back. I recorded it both ways. My mother listened through the headphones, frowned, and said, “Do it again, but don’t try so hard to get it right.” The third time, I caught her laughing in the background.

We had twelve days to empty the house. She was moving into a flat with an elevator, a word she pronounced with the satisfaction of someone who had spent forty years carrying groceries upstairs. I had expected her to be sentimental about the move and had prepared several tender speeches, none of which survived contact with her enthusiasm for the flat’s water pressure. I was the one who kept standing in doorways. She was the one who put the good china on the pavement with a sign that said FREE, then went out twenty minutes later to add PLEASE.

The recordings were her answer to my habit of rescuing things from the giveaway pile. What was I going to do with a colander whose base had rusted through? I said it didn’t have to do anything. She said that was generous of me, considering how much I complained about the size of my apartment. We compromised: I could keep any noise I liked. No storage unit, no bubble wrap. I downloaded an app that displayed each recording as a blue waveform, so that a cupboard shutting looked surprisingly like a mountain with a little village at its foot.

By the fourth day, I had recorded the bathroom light switch, the front gate, and the scrape of the bench my father had built too long for its alcove. To move it, you had to bring one end forward and wiggle the other. Every year at Christmas we performed this maneuver to make room for the tree. Every year my father said he ought to take an inch off the bench. The first Christmas after he died, my mother and I moved it without speaking. Then, halfway through, she said, in her own voice, “I ought to take an inch off this bench.”

That scrape was the only sound I tried to record without telling her. I waited until she went to buy packing tape, put my phone on the floor, and dragged the bench out. When I played it back, I heard the scrape and then a little gasp I didn’t remember making. I tried again and got the scrape and a truck going past. The third time I got what I wanted: a clean, unaccompanied scrape. It was the least interesting of the three. I sat on the bench for a while, listening to the truck go by again.

On Saturday a young man came for the kitchen table. His daughter, who was maybe six, walked around it with her palm flat against the edge. I warned him that one leg was shorter than the others and showed him the folded matchbook we used to level it. He put the matchbook in his shirt pocket with a seriousness I appreciated. While we worked out how to get the table through the door, his daughter crawled underneath and found the price of a bicycle I had written there in pencil when I was eleven. She asked if the bicycle was still for sale.

The last thing we packed was the kettle. My mother made tea and we drank it standing up, setting our cups on the windowsill between sips. Without the table, I could open the drawer all the way without stepping aside. I did, expecting that familiar rush of teaspoons, but of course there was nothing in it. My mother asked if I wanted to record that too. I said no. Then she opened it herself, peered into the far corner, and fished out the tiny screwdriver my father had used to fix his glasses. She put it in her handbag. Neither of us said a word about the giveaway pile.

For months after the move, I didn’t listen to the recordings. It turned out that the main thing I wanted, when I missed the house, was to tell my mother I missed it. She was usually sympathetic, though one evening she said, “You know, I spent a fair amount of my life wishing I could get out of that kitchen.” Then she told me about a night when she let the potatoes boil dry because she was reading a novel on the back step. I remembered the blackened pan. I had been told it was my father’s fault.

In February she called to ask if I still had the recording of the drawer. A friend of hers had been looking for replacement handles, and my mother had described ours as brass, with a little dip in the middle for your thumb. Her friend couldn’t picture it. Neither, it turned out, could I. I could remember how cold the handle felt early in the morning, and how it warmed if you stood there keeping the drawer open while you decided whether a piece of cake called for a fork or a spoon. The recording was no help at all.

I played her the third take anyway. There was the lift, the rattle, the laugh. Over the phone my mother laughed again, a little later than she had the first time. Then she asked if I could hear the snowplow. I said there hadn’t been any snow when we made the recording. “No,” she said, “out here. Right now. Listen.” She set the phone on her windowsill. For a few seconds I heard nothing, and then the plow came around the corner, its blade knocking over the seams in the road. When it had passed, my mother picked up the phone and told me what she could see. The man across the street had come out in his slippers. He was shoveling a path just wide enough for the dog.

# The Department of Small Repairs

On the first Saturday of every month, the city opened a room beneath the railway station where you could bring one broken thing. The rules were printed on a sheet of paper taped to the door: NO PHONES. NO MICROWAVES. YOU MUST STAY WITH YOUR OBJECT. That last rule was underlined twice. People assumed it meant there had been trouble with unclaimed toasters, but the volunteers had put it there because otherwise everyone went for coffee, and the room was too quiet.

Marta first came in November with a wooden duck. It was the kind that followed a child on a string, its wheels turning two flat orange feet that slapped the floor. One foot had split down the middle. Her son had graduated from university the previous summer and was now living in a city so flat, he said, that when you lost a dog you could watch it run away for three days. She had been saving that joke to tell someone in person.

“What kind of wood is it?” asked the man at the first table.

“I don’t know.”

“That’s all right. Neither do I.”

His name was Len. He took the duck apart and placed the pieces in a muffin tin. Beside them, in a compartment of its own, he placed a screw so small Marta could only see it when it caught the light. Then he asked her to hold the broken foot while he drew around it on a scrap of wood.

Above them a train came in. The ceiling trembled. At the next table a girl in a school uniform was learning to sew a button onto her own coat. She had buttoned it wrong on purpose so no one could see the gap. A woman with a suitcase sat with one stockinged foot resting on the other while a volunteer glued the sole of her shoe. It was an ordinary room, apart from the unusual number of people sitting still while something they needed was in pieces.

The new foot was paler than the old one. Len offered to paint it, but Marta said she liked being able to tell which one it was. He set the duck on the floor and drew it toward him. It made three good slaps, then fell on its side.

“I put the wheels on backward,” he said.

They laughed, although it wasn’t much of a joke. Then Marta told him the one about the dog.

By February she was a volunteer. Her first repair was a zipper on a cushion cover. She spent forty minutes coaxing the slider back onto the track, only for the cushion’s owner to turn the cover right side out and reveal a large burn in the shape of an iron.

“Did you want us to do something about that, too?” Marta asked.

“No,” the woman said. “My sister did that.”

She said it with such satisfaction that Marta didn’t ask another question.

Some things couldn’t be fixed. A boy brought in a snow globe with a crack at the base. Someone had already tried to seal it with candle wax. By the time he arrived, the little village inside stood dry beneath a blue sky, its snow gathered in an untidy drift along one wall. Len explained that even if they sealed the crack, he wasn’t sure how they’d get the liquid back in. The boy considered this.

“Can you make it snow one more time?”

Len turned the globe upside down and tapped the glass. A few flakes came loose. They fell much faster than snow should, but the boy watched until the last one landed.

In April, a council employee came downstairs carrying a clipboard. The station was being renovated. The room was needed for electrical equipment. She had been told, she said, that they offered a drop-off service.

“No,” Marta said, pointing at the rules.

The employee read the sheet. “Why can’t people drop things off?”

Marta looked around. Len was holding a lamp while its owner, an elderly man in a beautifully ironed shirt, tried to thread the cord through the base. Every time the cord appeared, the man reached for it too quickly and knocked it back inside. At last Len set down the lamp, took two pairs of tweezers from a drawer, and handed him one.

“Sometimes we need both of you,” Marta said.

They were given until June. On the last Saturday, people kept arriving with things that weren’t broken. The girl who had learned to sew on a button brought a cake in a tin with a perfectly sound hinge. The man with the lamp brought a photograph of it switched on. Someone brought a folding chair, circled the room twice looking for a place to put it, then unfolded it and sat down.

Marta had brought the duck. Her son was coming home the following week, and she had decided to give it to him, though she suspected he would say, quite reasonably, that he had nowhere to put it. She set it on Len’s table. He ran a thumb over the pale foot. It was already acquiring the grayish look of the older one.

“Needs a bit of oil,” he said.

“Does it?”

“No. I just thought we could do it anyway.”

So they did. At five they packed the muffin tins and took the sign off the door. Upstairs, the woman with the suitcase was waiting in the station café. She had asked the manager if they could use the back tables next month, and he’d said yes, provided nobody plugged anything in.

“What will we do about lamps?” Len asked.

“Bring one and find out,” she said.

The floor in the café was tiled, so Marta put the duck down to see how it sounded there. Louder, it turned out. It slapped its way past a man buttering a scone and stopped under the chair of a little girl. Marta crouched to retrieve it, but the girl had already slipped down from her seat. She picked up the string and looked at Marta.

“Can I take it back the other way?”

Marta moved her chair out of the way.

# The Four Minutes

The clock at the end of Mercy Street was four minutes slow. Everyone knew it, including the man who came twice a year to wind it, though he was under the impression that only he knew.

The clock had once belonged to a department store. When the store shut, the building became a pharmacy on the ground floor and six apartments above. The clock stayed where it was, bolted to the brick over the old entrance, which was now a wall. People still said, “Meet me under the clock,” and stood in front of the wall feeling a little foolish.

On the first Tuesday in November, a woman called Ruth arrived with a ladder and a municipal work order. The order said REMOVE REDUNDANT TIMEPIECE. In the space marked REASON, someone had typed INACCURATE.

She was extending the ladder when a man carrying two cups of coffee stopped beside her.

“How inaccurate?” he asked.

“Four minutes.”

“Is it getting worse?”

“Apparently not.”

He considered this. “That’s quite good, then.”

Ruth had worked for the city for nineteen years. She knew the difference between a man who wanted an answer and a man who had brought a second coffee in the hope of having a conversation. She took the coffee.

His name was Daniel. He used to meet his wife under the clock on Tuesdays, he said. She finished work at five and took the bus into town. He walked from the print shop. They had dinner at the place that was now a shop selling expensive soap.

“And now?” Ruth asked.

“Now I buy a coffee for myself and, as you can see, make poor decisions about the second.”

He said it lightly. Ruth looked down at the lid. Someone had drawn a small S on it in blue marker.

“Sugar,” Daniel said.

“I didn’t ask.”

“You looked like you might.”

She drank it. There was too much sugar.

From the top of the ladder she could see into the first-floor apartment. A child in a school uniform was trying to feed a piece of toast to a sleeping dog. The child looked up, startled, and Ruth raised her work order in explanation. The child raised the toast.

The clock’s casing was held shut by two screws, one of which had been painted over so many times it looked like a lump of chewing gum. Ruth scraped the paint away. Inside, someone had tucked a folded receipt between the casing and the mechanism. It was from the department store, dated thirty-one years earlier, for two pillowcases and a lamp. On the back, in pencil, was written: *If you alter the hands, do not alter the pendulum.*

She called her supervisor.

“Can I correct it instead?”

“Is that cheaper?”

“Almost certainly.”

“Then why did we send a van?”

“You always send a van.”

There was a silence during which Ruth could hear him eating something crisp. “Use your judgment,” he said at last, in the tone of a man who expected not to hear about it again.

At noon, Ruth moved the minute hand forward. The mechanism accepted the change without complaint. She put the receipt back where she had found it and climbed down.

Daniel was still there, sitting on the low wall outside the pharmacy.

“You’ve fixed it,” he said.

“Yes.”

He checked his watch. The clock and the watch agreed. He put his hands in his coat pockets.

“My wife used to set her watch by that clock,” he said. “She knew it was slow. She’d do it while I was standing there telling her it was slow.”

“Why?”

“I thought she was doing it to annoy me.” He smiled. “That was a perfectly good reason, as far as she was concerned.”

Ruth folded the ladder. Across the street, a delivery driver was arguing with a parking meter. A pharmacist came outside to eat an apple. Overhead, the child had opened the window, and the dog, now awake, put its nose out into the cold.

“Her bus was always late,” Daniel said. “No more than a few minutes, usually. She hated making anybody wait. One day I told her I went by the clock, so as far as I was concerned she was early.”

“Did you?”

“No. I went by my watch. I liked having a few minutes to stand here and look for her.”

He sounded surprised to have said it. Ruth busied herself with a strap that had twisted around the ladder.

At twelve fifteen, Daniel said goodbye. He thanked her for drinking the coffee. She thanked him for buying it. He went away in the direction of the expensive soap, walking a little sideways at first as he tucked one glove into the other.

Ruth put the ladder in the van. She completed the work order, crossing out REMOVE and writing ADJUSTED. She was about to start the engine when she noticed something in the side mirror.

A woman had stopped under the clock. She was looking up at it, then at her phone. She looked up again. The expression on her face was not annoyance but calculation. A moment later she put her phone away and ran toward the bus stop.

Ruth watched her catch the bus.

The following Tuesday, Ruth was back on Mercy Street to replace a bent street sign. It was nearly five when she finished. As she came around the corner, she saw Daniel by the wall with a coffee in each hand. He held one out to her.

“No sugar this time,” he said. “I had to guess about the milk.”

There was a little too much milk, but she didn’t tell him that. She had parked on a yellow line and meant to explain that she could only stay a minute. Instead she asked him what his wife’s name was.

“Susan,” he said. Then he took a sip of coffee and added, “She couldn’t stand that restaurant, by the way. We went every week for eleven years before she told me.”

Ruth laughed. Across the street a bus pulled in, and Daniel turned, without quite meaning to, to see who got off. Ruth stayed until the next bus came.

# The Things We Keep Until Thursday

On Thursdays, the city sold what it had found. For twenty years the sale had taken place in the basement of the old bus depot, where the pipes knocked even in summer. Umbrellas went for a dollar, bicycles for ten, and everything with a cord was understood to be a wager. Once, a man bought a toaster and found inside it a slice of bread so thoroughly fossilized that he brought it back the next week to show us. We put it on a saucer beside the cash box. By Christmas someone had bought that, too.

I worked the counter with a woman named Bea, who had been there long enough to recognize certain umbrellas by the sound they made opening. She disliked putting a price on anything before she had looked through it. She did not expect to find money. What she generally found was a reason not to sell the thing yet.

There had been a red schoolbag with a note inside that said, in a child’s tall handwriting, **tell Dad I can do the deep end**. There had been a pair of dancing shoes with the left heel repaired in three different colors of thread. Bea had kept the shoes through two changes of mayor.

“What if she stopped dancing?” I asked.

“Then she can come back and tell me herself.”

One October, a bus driver brought us a yellow cake tin. On the lid someone had stuck a strip of masking tape and written **MARTIN, THURSDAY**. There was no cake inside. Instead there were eleven photographs, each of the same small apple tree. In the earliest picture, the tree was tied to a broom handle. In the latest, two apples hung from a branch that looked hardly strong enough to bear them.

A man phoned about the tin that afternoon. He knew about the dent in the lid and the apple tree. Bea told him our hours. He said he’d be down once he’d finished putting up a shelf.

The next Thursday he called again. He had missed the bus. The following week he was waiting for a plumber. In November he said his sister was visiting, and Bea, who usually wrote down every word a caller gave her, stopped taking notes. Before she hung up she asked whether Martin was his name.

“Yes,” he said. Then, as if she’d asked a second question: “It’s my wife’s writing.”

We put the tin on the shelf behind the counter, between a motorcycle helmet and a paper sack of knitting. By February Martin had quit calling. I learned to slide the tin forward when I dusted, so that the clean circle underneath it wouldn’t show.

That spring the city decided to close the depot. A new lost-property office would open across town, in a building with level floors and a computerized inventory. The manager sent us a spreadsheet in which every object had to be either *claimed*, *disposed of*, or *transferred*. Bea added a fourth column and called it *coming*. The manager deleted it. Bea printed the spreadsheet and drew the column back in with a ruler.

On our last Thursday it rained so hard that customers had to shout their offers over the water running through the downspout. The bicycles went first. A young woman bought the dancing shoes without trying them on. After she’d paid, Bea came around the counter and showed her how to wind the ankle straps so the buckles wouldn’t scuff the leather. She was still holding one shoe when the woman reached to take it. For a second neither let go.

At four, with an hour left before closing, I called Martin. He answered on the sixth ring.

“I know,” he said before I’d finished introducing myself.

I told him I could bring the tin over.

“No, no. I don’t want you doing that.”

Behind him a kettle came to a boil. He set the phone down without saying anything and I waited through the clink of a spoon against a cup. When he came back he asked if the number nine still stopped outside the depot. I said it did.

He arrived twenty minutes after we locked the doors. Bea had already left with her ruler sticking out of her handbag. I saw him through the glass, standing under the narrow lip of the roof, trying to fold a newspaper around a loaf of bread. He held the loaf out to me when I let him in. It took me a moment to understand that he’d brought it for us.

“The cake was a lemon one,” he said when I put the tin on the counter. “She made it on Tuesday. I was supposed to take it to my brother on Thursday, but I ate it.”

He picked at the masking tape with his thumbnail. Then he flattened it again.

“And the photographs?” I asked.

“Oh. Those were for my brother, too.”

He opened the lid and dealt the photographs onto the counter, face up. In the picture with the two apples he pointed to a patch of brown in the bottom corner. I’d always taken it for a dead leaf.

“That’s her slipper,” he said. “She was holding the branch still. I kept telling her to get out of the picture.”

He laughed, and I did too, though a second later than he did. He gathered up the photographs without putting them in order. On his way out he stopped to tuck the tin under his coat. The newspaper he’d used to wrap the bread lay wet on the counter, its ink coming off on my hand.

I took half the loaf home and left half for Bea in the staff fridge. In the morning I remembered that neither of us was going back. I called the depot, thinking a cleaner might answer, but our number had already been disconnected.

For weeks afterward I found myself looking for things to mark the old hours. At four on Thursdays I’d turn the radio on or put the kettle to boil. Once I went down to the depot without quite deciding to. The doors were papered over, but the number nine still stopped outside. A woman got off carrying a young tree in a plastic pot. She set it down on the pavement, pulled a glove off with her teeth, and called somebody to come help her carry it home.

On the first Saturday of every month, the public library in my neighborhood puts a sign beside the book return: **BRING US YOUR BROKEN THINGS.** The first time I saw it, I assumed it announced an unusually ambitious poetry workshop. In fact, the library was hosting a repair café. Volunteers sat at folding tables with sewing kits, screwdrivers, and the little dishes people use to keep screws from rolling away. You could bring one thing, and someone would try to fix it with you. The sign promised nothing about success. This struck me as a refreshing way to advertise.

I brought a kitchen clock that had stopped at 4:17. It had hung above my parents’ stove for most of my childhood, gathering a faint brown varnish that no amount of wiping would remove. My mother gave it to me when she redid the kitchen. “It’s always been a little fast,” she said, though I remembered her setting it fast on purpose. She wanted five extra minutes in the morning. We all knew about the five minutes, and some mornings I would stand in the kitchen explaining to her that we had time for another piece of toast. She generally disagreed.

The volunteer assigned to my clock was a woman named Ruth, who wore her reading glasses on a length of green shoelace. She asked what I had tried. I said I had changed the battery. She asked whether I had thrown the old battery away. I said no, that it was on my desk at home. “Good,” she said. “Then there are two things we haven’t learned yet.” She tested the battery I had installed and found it dead. Then she handed me a fresh one. I put it in. The clock remained at 4:17. I was relieved not to have come all that way for a battery.

At the next table, a boy waited while a volunteer sewed the leg back onto a stuffed rabbit. The boy had insisted on holding the rabbit’s hand, which meant there was very little room for the volunteer to work. His father suggested he move. The volunteer said she could manage. Every few stitches she turned the rabbit over and asked the boy how it looked. He kept saying the leg was crooked. Finally she showed him the other leg, which was also crooked. They considered this together. He asked if she could make the two legs crooked in the same direction.

Ruth took the clock apart. On the back of the face, where nobody had been expected to look, someone had penciled a price: $2.50. My mother had told me it came from a yard sale, but I had imagined she meant a yard sale she had gone to as an adult. When I sent her a picture of the price, she called. She had bought it when she was twelve, for her first bedroom after her sister moved out. I knew the story of that bedroom, including the curtain she had sewn from a sheet. The clock had never come up.

While I was on the phone, Ruth figured out what was wrong. The minute hand was bent just enough to catch the hour hand as it passed. I’d been lifting the clock by its rim to dust it, but once, when I climbed onto a chair to change the time, I’d pressed my thumb against the face. I remembered this because I had almost dropped it. Ruth showed me how to ease the hand away from the face, then let me turn the little wheel on the back. At 4:17 the hands passed without touching. We went around again to make sure.

I’d expected to leave the moment the clock worked. Instead, I stayed to help a man look for a button. He had come in wearing the coat that needed it and had to take it off every time we found a likely match. There was a coffee tin full of buttons, most of them too shiny. We finally found one that looked right until he held it beside the others, whereupon it turned out to be blue. He stood there for a while with his coat off. Then he asked if there were three more like it. There were seven.

On my way out, I passed the rabbit on a windowsill. Its owner had gone to wash his hands, and his father was guarding it. Both legs now pointed a little to the left. I told the father it looked good. He said that the leg had been coming off for weeks and he’d kept offering to buy another rabbit. “Same one,” he said. “I found it online.” I had done something similar for my mother a few years earlier, replacing a chipped bowl with an identical one. She thanked me, put it away, and carried on eating her cereal from the chipped bowl.

At home I hung the clock above the stove and set it by my phone. The next morning, while I waited for the kettle, I called my mother and asked why a twelve-year-old needed a clock in her bedroom. “I didn’t,” she said. “I needed something to put on the wall.” She’d had a nail left over from a picture her sister took when she moved. She bought the clock with her own money and carried it home under her shirt because it was raining. I asked whether her sister had been pleased to move out. My mother thought for a moment and said she’d never asked.

The clock ran slow that first week. I had fixed one problem and discovered another, which might explain why I’d remembered my mother adjusting it so often. On Sunday I stood on a chair and moved the hands forward, taking care where I put my thumb. My mother was coming for lunch. She arrived early, carrying the chipped bowl with a dish towel stretched over it. Inside were strawberries she’d hulled that morning. While I was looking for the colander, she glanced up at the clock. “You know that’s fast,” she said. It was. I gave her a strawberry. We had a few minutes before lunch.
