The city kept its lost property in a former swimming pool. The deep end held bicycles; the shallow end, umbrellas. On rainy days people came down the tiled steps and pointed to a black umbrella among two hundred others. When asked what distinguished it, they almost always said, “It’s mine,” with a conviction that made Ada wish this were admissible evidence.

She had worked there for eleven years. She knew that people embroidered their names into hats they disliked and left no identifying marks on things they couldn’t bear to lose. She knew that a child could describe a missing glove with greater precision than a grown man could describe his briefcase. She knew that if someone began by saying the object wasn’t worth much, the conversation would take a while.

One Tuesday a bus driver brought in a paper bag containing a single pear and a house key. The pear had ripened past the point at which Ada could put it on the shelf, and the key had nothing to distinguish it except a dot of yellow nail polish.

“Did you see who left it?”

“If I’d seen who left it,” the driver said, “I’d have shouted.”

Ada gave him a receipt for one key. After he left, she ate the pear over the staff sink. It was the best pear she’d had all year, and she felt briefly, absurdly, like a thief.

That afternoon a woman called about a blue casserole dish. Ada found three. The woman said hers had a chip on the handle, which eliminated one. Then she said there might be a little baked cheese stuck to the underside of the lid.

“There is,” Ada said.

“Oh, good. My sister said she soaked it.”

The woman came in the next morning and carried the dish away wrapped in a bath towel. She was six steps up when she turned around.

“Did you have to look at the cheese?”

“Yes.”

“Sorry about that.”

“It was a very small amount of cheese,” Ada said, and the woman went on up.

At home Ada had a drawer full of keys to places she no longer lived. One opened a flat above a bakery where she had learned to sleep through the arrival of flour. Another belonged to a building that had been demolished. She could have thrown that one out, but she liked the definiteness of it. There was no risk of discovering she still needed it.

The yellow-dotted key remained on the shelf for two weeks. Then a boy came in for a trumpet and, while Ada was checking the serial number, asked whether anybody ever left food on the bus.

“All the time,” she said. “Why?”

“Just wondered.”

He was wearing a school uniform with the knees gone shiny. His mother stood at the counter, buying time for him to check that everything was in the case. He counted the mouthpieces twice. There was only one.

“What kind of food?” Ada asked.

“A pear, maybe.”

His mother looked at him. “You said you ate that.”

“I was going to.”

Ada took the key down from the shelf. The mother put her hand flat on the counter.

“I changed the lock,” she said.

“Good,” said the boy. He closed the trumpet case and opened it again.

“I thought you’d dropped it outside the house.”

“I thought so too.”

Ada set the receipt beside the key and turned it so the mother could read the date. The mother had paid a locksmith on a Sunday. She told Ada the price, then told her how long the man had been there, which was twenty minutes. She seemed to be hoping that Ada, who had a municipal badge and a pen on a chain, might be able to do something with these facts.

“Was the pear still in the bag?” the boy asked.

“Yes,” Ada said.

“Was it any good?”

“It was excellent.”

“I told you it was ripe,” his mother said. “You always wait until they’re brown.”

For a moment the boy looked as if he might object. Instead he put the old key in the little compartment beside the mouthpiece and snapped the case shut. His mother reached for the handle, but he was already carrying it.

That evening Ada went home by way of the bakery. It was still there, although the bread was displayed in the window now, where the sacks of flour used to go. The man behind the counter was slicing a loaf for a customer. Ada joined the queue. She hadn’t meant to buy anything, but once she was inside she remembered how good the bread was toasted.

When it was her turn, she asked who lived upstairs.

“I do,” the man said. “Why?”

She told him about the key. He wiped his hands on his apron and said he’d had some trouble with that lock. If she still had the key, would she mind bringing it in? The spare his landlord had given him didn’t work.

The next day she brought all the keys, having discovered she couldn’t tell the bakery key from the one to the demolished building. The man put a sign in the window and led her around the side. The first key wouldn’t go in. The second went in but wouldn’t turn. The third opened the door.

From the bottom of the stairs Ada could see the old green paint on the banister, worn through to the wood where she had put her hand every morning. There was also a pair of enormous orange slippers on the landing. She had been about to ask if she could go up and look. The slippers made her realize what an odd request that would be.

“Do you want to keep it?” the man asked.

“No,” she said, and gave him the key.

He lifted the door slightly by the handle as he locked it. She’d forgotten about that. In winter, when the wood swelled, she used to have to lift it with both hands.

“Does the bedroom still smell of bread in the morning?” she asked.

The man considered this. “I don’t notice it anymore.”

Neither had she, by the time she moved out. But she noticed it now, standing beside him in the narrow passage, and stayed until he had tested the key once more.

# The Drawer That Stuck

The first thing I took to the repair café was a toaster that worked. I had misunderstood the sign. It said BRING SOMETHING BROKEN, but underneath, in smaller letters, it said OR COME FOR TEA. I read this as a loophole so conspicuous it must be a test. I put the toaster in a shopping bag and carried it six blocks.

“What’s wrong with it?” asked a woman named Ruth.

“Sometimes the toast comes out a little uneven.”

“What kind of bread?”

I told her.

“Oh,” she said. “That bread is always doing that.”

She gave me a cup of tea.

The café met on Saturdays in the basement of a church. There were long tables, an urn that made a convincing imitation of distant traffic, and a row of extension cords taped to the floor. The volunteers wore name tags with their specialties written beneath their names. RUTH — ELECTRICAL. GUS — WOOD. NADIA — SEWING. One man’s tag said PETER — PATIENT. He was sorting screws.

I had moved to the neighborhood in January. By April I knew which grocery store sold good apples and which bus driver would wait if you ran. These were useful things to know. I did not yet know anybody well enough to ask them to help me carry something upstairs.

At the next table, a boy had brought in a clock shaped like a cat. Its tail was supposed to swing. Ruth removed the back and asked him to hold the screws. After a while she asked him to hold the spring. He took both assignments seriously, but when she asked him what time he wanted her to set it to, he said, “Six.”

It was eleven in the morning.

“Six is when my dad gets home,” he explained.

Ruth set it to the actual time. “That way you’ll know how long you’ve got.”

The following Saturday I brought a drawer. It came from a little pine desk that had belonged to my father. You could open it if you pulled hard with both hands, but then it came all the way out and hit you in the stomach. My father had dealt with this by keeping things he rarely needed in it: spare shoelaces, old passports, the manual for a radio he no longer owned. When I inherited the desk, I added my own expired passport and pushed the drawer shut.

Gus turned it upside down. “Where’s the rest of it?”

“At home.”

“I can’t tell why it sticks without seeing what it sticks to.”

I had been hoping this would be the kind of repair that took ten minutes. The desk was up two flights of stairs, and the last time I’d moved it, my father had been at the other end. We’d both insisted on walking backward so the other one could see where he was going. We made it as far as the landing before realizing that wasn’t possible.

“I’ll bring it next week,” I said.

Peter, who was eating a biscuit over a tray of washers, asked how far away I lived.

“Six blocks.”

“Have you got stairs?”

“Yes.”

He picked up another biscuit for the road.

We got the desk downstairs by taking the drawers out and carrying it on its side. Peter went first. At the landing he set his end down and studied a crescent-shaped dent in the wall.

“That from the desk?”

“Yes.”

“Must have been coming up, then. We’re doing beautifully.”

Outside, we stopped twice. The first time was because Peter wanted to change his grip. The second was because a woman walking a small dog asked how much we wanted for the desk. Peter looked at me. I said it wasn’t for sale.

“Everything’s for sale,” she said, not aggressively. She had already leaned down to untangle the dog’s lead from a parking meter. “But you don’t have to sell it to me.”

By the time we got back, somebody had put the drawer behind the tea urn. Gus fetched it, slid it halfway into the desk, and pressed down on one corner. Then he took it out, rubbed chalk along the sides, and slid it in again. A little patch of chalk had rubbed off near the back.

“Here,” he said.

I put my finger where he pointed. The wood felt no different there than anywhere else.

Gus took two curls off the drawer with a hand plane and tried it again. It went all the way in. He opened it with one finger hooked around the knob.

“That’s it?” I asked.

“Want me to put it back?”

He showed me how to rub a candle along the runners. I did one side and he did the other. When we turned the drawer over, a photograph dropped from the narrow space behind its front panel. It showed my father at a picnic table, holding half an orange. Somebody just outside the frame had evidently asked him a question, because his mouth was open and his eyebrows were up. I turned the picture over. On the back he’d written a phone number without a name.

I waited for some more information to occur to me. None did. I put the photograph in my pocket.

Peter and I carried the desk home. At my door I asked if he wanted to come in for coffee. He said he’d already had enough tea to hear his own pulse, but he came in anyway. I had two chairs, one of which wobbled. He sat in that one and wedged a folded envelope under its short leg.

“You could bring that in,” he said.

“I could.”

“Or you could leave the envelope.”

After he went home, I opened the drawer a few times. If I pulled it with the old amount of force, it still came out and hit me. I had to learn to use less.

For a while I kept the photograph on top of the desk. Later I put it in the drawer with the passports. I thought I might forget it was there, but the drawer turned out to be a good place for things I needed all the time: scissors, tape, the little screwdriver that fits the screws in my glasses. I see the photograph most days now. Sometimes I take it out. More often I just move it aside to get at something underneath.

# The Department of Misplaced Things

On the first Thursday of every month, the city auctioned off whatever had gone unclaimed at the Department of Misplaced Things. Umbrellas sold in bundles of twelve. Bicycles went individually unless they were tangled beyond the patience of the auctioneer. Once, a woman paid forty dollars for a suitcase that turned out to contain forty-one dollars and a note that said, *Don't spend it all in one place.*

For thirty years, my mother ran the department from a brick building behind the bus depot. She disliked the phrase *lost property*. “The property knows exactly where it is,” she said. “It's the people who are confused.”

When she retired, I took two days off work to help her clear out her office. By noon on the first day we had filled one box, mostly with shoes she kept under her desk. Every time I picked something up, she asked me to wait while she checked whether it belonged to her.

“Who else would own a mug that says WORLD'S OKAYEST MOM?”

“You gave me that,” she said.

“I know.”

“I thought you might want it back.”

At the bottom of her desk drawer, beneath a roll of peppermints gone soft in their wrappers, I found a claim ticket dated October 14, 1998. All the fields were blank except the one labeled DESCRIPTION.

*One small blue glove. Left.*

I remembered the glove. Or I remembered the right one, which had stayed in our coat closet for years after its partner disappeared. It was blue wool, with a yellow stripe around the wrist. My grandmother had knitted the pair and made the thumbs too long. When I wore them, I could pinch the empty ends and pull them off without using my teeth.

“Was that mine?”

My mother leaned over. “Yes.”

“Did somebody turn it in?”

“No.”

“Then why did you make a claim ticket?”

“So you would go to school.”

This sounded enough like her that I put the ticket in the recycling pile. She waited until I bent down for another pair of shoes, then took it out.

Around three, a man came in looking for a green umbrella. My mother had already packed her nameplate, but she set it back on the counter before asking him what kind of green.

“Green green,” he said.

She brought out a golf umbrella the color of a billiard table, a folding one with a lime handle, and a long, dull green one with a wooden duck's head. He reached for the duck.

“Before you open it,” my mother said, “is there anything you can tell me about the inside?”

He thought for a moment. “There's a hole my wife sewed up with dental floss.”

My mother undid the strap. He held the umbrella sideways between them while she peered under it. There, near the tip of one spoke, was a little white seam.

“She said thread wouldn't stand the rain,” he said.

“Did it?”

“I don't know. She used the floss.”

He tucked the umbrella under his arm and went out. It was raining. Through the window we watched him pull up his hood and walk toward the bus stop.

My mother opened the ledger and wrote *returned*.

“Did you ever give somebody the wrong thing?” I asked.

“Probably. A man once described a watch down to the scratch across the face. I gave it to him. Two weeks later a woman came in and described the same scratch.”

“What did you tell her?”

“That I'd given it to a man.”

“What did she say?”

“‘Of course you did.’” My mother closed the ledger. “I still don't know what she meant.”

We ate dinner that evening at the diner across from the depot. Without asking, my mother tipped the pickles from her plate onto mine. I had stopped liking pickles years before. I ate one anyway, and it turned out I liked them again.

“Why wouldn't I go to school?” I asked.

She wiped her thumb on her napkin. “Your grandmother had just died. You thought if we found the glove, she could finish it.”

“Finish it?”

“The thumb was too long. She'd promised to fix it.”

I remembered standing beside my grandmother's chair while she measured the thumb against mine. I also remembered her fixing it. She was wearing a pink cardigan in both memories. I didn't tell my mother about the second one.

“Every morning you wanted to go back to the bus stop and look,” she said. “I told you I'd put in a ticket. Then it would be my job.”

“What did you do?”

“I looked. There wasn't much to the bus stop.”

On our second day, I went back to the office alone. The new manager was coming in Monday, and my mother had asked me to empty the kettle and leave the good scissors. There was one last thing on her desk, a mug with two peppermints in it. I put the peppermints in the bin and wrapped the mug in my scarf.

On the way out, I heard someone try the front door. A girl stood on the other side of the glass, maybe ten or eleven. I unlocked it and told her we were closed.

“I know,” she said. “Can I ask anyway?”

She'd left a library book on the number nine. I asked what it was called. She didn't know, so I asked what it was about.

“A horse,” she said, then added, “Not right away. At first it's about this boy who sweeps up.”

There were three library books in the paperback bin. One had a horse on the cover. I handed it to her, but she shook her head. Then she picked up a book with a picture of a red barn and flipped to the middle. From between the pages she took a flattened straw wrapper folded into a tiny staircase.

“Page sixty,” she said.

It was page fifty-eight. I leaned over the counter to see what happened there. A man was explaining how to tell whether a horse was asleep. The girl saw me reading and kept her finger on the page until I got to the end of the paragraph. Then she put the staircase back and shut the book.

# The Department of Ordinary Sounds

The first sound my mother asked me to bring her was the kitchen drawer.

“Not the cutlery,” she said. “The drawer itself.”

I knew which one she meant. In the house where I grew up, the drawer next to the stove had a wooden runner that swelled in summer. You had to lift the handle as you pulled. If you forgot, the drawer would come halfway out and stop with a sound like someone clearing his throat before disagreeing.

The house had been sold twelve years earlier. My mother was about to turn eighty, and I had asked what she wanted for her birthday. I had been expecting her to say slippers.

“Do you want me to see if the people who live there now will let me record it?”

“Oh, they’ll have fixed it by now,” she said, and went back to peeling her pear.

At the time I worked for the municipal archive, where we had exactly one recording of a drawer. It was in a forty-minute interview with a retired midwife who stopped halfway through to get a photograph. For years, researchers had skipped those eleven seconds to get to the part about the maternity ward. I put on headphones and listened. The drawer was metal. There was a little rolling noise at the end, possibly a pencil.

I brought the recording to my mother anyway.

“No,” she said. “But play it again. I like how she keeps talking from across the room.”

That should have been the end of it. Instead, I spent a Saturday visiting secondhand furniture shops. The dealers were happy to let me open their drawers, though one followed me around afterward, rubbing candle wax on everything I had touched. I came home with seventeen recordings, none of them right, and an oak bedside table I hadn’t meant to buy.

By then I was interested in what else the archive might be missing. We had the high school band playing at the opening of the bypass, the mayor’s speech, and the scissors going through the ribbon. We didn’t have the rattle of the old bus that took people into town before the bypass opened. I asked our director if I could put out a call for ordinary sounds.

“As long as you don’t call it a department,” she said. “Departments have budgets.”

By the end of the first week, the Department of Ordinary Sounds had received six recordings of rain, a dog drinking from a mop bucket, and a ninety-minute cassette labeled *Gill’s boiler, possibly October*. Gill had apparently set up a recorder to catch a noise the plumber insisted she was imagining. At minute eighty-three there was a tremendous knock, followed by a woman shouting, “There! You bastard!”

I wanted to put that one in the listening room. Our director said we’d need Gill’s permission.

A woman named Nadia brought us the sound of her father preparing an orange. She had recorded it by accident while trying to get him to tell a story about his childhood. He refused, on the grounds that she already knew it. On the recording there was the scratch of his thumbnail breaking the skin, then the small wet sounds of the peel coming away. In the background a radio announcer read the shipping forecast.

“Do you know what he did after that?” Nadia said. “He gave me the whole orange. I was thirty-four. I’d come to tell him I was getting divorced, and I never got around to it.”

I asked if she wanted that in the catalog description.

“God, no,” she said. “Put down that it was a big orange.”

Not everyone wanted a sound preserved. A man who had spent forty years repairing shoes came in to hear a recording of his old stitching machine. After a few seconds he took the headphones off.

“Is that the whole thing?”

“There’s another two minutes.”

“I know what it does,” he said. He asked if we had anything from the public pool. He used to swim on Tuesdays, when the shop was closed. We found a recording made for a school project and sat together listening to children yell underneath the huge, hollow noise of the ventilation system. When I offered him the headphones again, he said he preferred it coming out of the little computer speakers. It sounded farther away, which was how he used to hear it from the warm bench where he put on his socks.

I never found the kitchen drawer. What I did find, while looking through my own files, was a video I’d taken in my mother’s flat. I was trying to show her how to send a video. The camera pointed at the table for most of it. We were having tea. At one point she said, “Look, that’s you,” and I said, “No, that’s my thumb.”

She laughed once, very suddenly, and set her cup down.

I knew the cup by the sound. It was the heavy green one with a foot just narrow enough to sit inside the rim of its saucer. When she set it down carelessly, it struck the rim first, then slid into place.

For her birthday I brought the video and a pear cake. She watched the video twice.

“You had a terrible time teaching me that,” she said.

“You kept taking pictures of your knees.”

“They looked all right in those trousers.”

Then she asked me to send her the video, so I did. While I cut the cake, she propped her phone against the sugar bowl and tried to send a video back. She wanted to do it without my looking. I kept my eyes on the cake, even when I heard her mutter that she’d got the ceiling again.

Later, on the bus home, I watched what she’d sent. There were eight seconds of the ceiling, then a view of my hands cutting two uneven slices. From somewhere off camera my mother asked for the smaller one. While I was still deciding which to give her, her hand came into the frame and took the bigger slice. I’d been standing right there and hadn’t noticed. I watched it again.

samples.result:
The library lent out sounds in blue tins, each about the size of a peppermint box. Most people borrowed rain. There were fourteen kinds, including rain on a parked car and rain coming through a ceiling into a saucepan. The second was popular with people who had moved away from town and wanted to remember why.

On my first day behind the desk, my aunt showed me how to test a return. You opened the tin just far enough to admit a fingernail. If it was a recording of a horse, you might get a single hoof. If it was a conversation, you might get a word you could spend the rest of the afternoon trying to place.

“Don’t open anything all the way in here,” she said. “A man played a wedding reception once and we had to shout over it until closing.”

I had come home for six weeks to clear out my father’s hardware store. Working at the library gave me somewhere to go when I couldn’t face another drawer full of screws. My father had sorted them by length but not by type, a system I’d complained about when he was alive. Now I kept finding myself holding two screws up to the light, checking whether he’d got it right.

On Thursday, a woman in a green cycling helmet set a tin on the desk.

“Could you put this back without telling Arthur I took it?”

“Who’s Arthur?”

She leaned sideways to see past me. My aunt was in the workroom eating an orange.

“Your father knew me,” she said.

This was how people introduced themselves to me now. Sometimes they’d say it before they said their names.

She was called June. She’d worked at the bakery next door to the hardware store until it closed. The tin she’d returned was labeled *End of the day, Bell Street, 1998*. I knew the year because it was the summer my father put in a new shop door. The old one swelled every August and had to be kicked at the bottom. He’d taken it off its hinges on a Tuesday, and I’d spent the rest of the week kicking the new door out of habit.

“What’s on it?” I asked.

“Mostly me,” June said. “I don’t know why I keep borrowing it. I can hear myself perfectly well at home.”

She tucked her helmet strap under her chin and left. I checked the card in the back of the tin. She’d borrowed it eleven times in three years. Arthur had never borrowed it.

That evening I carried the tin over to the store. I’d sold the counter to a man who planned to turn it into a kitchen island. Without it, the room looked wider and less useful. I sat on the step stool my father wouldn’t let customers use because one of its feet was shorter than the others.

I opened the tin.

A broom scraped the pavement. A bus pulled away. Someone was struggling to collapse a metal display rack, and a woman said, “You’ve got to lift it first.” I recognized June, though her voice was lower then, or perhaps she just had a cigarette in her mouth.

Then came the kick against the door. It made a hollow sound I felt in the toes of my right foot.

“Did you get the milk?” I asked.

I was fifteen. I’d remembered myself at fifteen as nearly grown, but I sounded about nine.

“Ah,” my father said.

“You said you’d get it.”

“I said ah.”

“You always say ah.”

There was a pause. I shifted my weight on the stool. Whatever came next, I thought, might be something I’d forgotten about the two of us. I’d been listening for his voice since he died. Once, in the supermarket, I followed a man who cleared his throat the way my father did, all the way from the freezer aisle to produce.

On the recording my father said, “June, have you got any milk?”

“Not for you.”

“Right,” he said. “I’d better go, then.”

He rattled his keys. I heard him walk away.

June swept for a while. Then she asked me what was wrong.

“Nothing,” I said.

“All right.”

The broom went on scraping. I expected a confession, or at least a sniff. Instead I heard myself ask whether she wanted me to hold the dustpan. She did. The two of us spent some time chasing a piece of cellophane that kept blowing out of it. When we finally caught it, June said, “There you are, you little sod,” with such quiet satisfaction that I laughed aloud in the empty shop.

The tin went silent. I shut it and sat awhile longer. I still didn’t know what had been wrong. It surprised me that there was something about that girl I couldn’t find out just by remembering harder.

The following Thursday, June came in without her helmet. Her hair was flat on one side anyway.

“Who’s Arthur?” I asked her.

“My husband. He thinks I go swimming.”

“Do you?”

“Occasionally. I don’t like to lie outright.”

I got the tin. She turned it over in her hands. The blue paint had worn away at the corners.

“I played it,” I told her.

“Oh, good,” she said. Then she looked at me more closely. “Was that you with the dustpan?”

I said it was.

“Well, I’ve had you down as the paper boy all these years.”

She laughed, and I heard how little her voice had changed. I asked if she wanted to borrow the tin again. She said she’d think about it, and stood at the desk for a bit, looking at the rack of postcards nobody ever bought.

“Did he come back with the milk?” she asked finally.

I didn’t know. But there was a grocery shop still open on the corner, and I hadn’t had tea yet. I asked my aunt to mind the desk and went out to get a pint. When I came back, June had taken off her coat. My aunt had found three cups and was running the hot tap to warm them.

samples.result:
At the train station where my father worked, the lost property office had no clock. This was not because the railway believed that lost things existed outside time. It was because someone had taken the clock down to change the battery and left it on a train.

My father told this story whenever someone asked him the time. I believed it until I was twelve, when I found the clock in a drawer beneath a stack of forms. Its hands stood at twenty past nine. I brought it out to him, pleased with myself in the merciless way of children who have caught an adult lying.

“Ah,” he said. “It came back.”

On school holidays, I sat behind the counter and did my homework. When I finished, my father let me sort the umbrellas. I liked deciding what counted as brown. There was the brown of a dog asleep in sunlight, the brown of tea before milk, and the brown of an umbrella that wanted very badly to be black. On the forms, all of them were BRN.

My father kept the umbrellas in a barrel. Everything else went on shelves, except for a cello, which sat upright in the chair beside the filing cabinet. During a week of heavy rain, my father moved the chair away from a leak in the ceiling. He moved my homework, too, but only after I asked.

Some people turned up so sure of what they had lost that they were unable to recognize it. A man once insisted that his briefcase had a brass clasp. My father set a briefcase with a silver clasp on the counter. The man shook his head. My father opened it and turned it around. Inside were three oranges and a photograph of the man standing beside a horse.

“That’s my horse,” the man said, still doubtful.

Other people remembered things no one could check. A woman looking for a red scarf said it smelled of her sister’s kitchen. My father brought out two red scarves and left her alone with them. She smelled the first one, then the second, then the first again. In the end she went away without either. My father folded them and put them back. One was a little damp where she had held it to her face.

The cello stayed for nine months. I asked how anyone could forget a cello, and my father said the trick was to carry it every day. Carry a cello once and it takes up your whole mind. Carry one for twenty years and you can get off a train thinking about whether you need potatoes.

This explanation pleased me so much that I tried to forget my schoolbag. I thought about potatoes all the way home. When I got there, I still had the bag, but I had left my coat on the train. My father made me fill in a form.

Years later, when the station was being renovated, the railway moved lost property to a warehouse at the end of a bus route. My father was offered a job there. He went out to look at it and found a bright room with a barcode reader. There would be no counter. People would describe their things online and, if there was a match, pay to have them posted.

“They’ll get more back this way,” he told me.

He meant it. He retired anyway.

On his last Saturday I helped him empty the office. The cellar smell I had always attributed to the building turned out to belong to the umbrella barrel. We carried it onto the platform. In the sunshine, I could see that the wood was stained purple in places. My father said it had come from a pub. I had the sudden, childish feeling that he ought to have told me this before.

At the back of a shelf we found a biscuit tin full of single gloves. My father tipped them out and began trying to make pairs. I reminded him that the warehouse van was due at eleven.

“I know,” he said, slipping a small blue glove over two fingers.

He found another blue one, a little larger, with a different pattern at the wrist. He laid them side by side. They were both left hands.

While he looked through the pile again, I opened the drawer and took out the clock. There was no battery in it. I asked him why he had kept it all those years.

“Somebody might want it,” he said.

“Who? It belongs to the railway.”

He took it from me and turned it over. On the back, written in nail polish, was a name I recognized as my mother’s. She had worked in the station café before I was born. She used to put her name on everything she brought to work because the café manager had the same taste in crockery.

“She loaned it to me,” my father said. “I kept meaning to get her another one.”

My mother was alive and living twenty minutes away. She and my father had been divorced for sixteen years. I called her from the platform and asked if she remembered the clock.

“Of course,” she said. “Does it still gain seven minutes a day?”

I looked through the office window at my father. He had found two gloves that might have been a pair. He laid one on top of the other, checking the thumbs.

“I don’t know,” I told her. “Do you want it back?”

There was a pause. I could hear a cupboard opening and the clink of a cup being set down.

“No,” she said. “But tell him I want my biscuit tin.”

I went back inside and picked up the lid. It was blue, with a picture of a yacht leaning into the wind. My father looked at it for a moment, then swept the gloves into a cardboard box for the warehouse. He wiped the tin with the sleeve of his shirt and pressed the lid down all the way around.

“You can take that to her,” he said.

“You could take it yourself.”

He pulled his coat off the back of the chair. “I suppose I could.”

samples.result:
The first thing I repaired at the Saturday repair café was a toaster. I say “repaired” because that is what I wrote on the form, but what I actually did was turn it upside down and shake it. A piece of toast fell out. The owner, a man named Leonard, watched me do this with the grave attention of someone observing a medical procedure he suspects he could have performed at home.

“How much?” he asked.

“Nothing.”

He looked at the toaster, then at me. “Well, you’ve priced it right.”

We worked in the basement of a library, beneath a room where children were learning to play the recorder. Every so often a note would come through the ceiling all by itself, as if one child had remembered something the others had forgotten. Our tables were marked ELECTRICAL, CLOTHING, BICYCLES, and OTHER. I sat at OTHER. In theory this was because I had a broad range of skills. In practice it was because I had arrived after everyone else had chosen a table.

The toaster was my only success for three weeks. I made a pepper grinder worse. I spent an hour trying to open a jewelry box before its owner mentioned that she had the key. When a woman brought in an umbrella that wouldn’t close, I got it closed, and we were both so pleased that neither of us thought to open it again until she was halfway up the stairs.

Then a girl named Nell brought me a globe.

It was the sort that sat in a cradle and spun on a tilted rod. The rod had snapped at the bottom, and the globe kept tipping out onto the table. Nell stopped it each time with the flat of her hand.

“Can you fix it without changing anything?” she asked.

“Probably,” I said, which was how I answered questions when I hadn’t yet looked at the thing.

She showed me what she meant. Someone had drawn a line across the globe in blue ballpoint pen. It started in Leeds, went diagonally down through the Atlantic, crossed the bottom of South America, and ended in open water. The line was faint in places where somebody had rubbed it with a thumb.

“My brother did that,” Nell said. “He thought if you went straight down from Leeds you’d come out in New Zealand.”

“He missed.”

“Yes, well, he was nine.”

She said this with the authority of someone who was now ten.

I took the globe out of its cradle and set it on a folded towel. At the top, the rod had a little brass cap that came off easily. At the bottom, the broken end was stuck inside a plastic fitting. I went to borrow a pair of pliers from the bicycle table.

When I came back, Nell had turned the globe so the blue line faced the ceiling.

“He says he didn’t do it now,” she said.

“Why?”

“He’s fourteen. He says that about most things.”

I pulled out the broken piece. It was shorter than I expected, which meant the rod had probably been loose for a long time. Under the table we kept a biscuit tin full of screws, washers, and pieces of things we had taken apart without ever getting them back together. Nell helped me spread the contents out. She was good at this. Most people looking for a small part move everything around at once. Nell picked up each piece, looked at it, and put it down somewhere she hadn’t looked yet.

We found a metal pin that was the right width but too long. I filed it down while she held the ruler. Upstairs, the recorders stopped. For a while the loudest thing in the room was a woman at the clothing table pulling a length of thread through a coat.

“What are you doing?” Leonard asked.

He had come back with the toaster. I thought, with a sinking feeling, that something else had gone wrong with it. Instead he set it down, plugged it in, and took a loaf of bread from his shopping bag.

“I’ve been thinking,” he said. “You should see it do one.”

It did two at a time. We ate standing up because every chair had something on it. Leonard had brought butter but no knife, so the woman from the clothing table washed her scissors and used the closed blades. Nell saved her crusts on a paper towel. She said she might want them later.

The pin fit. I put the globe back in its cradle and spun it harder than I meant to. We all watched it wobble. I reached to steady the base, but before I touched it, the wobble settled.

“Here,” I said.

Nell tried it herself, slowly. She stopped at the end of the blue line.

“What’s actually there?” she asked.

I leaned over. There wasn’t a name printed anywhere near it. The nearest lettering was so large that it seemed to describe half the world.

“Water, I think.”

“Just water?”

I was about to say yes. Then I remembered that when I was her age, I’d found a photograph of a man standing on the deck of a ship in weather so cold there was ice on the railings. I’d spent an afternoon trying to figure out which little patch of my school atlas he’d been standing in. I never found it. For months afterward, whenever I opened the atlas, I looked at the water first.

“I don’t know,” I said. “We could go upstairs and look.”

Nell considered this. From the stairwell her mother called that they were late. Nell tucked the globe against her chest. At the door she turned around, came back for the crusts, and put them in her coat pocket.

The next Saturday I found a library book on my chair. It was about the Southern Ocean. A slip of paper marked a photograph of a small gray bird riding a wave, its feet out of sight. On the slip, in handwriting I didn’t recognize, someone had written, *These sleep on the water.*

The book wasn’t checked out, so at closing time I took it upstairs. I meant to put it back on the shelf. Instead I got a library card.

On the first Monday of every month, the railway sold its unclaimed umbrellas. It sold the black ones for two dollars and the colored ones for three, because Mr. Vale, who ran the lost-property office, believed that anyone willing to carry a yellow umbrella ought to be charged for the pleasure.

Everything else went to auction twice a year. There were always more shoes than seemed reasonable. A person might leave a train without a hat, but how did they leave without a shoe? Mr. Vale had been asking this question for twenty-seven years. His assistant, Nina, once suggested that the answer was probably different for every shoe. He found this unsatisfying.

One Tuesday in November, a conductor brought in a kitchen chair.

“Carriage four,” she said.

“How did they get it on?”

“The doors open.”

“How did they forget it?”

The conductor shrugged. “Same way you forgot my birthday.”

Mr. Vale wrote *one chair, wooden, green*, on a tag, tied it to a rung, and wished the conductor a happy birthday. It turned out her birthday was in April. What annoyed her was that he hadn’t known enough to object.

The chair had a rush seat and one short leg. Nina slid a folded timetable under it and began eating her lunch there. From that angle she could see a slice of platform through the office window, low enough that passengers passed as a succession of shoes. On Friday she watched two pairs stop, turn toward each other, and remain still long after the train had gone. One person had a hole in the sole. She could see it each time he lifted his heel.

After three weeks, a boy came in and asked for the chair.

“Can you describe it?” said Mr. Vale.

“It’s uncomfortable.”

“Anything else?”

“Green. There’s a burn underneath.”

Nina tipped the chair over. There was indeed a dark oval on the underside of the seat.

“How do you burn the bottom of a chair?” she asked.

“With a toaster,” said the boy, and offered nothing further.

Mr. Vale unfastened the tag. The boy made no move to take the chair.

“Can I leave it here till four?”

“You’ve left it here since the seventh. I suppose we can manage another hour.”

At four, the boy returned with a woman wearing slippers inside plastic grocery bags. She walked slowly but refused his arm. At the sight of the chair she said, “Oh, you idiot,” and sat down.

The boy crouched to adjust the timetable under the short leg.

“It was on the train,” he told her.

“I know where it was. I put it there.”

This was the first Mr. Vale had heard of anybody putting a thing on a train without intending to take it off again. He lowered the lid of his lunch tin very quietly.

The woman had been moving out of a house. Her son had hired a van, and the men kept asking what was coming and what was going. She had put the chair on the pavement to sit on while she decided. Then the van went, her son went, and she took the chair to the station. She had bought it forty years earlier from a café that was closing down. It had cost less than her sandwich.

“I thought if I left it somewhere, I wouldn’t have to tell anybody they could throw it away,” she said.

“You could have told me,” the boy said.

“You’d have brought it back.”

He looked down at his hands, which were still on the chair leg.

Mr. Vale asked whether they would like him to put the tag back on. The woman considered this. Outside, an announcement began halfway through a sentence and gave up before naming the station.

“Do you need a chair?” she asked Nina.

“I have one at the desk.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

Nina looked at the chair behind her desk. It had wheels and could be raised or lowered by a lever. Nobody had ever asked if she needed it.

“Yes,” she said.

The woman got up. The boy took her arm this time, and they went out together. Visible through the window, the grocery bags made her feet look enormous. The boy had to shorten his stride so much he was almost walking in place.

The following morning, Nina found the folded timetable on her desk. Mr. Vale had sawed a thin round of wood from the end of a broom handle and glued it to the short leg. He had painted the new foot green. It was not quite the right green, and he had turned the chair to face the wall while it dried, as though it had done something wrong.

They kept it by the window. People trying to describe their missing things often sat in it. From time to time they surprised themselves by remembering a detail: a telephone number written inside a glove, or a set of keys with a little screwdriver attached. One man, who had come in about a briefcase, sat for ten minutes and then said it might be at home. It was. He called to tell them, and Mr. Vale, who had no place on his form for a briefcase that had never been missing, took down the message anyway.

In spring, the conductor brought in a single brown shoe. It was scuffed at the toe, with a new blue lace threaded through only the top two holes. Mr. Vale turned it over. There was nothing remarkable about the sole.

“Well?” said Nina.

He put the shoe on the shelf.

A week later, someone came for it. She was a woman in work trousers, out of breath from crossing the footbridge. She described the lace before Mr. Vale could ask. Then she sat in the green chair and took an identical shoe out of her bag. She set them side by side on her knees and pressed each toe with her thumb.

Mr. Vale was about to ask how she’d lost it. He had the words ready. But the woman was smiling down at the shoes, and after a moment he went back to counting the umbrellas.

# The Library of Unfinished Things

The first thing I borrowed from the library was a blue suitcase. I was twenty-four and had an interview in a city where I knew nobody. The suitcase had one wheel that clicked and a luggage tag that said JUNE in fading ink. I asked the librarian whether June was the previous borrower.

“June was the donor,” she said. “She stipulated that we keep the tag. She always wanted to travel more.”

I took June to Cincinnati. Neither of us got the job.

The library occupied a former laundromat between a bakery and a shop that repaired shoes. It had books, but only a few, and they mostly explained how to use the other things. You could borrow a drill, a sewing machine, a folding table, or a roasting pan large enough to accommodate the consequences of inviting both sides of the family. There were six umbrellas, which was exactly enough on a sunny day. Behind the desk hung a photograph of a man holding a tremendous cabbage. He had borrowed a shovel. The librarian, whose name was Ruth, thought he was giving the shovel too much credit, but she put up the picture anyway.

One winter a small wooden boat appeared in the front window. It was about the length of my forearm. The hull had been painted red, but the deck was bare and the mast lay beside it. I assumed it was a donation and asked when it would be available.

“It isn’t finished,” Ruth said.

“Who’s finishing it?”

“Well,” she said, “that’s what I’m trying to find out.”

The boat had belonged to a man named Arthur, who had moved into an apartment with no room for a workbench. He had brought it in wrapped in a bath towel, along with a paper bag of parts and a photograph of the actual boat, which his parents had owned when he was a child. On the back of the photograph he had written the year, then crossed it out and written a different year. Then he had crossed that one out, too.

Ruth put a card in the window: *Someone started this. Would you like to do a little more?*

A retired electrician named Sal took it home. He’d never built a boat, but he knew how to stand a mast up straight. He returned it a week later with the mast installed and a note explaining that he wouldn’t be doing the sails. He had spent forty years on ladders, he wrote, and had developed firm opinions about canvas.

The sails were made by a woman who came in to borrow a carpet cleaner. She used a handkerchief that had belonged to her father. It had a faint brown spot near one corner, which she positioned low on the mainsail. “That’s where he held his coffee,” she told Ruth. “I don’t see why the boat should get a clean one.”

By spring the boat had acquired a rudder, a coil of thread, and a tiny blue bucket made from the cap of a toothpaste tube. Nobody could agree whether the bucket was to scale. By then it had been there long enough that the people who objected to it would have been upset if anyone took it away.

Other unfinished things began to arrive. A woman brought a quilt with one empty square. Three people offered to fill it, and she discovered that she didn’t want them to. She took it home and finished it over the weekend. On Monday she brought Ruth a slice of banana bread, by way of apology or thanks. Her explanation made it difficult to tell, and Ruth ate it before asking.

Some projects did less well. A jigsaw puzzle stayed on the back table for a year because it was mostly sky and had no box. A man brought in a song his brother had started. The only lyric was “Tuesday, with its pockets full of rain.” It was a good line, but everyone who tried to write the next one made Tuesday sound like a person you wouldn’t want to sit beside on the bus. Eventually the man took the song back. He said he’d started hearing his brother’s voice again when he read it, instead of the voices of all the people trying to rhyme with rain. He seemed pleased enough with that.

Arthur came to see the boat late in May. Ruth called me because I had taken an interest in it, by which she meant I had once spent twenty minutes arguing about the bucket.

He wore a short-sleeved shirt with a pen clipped to the pocket. He looked at the boat for a long time. Then he said, “The sails were green.”

I felt unexpectedly ashamed. I hadn’t made the sails or told anyone what color to make them, but I had started to think of the boat as ours, and it occurred to me that this might be precisely what Arthur would dislike about it.

“Dad dyed them in the bathtub,” he said. “After that, if you took a bath, you came out a little green around the elbows.”

He bent closer to the window.

“Where’d you get that bucket?”

Ruth explained.

“Ours was a coffee tin,” Arthur said. “It rusted through. Dad kept putting it back on board anyway. You’d go to bail, and he’d say, ‘Quickly.’”

Arthur took the boat home. At the end of summer he brought it back with a photograph of it on his windowsill. Next to it was a pot of basil and a pair of reading glasses. The sail hung limp, of course. There was no wind in the apartment.

He asked to borrow the blue suitcase. His sister lived on the coast, and he hadn’t visited in years. Ruth checked it out to him, and I watched him pull it along the sidewalk past the bakery. The wheel still clicked. I’d meant to fix it after Cincinnati, but I’d returned the suitcase on a Monday morning on my way to work, and fixing it would have meant keeping it another day.

Halfway to the corner Arthur stopped and looked down at the luggage tag. He turned it over, found nothing on the back, and tucked it into the strap so it wouldn’t drag. Then he went on. From inside the library I could hear the wheel for a little while after he was out of sight.

On the last Thursday of every month, the library lent out sounds. You could borrow rain striking a canvas tent, the click of a good suitcase closing, or the noise a crowd makes when the person onstage forgets the words and everybody decides, at once, to help. These came in little gray boxes with brass hinges. There was no deposit, but you had to bring them back on time. People developed strong attachments to sounds they had not known they needed. The library had lost three copies of Someone Else Washing the Dishes.

I worked the Thursday desk. The job mostly involved checking hinges and explaining that no, we could not lend out silence. People were always disappointed by this. They imagined silence would come in an especially handsome box. In fact, the closest thing we had was Snow Falling on a Closed Swimming Pool, which contained, if you listened long enough, the faint ticking of the pool’s broken clock.

One November evening, a woman named Ruth brought in a sound she wanted to donate. She set a biscuit tin on the desk and said, “My kitchen, around four in the afternoon.”

“Anything in particular happening?”

“No,” she said. Then she thought about it. “The refrigerator, I suppose.”

I lifted the lid. There was the refrigerator, with a shallow rattle at the bottom of its hum. A truck went by. Somewhere beyond the kitchen a child said, “Wait, I wasn’t ready,” with the outrage of someone who had been perfectly ready a moment before. A chair scraped. Then came a tiny, regular clicking I couldn’t identify.

“That’s me,” Ruth said. “I was cutting coupons.”

We had a rule against taking sounds that belonged to other people. A kitchen was usually all right, but the child complicated things. I asked if she knew whose voice it was.

“Oh, that’s me too,” she said.

I looked at her.

“I grew up in that house. I bought it when my father moved out. Some afternoons it all gets mixed together.”

I listened again, and this time there was no child. There was a knife being sharpened, and a man clearing his throat after each pass along the steel, as though he had something to say about the result. Ruth leaned over the desk. Neither of us spoke until he put the knife down.

“He never used it after sharpening it,” she said. “He’d put it straight back in the drawer. Then he’d take out a different knife to cut an apple.”

“Why?”

“I asked him once. He told me to mind my own business.”

She laughed, but only after a second, as if giving him a fair chance to say something else.

I explained the other rule about donations: once a sound went into circulation, you couldn’t ask for it back. You could borrow it like anyone else, but there might be a waiting list. Ruth asked who in the world would want her kitchen. I took her over to the returns cart, where a shoebox labeled Upstairs Neighbor Finally Takes His Boots Off was waiting to be shelved. Its borrowing card had six names on it.

“What if I don’t like what somebody hears in it?” she asked.

I told her about a man who had borrowed Wind in a Pear Tree and brought it back furious because there was a bee. Nobody on staff could hear the bee. He’d grown up picking pears and could tell by the sound which side of the tree it was on. The next borrower was a woman who heard nothing but wind and kept the box open while she did her taxes. She returned it with a note asking us to thank whoever had planted the tree.

Ruth took the tin home. I thought that was the end of it, but she came back just before closing the following month. She had sold the house. The new owners were going to knock down the wall between the kitchen and the dining room, which she admitted was a sensible thing to do. For forty years, anyone carrying a roast to the table had needed another person to hold the door.

“But they’ll never know to ask,” she said, and slid the tin across the desk.

I gave her a donation form. Under DESCRIPTION she wrote Kitchen, 4 p.m. Under CONDITION she wrote Depends. Then she crossed that out and wrote Good.

The first person to borrow the kitchen was a young man who said he was looking for something to play for his dog while he was at work. I nearly told him the sound was too valuable for that. Instead I asked what kind of dog he had. A very old one, he said. Mostly deaf, but not entirely.

When he returned the tin, I asked how it had gone. He said the dog had shown no particular interest. He himself had started coming home for lunch. He would sit on the floor with the dog and eat a sandwich, and afterward he’d have to pick crumbs out of the dog’s coat. He said this as if it were a minor inconvenience that could not easily be resolved.

Ruth’s name went onto the waiting list in February. By the time her turn came, she had moved into an apartment with a refrigerator she described as ostentatiously quiet. I offered to find her a room where she could listen. She said she had groceries in the car, but she sat down anyway, right there at the desk, and opened the tin.

For a while I could hear only the people in the library: a zipper, a cough, the little slap of a picture book hitting the carpet. Then, from somewhere inside the tin, came a knock. Ruth looked up.

“That’ll be Mrs. Flynn,” she said. “She never could work the latch.”

She put one hand flat on the desk and started to get up. Then she remembered where she was. Neither of us moved for a moment. The knock came again, a little louder this time, and Ruth, still half out of her chair, called, “Come in, for heaven’s sake. It’s open.”

On the last Saturday of every month, the library put out a table of things found in returned books.

Most were ordinary: grocery lists, boarding passes, the occasional photograph of a dog. Once there was a crisp twenty-dollar bill. It drew a crowd of people who remembered, with increasing specificity, having used a twenty-dollar bill as a bookmark.

In April, there was a recipe card.

*Pear cake*, it said, in blue ink. Below that came a list of ingredients and, in a different hand, a note: *Not that bowl. The big one.*

A woman picked it up, turned it over, and put it down again. She walked to the door. Then she came back.

“Can I take this if it isn’t mine?”

The librarian looked up. “Do you know whose it is?”

“No. But I know which bowl.”

The librarian made her a photocopy. The woman folded it into her coat pocket and left.

The next month she came back with a pear cake. She set it beside the lost things, still in its pan, with a knife wrapped in a dish towel. By noon the cake was gone. The card was gone too, though nobody had seen who took it.

When the librarian brought the empty pan to the staff kitchen, she found a slip of paper tucked beneath it.

*You can use the little bowl if you do the pears last.*

The first thing I bought at the estate sale was a kitchen timer shaped like a tomato. The woman at the card table said, “That runs fast.”

“How fast?”

“Depends what you’re waiting for.”

She was eating a hard-boiled egg out of a paper towel. I waited for her to smile, but she was busy picking shell off it.

At home I set the timer for ten minutes and put it beside the stove. It rang in eight. I tried again while I was on hold with the electric company. That time it took eleven minutes and forty seconds. I wrote both results on the back of an envelope, then felt foolish and threw the envelope away.

A week later, my sister came over to teach me how to make our father’s bread. She’d brought his recipe, which called for “enough flour” and an oven “a little hotter than usual.”

“Did he tell you what that meant?” I asked.

“No. He used to tell me to take my rings off.”

We made two loaves. While they baked, we sat on the kitchen floor with our backs against the cabinets, eating the good butter on crackers. My sister told me she used to call Dad from the grocery store just to ask which apples to buy. She knew which apples. Sometimes she’d get all the way to the checkout and go back to produce so she could call him.

I’d set the tomato for forty minutes. After a while I got up and checked the bread. The loaves had split along the tops, the way his always did. I took them out and turned the timer to zero before it could ring.

“Is it done?” my sister asked.

“Yeah,” I said. Neither of us got up to get a knife.

The town installed a bench at the bus stop eleven years after the bus stopped coming.

This was not, as the newspaper suggested, a clerical error. The bench had been approved while the route was still running, and there had been a series of reasonable delays. The first contractor went bankrupt. The second delivered a bench too wide for the pavement. Then the pavement itself was found to belong, in part, to a man in Australia who had no objection to the bench but wanted someone to explain how he had come to own six inches of a town he had never visited.

By the time the bench arrived, the old bus shelter was being used by the bakery to keep its sacks of flour dry on delivery mornings. The bakers moved the sacks over.

Ruth sat there first. She had taken the seven-ten bus for thirty-two years, and her knees still woke her at six. At first she brought a newspaper. Later she brought two cups of coffee, because a boy named Sam passed the bench on his way to school and had once asked what she was waiting for.

“The seven-ten,” she’d said.

“Does it come?”

“It used to.”

He considered this. “Was it usually late?”

“Not eleven years late.”

He laughed hard enough to make her say it again.

On the first warm morning in April, Sam came by without his schoolbag. He sat down and told her that his father had moved out, and that he had known it was going to happen because on Sunday his father had taken the good kitchen scissors. Ruth didn’t ask about the scissors, though she wanted to. She gave him his coffee. They sat until the bakery opened and the baker came out to ask whether either of them knew where to buy a secondhand bicycle.

Sam did. He took out his phone to show her.

Years later, when the town proposed restoring the bus route, there was a crowded public meeting. Everyone wanted the bus. The trouble was, the new buses needed a wider turning space, and the bench would have to go.

“Can you move it down by the bakery?” someone asked.

The engineer checked his drawings. “It is by the bakery.”

“No,” said the baker. “By the door. Where we can bring out another chair.”

The first thing my father fixed after he retired was the kitchen clock. It had been seven minutes fast since I was nine. He took it down, set it by the radio, and hung it back up.

“What was wrong with it?” I asked.

“Nothing,” he said. “I used to need the seven minutes.”

He’d built them into the morning when my sister and I were little. Seven minutes to find a shoe, turn a permission slip over and discover the other place he had to sign, or stand at the end of the driveway while one of us ran back to the house to pee. We knew the clock was fast. He knew we knew. We still believed it when we were late.

That afternoon I went with him to the hardware store. He needed a washer for the outside tap. The man at the counter asked what size, and my father pulled the old one from his shirt pocket, wrapped in a square of paper towel.

On the way home he took the road past my old school. There was a little girl at the crossing with one arm out of her coat. Her father held her backpack while she tried to get the sleeve right side out. The crossing guard had already stepped into the road, so we waited.

My father drummed his fingers once on the steering wheel. Then he turned off the radio so we could hear what the girl was saying.

“I can do it,” she said. “Hold my other stuff.”

The city employed a woman to listen to the things people said into broken intercoms.

Most of it was “Hello?” followed by a pause, then “Hello?” in an entirely different voice. She liked the second hello better. The first was addressed to a machine. The second was addressed to the possibility that someone had heard.

On Tuesdays a man came to the old municipal swimming pool and said, “I have your towel.” The pool had been closed for eleven years. He always waited long enough for someone to come down the stairs.

One Tuesday he said, “I washed it.”

The woman took off her headphones. Outside her office, a custodian was trying to get a vending machine to release a packet of almonds. She went out and helped him rock it. Two packets fell. They ate them standing up.

“Sometimes,” the custodian said, “I think I should get a dog.”

“Do you want a dog?”

“No,” he said. “But I’d like to walk one.”

The following Tuesday, she went to the pool. The man was already at the intercom, carrying a towel with a faded cartoon shark on it.

“Would you mind if I waited with you?” she asked.

He moved his shopping bag so she could stand under the awning. It wasn’t raining yet, but it looked like it might.

After a while he said, “I know it’s closed.”

“I know,” she said.

A bus pulled up across the street. Neither of them needed it. They watched everyone get off anyway.

It was a kitchen chair, yellow, with one leg shorter than the others. The man who carried it in set it beside Dryer 6 and sat down.

“You know we’re closing,” said Bea, who owned the place.

**Room Tone**

My brother asked me to record the kitchen before we sold the house.

“What do you want me to do in it?” I asked.

“Nothing,” he said. “That’s the point.”

He works in film. He told me that after a scene, the crew stands still and records thirty seconds of the room doing nothing. They use it later, to fill the gaps between bits of dialogue. If you leave the gaps truly silent, people notice.

I set my phone on the kitchen table. The refrigerator came on. A truck went past. I shifted in my chair and started over.

The third time, I made it to twenty-two seconds before the mail came through the slot. It was a grocery circular addressed to my mother, who had been dead for nine months. Peaches were ninety-nine cents a pound. She would have bought six, put them on the windowsill, and spent the next four days telling me which ones I was allowed to eat.

I left the recorder running while I folded the circular. I opened the utensil drawer, though we’d already packed the utensils. A single birthday candle rolled forward in the empty tray.

That evening I sent my brother the file.

“Sorry about the noise at the end,” I wrote.

He called me.

“Open the drawer again,” he said.

I did.

“Yeah,” he said. “I’d forgotten it does that.”

Halfway out, the drawer caught. You had to lift it a little. I’d done it without thinking, the way you step over a crack in the pavement on your own street.

“Wait,” I said. “I’ll do it wrong so you can hear.”

At the laundromat, someone had taped a note to the change machine:

**IF IT TAKES YOUR DOLLAR, KICK THE LEFT SIDE. NOT HARD. IT’S OLD.**

I liked that last part. Whoever wrote the note had lost at least a dollar to the machine and still felt it deserved some consideration.

I was there to wash a sleeping bag I’d borrowed from my brother six years ago. He was coming over on Sunday. He hadn’t asked for the bag back, but I’d recently found it in the hall closet and remembered telling him I’d return it on Tuesday.

The change machine took my dollar. I kicked the left side, not hard. It gave me five quarters.

For a while I just stood there with the extra quarter in my palm. I could leave it on top of the machine, where the next person would find it. But then the next person might put in a dollar, lose it, and kick the machine, and I’d have interfered with a system that seemed to be working, more or less.

I put the quarter in my pocket.

On Sunday, I handed my brother the sleeping bag. He unzipped it and ran his hand along a seam near the foot.

“You washed it?”

“Yeah.”

“There was a twenty in here.”

There was a pause.

“Six years ago,” he added, as if that made it less likely I’d go back and check.

We went back and checked. The woman sweeping the laundromat listened to our story, reached into her apron, and pulled out a little spiral notebook. On each page she’d written a date and a list of things she’d found. A bus pass. A key with a blue cap. One earring, described as *heavy for its size*.

No twenty.

My brother thanked her anyway. On the way out, he stopped at the change machine and read the note.

“You wrote this,” he said.

“I didn’t.”

He pointed to the bottom corner, where someone had crossed out *very old* and written *old* above it.

“That’s exactly the kind of thing you’d spend time on.”

Outside, he tucked the sleeping bag under his arm. “Keep it next time,” he said. Then he thought about it. “No, actually. Ask me. I like knowing when you’re going somewhere.”

The library had a drawer labeled **THINGS FOUND IN RETURNED BOOKS**. In it were three bus tickets, a recipe for peach cobbler, and a photograph of a dog standing on a kitchen table, looking surprised by its own success.

There was also a note that said, “I can do Thursday, but not if we’re going to talk about the boat.”

Nora, who worked Saturdays, had been thinking about the boat for six years.

One rainy afternoon, a man came in and asked whether anyone had found a note in a copy of *The Complete Guide to Home Plumbing*.

“About Thursday?” Nora asked.

He took off his glasses. “Good grief. Yes.”

She fetched the note. He read it, laughed once, then read it again.

“Did you end up talking about the boat?” she asked.

“Oh, we talked about it all the time. That was the trouble. We’d go out for a sandwich and come home having priced an outboard motor.” He folded the note along its old crease. “Neither of us could swim.”

“Did you buy it?”

“No. We took swimming lessons. In the shallow end with a bunch of eight-year-olds. My brother was sixty-three and he kept trying to get out of putting his face in.”

He slipped the note into his coat pocket. Then he took it out again and handed it back.

“You know what,” he said. “I think I only wanted to see if it was still here.”

After he left, Nora opened the drawer. She put the note back where it had been, underneath the dog. On her way home she stopped at the municipal pool. She’d passed it every Saturday for eleven years. The woman at the desk said there was a lane free if she wanted it.

“I didn’t bring anything,” Nora said.

“We lend towels.”

Nora nearly explained that she meant a swimsuit, but she hadn’t meant a swimsuit. She’d meant she hadn’t planned to go swimming.

She asked when they closed.

My favorite thing about a library book is that sometimes a stranger has left something in it.

Not a note meant for you. Usually it’s a grocery list, or a bus ticket, or a photograph of a dog standing at the edge of a lake, looking back as if to say, *Well?* Whatever it is, the reader needed to put the book down for a minute. Then they finished it, or didn’t, and the bus ticket slipped far enough into the binding that nobody saw it when the book went back.

I once imagined a library that catalogued these things. You could ask the librarian for *all the bookmarks found in books about birds*, and she’d bring out a shoebox. In it: a recipe for soup, a receipt for a pair of shoes, an envelope with the arithmetic for how much someone could afford to spend that week. Perhaps an actual feather, though that would feel a little too on the nose.

What I’d really want to see is the collection from books nobody finished. There would be no reliable way to assemble it. A bookmark on page thirty-seven could mean the book was dull, or that the reader had a baby, or that on page thirty-seven they found the answer to the only question they’d opened the book to ask.

Anyway, if you borrow a book and find a picture of a dog by a lake, look at the back. People used to write the dog’s name.

On the morning the city took away the last public pay phone, someone called it.

The two workers looked at each other. One had already loosened the bolts. The other, whose name was Luis, picked up.

On Tuesdays, the library put a cart of books outside with a sign that said FREE. Nobody took the atlas. It was too big for a tote bag, and several of the countries had changed names. For three weeks it sat beneath a paperback about making your own curtains.

Then a woman named Ruth carried it home under one arm. She had no particular interest in geography. What she needed was something heavy to flatten the curling corners of a photograph.

The photograph showed her mother at a picnic table, laughing at someone outside the frame. Ruth remembered the day, the mustard drying on a paper plate, the wasp everyone insisted would leave if they ignored it. She could not remember the joke. For years she had assumed it would come back to her at some inconvenient moment, perhaps while she was trying to remember a password.

When she lifted the atlas a week later, the photograph lay flat. She opened the book at random and found a small pencil mark beside a town on the coast of Norway. Next to it, someone had written, in careful capitals, ASK LEON.

Ruth turned a few more pages, looking for Leon’s answer. She found a grocery receipt, a pressed leaf, and no other marks. Finally she tucked the photograph into the atlas, leaving just enough of its white border showing to mark the page. The next Tuesday she brought the book back. By noon, it and the book about making curtains were both gone.

The first thing Mara bought at the estate sale was a kitchen timer shaped like a tomato. She had come for a desk, but the desk was already sold, and the timer had a strip of masking tape on its underside. In blue ink someone had written: FOR DOING NOTHING.

At home she set it for ten minutes. Almost immediately she noticed a crumb on the table. She moved to brush it away, then wondered whether that counted. The crumb had been there since breakfast. It seemed capable of waiting. She put both hands flat on her knees and listened.

The refrigerator clicked off. Upstairs, a child practiced the same four notes on a flute, with a long pause before the fourth. A delivery truck stopped outside, and somebody called, “Not that door,” with surprising tenderness. Then the truck went away, and the child got the fourth note exactly right.

When the timer rang, Mara felt the small disappointment she used to feel when a teacher switched on the lights after a film. She brushed the crumb into her palm. It was a bit of toast crust, not quite large enough to account for how much attention it had required.

The next afternoon she set the timer again. This time the flute never started. Rain ran down the window in two thin lines that met halfway down. She watched the joined line gather speed. When the bell rang, she turned the tomato over and added a second strip: NOT FINISHED.

On Thursday mornings, a man named Luis set a yellow chair on the sidewalk outside his apartment. He never sat in it. He brought out his coffee, checked the sky, and went back inside.

The chair had belonged to his wife, who liked to peel oranges in the sun. After she died, he kept putting it out because Thursday was when the bakery across the street made raisin bread. The smell reached the chair before it reached the apartment. He liked knowing that.

For weeks, people walked around it. Then a bicycle courier sat down to eat a pear. A woman used it to retie her shoelace and stayed long enough to make a phone call she’d been putting off. One morning, Luis found a small boy standing on it, counting the pigeons on the bakery roof. The boy kept getting to seven before one flew away.

In November, rain loosened a joint in the chair. Luis carried it upstairs to fix it. By noon someone had put a milk crate in its place. It was too low for most people, but the courier sat down anyway, knees up by his ears.

The next Thursday, Luis brought the chair back. He meant to take the crate inside, but the baker came out with two heels of raisin bread and asked if he wanted one. Luis sat on the crate. From down there he could see that his wife had painted the underside of the seat yellow, too. She’d even painted the screws.

The first thing Mara noticed about the town was that nobody hurried when it rained. They stepped out of shops, opened their umbrellas, and continued whatever conversation the weather had interrupted. A butcher once stood ankle-deep in a gutter, explaining to a customer why he no longer believed in ghosts.

Mara had come to empty her father’s house. She had allotted three days: one for papers, one for furniture, and one for the kitchen, where he kept screws in teacups and tea in a tin labeled SCREWS. On the first morning, she found a pear still ripening on the windowsill.

She could remember buying it. Her father had wanted one pear, not two, and she’d teased him for making her stand in line for a single piece of fruit. He’d said he liked having something to look forward to on Thursday. At the time she’d thought he was being difficult.

Outside, rain darkened the brick wall. The neighbor was carrying two chairs from his shed to his porch. On his second trip, he waved at Mara through the window and pointed to the empty chair. She held up the pear. He went inside and came back with a kitchen knife.

They ate it in quarters, leaning forward so the juice wouldn’t run down their sleeves. The neighbor told her that her father had borrowed the chairs last summer and returned them painted blue. She asked what color they’d been before. He looked down, as if the wood might remind him.

The train station kept its lost property in a room behind the ticket office. On Tuesdays, when business was slow, Mara took everything out and dusted the shelves. She liked the umbrellas best. Opened indoors, they made the room look briefly like a place where weather happened.

One morning a man came in looking for a blue scarf. Mara brought him three. He examined each in turn, not touching them, then said he couldn’t remember which blue it had been. His wife had always called it the good scarf. He had never needed another name for it.

She set the scarves on the counter and went back to sorting keys. After a while the man picked up the plainest one. There was a repair near the fringe, a little ladder of stitches in purple thread. He slid his thumb over it twice.

“That’s not mine,” he said. “She would have used blue.” Then he folded it carefully, lining up the ends, and asked if he could wait there until his train came. Mara moved a box of single gloves off the spare chair. They sat without talking while the loudspeaker announced delays.

After he left, Mara put the scarves away. On the inventory card she had written BLUE three times. She crossed out the last entry and wrote BLUE, PURPLE MENDING. The next Tuesday she did the same for a coat with one wooden button. By the end of the month, she needed bigger cards for the umbrellas as well.

The laundromat on Fifth Street had a shelf of books nobody seemed to take home. There was a guide to raising orchids, a mystery with its final page missing, and an atlas that still showed a country my mother used to live in. On Sundays, while my clothes turned behind the glass, I opened the atlas to the same page.

One afternoon a woman sorting socks beside me leaned over and tapped a blue bend in the river. “That should be farther east,” she said. “Unless the river moved.”

“Do rivers do that?”

“This one did. My uncle went to bed with a vegetable garden and woke up with a boat landing.”

She folded a sock into its partner. I asked her whether she knew the town where my mother was born. She said she knew the bakery there, or at least the bakery that had been there when bread cost less than the paper they wrapped it in. Then she asked if my mother still made the little plum dumplings everybody made in September.

I had never heard of the dumplings. That evening I called my mother, who said of course she knew how to make them. She had stopped because my father hated cooked fruit. She had assumed I did too.

The next Sunday I brought six dumplings to the laundromat in a container with a cracked lid. The woman took one, bit into it, and asked if my mother was the one who always left the pits.

The laundromat on Alder Street had a shelf marked LOST PROPERTY. Most of the time it held one mitten, a plastic dinosaur, and the paperback nobody would admit to reading. Then, one Thursday, someone left a photograph of a woman standing beside a refrigerator in the middle of a field.

She wore slippers. An extension cord ran from the refrigerator toward the edge of the picture. On the back, in blue ink, somebody had written, “It worked.” By Saturday, three people had turned the photograph over to see if the other side offered a more satisfying explanation than that one.

The owner of the laundromat, Mrs. Patel, set a jar beside the photograph and invited customers to write down their theories. A boy proposed that the woman was trying to cool the whole world. His mother suggested that somebody had promised to help her move and had simply not arrived.

A week later, the woman herself came in with a bag of towels. She recognized the photograph and laughed. “That’s my sister’s field,” she said. “We had a picnic, and she didn’t want anybody putting warm potato salad back in the cooler.” She read every slip in the little jar.

Before leaving, she wrote a note of her own and folded it twice. Mrs. Patel waited until the towels were gone to open it. “Tell the boy we tried his idea first,” it said. “We left the door open all afternoon, but it only got colder if you stood close.”
