On the first warm Saturday in March, someone left a lemon on the windowsill of the laundromat. It was not in a bag or beside a forgotten basket. It sat alone in a square of sun, with a small green leaf still attached.

By noon, everyone had an opinion. The owner assumed it belonged to the woman who cleaned the dryers with vinegar. A boy in soccer cleats said it was a prize and asked what he had to do to win it. His father, folding a fitted sheet with mounting resentment, told him to ask the lemon.

I was there because my washing machine had stopped draining. I had brought a book, but the lemon was easier to pay attention to. It demanded nothing. Even the book wanted me to remember which brother had sold the horse.

Near closing, an older woman came in without any laundry. She went straight to the window and picked up the lemon. Then she took another from her coat pocket and set it in the same spot.

“Is that yours?” I asked.

“This one is,” she said, holding up the first lemon. “I left it here this morning to see if anybody would take it.”

“Why leave another?”

“Well,” she said, looking at the windowsill, “I brought it in case somebody had.”

The next Saturday, my machine was working again. I walked past the laundromat anyway. There was an orange on the sill. Someone had drawn a face on it in blue pen.

The first thing I ever found in a library book was a grocery list: eggs, lemons, something written so quickly it might have been either soap or soup. I was nine and had never considered that anyone could stop reading in the middle of a sentence to go buy eggs.

After that I shook every book before I opened it. Mostly I got crumbs. Once, from a book about whales, a photograph of a man holding a birthday cake fell into my lap. The cake leaned to the left. The man was watching it instead of looking at the camera.

I took the photograph to the librarian. She turned it over, but there was nothing on the back. Then she opened a drawer. Inside were two mittens, neither a match for the other, a playing card, and a key with a red cap. She put the man beside the key.

“How will he know where to look?” I asked. She said people usually came back for keys. Photographs were harder. I wanted to ask if we could put up a sign, but I couldn't think what it should say. HAVE YOU LOST A MAN? seemed likely to cause more trouble.

Last week I found that same book about whales at a used bookstore. It wasn't the same copy; this one had a coffee ring on the cover. Still, I opened it to the page I remembered. A blue whale's heart lay there in cross section, big enough to climb inside.

At home Mara set it for ten minutes and put the kettle on. While the water heated she opened a drawer that had been sticking since winter. A takeout menu had wedged itself behind the cutlery tray. On the back her father had written a phone number without a name.

She dialed. A man answered on the fourth ring, out of breath. She apologized and said she was trying to find out whose number this was. “Well,” he said, “you’ve found out it’s mine.” Then he asked her to wait while he let the old dog back into the house.

When he came back, he knew her father’s name. They had played chess on Thursdays at the library until the library got rid of its chess tables. “He always brought an orange,” the man said. “He could peel it in one piece. Did you know he could do that, too?”

Mara hadn’t known. She had never seen him eat an orange. She told the man this and heard him sit down; the chair made a little scrape. The timer went off. Mara cupped her hand over the lemon until it stopped rattling, then asked who usually won on Thursday afternoons.

The laundromat on Alder Street had a shelf labeled TAKE A BOOK, LEAVE A BOOK. For three years it held a waterlogged atlas, two detective novels, and a manual for a dishwasher nobody owned. Then someone left a notebook.

On the first page, in pencil: *What did you almost do today?*

By Thursday the answers had begun. A man had almost bought a pear but remembered the pears at home. Someone had almost called her brother. Someone else had almost stolen the notebook, which seemed fair enough, given the sign.

Over the winter the notebook filled. I read it while my clothes spun. The brother appeared again in February: *I called. He wanted to know how to cook rice.* Below that, in different handwriting, were instructions for cooking rice.

One evening the dryers stopped halfway through everybody’s loads. We stood around holding warm, damp sleeves as the owner went downstairs to check the breaker. A woman at the folding table opened the notebook. She read aloud the entry about the pear.

“That was me,” said the man beside her.

She looked up. “Were they any good? The ones at home?”

“No,” he said. “They made that noise when you bit into them. Like stepping in snow.”

The lights came back. Nobody moved for a second. Then the woman reached into her shopping bag, took out a pear, and cut it in half with a little folding knife. The man ate his half over the laundry sink so it wouldn’t drip.

On Tuesday the city installed a bench facing a brick wall. Everyone agreed it was a mistake. The river was behind it, along with the sycamores and the handsome old bridge. The wall belonged to a laundromat. Its only distinguishing feature was a pale rectangle where a sign had hung.

By Friday someone had drawn a small door inside the rectangle. It had a brass knob, a mail slot, and a welcome mat rendered in painstaking chalk. On Saturday a child sat on the bench and waited for somebody to come out. Her father sat beside her, holding two sandwiches.

Nobody came out. But the following week, an envelope appeared, tucked into a crack between the bricks. It was addressed to Whoever Lives Here. Inside was a recipe for lemon cake, with a note advising the reader to double the zest and not to apologize if the middle sank slightly.

After that came postcards, a photograph of a dog asleep in a wheelbarrow, and a question about whether grief counted as a reason to cancel dinner. Someone wrote Yes beneath it in chalk. Someone else added, But tell us where to leave the soup. An address appeared the next morning.

In November a city worker arrived with a wrench to turn the bench around. He set his toolbox down and read the wall. Then he sat for a while. When he left, the bench was where it had always been, and a new note said, in block capitals: NICE VIEW.

The city library had a drawer labeled THINGS FOUND IN BOOKS. Inside were the usual bookmarks, a few grocery lists, and a photograph of a dog sitting beside a birthday cake. On the back, someone had written, “He knew it was his.”

Mara worked the Thursday closing shift. When the library was empty, she sometimes opened the drawer and read one thing. Her favorite was a scrap of graph paper that said, “Tell Ruth about the moon.” She had found it in a manual for repairing washing machines.

One evening, a man came in ten minutes before closing and asked whether anyone had found a photograph. Mara pulled open the drawer. He looked at the dog for a long time before picking it up.

“That’s my mother’s handwriting,” he said. “She used to bake him a cake every year. Absolutely vile. Peanut butter and sardines.”

“Did he eat it?”

“He ate the candles once. We had to start counting them afterward.”

He slipped the photograph into his coat pocket. At the door he took it out again and held it by the edges all the way down the steps.

Mara turned off the lights, then turned one back on. She took the graph paper from the drawer and looked up the washing machine manual. It was still on the shelf, though nobody had borrowed it in six years. She tucked the note between the pages on replacing a drive belt. If Ruth ever came looking, she knew where to start.

On the last day of the year, the town librarian put a cardboard box beside the returns slot. A sign on it read: THINGS YOU MEANT TO SAY. She expected complaints about the heating. By noon someone had slipped in a recipe for plum cake and a single blue mitten.

The mitten belonged to a boy who came back for it after lunch. He said he had meant to say goodbye to winter, which he found unnecessarily long. The librarian gave him his mitten and explained that winter had several months left. He considered this, then asked for more paper.

At closing time, she took the box upstairs. There was a note thanking the bus driver for waiting, another asking whoever played the trumpet on Birch Street to keep practicing, and a third that said, simply, *I knew*. She turned that one over, hoping for a clue. There was none.

She had planned to go straight home, but the bakery was still open. In the window, beside a tray of buns, stood six purple plums. These were for tomorrow’s tarts, the baker told her. He sold them anyway and asked whether she had ever tried adding black pepper to cake.

Later, while the cake cooled, she called her sister. They had not spoken since August, when an argument about a borrowed ladder had turned into an argument about their mother. Her sister answered. Before she could say hello, the librarian asked, “Do you want to come over for plum cake?”

On the first warm evening of March, someone carried a kitchen chair out to the sidewalk. The chair was painted yellow, except where years of elbows had worn the wood bare. By the time I came home, a woman in a grocery apron was sitting in it, eating an orange.

She peeled it in one long ribbon and laid the peel across her knee. I knew her by sight, which is the way you can know somebody for eleven years without knowing whether they have a brother.

“Want half?” she asked.

I took half.

We watched a boy on a scooter try to get his dog to follow him over a crack in the pavement. The dog put one paw forward, thought about it, and sat down. Eventually the boy picked him up and carried him across. The crack was about as wide as a pencil.

Her name was Ruth. She had two brothers and did not recommend either one. The chair belonged to the man upstairs, who had put it out with the trash, though there was nothing wrong with it that she could see.

She got up to show me where one leg was a little short. I folded a receipt from my pocket and slid it under the foot. Ruth sat down again and rocked experimentally. Then she got up, pulled the receipt out, and handed it back.

From inside her apron she produced another orange.

“So,” she said, rocking a little, “tell me about your brothers.”

On the morning the laundromat closed, someone washed a single yellow curtain. It turned behind the round glass, rising and collapsing like a small weather system. Outside, a man unscrewed the sign. Every time his drill stopped, you could hear the curtain’s brass rings tapping the drum.

I had been coming there for eleven years and knew almost nothing about anyone. I knew that the woman who brought a book never turned a page until her wash began. I knew that a boy once fit entirely inside a laundry cart and, by the following spring, had to fold his knees. I knew that the owner kept a jar of loose buttons beside the register. If you found yours, she made you take a second one.

That morning she tipped the jar onto the folding table and invited us to help ourselves. I took a green button with a nick on its rim. It matched nothing I owned. The woman with the book picked out four white ones and laid them in a row before slipping them into her coat pocket.

When the curtain was dry, its owner shook it out. A warm gust traveled the length of the folding table and stirred the paper sign that said EXACT CHANGE. Then she folded the curtain over her arm, and we all stood aside to let her through.

I still have the button. Every few years I find it while looking for something else, and for a moment my hands smell clean.

On my first night at the Department of Undelivered Sounds, a man came in looking for a sneeze.

“Tuesday,” he said. “About half past four. I was on the bus and it went away right at the top.”

“Did you check your sleeves?”

He had. He’d also gone back to the bus depot. The driver let him walk up and down the aisle in case being there again might bring it on.

I was explaining that we didn’t handle sounds that had never been made when my supervisor, Anita, came out of the back with a jam jar.

“Try this.”

The man unscrewed the lid and sneezed so hard he knocked his glasses into the little dish where we kept the pens.

“How did you know?” I asked after he left.

“Same bus as me,” Anita said. “I heard him gearing up.”

The department was beneath a public swimming pool. All evening there was the noise of children jumping into water. At nine, the lifeguard blew his whistle, and afterward you could hear the enormous, unhurried work of the filters.

Most people came in for something they’d said. A woman wanted back the “fine” she’d given her husband when he asked whether he ought to take a job in another city. A boy of about seven wanted the swear word he’d whispered to see if the cat would tell. (It had not, but he was losing sleep.)

Sometimes people came for sounds they hadn’t been there to hear. We could release those only if nobody else had a claim. I once spent two weeks tracking down the proprietor of a demolished bowling alley so a woman could hear her best game again. Three strikes in the tenth. She played the jar three times at the counter. The third time she asked me to listen with her.

“Wait,” she said.

After the last strike, very faintly, someone laughed.

“That son of a bitch,” she said, delighted. “He bet me five dollars I couldn’t do it.”

I’d taken the job because my sister Nell had died the previous winter. She’d called while I was buying light bulbs, and I’d watched the phone ring until it stopped. I remember turning over two identical boxes and trying to work out why one cost three dollars more. I bought the more expensive bulbs. They flickered.

Nell hadn’t left a message. When I told Anita this, she asked for the date, then went downstairs. I hadn’t known there was a downstairs.

She came back empty-handed.

“There’s a fair amount from that evening,” she said. “Nothing addressed to you.”

“What does that mean?”

“Did you want me to bring up everything?”

I said yes too quickly. Anita went and put the kettle on. By the time it boiled, I’d changed my mind.

I worked there nearly a year before the pool closed for repairs. The council sent a plumber who took one look at the ceiling above our shelves and told us to move everything that couldn’t get wet.

“Where to?” Anita said.

He considered this. “Somewhere dry.”

We had six thousand jars, give or take. The branch library offered us its meeting room, provided we left it free on Wednesday afternoons for the chess club. We spent three nights packing. Anita brought old newspapers, and I learned to crumple them with my hands inside a drawer so the sound wouldn’t travel and set off the jars.

On the last night I found a jar that was warm. Its label gave a place I knew: the bus shelter outside the old supermarket. The date was years before Nell died.

Anita looked up from her packing. “Yours?”

“I don’t know.”

“Well, open it a little.”

There was the sound of rain on the shelter roof, and underneath it a plastic bag being shaken out.

“Put your arm through,” Nell said.

Then my own voice: “That’s the one with the eggs.”

“Other arm, then.”

I took my hand off the lid. I could just about remember the day. We’d bought groceries for our father, who’d hurt his knee. We were already wet when Nell decided we could get home under the shopping bag if we held it between us. The bag was nowhere near big enough.

I opened the jar again.

“Now run,” she said.

We didn’t run. You could hear it: six or seven walking steps, then a brief stop while one of us adjusted our grip. A car went by. I was about to close the jar when I heard myself say, “We could just get wet.”

There was a pause. Then the bag crackled as Nell lowered it.

“Oh,” she said. “Yeah.”

That was the whole thing.

Anita had finished packing her box. She was holding the flaps down with both forearms, waiting for me to pass her the tape.

“Can I take this one home?” I asked.

“Of course,” she said. “You’ll need to sign.”

The form asked whether the item had been recovered in full. I checked yes, then crossed it out and checked no, then asked for another form. Anita gave me one without looking at the first.

It was raining when we came out. We stood under the pool awning with a box each, waiting for the library van. Across the road, a man was trying to get his dog to go out from under the shelter of a shop. He’d step into the rain and the dog would stay put. Then he’d come back and explain something to it, quite earnestly. We watched him do this three times before he gave up and sat down beside the dog.

Anita set her box on the pavement and went back inside to find another roll of tape. I put mine down too. The rain had worked its way through a seam in the awning and was dripping onto my wrist. I could have moved a step in either direction. For a while I stood where I was.

The first thing my father forgot was how to whistle. He still put his lips together at the right points in a song, and if you were in the kitchen with him you could hear the small, industrious wind he made. I whistled along from the next room. For a while we were both able to pretend the sound was his.

The last thing he forgot was the price of a pear.

“Ninety cents,” he said at the grocery store, holding one up.

“Probably a little more now.”

He put it back. Then he picked up another from the same pile.

“How about this one?”

I bought six. That evening he ate one over the sink, cutting off pieces with a paring knife as he had all his life. In the morning there were five pears on the counter and his bed was empty. I found him on the porch in his socks, waiting for the school bus.

By October he was living in a place with a courtyard and a nurse named June who called him Mr. Frank. I began the work of emptying his house. In the drawer beneath the telephone, I found twenty-three keys in a margarine tub. One had a paper tag that said GOOD KEY.

I tried it in the front door, the back door, the garage, and the little metal box where he used to keep my report cards. It fit none of them.

The next Sunday I took it to him.

“Good key,” he read, and put it in his shirt pocket.

“Do you know what it opens?”

He considered this. “Did you bring the bad one?”

I went home and looked through the tub again. There were keys to a Ford he had sold when I was nine, to luggage we had never taken anywhere, to a padlock I remembered on the gate between our yard and the Halls’. The gate was gone. So were the Halls.

In the bottom of the tub was another paper tag, folded in half. It said BAD KEY. There was no key attached.

My father had spent thirty-eight years fixing things for the public schools. He came home with slivers of pencil in his cuffs and sometimes a whole doorknob in his coat. When I was little I asked if he could open any door in town.

“Only if somebody needs me to,” he said.

I remember being annoyed by this answer. I had wanted to know if he could get into the swimming pool at night.

I called the school district. A woman named Maribel told me my father had retired before the current maintenance records began. Then she asked if he was the Frank who used to bring a toaster to work.

“He said the staff room toaster burned on one side. He brought his own and took it home every Friday. We used to hide it on Fridays.”

“Why?”

“So he’d come looking for it.”

She laughed, then stopped. “We were twenty-two,” she said, as if that explained why anyone might want my father to stand in a doorway with his hands on his hips.

At my next visit the key was still in his pocket. I asked if he remembered the toaster.

“You have to turn the bread,” he said.

June brought us tea. My father waited until she left and slid his cup toward me.

“Too hot?” I asked.

“See if yours is any better.”

They tasted exactly the same. We traded anyway.

In November, a man came to buy the workbench. He was younger than I’d expected from his voice. He brought his daughter, who wore pajama pants and carried a tape measure. While we waited for him to back his truck up to the garage, she ran the tape along the bench, across the vise, and down to the floor.

“Seventy-one inches,” she told me.

“That sounds right.”

“It’s not. It’s seventy and three-quarters. I rounded for you.”

On the underside of the bench, exposed when we tipped it toward the truck, my father had penciled a line and written my name beside it. A second line, two inches higher, had my name again. I remembered standing on the bench while he measured from below, both of us pleased to have found a use for the ceiling.

“Do you want a picture?” the man asked.

I did. Then I helped him push the bench the rest of the way in.

The house sold in December. At the closing, I handed over three freshly cut keys. The buyer tested each of them while I stood on the walk. It was cold enough to see her breath when she came back out.

“They all work,” she said, sounding a little surprised.

My father died in January. June gave me a grocery bag containing his watch, his glasses, and a shirt with the good key still in the pocket. The paper tag had gone soft at the edges.

At home, I laid his things on the kitchen table. I put the key in the drawer with the spare batteries, then took it out again. I had spent months looking at locks and wondering which one he’d meant. Now I noticed how smooth the teeth were. Whatever it opened, he must have opened it nearly every day.

The following week, June called. She’d found a paperback with my father’s name in it. Did I want her to send it?

I said I’d come by. On my way I stopped at the grocery store and bought a pear. The cashier rang it up for eighty-seven cents.

“Is that right?” I asked.

She turned the little screen toward me. Pears were on sale.

I ate it in the parking lot before I went in. It was cold from the store and harder than it looked. I had to work at it, turning it in my hand to find the side that would give. By the time June came out with the book, I was down to the core. She tucked the book under her arm and held out the wastebasket from under her desk.

On the last day of the lost property office, someone came in for the piano.

Ruth had expected the umbrellas to go first. Rain was working its way through the station roof, and she’d propped the door open with a box of paperbacks and put out a sign: TAKE WHAT YOU CAN USE. By eleven, someone had taken the box.

The man who wanted the piano was wearing bicycle clips. He said his name was Daniel, and when Ruth asked if the piano was his, he said, “No, but I’ve got a receipt.”

The receipt was from a café that had closed nine years earlier. On the back, in blue ballpoint, someone had written: *If you ever find a piano, you owe me one.*

“Who wrote that?” Ruth asked.

“My sister.”

“Did you lose her piano?”

“I pushed it down a hill.”

Ruth waited. People often improved their stories if you gave them a moment.

“We were moving it,” he said. “I was in charge of the bottom end.”

The piano had arrived at the station during the renovation of the waiting room. In the paperwork it was listed as a package, dimensions unknown. It had taken four men to get it into the office, where it was immediately put to work supporting a microwave. Now a red sticker on the lid said it was to be collected on Monday for disposal.

“You’ll need a van,” Ruth said.

Daniel looked out at his bicycle. “I thought I might.”

He went away to make a call, and Ruth ate a pear over the wastebasket. Her daughter had offered to come down and help her clear the office, but Ruth had said there was nothing to clear. This was the kind of thing she said to her daughter and then spent an afternoon making true.

At noon a woman came in to ask where lost things would go after today.

“There’s a form online,” Ruth told her.

“But where do the things go?”

Ruth had been to the depot. It was a windowless building beside a roundabout, and to visit it by public transport you had to take a bus whose driver sometimes forgot there was a stop. She gave the woman the address.

“I haven’t lost anything,” the woman said. “I just thought I ought to know.”

A little after two, Daniel returned with a van and his sister. His sister was called Helen and had the receipt in her hand. She laid it on the counter and looked at Ruth.

“He told you about the hill, did he?”

“He said he was at the bottom end.”

“He was at the top. I was at the bottom. That’s why I’m still so cross.”

She took off her raincoat. Daniel went back out to find somewhere the van could stay without blocking the bus.

Ruth moved the microwave to the floor. Helen lifted the lid and played several notes, then the same notes harder, as if the piano might not have heard her the first time.

“Is it awful?” Ruth asked.

“Parts of it.”

She played something Ruth knew well enough to notice when Helen went wrong. Her father used to play it on Sundays, after lunch, with his belt undone by one notch. Halfway through, he would usually stop and ask whether anybody wanted a cup of tea. If nobody did, he made one anyway. Ruth realized she didn’t know how the piece ended.

Daniel came back. There was nowhere for the van. A bus was waiting, and its driver had got out.

“Just a minute,” Helen said.

The driver appeared in the doorway. Ruth knew him slightly. He’d lost a glove in February and had come in three times to see if she had it, each time taking the remaining glove from his pocket to show her. Now he stood with his hands at his sides until Helen finished. The last few notes were nothing like what Ruth had expected. There was a little descending run, then a pause long enough for her to think it was over, then one more note, quite low.

“Ten minutes,” the driver said. “I’ll go round the other way.”

They got the piano as far as the threshold before one of the front wheels came off. Daniel went to look for a brick. Ruth knelt and put her fingers under the corner, then took them out again. Years ago a porter had shown her how to move a filing cabinet alone. She could remember the porter’s wristwatch, which had a hairline crack across the face, but not what he’d done with the cabinet.

Her phone rang. It was her daughter, asking if she was home yet.

“No,” Ruth said. “I could use a hand, actually.”

“All right,” her daughter said. “I’ve got the kids.”

“Bring them.”

Daniel came back with half a brick. Helen told him not to put it there, and he asked where he should put it, and she said she didn’t know yet, but not there. Ruth went out to the platform so her daughter could hear her.

The rain had stopped. Across the tracks, a man on the far platform was walking briskly toward the footbridge, carrying a long yellow umbrella. Ruth recognized it by the black tape around the handle. It had been in the office since before Christmas.

He’d nearly reached the stairs when he stopped and looked up at the sky. Then he doubled back a few steps and put the umbrella on a bench, well in from the edge so it wouldn’t fall. He checked the clock and ran for his train.

Ruth watched the umbrella until her daughter said, “Mum? Which entrance?”

“The side one,” Ruth said, and went to prop it open.

The year the river moved, the city sent everyone on our street a change-of-address form.

We had not moved. Our houses stood where they always had, with their cracked steps and satellite dishes pointed at the same unpromising patch of sky. But the river, which had been the boundary between two municipalities since 1841, had cut across a bend during the spring flood. We went to bed in Bell and woke up in Overton.

The practical differences were these: our rubbish would be collected on Thursdays, our library cards would no longer work, and my father was now buried out of town.

My mother took the last development personally.

“He never liked to travel,” she said.

This was true. My father had once spent six weeks looking forward to a holiday and the entire holiday looking forward to getting home. On the drive back he had bought a bag of cherries from a roadside stand. That, in later tellings, became the holiday.

My mother called both municipalities. Bell said the cemetery remained in Bell. Overton said our house was indisputably in Overton. A woman in the county surveyor’s office said she could send a map.

“I know where everything is,” my mother told her.

Still, she asked for the map.

It arrived folded into a rectangle with a shiny advertisement for a septic company on the back. The new river was blue. The old one was a dotted line, like something we were meant to cut out with scissors.

My mother spread the map over the kitchen table and put a salt shaker on one corner, a pepper mill on another, and her elbows on the remaining two. She stayed like that for some time. I made tea around her.

“What are you looking for?” I asked.

“Where it decided.”

I’d seen the place from the road. Someone’s cornfield had become a shallow lake with fence posts sticking out. I could have shown her, but I had the sense not to point.

On Thursday the new rubbish truck came at seven in the morning. Everyone on the street had put their bins out except my mother. Ours was full, and when I offered to run it down she said, “They’ll be back next week.”

That afternoon we drove to the cemetery. The old bridge still stood, although now there was hardly anything under it. A boy in a red sweatshirt was riding his bicycle through the mud beneath the arch. We slowed down to watch him make it almost to the far bank before he had to put a foot down.

At the grave my mother pulled three strands of dead grass out of the lettering. Then she started telling my father about a piece of gutter that had come loose above the kitchen window. I had offered to fix it on Monday, but she’d said it wasn’t bothering her.

Without the river in its old bed, the cemetery was quieter. I could hear someone fastening a dog’s lead on the footpath. The clasp made a small, clean click.

“Do you want to go to the library?” I asked when we got back to the car.

“They won’t let us take anything out.”

“We can put something back.”

I had a book of my father’s in the glove compartment. He’d borrowed it three weeks before he died. It was a large, illustrated guide to pruning, and in the last winter of his life he had made notes on the pear tree in our garden: south branch crossing; leave the little one. By the time I found the book under his chair, I’d already paid for a replacement. I had been driving around with it for eleven months.

The librarian checked the barcode and told us we could keep it.

“We have one,” she said, and turned her monitor toward us, as though we might want to see the one we’d bought.

My mother put the book back in her bag.

At home, she fetched the stepladder while I found a screwdriver. I got up far enough to see why the gutter bracket wouldn’t hold: the wood behind it was soft. I told her we’d need to replace the board.

“Is that a big job?”

“Probably not,” I said. I’d never done it.

She held the ladder while I came down. Neither of us let go right away. Her hands were on the rails below mine, and there was a streak of green on her sleeve from where she’d carried it against the side of the shed.

We went to the hardware store in Overton. A man there told me how to take the gutter down without bending it. My mother listened, then asked him to explain it again, slower, while she wrote it on the back of the receipt.

The gutter took most of Saturday. We bent it anyway. On Sunday it rained, and water came out of the downpipe instead of pouring past the kitchen window. My mother stood at the sink for a while, watching the place where it no longer fell.

By summer the city had painted a white line across the road to mark the new boundary. It ran through the bus shelter, leaving the bench in Bell and the timetable in Overton. Nothing stopped anybody from sitting there. My mother did sometimes, on her way back from the cemetery. She said it was a good place to eat a peach because you could be as messy as you liked and wash your hands in the river afterward.

Late that August I went with her. She’d brought two peaches in a paper bag. Mine was hard near the stone; hers was so ripe she had to lean forward to keep from getting it on her shirt. She saw me looking and said my father would have taken hers back to the shop.

“He’d have eaten it first, though,” I said.

“Oh, certainly.”

We sat a little longer. A bus pulled up, and my mother waved it on. Then she finished her peach and held out her hand for my stone. I thought she meant to throw them both in the river, but she put them in the bag. On the way home she told me where in the garden we could try planting them.

On the morning the city began giving back its sounds, Mara received a padded envelope containing her father clearing his throat.

She knew it before she opened the envelope. The little cough came through the paper as she stood at the kitchen counter, trying to decide whether an egg could go bad one day after the date on the carton. Two dry notes, then a third, almost apologetic. For thirty years that sound had meant he was about to say something difficult or ask where the scissors were.

Inside was a brass disk the size of a coat button, and a letter.

*The Department of Public Works is pleased to return the enclosed material, recovered during repairs to the municipal water system. No response is required.*

Mara turned the disk over. Her father cleared his throat again.

“Well?” she said.

Her egg rolled off the counter.

By noon the neighborhood was full of noises nobody had heard in years. The corner grocer got back the bell from the shop he’d run before the rent went up. A woman on the fourth floor received the squeak of a hospital shoe and spent twenty minutes on the phone trying to give it back. The man who walked his greyhound in a raincoat came home to find his own eight-year-old laughter in the mailbox. He played it once on the front steps. The dog got up and looked behind him.

Mara put the disk in her pocket and took the bus to Public Works.

They were receiving claims in the basement. Someone had taped a sign to the door: PLEASE DO NOT TEST SOUNDS IN LINE. Ahead of her, a man held a shoebox in both hands. Every few seconds something inside it said *Next stop, Linden Avenue.*

“Linden Avenue hasn’t been a stop since 1994,” he told her.

“Do you want it to be?”

“No. The bus would have to turn right through my living room.”

He smiled, but he held the box very carefully.

At the counter, a clerk took Mara’s letter and asked what was missing.

“Nothing, technically,” Mara said. “I wondered if you had what came after this.”

She turned over the disk. The clerk leaned forward to listen.

“Speech is hard,” he said. “We get a lot of beginnings. People speak up to start, then they turn away, or the kettle comes on. Do you know where it happened?”

“My parents’ kitchen, probably.”

He passed her a form. There were boxes for the address, the approximate date, the weather, and any machinery that might have been running. For the first time in years she had reason to remember how the refrigerator in that kitchen used to shiver when it switched off. Once, when she was doing homework at the table, her father had put a hand on top of it and said, “I know, I know.”

Under *Approximate date*, she wrote *Any*.

“I need at least a year,” the clerk said.

She thought about picking the year he died, but he had hardly spoken that year. She thought about the year she went away to college, when he’d called her on Sundays until she told him she was usually out on Sundays. He’d believed her.

“1998,” she said. “August. Probably hot.”

The clerk entered the date. Somewhere behind the partition a drawer opened and a great many birds flew out of it, or made the sound of flying out of it. He waited for them to finish.

“What are you hoping he said?”

“Does that help you find it?”

“No,” he said. “Sorry. That was just me asking.”

She could have told him that in August of 1998 she had backed her father’s car into a low wall and waited all day for him to come home. She remembered how she’d planned to confess while he still had his shoes on, so he could go straight out and look. How he’d come into the kitchen, put his keys down, cleared his throat, and said—

That was the trouble. She knew he hadn’t shouted. She knew that afterward he’d sent her to buy bread, in the same car, while it was still light. She could remember every turn on the way to the bakery. She could remember a warm loaf on the passenger seat, sliding forward each time she braked. But whatever he’d said in the kitchen was gone, and for years she’d had the uneasy feeling that it had been something she was supposed to learn.

The clerk handed back her form. “We’ll call if anything turns up.”

Outside, it had rained while she was underground. Water stood in the little dents left by the feet of market stalls. She sat at the bus stop with an old woman who was eating cherries out of a paper bag.

“Want some?” the woman asked.

Mara took one. It was a little warm.

The woman cleared her throat. Not like Mara’s father. Quite a bit louder, in fact.

“I’ve got a stone in my shoe,” she said. “Would you mind holding these?”

Mara held the cherries while the woman took off her shoe. There was no stone in it. She shook it twice and ran a finger along the seam. Finally she peeled off her stocking and found a tiny curled leaf stuck to the bottom of her foot.

“How on earth,” she said.

Mara held the bag open for her. The woman dropped the leaf in with the pits.

On the ride home Mara put her hand in her pocket and found the disk. She thought she might play it once more before she got off. Instead she watched a boy on the sidewalk push a bicycle alongside a much smaller boy, who was telling him something at considerable length. The older boy kept having to walk into the grass to give him room.

At home she put the disk in the kitchen drawer, next to the scissors. Then she took the other egg out of the carton and cracked it into a bowl. It was fine. She got out a pan. From the apartment upstairs came three knocks, a long pause, and a fourth knock much softer than the others. Someone was hanging a picture. She turned down the burner a little so she could hear how it went.

The post office began accepting letters to buildings the year they closed the elementary school. You had to use the street address, not the name, and put a second stamp on the envelope. The extra stamp was for the reply.

I assumed this was something the postmaster had invented to keep himself busy. He was a man who had once mailed my father a single glove with the address written on the palm.

“No,” he said. “If it were up to me, we wouldn’t deliver to anybody without a mailbox.”

I wrote to the school on a Tuesday.

*Dear 41 Barlow Street,*

*Do you remember the day we put a fish in the piano?*

On Friday I got back a square of the brown paper teachers used to cover bulletin boards. In small, dented type, it said:

*The fish was in a sandwich bag. For eleven minutes there was water in the bottom of middle D.*

This was correct. We’d caught the fish in the drainage ditch at recess, and neither of us wanted to be the one to take it out of the piano. In the end Mara did it, because I told her I would and then stood there doing nothing. She carried the bag out under her sweater and emptied it into the ditch. Whether it was also a good day for the fish was something we had not thought to establish.

I had not spoken to Mara in twenty-three years. At first I knew exactly why. Later, if I told the story at all, I found I could make it sound as though we had simply gone to different high schools.

I wrote to the school again.

*What did Mara say to me on the last day? By the coat hooks.*

The school took two weeks to reply.

*The right sleeve of her coat was turned inside out.*

I went to see the postmaster.

“Can you ask a follow-up?”

“You can buy two more stamps.”

“But do they understand the questions?”

He slid the sheet of stamps back into its drawer. “My wife wrote to our old apartment and asked whether we’d been happy there. It said someone had painted over a wall outlet.”

“Were you?”

“We were always running out of outlets,” he said.

The demolition fence went up in April. On the gate was a notice advising the public that the building contained asbestos and was under video surveillance. Through the mesh I could see that somebody had already taken the brass letters off the wall. The pale shapes they’d left behind were easier to read than the letters had been.

I bought a book of stamps.

*Was I crying?*

*The heel of your left shoe kept striking the baseboard.*

*Was she crying?*

*She stood close enough to the window to fog it.*

I had remembered her standing by the door. The window was at the other end of the hall. I had to put the letter down for a while after that. In my version she had walked away before I could answer; I’d been rather fond of that detail.

I found Mara through the website of a veterinary clinic three towns over. The page showed her holding a rabbit with one hand under its bottom, a precaution none of us had taken with the fish. I wrote to the clinic’s general email address and asked the receptionist to pass on my number. Then I bought groceries, came home, and ate a nectarine over the sink. It wasn’t ripe. I ate the whole thing anyway.

She called the following evening while I was taking out the recycling.

“You’re not supposed to put the lids in,” she said, after I told her what the noise was.

I took the lid out of the bin.

We talked about our parents, who were alive in different proportions than they used to be. We talked about a boy in our class who could play the trumpet without moving his face. She had gone on a date with him at nineteen. He’d moved his face a normal amount. There was no second date.

Finally I asked if she remembered the last day of school.

“Sure,” she said. “You told everybody I was moving because my dad went to jail.”

“I told Ben.”

“Ben had a mouth the size of a garage.”

I leaned against the bins. Up the street a woman in slippers was trying to coax a dog off somebody’s lawn without stepping onto the lawn herself.

“I’m sorry,” I said. “You asked me not to tell anyone, and I told him at lunch.”

“Yes,” Mara said. Then she asked if I remembered saving her a seat on the bus that afternoon.

I didn’t.

“You made me sit on your backpack so Ben couldn’t get it. It had a thermos in it. Extremely uncomfortable.”

“Why did you sit there?”

“It was a long ride.”

We talked a little longer. Her son had got into making bread. He was fourteen and took any suggestion that he wipe the flour off the counter as a failure to support the arts. I said I’d like to meet him. She said that could probably happen, though on Saturdays he slept until one.

That night I wrote one more letter to the school. I didn’t have another question, so I told it about the fish. How Mara had returned it to the ditch, which the school couldn’t have seen from where it stood. How I’d held the door for her on the way back in and she’d wiped her wet hands on my shirt. I left the letter in the mailbox with the flag up.

The excavator arrived on Monday. They started at the far end, with the gym, and worked their way toward the coat hooks. I didn’t go to watch.

A week later the letter came back. The envelope was unopened, with a yellow sticker over the address and both stamps still good. I peeled one off, put it on a postcard, and wrote to Mara to ask what time the bread usually came out of the oven.

The first thing my father asked me to steal was a tree. He called on a Tuesday, while I was eating lunch over the sink.

“Bring the shovel with the red handle,” he said.

“Are we burying something?”

“Other way around.”

The tree was a pear, not much taller than he was, growing behind the house where I grew up. My father had sold the house in March. It was now November, and the new owners had put a trampoline exactly where our kitchen table used to be, if you counted through the wall.

“Did you ask them?” I said.

“I left a message.”

“When?”

He took a pair of work gloves out of his coat and examined them, as if the answer might be printed inside.

My mother had planted the pear tree the year she gave up smoking. She bought it with the money she’d saved in a mayonnaise jar and spent the rest on a pink blouse that made my father say, every time she wore it, “Well, look at you.” The blouse lasted longer than the resolution. The tree, which was supposed to produce two varieties of pear on the same trunk, had produced one small, very hard pear in twelve years. My mother put it on the windowsill and waited for it to ripen until my father used it to prop open the bathroom door.

The new owners weren’t home. There was a plastic dinosaur on the back step, flattened at the hips from having been shut in the door. My father picked it up and stood it on the railing.

“We can go to a nursery,” I said. “You can get a bigger one.”

“I don’t know where I’d put a bigger one.”

I had no idea where he meant to put this one. His new apartment was on the third floor, over a bakery. He insisted you couldn’t smell the bread from up there, although the first time I visited he opened the door and said, before he said hello, “They’ve burnt something.”

I put the shovel in the ground. The soil was wet enough to come up in slabs. Beneath the sod was a piece of blue china, and beneath that a worm. My father moved the worm out of the way with one finger.

“You know she didn’t even like pears,” he said.

“I know.”

“She liked those little ones in the tin.”

“Those are pears.”

“Well, she liked the tin.”

We dug a circle, then a bigger circle. Roots kept turning up where roots had no business being, under the path and out toward the clothesline. I had thought of a tree as a thing with a top and a bottom, and had brought a tarp sized for approximately that idea. My father sat on the overturned wheelbarrow and held one end of the tarp in his lap so it wouldn’t blow away.

At half past three, a woman came through the side gate with a child in a reflective vest. She had a bag of groceries in each hand. The child stopped short at the hole.

“Is it dead?” he asked.

“No,” said my father.

The woman set the bags down. A leek stuck out of one, trailing rainwater from its leaves.

“I got your message,” she said.

My father wiped his gloves on his trousers. “We can fill it in.”

“Oh, you can have it. I thought you meant the big tree.”

We all looked across the yard at the ash, which was taller than the house. I tried to imagine my father leaving a message about coming round to collect it. Evidently the woman had tried, too, and had got far enough to wonder what kind of equipment he might bring.

“Hang on,” she said. “He made something for it.”

The child went inside and came back with a square of plywood on a string. PEARS 5p, it said. On the back, in smaller letters, was NO CREDIT.

“He saw the label,” she said. The nursery tag was still looped around a branch, bleached nearly blank. “He’s been checking it before school.”

My father took the sign. “Five pence apiece?”

“For a bag,” the child said.

“You’ll want to have another think about that.”

The woman picked up her groceries. The child watched my father turn the sign over twice, then said, “You can keep it,” in the tone of someone who has given away a pet and hopes to hear where it will sleep.

I waited for my father to say thank you. Instead he got up and went to the hole. With the toe of his boot he nudged a slab of sod back into place. It sat too high. He stamped on it, then stamped again.

“Have you turned the heating on yet?” he asked the woman.

“We have. It makes a racket.”

“That’ll be the pipe behind the cupboard. There’s a wooden wedge on top of the boiler. I took it out for the inspection and forgot to put it back.” He showed her how wide the wedge was with his thumb and finger. Then he told her where the stopcock was, which window needed lifting before you pulled it shut, and why she shouldn’t pay anybody to come out about the extractor fan until she’d tried turning it off at the wall. I’d heard most of this before. The thing about the wedge was new to me.

The child helped us push the dirt back with the sides of his boots. Then he hung his sign on a low branch, where the price was legible from the kitchen.

On the way home my father carried the muddy shovel across his knees. We stopped outside the bakery. The lights were still on, and a woman inside was putting the unsold rolls into a paper sack.

“Do you want me to come up?” I asked.

“Yes,” he said, without looking over. Then he opened his door a little, closed it again, and said, “Actually, let’s go in here first. I’ve never been.”

On the last day of the laundromat, my father washed a single sock. He paid six dollars to do it. When I pointed out that he could have washed it in the sink, he said, “I could have washed it in the sink in 1987, too.”

That was the year he bought the place. The sock wasn’t from 1987. I checked.

I’d come with a recorder borrowed from the library. The idea was to get him talking about the laundromat: how he’d bought it with money from selling his taxi, how my mother had put a bowl of oranges by the change machine and gotten annoyed when people took them. I wanted to ask about the flood. I wanted to ask whether he remembered making me do my homework on top of dryer nine, which ran a little hotter than the others and kept my legs warm through my jeans.

He remembered the flood.

“Water came in,” he said.

I waited.

“From outside.”

I stopped the recorder.

At eleven, Mrs. Alvarez came in with her comforter. Dad had taken the sign down the night before, and she wanted to know why he’d done that if he was still open.

“Because I had a ladder yesterday,” he said.

“You could put up a paper sign.”

“I could.”

She stood there a moment, deciding whether the matter called for further intervention. Then she put her comforter in the big machine. Dad went over and opened the soap drawer for her, though she’d been coming in every Thursday since I was nine and knew how it worked.

He’d told me he was ready to be done. The new owner was going to sell tiles. There would be a rack of tiles you could pull out and tilt under a light, and a desk where you could sit down and discuss the cost of having a floor. Dad had shown me the plans. He was pleased that they’d decided to keep the little bathroom in the back.

Around noon I turned the recorder on again and left it on the folding table. I didn’t tell anybody. I wasn’t trying to catch a confession. I’d just noticed that as soon as I held it up, my father said everything twice as clearly and half as well.

A boy fed quarters into the change machine. It was an excellent machine, in that respect: it took a quarter and gave you a quarter. He kept doing it until his mother noticed.

The door made its familiar high noise. Dad had oiled the hinge any number of times. The noise turned out to come from the rubber sweep at the bottom, which he could have trimmed in thirty seconds. By the time he figured that out, he’d grown to like knowing when someone came in.

At two, Mrs. Alvarez folded her comforter with his help. For the first fold they stood far apart, arms spread. At each subsequent fold they stepped closer, until finally he pulled his hands out and she had the whole thing against her chest.

“What’re you going to do on Thursdays?” she asked him.

“I have to see about a tooth.”

“Every Thursday?”

“I don’t know how bad it is yet.”

She laughed, and then she asked him, quite seriously, to let her know.

The sock was still in the washer. I asked if he was going to dry it.

“No,” he said. “It’s yours.”

It was gray with a green heel. I’d bought a pack of them in college. He said he’d found it behind the lost-property bin when he pulled the bin out to sweep. I put it in my coat pocket. For the next hour, whenever I leaned against the folding table, I could feel the wet coming through.

We stayed until six, though nobody came in after four. Dad emptied the coin boxes, and I counted the quarters into paper sleeves. He kept sliding little piles toward me after I thought I’d finished. In the end we had one quarter that wouldn’t make up a roll. He went to the door and wedged it into the loose strike plate, which had rattled since the tile man came to measure.

That night, in my apartment, I listened to the recording. There was more of me on it than I’d expected. Me asking where the tape was. Me tearing it with my teeth. Me saying, “Dad,” three times, with no particular urgency, while I waited for him to turn around.

Then, in a stretch I didn’t remember at all, my father began to sing. It wasn’t loud enough to make out the words. I kept backing up, thinking I recognized the tune, and then losing it when a dryer came on.

I took the recorder over to his house the next morning. He was at the kitchen table eating toast on a paper towel. I played him the part with the singing and asked what song it was.

“That’s not me,” he said.

We listened again.

“It’s you.”

It was. I’d been standing by the folding table, putting tape on a box. With the dryer going I’d apparently felt free to sing.

“Your mother used to sing that,” he said.

I waited for him to name the song, but he didn’t know it either. He put another slice of bread in the toaster. While we waited for it to come up, I played the little stretch again, this time with the recorder between us on the table. There was a scrape I took for the box being dragged across the table. Then the dryer cut out, and you could hear my father, very close to the microphone, humming the next few notes. By then I’d stopped singing. He went on by himself for a little while.

On the last day of the ferry, the captain let everybody bring one thing that had never been allowed aboard.

He made the announcement himself, on the radio station that gave the lake temperature and the price of eggs. His daughter called while he was still in the studio to ask whether he meant it.

“Within reason,” he said.

“You can’t put that in afterward,” she told him.

By seven, someone had brought a goat.

The ferry had been losing money for eleven years, which was also how long people had been saying it was about to go. Now there was a bridge. From the wheelhouse you could see cars going over it in both directions, their headlights still on. The captain’s daughter had driven across that morning with a cup of coffee in the holder and been startled to find herself on the other side before the coffee was cool enough to drink.

Her name was Ruth. When she was nine, she had sat at the kitchen table making little timetables for the ferry, with a run at midnight in case somebody couldn’t sleep. She now worked in payroll. She had taken the day off and brought a folding chair.

“What’s forbidden about that?” her father asked.

“Nothing. It’s for you.”

“I’ve got a chair.”

“You’ve got a stool.”

He looked at the folding chair again. It was striped blue and yellow, the kind people took to the beach. He said he’d think about it.

On the eight-ten, Mr. Devi brought a tub of fish and cleaned them on the car deck. This had been explicitly prohibited since an incident involving Mr. Devi. At nine, three middle-schoolers brought their bicycles down the passenger stairs instead of walking them up the ramp. They wore helmets and came down very slowly, squeezing the brakes, so that the effect was less an act of rebellion than the delivery of three large and delicate parcels.

At ten-forty a woman came aboard carrying an iron.

“I want to plug it in,” she said.

The captain showed her the outlet by the vending machine. For the length of the crossing, while the ferry rolled a little in the wake of a Johnson outboard, she ironed a white shirt on a towel laid across the bench. Nobody knew what to ask her, so they let her work. As the boat came in, she slipped the shirt onto a hanger and held it high to keep the sleeves from brushing the rail.

Ruth knew what the iron was about. She remembered the woman from the years when she’d crossed every morning in a supermarket uniform, always with something to do: an orange to peel, a stocking to mend, a child’s permission slip to fill out against the window. Ruth remembered her asking once about an outlet. Her father had said no without looking up.

At noon Ruth went to the wheelhouse with two sandwiches. Her father ate the first half of his standing up. Below them, the goat had gone home, but a thin man in a suit was teaching someone to back a trailer.

“All these years,” Ruth said, “I thought you’d stop and they’d get another captain.”

“They might have. If I’d stopped.”

She’d meant it as a complaint and found she didn’t want to explain it. In the version she had taken for granted, there would be a substitute captain whom her father could criticize from the passenger deck. He would call her to report a rough landing. She could tell him not to be so hard on the new man.

“Did you ever let Mum steer?” she asked.

“Once. She didn’t like it.”

“What didn’t she like?”

“Couldn’t see where we were going.”

Ruth looked out. The landing was in plain sight.

“Fog,” he said. “She picked the day.”

They finished their sandwiches. Beyond the bridge a red truck appeared again between two stands of trees. Ruth had never quite understood where the old road went after it turned away from the lake.

The last crossing was at six-twenty. By then the forbidden things had given way to ordinary ones: laundry in a basket, a sleeping baby, groceries somebody had bought on the wrong side for the pleasure of carrying them back. At the last minute a man ran down the ramp with his keys in his hand. He stopped when he reached the deck and looked embarrassed. There was no car behind him.

“I always run,” he said to Ruth.

She moved her bag off the bench.

Halfway across, the engine changed note. People looked up. The ferry was slowing, though it was nowhere near the landing. A boy asked if they were stuck. His grandmother told him to wait.

Ruth went up to the wheelhouse. Her father was still at the controls. The striped chair stood open beside him.

“Come here a minute,” he said.

She stood where he stood. He pointed at a white house on the far bank, then at a notch in the trees. Seen from the ferry, the notch fit exactly over the chimney.

“That’s how I know I’m halfway,” he said.

She waited for him to tell her what he used it for. In fog he couldn’t have seen it, and on a clear day nobody needed to know when they were halfway. He sat down in the folding chair. The canvas gave a small, ugly squeak. He shifted his weight and it squeaked again.

Ruth kept her eyes on the house. The chimney moved out from under the notch. It happened so slowly that she could watch it happen, and then she couldn’t have said at what instant the two had come apart.

At the landing her father counted the passengers off, even the baby. Ruth folded the chair. They walked up the ramp together, and she asked whether he wanted her to drive him home.

“In a minute,” he said.

He had left the wheelhouse light on. From shore it looked considerably brighter than it ever had from inside. Ruth put the chair in the trunk and waited while he went back to turn it off.

On the first Thursday of every month, my father mailed me a pencil.

He worked at a hardware store and got them free from the man who sold the store its hinges. They were flat carpenter’s pencils, designed not to roll off a roof. Along one side, in green, was printed ASK ME ABOUT OUR HINGES. My father never included a note. He did, however, sharpen each pencil before he sent it, cutting away the wood with his pocketknife until the graphite emerged like a small, badly paved road.

We talked on Sundays. We discussed the weather, his neighbor’s fence, and whether the place where I bought my tires could be trusted. The pencils belonged to a separate correspondence.

The month he died I got two. One arrived on Thursday. The other arrived eleven days later, in an envelope the post office had put inside a clear plastic bag. WE CARE, the bag said. The pencil had punched through the envelope, and someone had taped its point to the flap. I appreciated the tape more than I appreciated the bag.

My sister and I went to clean out his house. She was good at opening drawers. I was good at standing in front of an open drawer and picking up one thing at a time.

“Do you want the colander?” she asked.

I said I had a colander.

“I know you have a colander. Do you want *this* colander?”

It was the aluminum one he used to rinse blackberries. In August he brought them home in empty sour cream tubs, and if you opened the wrong tub there would be sour cream, which always seemed like a breach of the arrangement.

“Yes,” I said.

She set it by my coat. After a while I realized she was doing this with everything she wanted me to have. I went to put on my coat and found a colander, a socket wrench, and a picture of myself at nine, kneeling beside a hole I had dug in the yard. I remembered the hole. I had wanted to see whether the dirt would change color if I went deep enough, and it had. This remains one of the most satisfying results of any work I’ve undertaken.

In the garage there was a shoebox filled with pencils. Below it, on the workbench, Dad had screwed down a little block of wood with a notch cut in it. You could rest the pencil in the notch and shave it without holding it in your other hand. For the last year or so he’d had trouble with his left hand. He told me it was funny what you missed. He hadn’t missed opening jars, because there were tools for jars. He missed taking a sock off with one motion.

I tried the block. It took several passes to get through the paint. I kept pressing too hard, and on the third or fourth pass the blade jumped and sliced the pad of my thumb.

My sister washed the cut at the kitchen sink. She’d been a lifeguard in high school and still approached minor injuries with a degree of authority I found comforting.

“What were you trying to do?”

“Sharpen a pencil.”

“Did you need a pencil?”

“No.”

She wrapped a bandage around my thumb and went back to the pantry. After a minute she called out, “I kept thinking I’d get to tell him the dishwasher works.”

She’d installed it herself the weekend he went into the hospital. He’d sat at the kitchen table reading the instructions to her and then, when she asked him to stop, reading them silently with his lips moving. On Sunday morning she ran it for the first time. The measuring cup on the top rack came out clean, including the little hollow in the handle where the old machine always left a grain of rice.

I took the shoebox home. For months I used the pencils for grocery lists and crossword puzzles, the latter with some difficulty; a carpenter’s pencil can fill in most of a square before you decide what letter you meant. When a pencil wore down, I sharpened it over the trash with a utility knife. The shavings smelled faintly of the aisle where Dad used to stand with his lunch in a paper sack, eating one half of a sandwich and keeping the other half folded up so he could go help somebody.

In the spring my sister called to ask if I remembered how deep he planted his peas. I didn’t. We both looked it up, separately, while we were on the phone, and came back with different answers.

“An inch,” she said.

“Two inches.”

“That sounds deep.”

“It does.”

Neither of us hung up. I could hear her walking outside, then the metal scrape of the back door she’d been meaning to fix since she bought the place. I asked if she still had the door propped open with a brick. She said yes, and that the brick was doing an excellent job.

A week later I found a small paper envelope in the mailbox. Inside were six peas and a torn piece of the seed packet. My sister had circled the planting instructions, which said one inch. Beneath that, in her cramped handwriting: TWO IF YOU LIKE.

I planted three at each depth. I’d intended to label them, but the phone rang while I was doing it, and afterward all six places looked the same. I went inside for a glass of water and stood drinking it at the sink. There was still a blackberry seed caught under the rolled rim of the colander. I’d tried to get it out before, with a toothpick, and the toothpick had broken.

Out in the yard, a squirrel was nosing around the place I’d planted the peas. I knocked on the window. It sat up and looked directly at me, its front paws held loose against its chest. Then it went back to what it was doing, and I put down my glass and went outside.

On the last day of the municipal lost-and-found, a woman came in looking for the sound of her brother coming home.

“Which part?” I asked.

She had expected trouble with *sound*. She had prepared a little speech about how she knew this wasn’t an ordinary lost-and-found and how the man at the bus depot had assured her. My question seemed to annoy her more than disbelief would have.

“The whole thing,” she said.

I showed her the form. Under DESCRIPTION there were six lines. She took off her gloves and wrote: *Key missing the lock, twice. Door. Two steps. Keys in the blue bowl.*

“Did he always miss twice?”

“Once when he was sober,” she said, and added it to the form.

We had until five. At five the building would become the property of a company that made alarms for refrigerators. They had bought the building for its loading dock and were indifferent to the vault, which was the only room in town in which you could hear a pin drop on a carpet. I knew because I had dropped one. It sounded like the smallest possible person sitting down.

The woman’s name was Irene. Her brother’s was Paul. He had been dead twelve years, which put his homecoming in the old stacks, assuming we had it at all. Ordinary sounds were harder to find than exceptional ones. We had three drawers of lightning hitting churches, all carefully labeled. The drawers for footsteps, on the other hand, had been misfiled during a renovation and never entirely put right.

“Was there a dog?” I asked.

“No.”

“Television usually on?”

“No. Well, yes. I turned it down when I heard him.”

That gave us something. We filed a surprising number of sounds by what stopped just before them.

I took her downstairs. Visitors weren’t supposed to go downstairs, but there was nobody left to tell me so. My supervisor had spent the morning packing his plants into a box that said EVIDENCE and had gone home at eleven.

In the old stacks, each recording lived on a strip of brown paper wound around a wooden spool. You drew the paper through two fingers to hear it. It was important not to pull too fast. You could give a child a man’s voice by accident, which upset people even when they knew what you’d done.

We found a likely box under TELEVISION, MUTED. Irene stood next to me while I tried the first spool. A remote clicked. A door opened. Someone said, “Don’t get up, it’s only me.”

“No,” she said.

The next was a sitcom laugh cut in half, then a dead bolt and a bag of groceries being set down rather hard.

“He never bought groceries,” Irene said.

“Never?”

“He bought mustard once. We already had mustard.”

She pulled out a chair. I went on with the spools. After a while she took one herself and began listening. At four we ate the biscuits I’d been saving for my supervisor’s farewell. At twenty past, we heard a key scrape brass, stop, scrape again. There was a soft burr from the bottom of the door.

Irene took hold of my sleeve.

One step. Two. The keys struck the bowl and spun against its side. Just before the paper ran out, there was a little breath, close enough to stir the hair in my ear.

“That’s me,” she said.

I wound it back. We listened again.

“I used to hold my breath for the bowl,” she said. “If he made it that far, I knew I could go to bed.”

I put the spool on the table and went upstairs for an envelope.

When I came back, she’d wound the paper so tightly that the outer edge had puckered. I showed her how to loosen it with her thumb.

“I don’t think I want to take it,” she said.

I put the envelope down anyway. People changed their minds a lot at the counter. One man had come in every Thursday for a year to listen to the starter motor of a car he’d hated.

“Can we hear the one with the groceries again?” she asked.

It took me a minute to find it. She closed her eyes as the bag hit the floor. Somewhere inside it, glass knocked against glass.

“Mustard,” she said.

“Could be.”

“He left it in his coat for three days. Then he went looking for it in the fridge and got angry with me for using it all.” She laughed, and then, because she had laughed, told me the rest: he’d found the jar in his pocket while they were on the bus and held it up without a word. She’d looked out the window rather than give him the satisfaction. At that point in the story she had to stop and take a drink of water. She wiped the rim of the glass with her sleeve before giving it back to me.

At five the man from the refrigerator company knocked on the front door. I could see him through the glass, holding a ring of keys and trying to peer past his own reflection.

“What happens to the ones nobody takes?” Irene asked.

I’d been told to leave them where they were. My supervisor said you couldn’t throw away something that belonged to nobody without first demonstrating that it belonged to nobody. This had struck him as very funny on Monday. By Friday he’d stopped saying it.

Irene took the spool with the groceries. She put it in her coat pocket without the envelope.

I let the man in. He had a clipboard and wanted me to show him the loading dock. On the way there I heard Irene start down the front steps, stop, and come back to pull the door shut. It stuck at the bottom. I’d been meaning to fix it for years. Through the wall I heard her give it one good, impatient shove, the way I did every evening, and then it caught.

On the ninth day after the river came through, we opened a lost-property office in the high school gym. We had six folding tables, a pad of claim forms, and a rule against plugging anything in. By noon somebody had plugged in a lamp. It worked. For the rest of the week people brought things over to see them in its light, though the gym was perfectly bright.

The first thing I tagged was a wooden spoon. I wrote FOUND AT CORNER OF THIRD AND ELM, which made it sound as if the spoon had been waiting for a bus. Later, when we ran out of tags, we wrote directly on things. A white refrigerator door said BEHIND THE LIBRARY in blue marker.

The door had no refrigerator attached. It lay flat across two milk crates, and people rested their coffee on it while filling out forms. On Friday a woman in a green raincoat came in, saw it, and said, “Oh, good.”

She turned it over. Three mugs hit the floor. One broke.

“Sorry,” she said, without looking up.

On the other side were pencil lines, dates, and names. Some of the lines had been drawn over so many times that the pencil had scored the enamel. The lowest one said JUNE, SHOES ON.

“That’s mine,” she said.

The claim form asked for an identifying feature not visible to staff. I asked her if there was anything written under the rubber seal.

“How would I know?”

“Sometimes people put things there.”

“Do they?”

I had no idea. I lifted the seal with my thumbnail. A little brown water came out.

June, it turned out, was her sister. The woman was Ruth, which was also the name beside most of the lines. There were a few for a boy called Ian, and one, nearly six feet up, for a visiting cousin whose arrival had apparently been an event.

“My mother started it on the kitchen wall,” Ruth said. “Then she painted the kitchen.”

Her mother was in a motel off the interstate, in a room with a microwave on top of a microwave. The first one didn’t work. Ruth had asked the manager why he didn’t take it away, and he said the second one would be too low.

I got as far as writing Ruth’s name on the form before a man at the end of the table said, “That came off my fridge.”

We looked at him. He had been in every day that week. He’d found one of his lawn chairs on Tuesday and had kept coming back because, as he explained, he used to have two.

“Mine had that dent,” he said, pointing to the bottom corner of the door.

Ruth pointed to her name.

“I see that,” he said. “I’m not saying it makes sense.”

He took out his phone. He had a picture of his dog asleep in front of a refrigerator with a dent in the bottom corner. It was a very good picture of the dog. You couldn’t see much of the refrigerator.

“Did you buy it used?” Ruth asked.

The man thought about it. “I got it from a lady on Spruce.”

“That’s my mother.”

In the gym behind us, somebody dropped a drawer full of cutlery. We waited for the noise to die down.

“She told me she put it out for the scrap man,” Ruth said.

“No. I gave her sixty dollars.”

Ruth ran her finger along one of the pencil lines. I thought she might ask him why he’d left them there. Instead she asked if the fridge had worked.

“For four years,” he said. “Freezer was terrible.”

“Yes,” she said. “It was.”

I put the claim form between them. The man looked down at the box marked REPLACEMENT VALUE and laughed. Then he asked Ruth whether she’d seen a green lawn chair anywhere near the library. She hadn’t, but she asked what kind of green, and he said the kind that starts out green and gets whiter every summer. She said she’d keep an eye out.

The door was too wide for the trunk of her car. We lowered the back seats and slid it in from the passenger side. Halfway through, Ruth said, “Hang on,” and I thought we’d caught a hinge on something. But she was looking at a line near the top.

“October,” she said. “I must have been home from college.”

It was higher than the one before it by less than the width of the pencil mark.

“She said I hadn’t grown,” Ruth said. “I made her do it again.”

There was, if you leaned in, a second line.

When we got back inside, the man was on his knees with a dustpan, sweeping up the mug. He’d put the two that hadn’t broken on my chair. One was his.

“Sorry about the table,” Ruth said.

“It wasn’t a very good table,” I told her. This was untrue. It had been exactly the height you wanted a table to be.

On Monday she came back with the door. She and her mother had taken pictures of all the marks. Her mother wanted to know whether she’d be charged for leaving it with us.

“People have been setting their coffee on the floor,” I said.

We put the door back on its crates, writing side down. Ruth pressed on each corner to make sure it wouldn’t tip. Then she took a pencil from the box of claim forms and crouched beside it. I could hear the pencil moving but couldn’t see what she wrote.

After she left, I got down on my knees and looked. On the underside of the door, beside JUNE, SHOES ON, Ruth had written the name of the gym and the date. The pencil had barely taken. I had to turn my head sideways to read it.
