On the last day of the ferry, my father brought a spirit level.

He had spent thirty-one years telling passengers not to lean against the rail, and now, retired and wearing a good blue shirt, he leaned against it himself. He took the level from his coat and laid it flat on the rail. The bubble slid to one end.

“There,” he said.

“What?”

“People always asked if the river was level.”

“Was it?”

“Not if you ask on a boat.”

The bridge had opened at six that morning. From the deck we watched cars cross it without slowing. This was the marvelous thing about the bridge, apparently: you could go over the river without noticing it. The mayor had said as much on the radio. He called it giving people back their time.

I had come home to help my father decide whether to sell his house. I had a folder in my bag. In the folder were photographs of a flat near me, with a lift and a grocery store downstairs. I had circled the grocery store on the map. As soon as I did it I knew he would make fun of the circle, so I drew another around the pharmacy to make it look like a system.

The ferry was crowded. Some people had brought their children, who were disappointed that nothing was going to happen to the boat. It wasn’t going to be sunk or blown up. On Monday two men would take it upriver to a yard and see what it was worth.

“Did you ever go across just for fun?” I asked my father.

“Once,” he said. “With your mother. Before I worked here. We went to buy a cooker.”

“That doesn’t sound like fun.”

“We came back without the cooker.”

He took the level off the rail and wiped it on his sleeve. I waited for more, but this was the whole story, or all he was willing to part with.

At the far landing a woman struggled down the ramp with a shopping trolley. One of its wheels had turned sideways. The deckhand offered to lift it, but she told him to wait and gave the wheel a good kick. It straightened. Then she came aboard and parked next to us.

“Are you going to tell me off?” she asked my father.

“For what?”

“I haven’t paid.”

“I don’t work here.”

“You told me that yesterday.”

She reached into her coat and brought out three coins. The fare had gone up years ago and then gone up again. My father looked at the coins and told her she was two pence short. She put them back in her pocket.

“Never liked you,” she said.

They stood together without speaking as the deckhand raised the ramp.

When I was nine, I missed the last ferry home. I’d gone across with a friend who said there was a horse in a field that would let you sit on it. There was a field. We spent the afternoon trying to catch grasshoppers in our socks, and when we got back to the landing, the ramp was up and the ferry was halfway across. My friend lived on that side. She went home for her tea.

I thought my father would come back for me if he saw me, so I took off my yellow jumper and swung it over my head. Nobody on the boat moved. It was getting cold, but I was afraid to put the jumper back on in case that was the moment he looked.

Eventually a lorry came down the road and stopped beside me. My mother got out of the passenger side. She had persuaded a man delivering washing machines to take the long way round. She put my jumper back on me, poking my fingers through the cuffs one by one, as if I were much younger than nine. I asked her if Dad was angry.

“Oh, he’s furious,” she said. “He’s making you an egg.”

On this last crossing I tried to find the place where I’d stood. There was a new shelter, and the fence looked too far back. I’d always pictured my father looking straight at me and being unable to turn the boat. It occurred to me now that he might have been inside, checking the takings, with no idea I was there.

The woman with the trolley got off first. My father waited until the deckhand had shut the little gate across the ramp, then knocked on the wheelhouse door and passed the level through the window. The man inside took it and turned it over. There was a strip of masking tape on the underside with a name written on it.

“I wondered where that went,” the man said.

“Your dad lent it to me.”

The man ran a thumb over the tape. “What for?”

“Putting up a shelf.”

“You taken the shelf down?”

“No,” said my father. “It’s a bloody good shelf.”

Up at the road, the bus was already rounding the corner. Neither of us ran. I took out my phone to look up the next one, but my father read the timetable on the pole. Forty minutes.

Across from the stop was the shop that used to sell cookers. There were two armchairs in the window and a notice saying you could come in and try them. My father read the notice aloud. Then he opened the door and held it for me.

A young man came out from behind the counter. He wanted to know what sort of thing we were after. My father said we were waiting for the bus. The young man looked at the clock and said we might as well sit down.

My father took the green chair. I sat in the other one and put my bag between my feet. After a while he pointed to a delivery van coming down the hill. It was nearly at the river before the driver saw the sign and turned. My father kept his hand raised a little longer, though from the road it would have been hard to see him through the glass.

On the last day of the municipal pool, somebody stole the clock. They left the screws in a neat pile on the lifeguard’s chair. At ten past nine, according to my phone, my mother stood beneath the pale circle on the wall and said, “Good. Now nobody can tell me my break is over.”

She’d been retired for eleven years.

I had agreed to record the building before they tore it down. This was my idea, though by then I’d explained it to so many people that I’d come to resent whoever had thought of it. The city archivist wanted dates, names, and a brief account of the roof repairs. I wanted the sound of a bare foot slapping a wet tile. Each of us thought the other was missing the point.

My mother brought a grocery bag containing her old whistle, two egg sandwiches, and a padlock whose combination she’d forgotten. She rattled the padlock at me.

“You used to open this.”

“Thirty-six, ten, twenty-two.”

She spun the dial. It opened.

“Why have you got room for that in your head?”

“I don’t get to choose.”

“Apparently not,” she said, and put it back in the bag.

The pool had closed to swimmers in August. Now it was November, and the only water left was a green puddle over the drain in the deep end. A beach ball lay down there, soft on one side. The blue lane markings looked freshly painted. From the edge you could see a hairline crack running through all six lanes, as if somebody had tried to fold the pool in half.

I put a microphone on a stand and asked my mother to walk from the changing rooms to the shallow end. She took off her shoes. Halfway across, she stopped and picked up a hairpin.

“Keep going,” I said.

“You want somebody to step on this?”

There was nobody else in the building. I started to say so, then watched her carry the hairpin to a trash can that had no liner. It made a sound like a coin dropped into a well. I’d already stopped recording.

We tried the whistle next. She gave it one short blast, and a pigeon came out of a hole in the ceiling. Neither of us had known it was there. It flew the length of the pool twice before finding the open door, and my mother laughed so hard she had to sit down.

“Did you get that?” she asked.

I had, but the whistle had overloaded the microphone. On playback it sounded as though somebody had torn a piece of paper close to my ear.

During lunch my mother told me about a woman who had come every Tuesday for nine years and never got in the water. She sat on the lowest bleacher in a purple bathing cap and read the newspaper. When the woman stopped coming, my mother called the number on her membership form. The woman answered on the second ring. She’d started taking an upholstery class. She had a chair at home that needed doing.

“What did you say?” I asked.

“I asked her what color.”

“What color?”

“Oh, I don’t know,” my mother said. She pinched a strip of egg white out of her sandwich and ate it. “I only remember how relieved I was when she picked up.”

After lunch we went to the changing rooms. The locker doors were different enough that I recorded six of them, then felt sorry for the seventh and recorded that too. My mother sat on the wooden bench and turned the padlock dial back and forth. She had taught me to swim in this building, but not during her shift. After closing, she’d get in up to her shoulders and hold a nickel flat on her palm, just below the surface. If I put my face in, I could have it. I must have made two dollars that summer, all of it from the same nickel. I kept forgetting to take it out of my swimsuit, and she kept finding it in the washing machine.

“Would you talk about teaching me to swim?” I asked.

She looked at the microphone. “You never liked to get your ears wet.”

“Right.”

“You’d get your whole head under, then come up with one ear still dry. I wish I knew how you did that.”

I waited for more. She turned the dial again.

At four, the man from Public Works arrived to lock up. It turned out he had taken the clock. His daughter had learned to tell time by it while waiting for her brother’s swimming lessons to end. He’d put it in his truck, then worried all day that he ought to have asked somebody. My mother told him that if anyone wanted it back, he should say she’d taken it.

“You don’t work here anymore,” he said.

“That’s why it’ll take them a while to find me.”

He gave us five minutes. I went back for the microphone stand and found my mother on the lifeguard’s chair, putting on her shoes. Without the clock above her, I could see where somebody had tested three shades of blue on the wall and painted over only two of them.

“Want a hand?” I asked.

“In a minute,” she said. “I’ve got a stone in here.”

She shook her shoe into her palm. I had my headphones on, and I could hear the little knocks she gave the heel, the laces brushing the metal chair, the man out in the lobby trying one key and then another. I could hear myself breathing. I held still while she checked the other shoe.

Months later, the archivist asked me to identify a voice on the recording. I put on my headphones. There was my mother saying *In a minute*, but that wasn’t the part he meant. He meant the voice after hers, so low I had to turn it up. It was me. I said *Okay*.

I almost wrote back that it was nobody. Then I gave him my name.

On the last night of the Orpheum, my mother sold one ticket to a man who did not want to see the film.

“What do you want to do, then?” she asked.

“Sit in my seat.”

She tore the ticket down the middle. “You people are going to discover benches and it’ll be the ruin of me.”

The man laughed. He had been coming on Thursdays for thirty-one years. Neither of us knew his name. On the seating chart in the box office, my mother had marked G9 *man with own salt*.

The buyer was turning the Orpheum into a pharmacy. He’d offered us the letters from the marquee, which was decent of him, but my mother said she had nowhere to put a seven-foot O. She’d already made the decision once, she said, when we took down the first O, the one that fell in 1998 and landed around a bicycle.

I’d come home with a recorder borrowed from work. I edit sound for nature documentaries. When you hear a beetle walking across a leaf, there’s a good chance you’re hearing me squeeze a cabbage. I’d been explaining this to my mother for fifteen years and she still told people I worked with beetles.

“What are you recording?” she asked.

“The room.”

She looked at the recorder, then up at the ceiling. “The whole thing?”

I told her about room tone: how even when nobody’s speaking, an empty kitchen sounds different from an empty church. When you take a cough out of somebody’s interview, you have to put a little of the room back in. Otherwise you can hear the hole.

“Well, don’t take out my cough,” she said. “I’ve had it since March.”

At seven she started *Local Hero*. It was the film she’d shown on opening night, though not at first. On opening night she’d meant to show *Tootsie*, but the distributor sent the wrong cans. My father told the audience there had been a change of management and the new management felt strongly about Scotland. My mother was the new management. She was twenty-six and pregnant with me and she was in the box office eating an egg sandwich. In later years, when she told the story, it was important to her that the sandwich not be left out.

I went down to the front row and put on my headphones. Through them I could hear the ventilation rattle over the left exit, and the little ticks the screen made as it warmed. Someone unwrapped a sweet for what felt like twenty minutes. Then a woman behind me whispered, “Just put the whole thing in your mouth.”

After the credits, people lingered in the lobby. They took pictures of the carpet, which had been the subject of a petition in 2006. A woman asked if she could buy a seat. My mother gave her a socket wrench and told her to see how badly she wanted it.

By eleven only the man from G9 was left. I found him standing in the aisle with his coat on, staring down at the seat next to his.

“My wife hated this place,” he said.

I’d been preparing for a different sentence and had already arranged my face.

“Too cold,” he said. “She waited in the car. She liked the radio.”

He asked if I could help him find something. One night he’d dropped a pound coin and it had rolled down under G8. This would have been ten or twelve years ago. He knew there was no chance, he said. We got out our phones and got down on our knees anyway. We found three pen lids, a boiled sweet still in its wrapper, and a key. He tried the key on his front door when he got home and called the box office to tell my mother it hadn’t worked.

At midnight I asked her to sit with me while I made the recording. She picked G8. I set the recorder on the armrest and told her we needed to be quiet for a minute.

After eleven seconds she said, “I don’t remember what your father sounded like when he answered the phone.”

I reached for the recorder and she put her hand on my wrist.

“I remember him talking to me. I remember him calling up the stairs. But there was a way he said hello when he didn’t know who it was. Very grand. As if we’d been expecting a call from the palace and he didn’t want to give away that he’d been in the bath.”

She tried it twice. The first time she made herself laugh; the second time she got it, I think, because she stopped smiling and looked straight at the blank screen.

We sat another minute. Then my mother said she’d left half an egg sandwich in the box office and did I want it. I did.

Months later, I opened the file at work. The minute after she imitated him was no good as room tone. She moved her feet and I sniffed and there was a sound I couldn’t place until I remembered the two of us passing her keys back and forth in the dark, neither of us wanting to be the one to get up and lock the door.

I sent her the whole thing. She called me that evening.

“Was that me saying hello?”

“Yes.”

“Play it again,” she said, though she had the file right there. So I held my phone up to the speaker. When it finished, I could hear her moving around in her kitchen. She put the kettle on. Neither of us hung up.

The city kept the sounds of demolished buildings in a basement beneath the tax office. You could request one by address, provided you knew the address as it had been at the time of demolition. This was harder than it sounded. Streets had been straightened, houses renumbered, and in one neighborhood an entire block had once been known as “behind the good bakery.”

My mother had worked in the basement for thirty-one years. When I was little and had to wait for her after school, she let me listen to buildings nobody had requested. A knitting factory. A swimming pool in winter. The last wooden escalator in a department store where, according to my mother, you used to be able to buy a single glove.

“Why would you buy one glove?”

“Because you lost one glove,” she said.

This struck me as such a sensible arrangement that for years I assumed it was still possible.

After she died I went down to the basement to clear her desk. Her replacement, a man named Paul, had already put most of her things in a copier-paper box. He made a point of showing me that he hadn’t thrown away the yogurt spoon in the drawer.

“I didn’t know what was personal,” he said.

“It’s all personal now,” I said, which sounded unkind, though I hadn’t meant it that way. I put the spoon in my coat pocket.

Paul asked whether I wanted to hear anything while I was there. I gave him the address of the house where I’d grown up. It had been demolished to make room for a building with balconies too narrow for chairs.

“Which room?”

“The kitchen.”

“We have morning or evening.”

I chose evening.

The listening booth was smaller than I remembered. Someone had replaced the old swivel chair with a stackable plastic one, and the headphones had a fresh foam cover. I could see Paul through the glass, looking studiously at his computer.

For a while there was only the refrigerator. Then came the click of a burner trying to catch, a drawer opening against a person’s hip, my mother saying, “Well, use the big one, then.”

I took off the headphones.

There was no particular tenderness in the way she said it. She was a little annoyed. That was the problem. All week people had been telling me how patient she was, and here, at last, was somebody who had actually known her.

I put the headphones back on.

A pot struck the sink. Water ran. Someone in the next room was practicing the first seven notes of “Good King Wenceslas” on a recorder. It had to be me. I waited for my mother to tell me to stop. Instead, she sang the eighth note. I started over and she did it again. The third time, she came in early and we both laughed.

I didn’t remember this. I remembered hating the recorder. I remembered that the cleaning rod had a slot in one end, like the eye of a needle, and that I’d never been able to get the cloth through it. If you’d asked me that morning whether my mother ever sang, I’d have said only in the car, and only when she thought I was asleep.

When I came out of the booth, Paul offered to make me a copy. I imagined listening to it in my own kitchen. I imagined stopping it just before we laughed, to see if I could catch what was funny.

“Not today,” I said.

I took the box upstairs. At the tax counter a woman was arguing that her house had never had a garage. The clerk turned his screen to show her a photograph of the garage, and she peered at it for a good long time.

“Oh,” she said finally. “That’s where he kept the boat.”

Outside, it had started to rain. The copier-paper box had handholds that let the rain in, so I ducked beneath the awning of a hardware store and shifted my mother’s things into my canvas grocery bag. There was less than I’d thought: a cardigan, some aspirin, three photographs, a book of crossword puzzles with all the long answers filled in. She’d left the short ones for later, or perhaps she just didn’t like them.

A boy came out of the hardware store holding a key by its bright new teeth. His father told him to put it in his pocket. He did, then took it out again.

“Can we try it as soon as we get home?”

“How else are we going to get in?”

The boy considered this. Then he ran a little way ahead into the rain, holding the key out flat on his palm.

I went into the hardware store. I needed nothing, but I wasn’t ready to take the bus. A woman behind the counter asked what she could do for me, and I found myself holding up the spoon.

“Could you bend this back?”

The handle was crooked. I’d noticed it when Paul took it from the drawer, but not until I asked did it occur to me that my mother might have bent it on purpose. She had arthritis. There might have been a way she liked to hold it.

“Actually,” I said. “Leave it.”

The woman handed it back. On my way out I saw a display of work gloves, clipped together in pairs. I asked if she ever sold just one.

“Which hand?”

I hadn’t expected to get that far.

“Left,” I said.

She went into the back and returned with a red glove, a little dusty at the cuff.

“What happened to the right?”

“Man bought it in November.”

She charged me half the price of a pair. I put the glove on to carry the bag home. By the time I reached my stop, I’d worked out that the spoon fit the left hand better than the right, if you held it with your thumb along the bend. I ate my yogurt that way the next morning. It took a while.

The first thing my mother put in the museum was a potato masher.

She wrote the label on the back of a gas bill: *Bent on the occasion of your father trying to open the bathroom window.*

“Why was he opening it with a potato masher?”

“The latch was stuck.”

“Why didn’t he use a screwdriver?”

“He had a potato masher.”

The museum occupied the narrow shelf above the washing machine. There was room for perhaps eleven objects, less if one of them was a hat. My mother had been given six months to live and had responded, in part, by becoming very particular about which nouns she used. The shelf was a museum. Her morphine was Tuesday. The hospice nurse, whose name was actually Grace, she called Grace, because, she said, you couldn’t improve on everything.

I told my brother about the museum on the phone.

“Is she doing that thing where she wants us to ask about Dad?”

I looked at the masher. My father had left when I was twelve. For a while he sent birthday cards with the ages of much younger children printed on them, altering the numbers in pen. On my sixteenth birthday I got a card that said *You’re 6!* with a slender blue one squeezed in.

“I think she wants us to ask about the masher,” I said.

The second exhibit was a sandstone-colored button, which my mother attributed to “one of those coats I hated but wore for twenty years.” The third was a set of keys she had found in a pear tree in 1989. She’d put a notice in the post office. A man had called to ask how high up they’d been. When she told him, he said they couldn’t be his.

“Did you ask why?”

“It was his dime,” she said. “I figured he’d tell me if he wanted to.”

On Thursday I brought a shoebox down from the attic. It contained our school pictures, my grandmother’s wedding license, and a blue ribbon my mother had won for a sponge cake at the county fair. I laid the ribbon on the shelf while she supervised from a folding chair.

“Not that,” she said.

“Why not?”

“It already says what it is.”

I turned it over. On the back, in pencil, someone had written *slight dip in center*. I showed her.

“Oh,” she said. “In that case.”

My brother arrived in late October with a carry-on bag and a paper sack of apples. He stood in the laundry room reading the labels. Then he picked up the potato masher and slid his thumb along the crooked handle.

“I did this,” he said.

My mother opened one eye. “Did you?”

“Dad was holding it. I stood on it.”

“What on earth for?”

“He told me to.”

He lowered one foot onto the base of the laundry hamper to show us how he’d done it. There was something so familiar about the care he took demonstrating this stupid thing that I suddenly wanted to be twelve again, to have the old privilege of telling him nobody cared. Instead I asked him if the window had opened.

“Oh, sure,” he said. “We broke it.”

My mother laughed until Grace had to come see what was going on. Later I asked if she wanted me to change the label.

“Put his name on it,” she said. “Don’t take your father’s off.”

My brother stayed. He made applesauce, which neither of us knew she disliked until she was too tired to be polite. We ate it ourselves, cold, standing in front of the refrigerator. On the last night there was a load of towels in the dryer. Every so often a metal zipper struck the drum. I kept thinking I ought to get up and stop it. I didn’t want to let go of her hand, and I didn’t want to ask my brother to let go of the other one.

In January we emptied the house. My brother took the masher. I took the keys. We left the folding chair out by the curb. A woman walking a spaniel sat in it while she waited for the dog to finish smelling the hedge. When I went out to tell her she could have the chair, she said she didn’t need it, but would I mind if she sat a little longer?

I said no. Then I went back inside and got the other chair, the good one we’d been meaning to sell.

We sat there in our coats. The dog finished with the hedge and came to inspect my boots. I had the keys in my pocket. They were on the kind of ring you have to pry apart with a thumbnail, and there was a little brass key among them that looked as though it had opened a diary or a cashbox.

I told her about the pear tree.

“How high up?” she asked.

Of course I didn’t know. It was the one part of the story I’d never thought to ask about.

“High enough that a man ruled himself out,” I said.

The woman considered this. “I lost a set of keys once,” she said, “and my husband said, ‘Where did you have them last?’ and I said, ‘If I knew that, Dennis, I wouldn’t have brought it up.’”

The dog sat on my foot. I could feel his warmth through the boot, which was surprising, as it was a very good boot.

“Did you find them?” I asked.

“Dennis did. In his coat.”

Across the street someone was bringing in the bins. The woman loosened the leash a little, and the dog settled more of his weight against my ankle. I’d spent the morning deciding what to do with the last of my mother’s things. There was still a broom in the kitchen, and a saucepan of water I’d put on for tea before remembering I’d packed the cups. In a minute I would go back in and turn off the stove. For now I asked her whether Dennis had had the decency to look embarrassed.

The salvage man said he could take the kitchen door, but not on its own. He bought by the room. If we wanted him to take the door, he’d take the cupboards, the sink, the taps, and the strip of copper pipe that ran behind the stove.

“How much?” my sister asked.

He named a figure.

“No,” she said. “How much for you to leave the room and just take the door?”

He looked at her for a moment. He had already been to seven houses on our road. By Friday there would be nobody left on it. I imagine he was tired of being asked to do things that fell somewhere between a favor and a transaction.

“I can lend you a screwdriver,” he said.

After he left, Ruth made coffee in the saucepan. The kettle had gone in a box marked BATHROOM, for reasons neither of us could reconstruct. We drank standing up. The kitchen table was already in my garage, where it had acquired one short leg. On the kitchen floor it had never wobbled.

“You don’t even have to hang it,” she said. “You could put it behind something.”

“Behind what?”

“The table.”

Our father had marked our heights on the door in pencil. The earliest marks were horizontal, with our initials and the dates written so small you had to put your face right up to the wood. Later he got a ballpoint pen and his handwriting grew enormous. At sixteen I was five foot nine, according to the door. The nurse at my last physical had put me at five eight and a quarter. I’d considered telling her that we had documentary evidence.

Ruth fetched the screwdriver. The screws had been painted over so many times that there was nowhere to put its tip.

“Knife,” she said.

“Bathroom box.”

She laughed, then stopped, as if I’d interrupted her.

The company building the reservoir had given us a brochure that showed the valley in blue. You could still see the roads underneath, thin and gray, including the spur to our house. Ruth had asked the company’s representative why they’d left the roads on the map.

“So you can see where you are,” he said.

She put her finger on the bend above our driveway. “I know where I am.”

He was a young man with a wedding ring that seemed too big for him. He looked down at the brochure as though the answer to her objection might have been printed in a corner he hadn’t read. Finally he said, “My dad would hate this.” It was the only thing he said all afternoon that Ruth didn’t argue with.

I found a loose utility blade on the windowsill and scraped the paint from the top screw. The blade slipped and opened the pad of my thumb. Ruth handed me a coffee filter to wrap it in. We’d packed the bandages, but there were sixty coffee filters.

“You never wanted this door till yesterday,” I said.

“Yes, I did.”

“You could have said.”

“I did. At Christmas.”

At Christmas she’d said somebody should do something about the door. I’d thought she meant it was sticking.

She scraped at the lower hinge while I held my thumb. From where I stood I could see how close the last two marks were. I remembered that measurement. I’d come home from my first semester at college and Ruth had made me take off my shoes. She had not grown since August, but she suspected I had got shorter, and wanted it on the record. Dad had been frying onions. He’d let her do the measuring and then, without taking his eyes off the pan, told her where to find his pen.

“Do you want me to bring it to your place?” I asked.

“No,” she said.

We listened to a truck go by. You could tell, by then, which trucks were going to stop at a house and which were taking the road all the way to the works. There were only two houses left with anything in them.

“I thought you wanted it,” she said.

I looked down at her. She was still crouched by the hinge, making small, patient turns with the blade. I’d spent the week thinking she was giving me one more thing to carry. It hadn’t occurred to me that she might be doing something for me in a way that let me complain about it.

“I think I do,” I said.

“Well, hold it, then. This one’s coming out.”

With the two top screws gone the door leaned into my arms. It was much heavier than I’d expected, though I’d opened it thousands of times. I called to Ruth to wait. I needed to get my knee under it. She waited.

We took it out through the front of the house. At the porch she went first and told me when the step was coming. We rested the door across the bed of my truck while I looked for something to pad it with. Ruth took off her sweatshirt and folded it under the end with the writing. The other end could rattle all it liked, she said. There was nothing on it but a boot print, and that was probably mine.

Before we left I went back for the saucepan. From the front hall I could see clear through the kitchen to the window. A strip of late sun fell across the place where the table used to stand. There was a pale square on the floor beneath it, with four dark dents at the corners. I stood there trying to decide which dent had held the short leg. I could have figured it out by walking around to the other side, but Ruth honked, and I took the saucepan off the stove and went.

At my house we set the door down on the garage floor and stood the table on it. All four legs met the wood. Ruth pushed down on a corner, then another. Neither of us could make it rock.

“Of course,” she said, though neither of us knew why.

On the last Thursday of every month, the city sold the things people had left on buses. Umbrellas went for a dollar, bicycles for twenty, and musical instruments for whatever the auctioneer thought he could get before somebody asked him to demonstrate one.

My mother went for the gloves. She had only one hand, and the city sold single gloves by the bag.

“Somewhere there’s a woman making out like a bandit on the lefts,” she told me. “I hope she has my taste.”

She took the bus to the auction even after I bought a car. She said it improved her odds of finding something good if she traveled by the method through which it had been lost. I pointed out that she had once found a perfectly good bread machine on the curb without first spending the afternoon on the curb herself.

“You don’t remember everything I did when you were at school,” she said.

The winter she stopped going, I went in her place. I told myself I was looking for a glove with a long cuff, because her coat sleeve rode up when she reached for the kettle. What I wanted, though I wouldn't have said so then, was to go somewhere she was expected.

The auctioneer looked past me.

“Your mother coming?”

“Not today.”

He moved a folding chair out from behind his table. It was the only one with a cushion.

I bought a bag of gloves and, for reasons I couldn’t explain at the time, a green suitcase. It had one wheel and a strip of masking tape across the handle. Somebody had written *WEDNESDAY* on the tape in blue pen.

Inside was a red sweater, a toiletry bag containing seven hotel soaps, and a jar of soil wrapped in a tea towel. There was also a photograph of a woman kneeling beside a newly planted tree. She had one hand on the trunk, not holding it upright so much as checking whether it could stand on its own. On the back was a phone number.

I called from the parking lot.

“Is the jar broken?” the woman asked.

I told her it wasn’t.

“Good,” she said. “You can keep the rest.”

Then, after a pause: “Actually, how big are you?”

I told her I was five foot eleven.

“The sweater won’t fit you. I don’t know why I said you could keep it.”

We agreed to meet at the end of the number six line, where there was a bakery with a bench in the window. I brought the whole suitcase. She arrived with a shopping trolley and a paper bag warm enough to fog her glasses when she opened it.

We ate cheese pastries off napkins. She examined the wheel that wasn’t there.

“That came off before the bus,” she said. “I’d like you to know I didn’t abandon it for that.”

“Why did you?”

“I got off to help a man with his trolley. By the time we got him turned round, the driver had gone.” She brushed a flake of pastry onto her napkin and folded it in. “The man said I should’ve let him manage. Which was true, but he could’ve waited a minute to say it.”

I gave her the jar. She took it out of the towel and turned it over to look at the bottom, the way you would with a jar of jam you suspected might be nearly finished.

“My sister was selling her house,” she said. “I went up to help. We took a bit of the garden each.”

I asked if it was from under the tree.

“What tree?”

I showed her the photograph.

“Oh, that’s the neighbor,” she said. “My sister took the picture because she thought the tree was too close to the drain.”

She put the photograph in her coat pocket anyway.

At home I tipped the gloves onto the kitchen table. Nearly all of them were lefts. There was one good right, made of brown leather, with a lining that came out when I pulled my fingers free. I pushed it back in with the handle of a wooden spoon.

My mother was asleep in her chair. On the floor beside her was the television remote, which she had lately taken to dropping and pretending she hadn’t wanted. I put it on the arm of the chair. She opened her eyes.

“How much did you spend?”

“Four dollars.”

“How much did you spend on things you went there for?”

“One dollar.”

She considered this and nodded. I showed her the glove. She tried it on, tugging at the cuff with her teeth. It reached almost halfway to her elbow.

“Too nice for the bus,” she said.

A week later, she asked me to take her out. She wore the glove. I brought the car round, but she was already standing at the bus stop, so I parked again and went to wait with her.

When the number six came, she let it go.

“Wasn’t that ours?” I asked.

“I haven’t decided.”

It was cold enough that I kept moving my toes inside my shoes. Across the street, someone was trying to carry a mirror out of a narrow shop door. A man on the pavement stopped to help. For a while the mirror reflected only brick; then they tilted it, and there we were on the other side of the road, my mother in her good glove and me with my shoulders up around my ears. I’d been standing half a pace behind her. In the mirror it looked as though I were waiting in a very short queue.

I moved up beside her.

“Do you want to go somewhere,” I asked, “or did you just want to come out?”

“I wanted to see if I could still get down the front steps.”

“You did.”

“Yes,” she said. “Then I wanted to see if you’d leave the car.”

The next bus came. She raised her gloved hand. When the doors opened, she asked the driver where he was going, although we could both read the sign. He told her. She looked at me to see if I was coming.

The woman from the sound archive asked us to turn off the refrigerator.

“How long?” my father said.

“Three minutes.”

“It takes longer than that to get cold again.”

She looked at me. I unplugged it.

Our house was one of forty-six being knocked down for the new flood channel. The county had offered each household a truck, six months’ storage, and a recording of one room. My father had turned down the truck because he owned a truck, turned down the storage because he didn’t believe it would be dry, and accepted the recording because he wanted to see how anybody could make a recording of a room with nobody talking in it.

The woman’s name was Ruth. She had a small microphone with a fur cover. My father asked if she had to brush it.

“Sometimes,” she said, and showed him the comb.

He liked her after that.

We had chosen the kitchen. Or rather, I had written *kitchen* on the form while my father was in the garage finding a pen. I’d spent the previous two weekends packing that room. At the back of the junk drawer I’d found eleven keys, some gray birthday candles, and a note in my own childhood handwriting that said PLEASE BUY PEARS. On the reverse, my father had written a tire size. I put it in the box with the cutlery rather than try to decide whose rubbish it was.

Ruth set up the microphone by the bread bin. She told us we could stay as long as we sat still.

“What if a car goes by?” my father asked.

“Then we’ll have the car.”

“What if the phone rings?”

“Does it often?”

“Not anymore,” he said.

Ruth started the recorder.

For the first few seconds I could only hear my own breathing. Then there was a tick above the stove, where the clock had been. My father had taken it down that morning. I looked up anyway; there was a round patch of clean wall and, through the wall, a small intermittent ticking I’d apparently been giving the clock credit for all my life.

A car went by.

My father sat with his hands flat on his knees. At seventy-four he still had the forearms of somebody who could carry a washing machine with one other man. He had been offered a ground-floor apartment near a bakery. He’d taken it, then complained that the bedroom window looked onto the bakery’s loading bay. When I pointed out that the trucks would come early, he said he knew when trucks came. He’d driven one for thirty-eight years.

His route used to bring him home at four in the morning. When I was little I would wake to the hinge on the back door, then the kettle, then the click of the teaspoon he set down on the counter. Some mornings I padded out and sat with him. He let me dunk toast in his tea, although he objected to the crumbs.

When I was twelve I began staying in bed. I could hear the hinge, the kettle, the teaspoon, and sometimes his steps coming as far as my door. He never knocked. At the time I thought this was evidence that we understood each other.

Somewhere in the second minute my father’s chair creaked. His eyes went to Ruth. She shook her head a little to say it was fine.

When the three minutes were up, she put headphones on him first. I watched him listen. Halfway through, he lifted one ear cup.

“Is that me?”

“The chair?” Ruth said. “Yes.”

“No, before.”

She backed up the recording. He listened again, then handed me the headphones.

At first there was just the soft, steady sound of the room. Then I heard myself take two short breaths close together, almost a sniff.

“You used to do that,” he said. “Before you came out.”

I took off the headphones. “You could hear me from the kitchen?”

“Not from the kitchen.”

Ruth began winding a cable around her hand.

“I thought you were asleep most of the time,” my father said. “But then I’d hear that and put another piece of bread in.”

I tried to remember whether, on the mornings I’d stayed in bed, he’d come to my door before or after he made his toast. I could remember the stripe of light under the door, and how I used to move one foot into it and take it out again.

“Did you eat both pieces?” I asked.

“Usually.”

Ruth gave us a card with a link on it. My father turned it over, looking for the rest of the instructions, and I told him I’d put the file on his phone. He walked her out to her car. Through the window I saw him stop her before she drove off. He had remembered the comb, which she’d left next to the bread bin.

I plugged the refrigerator back in. It shuddered and settled into a hum so familiar I hadn’t noticed it was gone.

My father came in and asked if I was staying for lunch. I’d said earlier that I couldn’t. I had a call at one, and if I left now I could make it from my own desk, with the door shut and all my papers where I wanted them. I texted to ask if we could do it at two.

“There’s not much,” he said, looking in the refrigerator we’d spent the week emptying. “I could make toast.”

I took two plates out of the box. He put the bread in and pushed down the lever. Before the toast came up he pushed it down a second time, because it was an old toaster and that was what you had to do. I’d forgotten. I stood there while he did it, holding the plates, though there was a clear place on the counter where I could have put them down.

samples.result:
My mother left me half a cow.

“The back half,” my brother said.

The lawyer took his glasses off. “An undivided interest in the whole animal.”

“That seems worse,” I said.

My brother had driven four hours to the lawyer’s office with a hard-boiled egg in his shirt pocket. Halfway through the will he had taken it out and begun peeling it into his hand. This was the first time we’d been in a room together in six years, and I’d forgotten how much I enjoyed watching him make other people uncomfortable.

The cow’s name was Linda. She lived on twelve acres that my mother had left, in their entirety, to a woman named Pam.

“Who is Pam?” I asked.

“Her wife,” my brother said.

The lawyer put his glasses back on. Apparently he had been waiting to see which of us would tell me.

* * *

Pam was sitting on an overturned bucket when we pulled up. Linda stood beside her, licking a broom. There were flecks of blue paint on Linda’s tongue.

“Your mother said you’d both come if there was a cow involved,” Pam said.

“I would have come for other reasons,” I said.

Pam gave me a little nod, as if I’d told her which way I’d driven.

She went inside to make coffee. My brother took a pair of fence pliers from the bed of his truck and walked away. I followed him because I didn’t know where else to go.

At the far end of the pasture he slipped the jaws of the pliers under a staple and rocked it out of a post. He caught it as it fell and put it in his pocket.

“Did you go to the wedding?”

“Yes.”

“Did you have cake?”

He looked at me.

“I don’t know why I asked that.”

“Lemon,” he said.

He handed me the pliers and showed me how to get the next staple. I pulled instead of rocking and the whole post shuddered.

“She had your number,” he said.

“I know.”

“You had hers.”

“I know.”

“You can rock it harder than that.”

We got nine staples out before Pam called us in. My brother counted them onto the porch railing, then counted them again. When he was seven he’d stepped on a roofing nail and had to get a shot. I remembered holding his shoe in the emergency room. Our mother kept asking me to put it down, and I wouldn’t. I’d been charged with watching him and I wanted to be able to hand him back every part of himself she’d given me.

* * *

In the kitchen there were four different kinds of mustard in the refrigerator door. My mother had always said she couldn’t taste the difference between mustards. I wondered whether she’d lied to save money, or whether Pam liked mustard and my mother had enjoyed bringing home one she hadn’t tried.

Pam was on the phone rescheduling a dentist appointment. She kept saying “Tuesday” and the person on the other end kept offering her Thursdays. I sat at the table and listened. There was no reason the person on the other end should know anything had happened.

When she hung up, Pam said, “I’d like to keep Linda.”

“You can have my half,” I said.

“Mine too,” my brother said.

“All right. I thought I might have to buy you out. I looked up what a cow costs and it turns out everybody thinks their cow is exceptional.”

“Is Linda?” I asked.

“No. She’s a pretty good cow.”

Pam poured the coffee. Then she said, “I don’t actually think she knew you’d come. She wanted you to. I made it sound like she was sure.”

I looked down at the table. It was the one we’d had growing up, with a pale ring where my brother had set a saucepan of hot oil while trying to make doughnuts. He’d made one doughnut and we’d eaten it standing over the saucepan, tearing off pieces too hot to hold.

“Did she tell you why we stopped talking?” I asked.

“She said you two had a fight about a coat.”

“It was a coat,” I said. “There’s not going to be a version where it isn’t a coat.”

Pam waited. She didn’t ask about the coat. After a while I told her anyway.

* * *

It was dark when we left. My brother drove ahead of me for a while, until he took the north ramp and I took the south. I’d made it to the next exit when he called.

“Did you see where I put those staples?” he asked.

“On the porch rail.”

“Right.”

Neither of us hung up. The road was freshly paved and so smooth I could hear him flick his turn signal on. I pictured him holding the phone to his ear and told him to put me on speaker.

“You are on speaker,” he said. “I have a nicer truck than you remember.”

Then he asked what I was doing Tuesday.

“Working.”

“After work.”

“Probably eating.”

“Okay,” he said. “I could do that.”

He lived four hours from the lawyer’s office, but only forty minutes from me. I had known that, more or less. I’d never looked up the route.

At the next light I asked if he still made doughnuts.

“I never made doughnuts,” he said.

“You made one.”

“There was another one. You went to bed.”

This bothered me all the way to my turn. I’d been telling the story of that doughnut for years. The way I told it, we’d been too impatient to wait for a second one, which was true of me, anyway.

“Was it any better?” I asked.

“The second one?”

“Yeah.”

He thought about it. “I let the oil get hotter. It puffed up like it was supposed to.”

I turned onto my street. Somebody had put their trash out a day early and three other houses had followed suit, including mine. I pulled into the driveway and left the engine running.

“How hot?” I asked.

“I don’t remember,” he said. “We can look it up.”

samples.result:
The first time my mother called to ask how to make rice, I gave her instructions. The second time, I understood that she wanted me to come over.

She had made rice for forty years in a pot with a dent in the lid. On the phone she said, “Is it two cups of water?” and I said, “I’ll be there at six.”

When I arrived, there were potatoes in the oven.

“I changed my mind,” she said.

My father had been dead for seven weeks. His coat was still on the hook by the back door, but she had canceled his subscription to a woodworking magazine the day after the funeral. She had always hated that magazine. He used to leave it open on the kitchen table to photographs of rooms with no evidence of anyone eating in them.

“He got six more issues on the renewal,” she told me. “I asked for the money back.”

“Did they give it to you?”

“They gave me six more issues.”

After dinner she asked if I wanted the dining-room table. I said I didn’t have room. She asked if I wanted the good scissors. I said she might still need the good scissors.

“I know,” she said. “I wanted to see what you’d say.”

In the town where I grew up, there was a man who sharpened knives out of a van. You heard his bell from inside the house and ran out carrying whatever had disappointed you lately. The knife man would take the blade between his fingers and look down its length, giving it the grave, particular attention that, as a child, I believed adults could have whenever they wanted.

My mother wanted to know if he still came around. The kitchen shears had got so bad she was opening bags of frozen peas with her teeth.

I took out my phone.

“Not now,” she said. “I just wondered.”

On the way home I stopped for gas and looked him up anyway. I found a photograph of his van on a local history page. In the comments, a woman remembered that he’d sharpened her ice skates. A man remembered that he wouldn’t sharpen ice skates, not even if you asked twice. No one seemed to know his name.

The next Tuesday, I bought my mother new kitchen shears. She snipped the air a few times and said they were very nice. Then she showed me that the old ones had a notch for cracking walnuts. The new ones didn’t.

“When did you last crack a walnut?” I asked.

She opened a drawer and took out a walnut.

It was the first time I’d heard her laugh since the funeral. She leaned against the counter and laughed while I stood there holding the walnut. After a while she stopped, looked at me, and started again.

“Your father bought a pound of them at Christmas,” she said. “He thought the squirrel might like one.”

“Did it?”

“He gave it the pound.”

She put the walnut back in the drawer. I put the new shears in beside it. Over dinner she told me the squirrel had buried several of the walnuts in the window box. My father had dug one up by accident when he went to plant the geraniums. He brought it inside to show her. The soil was still cold that day, she said. She remembered because he had put his hand on the back of her neck.

By November, I was going over on Tuesdays whether she called or not. She sometimes cooked and sometimes left a note on the door telling me to meet her at the diner. Once I found her in the driveway with my father’s coat on, trying to decide whether there was enough light left to wash the car. I said we could do it Saturday. She said there would be light on Saturday whether we washed the car or not, and handed me the hose.

To reach the middle of the roof, I stood on the sill with the driver’s door open. Water ran down my sleeve, all the way to my elbow. My mother told me to mind the upholstery. It occurred to me that my father must have managed to get the middle of the roof without opening the door. I couldn’t picture how. For years I’d assumed there would come a day when I’d run out of things I didn’t know about him.

After we dried the car, she asked if I wanted to stay for dinner. I’d been about to ask her the same thing, although it was her house.

We made rice. She measured the water in a cup printed with an advertisement for a bank that didn’t exist anymore. While we waited she took the scissors from the drawer and tried the walnut. The shell slipped out of the notch and rolled under the refrigerator.

“Leave it,” she said.

I was already on my knees. There was a surprising amount of room under there. I found a twist tie, two nickels, and one of the little white buttons my father used to lose from his shirts. I put everything on the table, including the walnut.

My mother picked up the button. “That’s from my green blouse,” she said.

She went upstairs to get it. I could hear her opening and shutting drawers. The rice began to boil, and the dented lid rattled in its familiar, uneven way. I turned down the burner. I had never noticed before how low you could turn it and still have it do what it needed to do.

When she came back, the blouse was on a hanger. She laid it out beside our plates. There was a loose white thread where the button had been, and she asked me to hold it up to the light while she threaded a needle. It took her three tries. I kept thinking I should offer to do it, but she had nearly got it the second time and I wanted to see her get it. When she did, she pulled the thread through with both hands and told me to go ahead and eat. I brought my plate over and sat beside her.

samples.result:
On the last day of the municipal sound archive, a woman came in asking for the noise a particular swimming pool made at four in the afternoon.

“Underwater or above?” I asked.

She set her bag on the counter. “You have both?”

“We have underwater at four-oh-six. Above, there’s a gap between three-fifty and four-twenty. The lifeguard taped over it with his band.”

“They any good?”

“They get better.”

She thought about this. “Underwater, then.”

I brought out the headphones with the intact foam and found the file. The pool had closed twenty-three years earlier. I knew the recording well enough to identify the slap of the vacuum hose against the ladder and the little descending roar of someone doing a cannonball. At the end, the man holding the microphone came up for air and said, very distinctly, “Cold where the sun isn’t.”

The woman listened twice.

“Can I take it home?”

I glanced at the notice taped to the counter. We’d been told not to distribute material while the council decided what to do with the collection. The council had given itself six months to decide and us until five o’clock to leave the building.

“Have you got your phone?” I asked.

She took a blue flash drive from her bag instead. It was attached to an enormous brass key.

“Swimming pool key,” she said when she saw me looking. “They never asked for it back.”

“You worked there?”

“I lived there. My dad was the caretaker. There was a flat behind the changing rooms.” She put a finger on the key, still plugged into my computer. “Does the person holding the microphone say anything else?”

I played her the beginning, where the man cleared his throat. Then I found the above-water recording from three-forty, in which he asked somebody named Gary whether the lead would reach.

“Dad,” she said, fondly and with some exasperation, as if he’d just come in wearing shoes she’d asked him to throw away.

I made her a folder. While the files copied, she told me the flat had no windows on the pool side, for privacy, but if you sat on the kitchen counter with your feet in the sink you could look through a vent and see a little square of water. She’d done her homework there in summer until her father caught her and made her scrub the heel marks off the draining board.

“I thought we were poor,” she said. “Well, we were. But imagine getting home from school and having a pool.”

I asked if she wanted the lifeguard’s band too.

“Absolutely not,” she said. “That was Gary.”

After she left, I ate my lunch on a packing crate. Downstairs, someone dragged a desk across the tile in short, furious installments. There was still half a roll of red stickers on my desk, which we were supposed to put on things that belonged to the council. I stuck one to my apple.

At three, my brother called. He wanted to know if I’d changed my mind about the piano.

Our mother had been dead for nine weeks. In that time we’d found homes for seven dining chairs, an exercise bicycle, and a freezer full of plums. The piano was the only thing we both wanted and neither could take.

“The school can collect it Tuesday,” he said.

“I know.”

“They’ve got a man with a ramp.”

“You told me.”

I could hear him turning the pages of something. He always found a little job for his hands when a conversation wasn’t going well.

“Do you remember her playing it?” I asked.

“Of course I do.”

“When?”

The pages stopped. After a while he said, “When she was waiting for the potatoes.”

That was right. She played standing up, just the right hand, for as long as it took the pot to boil. Mostly songs from commercials. Once, when the plumber was in, she played the first eight bars of something grand and difficult, and I realized she knew exactly how much music she was withholding from us.

“Let the school have it,” I said.

My brother said okay, but neither of us hung up. Then he asked if I wanted the plums. I said I’d already taken four bags. He said that wasn’t an answer.

At four-forty, the woman with the pool key came back. She had listened to the recording in her car and wanted to correct something.

“It isn’t ‘cold where the sun isn’t,’” she said. “It’s ‘hold where the sun hits.’ He’s telling Gary where to stand with the cable. There was one dry patch by the rail.”

I played it through the little speakers on the counter. She leaned in. Hold where the sun hits. I could hear it now, although if I looked at my original notes, I could still hear the cold.

“Do you want me to change the transcript?”

She took a while to answer. Outside, the man who came to lock up was trying his keys in the bicycle shed. He had a bicycle of his own, a yellow one, which meant he had to lock the shed, wheel his bike to the front, lean it against the wall, lock the building, and then tuck his trouser cuff into his sock before he could go home. I’d watched him do it every weekday for eleven years.

“Put both,” she said.

So I did. I saved the file, shut the computer down, and carried my apple and the last of my things outside. At the bicycle shed, I asked the man if I could hold his bike while he locked the door. He looked surprised, then passed it to me by the saddle.

The front wheel swung round and rested against my shin. There was a bell on the handlebars, its chrome worn dull in the exact place his thumb would reach it. I’d never heard it ring. I kept my hands where they were and waited for him to finish.

samples.result:
The first thing Mara’s father forgot was how to make a small pot of coffee. He still knew how to make a large one. Every morning he filled the machine to twelve cups, drank one and a half, and poured the rest into a succession of unsuitable containers. When Mara came on Sundays, there was coffee in the pickle jar, the gravy boat, and the blue vase her mother had won at a church raffle.

“You could pour it down the sink,” she said.

“I could pour your coffee down the sink,” he said, and handed her a mug.

Across the street, the city was replacing a water main. The crew arrived at seven and ate lunch at eleven fifteen, sitting along the low wall in front of the house. One Sunday Mara found her father counting them from the living room.

“Five,” he said.

“Six. There’s a man in the truck.”

“He brings his own.”

The next day she called at eleven twenty and heard unfamiliar voices in the kitchen. Her father said he couldn’t talk. He was looking for the sugar bowl.

By Thursday there was a coffee station on the front porch: mugs, sugar, a spoon on a saucer, and a handwritten sign that said PLEASE LEAVE THE SPOON. The crew left the spoon. They also left the mugs, although not always the right mugs. A red one that said WORLD’S OKAYEST DAD appeared among the good china. Mara took it inside, washed it, and put it back out.

The woman who drove the excavator was named Ruth. She had a gold front tooth and a son who sold insurance in Ohio. Mara knew these things because her father told her, and then told her again. When Mara finally met Ruth, she was surprised to find her younger than herself.

“He says you play piano,” Ruth said.

“I used to.”

“He said you’d say that.”

Mara had been trying to persuade her father to move. There was an apartment available near her, on the ground floor, with a grocery store close enough to walk to. She had taken pictures of the rooms and put them in an envelope. He kept the envelope under the short leg of the kitchen table. It was precisely the right thickness.

In October the crew reached the end of the block. They filled in the trench, laid a temporary strip of asphalt, and took away the portable toilet. On their last morning Ruth brought a cake. She had ordered it from a supermarket and asked for THANKS, FRANK, but the decorator had written THANK FRANK. Her father said it was a good idea, and somebody ought to.

Mara came on Monday instead of Sunday that week. At eleven ten, her father carried the pot out to the porch.

“They finished,” she said.

“I know.”

He set out three mugs. She watched him go back for the other two.

It was cold enough that she could see the steam. On the new asphalt someone had chalked a number and drawn a long arrow toward the curb. She thought it would be gone by the next rain, but it stayed there all winter.

No one came for coffee that Monday. At eleven forty her father took in the mugs, and she poured the coffee down the sink. Then he got out the bread and made her a sandwich. It was only when she lifted the top slice that she saw he’d cut the cheese into six little squares, arranged in two rows, the way he had when she was a child and refused to eat a slice whole. She’d forgotten about that. She put the bread back and ate the sandwich.

He moved in March. He was the one who brought it up. The basement stairs were getting to be a nuisance, he said, and someone had built them too steep. He had built them himself in 1978. Mara told him the apartment was still available. It wasn’t, but by evening she’d found another one in the same building, on the second floor, across from the laundry room. It cost eighty dollars a month more and had a better kitchen.

While they packed, he wanted to know what would happen to the spoon.

“We’ll take it,” Mara said.

“It’s not ours.”

She turned it over. The handle was stamped with the name of a hotel that had burned down before she was born.

“Where’d you get it?”

“Your mother.”

This seemed, to both of them, to settle the matter.

The first Sunday in the apartment, Mara brought bagels. Her father had made a large pot of coffee. He poured her a cup and asked whether she’d had trouble finding him.

“No,” she said, although she had gone automatically to the old house. She had pulled up in front and turned off the engine. Someone had already taken down the porch light, leaving two capped wires sticking out of the siding. The new owners were going to paint.

Across the hall a dryer stopped. A moment later it started again.

“Those people have been in there all morning,” her father said.

“Maybe their dryer broke.”

“I meant different people.”

He took a drink. Mara unwrapped the bagels. She had brought two kinds of cream cheese but no knife, and he opened a drawer and found the spoon.

For a while they ate without talking. Then a woman backed out of the laundry room, dragging a basket with a broken handle. Mara held the door for her. The woman thanked her and went three doors down, where a child opened up and immediately asked if his sheets were dry.

Mara turned back. Her father was at the counter with the coffee pot in his hand. She thought he meant to empty it and moved aside to give him the sink.

“Could you see if she takes milk?” he said.

By the time Mara reached the woman’s door, it had closed. She could hear the child inside, explaining something at great length. She stood there with her hand raised and waited for him to finish. Then she knocked.

samples.result:
The city kept its lost sounds in the basement of the public library. You could go down on a Tuesday and ask for the click your old refrigerator made just before the motor came on. If you filled out a green slip and could approximate the click with your tongue, the clerk would take you to a listening booth.

You weren’t allowed to take the sound home. People had tried.

Mara worked the desk on Tuesdays. Most of her customers were after voices, which the city did not collect. She explained this so often she had stopped trying to make it sound kind.

“We might have the chair he sat in,” she would say. “If it made a noise.”

One afternoon a girl in a bicycle helmet came in with a manila envelope under her arm.

“I lost the sound of a bridge,” she said.

“Which bridge?”

“The footbridge on Mercer. Before they fixed it.”

Mara found the entry: *Mercer footbridge, loose deck board, east end. Two reports of tripping. Removed May 6.* She fetched the sound and set it playing in the booth.

The girl listened three times. The board gave a flat wooden clap, followed by a smaller one as it settled. On the third play the girl put her forehead against the glass.

“Is that it?” Mara asked when she came out.

“Yes. Can I bring my brother?”

“Of course.”

“Can we come after six?”

“We close at five.”

The girl considered this. “He won’t get off the bridge until dark.”

Mara waited for an explanation, but the girl was already sliding the envelope toward her. Inside was a petition with twelve signatures. At the top, in pencil, someone had written: *Please put the noise back.*

The brother was nine. He was blind. Until May 6, he had crossed the footbridge alone on his way home from school. The loose board told him where he was supposed to stop and reach through the rail for the low branch of a willow. From there he could tell which way the wind was moving over the canal. This mattered to him for reasons his sister couldn’t explain.

After the repair, he could still cross the bridge. He just couldn’t find his place on it. He spent his afternoons trying.

“There are other ways to mark a spot,” Mara said.

“I know. I offered to paint it.”

They looked at each other.

“That was a pretty bad offer,” the girl admitted.

Mara called Public Works. The man who answered remembered the board. His father had been one of the people who tripped on it.

“Then you know exactly where it was,” Mara said.

“Sure. But I’m not putting it back.”

He was willing to meet them on Thursday. He arrived with a tape measure and an orange vest over his good shirt. The girl came with her brother, who introduced himself as Leon, and asked them all to stand back because he was in the middle of something.

They stood back. Leon went slowly along the bridge with his cane. Halfway across he stopped, retraced a few steps, and knelt to feel the edge where the boards met the rail.

“Did you find it?” his sister asked.

“No. I found a screw that needs tightening.”

The man from Public Works took a pencil from his pocket.

Watching them, Mara remembered a sound she had never looked for in the basement. When she was small, her mother had taken in sewing and kept a saucer of pins beside the machine. Some nights, long after Mara had been put to bed, she would hear her mother tip the pins from the saucer into a tin. Then the kitchen light would go out. Mara had hated that sound on the nights she couldn’t sleep. It meant the person she was waiting for had finished everything and forgotten to come.

Years later, her mother told her she used to stand outside the bedroom door on those nights, trying to tell from Mara’s breathing whether she was still awake. By then they lived in different states. They had this conversation while Mara was buying onions.

“Would a different noise work?” she asked Leon.

He stood up. “How different?”

The man from Public Works had a socket wrench in his bag. He tapped it against the rail. The rail rang, not beautifully. A woman walking a dog stopped to see what they were doing. Leon tapped the same spot with his cane. It barely made a sound.

“My cane’s not a wrench,” he said.

“No,” the man agreed. He took the rubber cap off the end of the rail and put it back on. Then he asked Leon to show him how he swept his cane when he walked.

The following Thursday there was a little steel plate on the inside of the rail, low enough to catch with a cane, with three raised ribs. Leon passed it once without touching it. On the return trip he drew his cane across all three. It sounded like someone riffling a very short deck of cards.

“Closer to the tree,” he said.

The man moved it two inches.

Mara had brought the old sound in a portable player, though she hadn’t told anyone. She had pictured giving it one last play on the bridge. Now she kept her hands in her coat pockets. Leon’s sister had got bored and was rolling a pill bug gently from one palm to the other. A cyclist rang his bell. Everyone moved except Leon, who was already out of the way.

When Mara got back to the library, she called her mother. She had meant to ask about the tin, but her mother wanted to know how long potatoes lasted after they sprouted. Mara looked it up. They disagreed about what the instructions meant by *firm*.

While they talked, Mara filed the sound of the loose board. On the reverse of the original green slip there was a box marked *Further action*. She wrote, *Leave the screw at the east end alone until Leon shows you which one it is.*

Then she turned off the basement light. Her mother was still on the line, opening drawers, looking for the small knife.

I’d make the accident of where you’re born matter less.

A child should get to find out what they love and what they’re good at before hunger, war, or poverty decides what their life can be.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
I’d make it possible for anyone to walk away from a situation that’s hurting them without having to gamble their survival.

A person could leave an abusive home without becoming homeless, quit a dangerous job without losing access to medicine, or flee persecution without having to find a country willing to let them in.

It wouldn’t make people kinder. But it would make it harder to turn someone’s need to survive into a reason they have to stay.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
I’d make it so no one had to depend on another person’s goodwill to stay alive. Food, clean water, shelter, and basic care would be things you could count on, not things someone could take away to make you obey.

It wouldn’t make people kinder. But it would give more people the freedom to say no, to leave, and to decide what to do with a life they weren’t spending all their strength just trying to keep.
